title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
Reading




Compulsory: (castro2020turning?).
Course material: Compartmental Models, The Reproduction Number, The Final Size of an Epidemic.
The SIR model is a small system of three ODEs (Kermack and McKendrick 1927; Keeling and Rohani 2008). The solve_ivp workflow from Solving Initial Value Problems applies unchanged: the state is now a vector.
\[
\dot S = -\beta SI, \qquad \dot I = \beta SI - \gamma I, \qquad \dot R = \gamma I .
\]
The state has three components, but \(S + I + R = 1\) is conserved, so only two are independent.

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
Prediction






Exercise



For \(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\), \(S(0) = 0.99\), \(I(0) = 0.01\), use the formulas from The Reproduction Number and The Final Size of an Epidemic to predict the peak prevalence \(I_{\max}\) and the final size before you simulate.








Solution





Here \(R_0 = 3\). The peak prevalence is \(I_{\max} = I_0 + S_0 - \frac{1}{R_0}\bigl(1 + \ln(R_0 S_0)\bigr) \approx 0.304\), reached when \(S = 1/R_0 \approx 0.333\). The final size relation \(\ln(S_0/S_\infty) = R_0 (1 - S_\infty)\) gives \(S_\infty \approx 0.059\), so about 93% of the susceptibles are infected and \(R_\infty \approx 0.94\).

from amlab.epidemics import final_size, peak_prevalence

print(f"I_max = {peak_prevalence(3.0, 0.99, 0.01):.3f}")
print(f"final size = {final_size(3.0, 0.99):.3f}")

I_max = 0.304
final size = 0.931

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
Implementation






Exercise



Complete the right-hand side of the SIR model. The solver only needs one function that returns the three derivatives.
def sir_model(t, y, beta, gamma):
    s, i, r = y
    dsdt = # TODO
    didt = # TODO
    drdt = # TODO
    return [dsdt, didt, drdt]








Solution





def sir_model(t, y, beta, gamma):
    s, i, r = y
    dsdt = -beta * s * i
    didt = beta * s * i - gamma * i
    drdt = gamma * i
    return [dsdt, didt, drdt]



The solver call follows the usual pattern:
solution = solve_ivp(
    sir_model,
    t_span=(0, 160),
    y0=[0.99, 0.01, 0.0],
    args=(0.3, 0.1),
    t_eval=np.linspace(0, 160, 1000),
)
The reference implementation amlab/odes_1d/sir_model.py provides sir_model and the plotting helper plot_sir_model.








Figure 1: SIR dynamics for beta = 0.3, gamma = 0.1 (R0 = 3), S(0) = 0.99, I(0) = 0.01.

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
Validation
Check three facts against the theory: \(S + I + R\) stays equal to 1, the peak of \(I\) matches the formula, and the peak happens when \(S = 1/R_0\).

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

from amlab.epidemics import peak_prevalence
from amlab.odes_1d.sir_model import sir_model

sol = solve_ivp(sir_model, (0, 160), [0.99, 0.01, 0.0], args=(0.3, 0.1),
                t_eval=np.linspace(0, 160, 4001), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-12)
s, i, r = sol.y
print(f"max |S+I+R-1| = {np.max(np.abs(s + i + r - 1)):.1e}")
print(f"I_max simulated = {i.max():.4f}, formula = {peak_prevalence(3.0, 0.99, 0.01):.4f}")
print(f"S at the peak = {s[i.argmax()]:.4f}, 1/R0 = {1 / 3:.4f}")

max |S+I+R-1| = 6.7e-16
I_max simulated = 0.3038, formula = 0.3038
S at the peak = 0.3331, 1/R0 = 0.3333

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
What to look for

The susceptible fraction decreases monotonically.
The infected fraction rises, peaks and then falls.
The recovered fraction grows monotonically.
Changing \(\beta\) mostly affects how fast the outbreak grows.
Changing \(\gamma\) mostly affects how quickly the outbreak resolves.

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
Experiment






Exercise



Start from \(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\), \(I(0) = 0.01\) and change one thing at a time.

Increase \(\beta\) with \(\gamma\) fixed. What happens to the height and the time of the peak?
Increase \(\gamma\) with \(\beta\) fixed. Does the epidemic end sooner? Is it smaller?
Change \(I(0)\) from \(10^{-2}\) to \(10^{-5}\). Which quantities change: peak height, peak time, final size?









Solution





With \(\beta = 0.45\) (\(R_0 = 4.5\)) the peak rises from 0.30 to 0.45 and comes earlier, near day 17 instead of day 27. With \(\gamma = 0.15\) (\(R_0 = 2\)) the peak drops to 0.16 and the final size to 0.80; the epidemic is smaller, and it dies out a little sooner. With \(I(0) = 10^{-5}\) the peak height (0.30) and the final size (0.94) barely change, but the peak moves from day 27 to about day 61.

for beta, gamma, i0 in [(0.3, 0.1, 1e-2), (0.45, 0.1, 1e-2), (0.3, 0.15, 1e-2), (0.3, 0.1, 1e-5)]:
    run = solve_ivp(sir_model, (0, 300), [1 - i0, i0, 0.0], args=(beta, gamma),
                    t_eval=np.linspace(0, 300, 30001), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-12)
    i_run = run.y[1]
    print(f"beta={beta}, gamma={gamma}, I0={i0:.0e}: peak {i_run.max():.2f} "
          f"on day {run.t[i_run.argmax()]:.0f}, final R {run.y[2, -1]:.2f}")

beta=0.3, gamma=0.1, I0=1e-02: peak 0.30 on day 27, final R 0.94
beta=0.45, gamma=0.1, I0=1e-02: peak 0.45 on day 17, final R 0.99
beta=0.3, gamma=0.15, I0=1e-02: peak 0.16 on day 29, final R 0.80
beta=0.3, gamma=0.1, I0=1e-05: peak 0.30 on day 61, final R 0.94

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
Interpretation
\(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) enter the shape of the outbreak mainly through \(R_0 = \beta/\gamma\) (peak height, final size) and \(\beta - \gamma\) (early growth rate). The initial seed \(I(0)\) shifts the curve in time but hardly changes its shape.






Optional extension



Add Streamlit sliders for \(\beta\), \(\gamma\) and \(I(0)\), following Budworm: a Streamlit App. Show the peak prevalence formula next to the plot.

title: FitzHugh-Nagumo Model
text:
The FitzHugh-Nagumo model is a two-variable simplification of the Hodgkin-Huxley equations that keeps excitability and spiking (FitzHugh 1961; Nagumo, Arimoto, and Yoshizawa 1962). The version used in this course is
\[\begin{aligned}
\epsilon \dot v &= f(v) - w + I_{\text{app}}, \\
\dot w &= v - \gamma w,
\end{aligned} \tag{1}\]
with the cubic
\[
f(v) = v (1 - v)(v - \alpha), \qquad 0 < \alpha < 1 .
\]
\(v\) is the fast variable (membrane potential), \(w\) the slow recovery variable, \(I_{\text{app}}\) an applied current, and \(\epsilon \ll 1\) sets the separation of time scales.

title: FitzHugh-Nagumo Model
text:
Nullclines and geometry
\[
\dot v = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; w = f(v) + I_{\text{app}},
\qquad
\dot w = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; w = \frac{v}{\gamma}.
\]
The cubic \(v\)-nullcline and the straight \(w\)-nullcline organize the flow. Away from the cubic, \(\dot v\) is of order \(1/\epsilon\), so trajectories move almost horizontally. Near the outer branches of the cubic they drift slowly (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.5).

If the nullclines cross on an outer branch of the cubic, the fixed point is stable and the system is excitable (see Excitability).
If they cross on the middle branch, the fixed point is unstable and the system produces a relaxation oscillation.

Increasing \(I_{\text{app}}\) shifts the cubic upwards and moves the crossing from the left branch to the middle branch.








Figure 1: FitzHugh-Nagumo phase planes for alpha = 0.1, gamma = 0.5, epsilon = 0.01. Left: I_app = 0, excitable; one trajectory starting at v = 0.2 makes a single excursion. Right: I_app = 0.5, oscillatory; the trajectory settles on a limit cycle.

title: FitzHugh-Nagumo Model
text:
Implement the vector field






Exercise



Complete the FitzHugh-Nagumo vector field Equation 1. Remember to divide the \(v\) equation by \(\epsilon\).
def fitzhugh_nagumo(t, vw, i_app=0.5, gamma=0.5, alpha=0.1, epsilon=0.01):
    v, w = vw
    fv = # TODO: cubic nonlinearity
    dvdt = # TODO
    dwdt = # TODO
    return np.array([dvdt, dwdt])








Solution





def fitzhugh_nagumo(t, vw, i_app=0.5, gamma=0.5, alpha=0.1, epsilon=0.01):
    v, w = vw
    fv = v * (1 - v) * (v - alpha)
    dvdt = (fv - w + i_app) / epsilon
    dwdt = v - gamma * w
    return np.array([dvdt, dwdt])
This is amlab/odes_2d/fitzhugh_nagumo.py, which also contains an interactive animation.



Because \(1/\epsilon = 100\), the problem is mildly stiff. Limit the step with max_step or use method="LSODA" so that the solver does not step over the fast jumps.

title: FitzHugh-Nagumo Model
text:
Time series
Follow the CDIMA pipeline again: solve trajectories, inspect the phase plane, compute nullclines, and then animate the motion. Figure 2 shows the fast variable \(v(t)\) in the oscillatory regime.








Figure 2: Time series v(t) of the FitzHugh-Nagumo system for I_app = 0.5, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 0.5, epsilon = 0.01, starting at (v, w) = (0.3, 0). Each spike is a fast jump followed by a slow recovery.





The time trace and the phase plane explain the same phenomenon from two viewpoints.

Some initial conditions return directly to equilibrium.
Others produce a large transient spike before recovery.
In the oscillatory regime, every initial condition ends on the same limit cycle.

title: FitzHugh-Nagumo Model
text:
Interpret the parameters

Smaller \(\epsilon\) makes the jumps faster relative to the slow drift.
\(I_{\text{app}}\) moves the system between rest, excitability and repetitive firing.
\(\gamma\) and \(\alpha\) change the slope of the \(w\)-nullcline and the position of the cubic, and therefore where the nullclines intersect.







Exercise



For \(\alpha = 0.1\), \(\gamma = 0.5\), find the fixed point for \(I_{\text{app}} = 0\) and show that it is the only one.








Solution





Fixed points satisfy \(v/\gamma = f(v)\), that is \(2v = v(1-v)(v - 0.1)\). One root is \(v = 0\). The others solve \((1 - v)(v - 0.1) = 2\), i.e. \(v^2 - 1.1v + 2.1 = 0\), whose discriminant \(1.21 - 8.4\) is negative. So \((0, 0)\) is the only fixed point.









Exercise



Change the initial condition and \(I_{\text{app}}\) and watch how the time series changes. Use \(I_{\text{app}} = 0\) and \(I_{\text{app}} = 0.5\), and start from \((v, w) = (0.05, 0)\) and \((0.3, 0)\). Connect what you see to the nullclines in Figure 1.








Solution





For \(I_{\text{app}} = 0\) the fixed point \((0, 0)\) sits on the left branch of the cubic. The start at \(v = 0.05\) lies left of the middle branch and decays straight back to rest. The start at \(v = 0.3\) lies right of the middle branch, so \(v\) jumps to the right branch, drifts up, jumps back and returns to rest: one spike. For \(I_{\text{app}} = 0.5\) the crossing is on the middle branch, and both starts end on the same limit cycle with repeated spikes.

for i_app in [0.0, 0.5]:
    for v0 in [0.05, 0.3]:
        s = solve_ivp(fitzhugh_nagumo, (0, 4), [v0, 0.0], args=(i_app, gamma, alpha, eps), max_step=0.002)
        late = s.t > 2
        print(f"I_app = {i_app}, v0 = {v0}: max v = {s.y[0].max():.2f}, "
              f"range of v for t > 2 = {np.ptp(s.y[0][late]):.2f}")

I_app = 0.0, v0 = 0.05: max v = 0.05, range of v for t > 2 = 0.00
I_app = 0.0, v0 = 0.3: max v = 0.92, range of v for t > 2 = 0.00
I_app = 0.5, v0 = 0.05: max v = 1.30, range of v for t > 2 = 1.27
I_app = 0.5, v0 = 0.3: max v = 1.30, range of v for t > 2 = 1.27

title: The Modelling Workflow
text: Every model in this course goes through the same stages. The order matters less than making each stage explicit, so that you and your reader can check it.

title: The Modelling Workflow
text:
From question to model

Formulate. State the question. Choose state variables and parameters. Write one term for each process you include, and say why you left the others out.
Nondimensionalize. Rescale the variables so that the model has the fewest possible parameter groups. In the budworm model this reduces four parameters to two (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.7; ludwig1978qualitative?).
Analyse. Find equilibria and their stability, and see how they change with the parameters. This often answers the question without any simulation.
Simulate. Integrate the model numerically. Use simulation for what the analysis cannot give you: transients, global behaviour, many parameter values.
Validate. Compare with data and with limiting cases whose answer you already know.
Criticize. List the assumptions again. Which one would change the conclusion if it failed?

title: The Modelling Workflow
text:
Why nondimensionalize?
A model with units has redundant parameters. Rescaling time and state by natural scales groups the parameters into dimensionless combinations. You learn which combinations control the behaviour, and you reduce the parameter space you need to explore. Sections 3.5 and 3.7 of Strogatz (2024) show the procedure on worked examples, and you will apply it to the budworm in The Spruce Budworm Model.

title: The Modelling Workflow
text:
The lab workflow
Laboratory sessions follow six steps. You will see them as section headings in the lab pages.

Prediction. Before you run anything, write down what you expect: how many equilibria, which one is stable, whether the solution oscillates.
Implementation. Write the right-hand side, the solver call and the plots. Keep functions small and documented.
Validation. Check the code against something you know: a conserved quantity, an equilibrium, an analytical formula.
Experiment. Change one parameter or initial condition at a time and record what changes.
Interpretation. Explain the result in terms of the model: which term dominates, which equilibrium the trajectory approaches.
Limitations. Say what the simulation cannot tell you, and which assumption is responsible.

Each lab has a core activity that everyone should complete, and optional extensions for those who finish early.






Exercise



The exponential decay model \(\dot y = -\lambda y\) with \(y(0) = y_0\) has solution \(y(t) = y_0 e^{-\lambda t}\). Use it to design one validation test for a numerical ODE solver.








Solution





Solve the model numerically with \(\lambda = 0.5\), \(y_0 = 2\) on \([0, 10]\) and compare with the exact solution. The maximum absolute error should be small and should decrease when you tighten the tolerances.

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

sol = solve_ivp(lambda t, y: -0.5 * y, (0, 10), [2.0], t_eval=np.linspace(0, 10, 50), rtol=1e-8)
error = np.max(np.abs(sol.y[0] - 2.0 * np.exp(-0.5 * sol.t)))
print(f"Maximum error: {error:.2e}")

Maximum error: 2.17e-07

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text: You now estimate \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) from a time series of daily new cases. This is your first parameter estimation problem of the course.

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
The data
amlab.epidemics.load_cases() reads data/epidemic/cases.csv with columns date,new_cases (see data/epidemic/README.md). If the file does not exist, it returns synthetic data and prints a warning: a deterministic SIR epidemic with \(R_0 = 3\) (\(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\) per day) in a population of one million, with random reporting noise and a fixed seed. The figures on this page use the synthetic data unless you add a real file. With synthetic data you know the true parameters, so you can check whether the fit recovers them.

import numpy as np

from amlab.epidemics import load_cases

days, cases, synthetic = load_cases()
print("Synthetic data:", synthetic, "| days:", len(days), "| total cases:", int(cases.sum()))

Synthetic data: True | days: 120 | total cases: 945521

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
The observation model
The SIR model predicts fractions. The data are counts of new infections per day. The expected number of new cases on day \(d\) is
\[
\mu_d = N\,\bigl(S(d-1) - S(d)\bigr),
\]
the number of people who left the susceptible class during that day. sir_incidence(days, beta, gamma, i0, N) computes \(\mu_d\).

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Before fitting, estimate the growth rate from the early data by eye: on a log scale, the rising part of the curve is roughly a straight line with slope \(\beta - \gamma\). What slope do you expect for the synthetic data?








Solution





The synthetic data use \(\beta = 0.3\) and \(\gamma = 0.1\), so the slope of \(\ln c_d\) is \(\beta - \gamma = 0.2\) per day: cases double about every \(\ln 2 / 0.2 \approx 3.5\) days. A straight-line fit to the first weeks gives a value close to this.

early = (days >= 5) & (days <= 30) & (cases > 0)
slope = np.polyfit(days[early], np.log(cases[early]), 1)[0]
print(f"slope of log(cases) for days 5 to 30: {slope:.3f} per day")

slope of log(cases) for days 5 to 30: 0.200 per day

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
Implementation
Least squares chooses the parameters that minimize \(\sum_d (\sqrt{\mu_d} - \sqrt{c_d})^2\), where \(c_d\) are the observed counts. The square root reduces the weight of the large counts near the peak, since count noise grows with the mean.






Exercise



Complete the residual function for a population of \(N = 10^6\). Here i0 is the initial infected fraction.
from scipy.optimize import least_squares

def residuals(log_params):
    beta, gamma, i0 = np.exp(log_params)   # log scale keeps parameters positive
    model = # TODO: sir_incidence(...)
    return # TODO: sqrt(model) - sqrt(cases)

result = least_squares(residuals, np.log([0.25, 0.12, 1e-5]))








Solution





amlab.epidemics.fit_sir_incidence implements exactly this, with bounds on each parameter. It takes the initial number of infected people in the guess instead of the fraction.

from scipy.optimize import least_squares

from amlab.epidemics import sir_incidence


def residuals(log_params):
    beta, gamma, i0 = np.exp(log_params)
    model = sir_incidence(days, beta, gamma, i0, 1e6)
    # clip tiny negative values produced by the ODE solver
    return np.sqrt(np.clip(model, 0, None)) - np.sqrt(cases)


result = least_squares(residuals, np.log([0.25, 0.12, 1e-5]))
beta_hat, gamma_hat, i0_hat = np.exp(result.x)
print(f"beta = {beta_hat:.3f}, gamma = {gamma_hat:.3f}, i0 = {i0_hat:.1e}")

beta = 0.303, gamma = 0.103, i0 = 9.2e-06






import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from amlab.epidemics import fit_sir_incidence, sir_incidence

N = 1e6
fit = fit_sir_incidence(days, cases, population=N)
print(f"beta = {fit['beta']:.3f}, gamma = {fit['gamma']:.3f}, R0 = {fit['r0']:.2f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.plot(days, cases, ".", color="gray", label="data")
ax.plot(days, sir_incidence(days, fit["beta"], fit["gamma"], fit["i0"], N), "tab:red", label="SIR fit")
ax.set_xlabel("Day")
ax.set_ylabel("New cases")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

beta = 0.303, gamma = 0.103, R0 = 2.95








Figure 1: SIR fit to the full incidence curve. Dots: data. Line: fitted model.

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
Validation
With the full curve, the fit should recover values close to \(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\). Check the residuals: they should look like noise, with no systematic pattern before or after the peak.

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
Experiment: identifiability
A parameter is identifiable if the data determine it. Now treat the population size \(N\) as unknown too (fit_population=True); in a real epidemic you rarely know how many people can actually be reached. Fit only the first \(T\) days for several values of \(T\).

print(" T   beta-gamma    R0          N")
for T in [20, 30, 40, 60, 90, 120]:
    f = fit_sir_incidence(days[:T], cases[:T], population=N, fit_population=True)
    print(f"{T:3d}   {f['beta'] - f['gamma']:.3f}      {f['r0']:8.2f}   {f['population']:.3g}")

 T   beta-gamma    R0          N
 20   0.220          3.79   7.37e+06
 30   0.189          2.94   1.46e+06
 40   0.209        143.16   2.25e+05
 60   0.204        205.26   8.18e+05
 90   0.201          2.83   1.01e+06
120   0.200          2.94   1e+06


The growth rate \(\beta - \gamma\) is close to the true 0.2 for every \(T\). \(R_0\) and \(N\) are not: before and around the peak (near day 55), the fit can return values far from the truth, including very large \(R_0\) with a small \(N\), and these fits have a lower cost than the true parameters. During exponential growth \(I(t) \approx I(0)e^{(\beta-\gamma)t}\), so very different combinations of \(\beta\), \(\gamma\) and \(N\) produce almost the same curve. Only the decline of the epidemic pins them down.

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
Limitations

The fit assumes the SIR model is correct. Real outbreaks involve interventions that change \(\beta\) in time.
Reported cases are a variable, unknown fraction of true infections.
Least squares gives a point estimate. Quantifying uncertainty needs bootstrap or Bayesian methods, as in (castro2020turning?).

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
Optional extension



This page is optional in Session 8. It applies the CDIMA pipeline to a second oscillator. Session 9 returns to it in Relaxation Oscillations.
The Van der Pol oscillator, introduced by van der Pol for electrical circuits with triodes (vanderpol1926relaxation?), is a prototypical nonlinear system that exhibits self-sustained oscillations. For a wide range of initial conditions, trajectories converge to a stable limit cycle.
In the form we will use in this course, the system is written as (Strogatz 2024, chap. 7.5):
\[\begin{aligned}
\dot x &= \mu\,(y - f(x)) \\
\dot y &= -\frac{x}{\mu}
\end{aligned} \tag{1}\]
where \(\mu>0\) controls the strength of the nonlinearity (and the fast-slow character for large \(\mu\)), and
\[
f(x) = \frac{x^3}{3} - x.
\tag{2}\]

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
Nullclines and Fixed Point
The nullclines are especially simple in this model:
\[
\dot x = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad y = \frac{x^3}{3} - x,
\qquad
\dot y = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x = 0.
\]
They intersect at the origin, so \((0,0)\) is the equilibrium point. For the parameter regime used in this session, the main long-run object of interest is not the equilibrium itself, but the attracting limit cycle around it.








Figure 1: Phase plane of the Van der Pol system with mu = 3. Trajectories are shown for different initial conditions (IC as x-y, marked black). Generated with scipy.integrate.solve_ivp() and matplotlib.

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
Implement the Vector Field






Exercise



Complete the Van der Pol vector field Equation 1.
def van_der_pol(t, xy, mu=1.0):
    x, y = xy
    dxdt = # TODO
    dydt = # TODO
    return np.array([dxdt, dydt])








Solution





def van_der_pol(t, xy, mu=1.0):
    x, y = xy
    fx = x**3 / 3 - x
    dxdt = mu * (y - fx)
    dydt = -x / mu
    return np.array([dxdt, dydt])



Follow the same pipeline as in CDIMA: Phase Plane: define the right-hand side, solve the initial value problem, compute nullclines, and then animate the resulting trajectory.

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
The Stable Limit Cycle
For every \(\mu > 0\) the Van der Pol system has a unique, stable limit cycle; this follows from Liénard’s theorem (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.4).






Exercise



Plot this limit cycle as an \(x(t)\) against \(t\) plot for \(\mu = 3\) and the initial condition \((2, -2)\), and verify that it matches the phase plane trajectories. Figure 2 shows the expected result.








Solution





sol = solve_ivp(van_der_pol, [0, 40], (2, -2), args=(3,), t_eval=np.linspace(0, 40, 4000))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(sol.t, sol.y[0])
ax.set_xlabel("Time (t)")
ax.set_ylabel("x(t)")
plt.show()
The maximum of \(x(t)\) is close to 2, the largest \(|x|\) on the closed orbit in Figure 1.











Figure 2: Time series of x(t) for the Van der Pol system with mu = 3 and IC: (2, -2). Generated with scipy.integrate.solve_ivp() and matplotlib.

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
The Role of \(\mu\)
The amplitude and period of the limit cycle depend on \(\mu\).

For smaller \(\mu\), the oscillation looks smoother and less sharply separated into time scales.
For larger \(\mu\), the motion develops a clear slow-fast structure.
The trajectory spends long intervals drifting near the cubic nullcline, then jumps rapidly between branches.

This is the characteristic relaxation-oscillation picture.

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
What to Look For

Different initial conditions approach the same closed orbit.
The transient depends on the initial state, but the long-run behavior does not.
The time trace \(x(t)\) reflects the same slow-fast pattern you see in the phase plane.







Exercise



Play with the parameter \(\mu\) (try 0.5, 1, 3 and 10) to see how it changes the shape of the limit cycle, its amplitude, its period and the transient dynamics.








Solution





The amplitude of \(x\) stays close to 2 for every \(\mu\). The period grows with \(\mu\): about 6.4 for \(\mu = 0.5\) and 19 for \(\mu = 10\). For large \(\mu\) it approaches \((3 - 2\ln 2)\mu\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.5). Small \(\mu\) gives a nearly sinusoidal oscillation; large \(\mu\) gives slow drifts along the cubic nullcline and fast jumps between its branches.

for mu_test in [0.5, 1, 3, 10]:
    t_end = 40 + 30 * mu_test
    s = solve_ivp(van_der_pol, (0, t_end), [2, -2], args=(mu_test,),
                  t_eval=np.linspace(0, t_end, 200001), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-11)
    late = s.t > t_end / 2
    x_late, t_late = s.y[0][late], s.t[late]
    up = np.where((x_late[:-1] < 0) & (x_late[1:] >= 0))[0]
    print(f"mu = {mu_test}: amplitude {x_late.max():.2f}, period {np.diff(t_late[up]).mean():.2f}, "
          f"(3 - 2 ln 2) mu = {(3 - 2 * np.log(2)) * mu_test:.2f}")

mu = 0.5: amplitude 2.00, period 6.38, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu = 0.81
mu = 1: amplitude 2.01, period 6.66, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu = 1.61
mu = 3: amplitude 2.02, period 8.86, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu = 4.84
mu = 10: amplitude 2.01, period 19.08, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu = 16.14

title: Bistable Switches
text: A bistable switch is a system with two stable states and a threshold between them. You met one in Bistability for the budworm. In cell biology, switches let a cell make a lasting decision from a transient signal. Gardner, Cantor and Collins built one from two genes that repress each other, and predicted the conditions for bistability with a two-variable model (gardner2000construction?).

title: Bistable Switches
text:
The toggle switch
Let \(u\) and \(v\) be the concentrations of two repressor proteins. Each one represses the promoter of the other:
\[
\dot u = \frac{\alpha_1}{1 + v^{\beta}} - u, \qquad
\dot v = \frac{\alpha_2}{1 + u^{\gamma}} - v .
\tag{1}\]
\(\alpha_1, \alpha_2\) are the effective synthesis rates, \(\beta, \gamma\) describe the cooperativity of repression, and the \(-u\), \(-v\) terms are degradation and dilution (gardner2000construction?).

title: Bistable Switches
text:
Geometry of the switch
The nullclines are \(u = \alpha_1/(1 + v^\beta)\) and \(v = \alpha_2/(1 + u^\gamma)\). When repression is cooperative (\(\beta, \gamma > 1\)) and the two synthesis rates are balanced and large enough, the nullclines cross three times: two stable states (one gene on, the other off) and a saddle between them. The stable manifold of the saddle separates the two basins (gardner2000construction?).








Figure 1: Toggle switch with alpha1 = alpha2 = 10 and beta = gamma = 2. Nullclines (blue: du/dt = 0, red: dv/dt = 0) cross three times. Trajectories from different initial conditions end in one of the two stable states (black dots); the open dot is the saddle.

title: Bistable Switches
section: Why it works as a memory
text:
Why it works as a memory
A transient signal that pushes the state across the separatrix, for example an inducer that temporarily inactivates one repressor, flips the switch. When the signal is removed, the system stays in the new state. Gardner et al. showed this experimentally in Escherichia coli: the toggle switched between states in response to transient chemical or thermal induction and kept its state afterwards (gardner2000construction?).
The same structure appears in the budworm: two stable states, a threshold, and hysteresis when a parameter changes slowly (Hysteresis).






Exercise



Take \(\beta = \gamma = 1\) (no cooperativity) and \(\alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = \alpha\). Show that the symmetric fixed point \(u = v\) is the only fixed point with \(u = v\) and find it.








Solution





With \(u = v\): \(u = \alpha/(1 + u)\), so \(u^2 + u - \alpha = 0\) and \(u = (-1 + \sqrt{1 + 4\alpha})/2\), the only positive root. For \(\beta = \gamma = 1\) the nullclines are hyperbolas that cross only once, so this fixed point is the only one and there is no bistability. Cooperativity is needed for the switch (gardner2000construction?).

title: Bistable Switches
text:
Session wrap-up
Part I of the course ends here. You have seen the main behaviours of low-dimensional systems: equilibria and their stability, bistability and hysteresis, limit cycles and Hopf bifurcations, excitability and relaxation oscillations. Part II couples many oscillators together.

title: Saddle-Node Bifurcation
text:
Reading




Compulsory: Strogatz (2024), Section 3.7.
Recommended: (murray2002mathematical?), Chapter 1 (continuous population models for single species).
A bifurcation is a qualitative change in the dynamics as a parameter crosses a critical value: fixed points appear, disappear or change stability. In one dimension, the basic way to create or destroy fixed points is the saddle-node bifurcation (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.1).

title: Saddle-Node Bifurcation
text:
Normal form
The prototype is
\[
\dot x = \mu + x^2 .
\tag{1}\]

\(\mu < 0\): two fixed points \(x^* = \pm\sqrt{-\mu}\). The negative one is stable, the positive one unstable.
\(\mu = 0\): one half-stable fixed point at \(x^* = 0\).
\(\mu > 0\): no fixed points.

As \(\mu\) increases through 0, the two fixed points approach each other, collide and annihilate. Near any saddle-node bifurcation of a smooth 1D system, a Taylor expansion reduces the dynamics to Equation 1, which is why it is called a normal form (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.1).

title: Saddle-Node Bifurcation
text:
Conditions
At a saddle-node bifurcation of \(\dot x = f(x; \mu)\), a fixed point is also a point of tangency:
\[
f(x^*; \mu_c) = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x^*; \mu_c) = 0 .
\tag{2}\]
The linearization gives no information at \(\mu_c\): the decay rate \(|f'(x^*)|\) goes to zero, and perturbations relax more and more slowly as \(\mu \to \mu_c\). This is called critical slowing down.

title: Saddle-Node Bifurcation
text:
Bifurcation diagram of the budworm
Apply Equation 2 to the budworm model with \(k\) as the control parameter and \(r = 0.56\) fixed. Figure 1 plots the positive fixed points against \(k\).








Figure 1: Bifurcation diagram of the budworm model for r = 0.56. Solid: stable fixed points. Dashed: unstable. Saddle-node bifurcations occur near k = 6.45 and k = 9.94.





The diagram has an S shape. The middle branch is unstable. At each fold, a stable branch meets the unstable branch in a saddle-node bifurcation.
You can find the folds numerically by checking where the number of equilibria changes:

counts = [len(budworm_equilibria(0.56, k)) for k in np.linspace(2, 16, 1400)]
k_grid = np.linspace(2, 16, 1400)
changes = k_grid[1:][np.diff(counts) != 0]
print("Number of equilibria changes near k =", np.round(changes, 2))

Number of equilibria changes near k = [6.45 9.94]








Exercise



Show that the saddle-node conditions Equation 2 for \(f(x) = rx(1 - x/k) - x^2/(1+x^2)\) can be solved for \(r\) and \(k\) in terms of the double root \(x\).








Solution





For \(x \neq 0\) divide \(f = 0\) by \(x\): \(r(1 - x/k) = x/(1+x^2)\). Tangency of the two curves means equal slopes: \(-r/k = (1 - x^2)/(1 + x^2)^2\). Substituting \(r/k\) into the first equation gives
\[
r = \frac{2x^3}{(1 + x^2)^2}, \qquad k = \frac{2x^3}{x^2 - 1}, \qquad x > 1,
\]
as in Strogatz (2024), Section 3.7. These curves are used on the next page.

title: Budworm: Integration and Time Series
text: You now integrate the budworm model from Budworm: the Model in Code in time (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.7; Virtanen et al. 2020).

title: Budworm: Integration and Time Series
text:
Implementation: numerical integration
The app on the next page calls this function repeatedly, each time continuing from the last state.






Exercise



Create a function that evolves the system forward in time and appends the result to existing arrays.

Function name: evolve_spruce_budworm
Inputs: t (time array), x (population array), r, k, t_eval (duration to evolve).
Use solve_ivp with method="RK45", the adaptive step size Runge-Kutta method, starting from the last values of the arrays.
Concatenate the new results with np.concatenate and clip negative values with np.clip.
Return the updated t and x.

def evolve_spruce_budworm(t: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, r=0.5, k=10, t_eval=50):
    """Don't forget the docstring and type hints"""
    t_span = (t[-1], t[-1] + t_eval)
    t_points = # TODO: evaluation points along t_span, use np.linspace

    solution = solve_ivp(
        fun=spruce_budworm,
        t_span=t_span,
        y0=[x[-1]],
        t_eval=t_points,
        args=(r, k),
        method="RK45",
    )
    # TODO: concatenate solution.t and solution.y[0] to t and x
    # TODO: ensure non-negative population with np.clip
    return t, x

args passes r and k to your ODE function.
The initial condition is [x[-1]], the last population value, as a list.









Solution





def evolve_spruce_budworm(t, x, r=0.5, k=10, t_eval=50):
    """Evolve the budworm ODE for t_eval time units and append the result."""
    t_span = (t[-1], t[-1] + t_eval)
    t_points = np.linspace(t[-1], t[-1] + t_eval, 1000)
    solution = solve_ivp(spruce_budworm, t_span, [x[-1]], args=(r, k),
                         t_eval=t_points, method="RK45")
    t = np.concatenate((t, solution.t))
    x = np.clip(np.concatenate((x, solution.y[0])), 0, None)
    return t, x

text:
Implementation: time series plot
This plot shows how the population evolves from the initial condition.






Exercise



Create plot_spruce_budworm(t, x) that plots population against time in green, with the y axis starting at 0 (populations cannot be negative), a grid, labels and a title. Return the figure and axes. Figure 1 shows an example.








Solution





def plot_spruce_budworm(t, x):
    """Plot the budworm population against time."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
    ax.plot(t, x, color="green")
    ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
    ax.set_xlabel("Time")
    ax.set_ylabel("Budworm population")
    ax.set_title("Spruce budworm population dynamics")
    ax.grid()
    return fig, ax

The trajectory in Figure 1 starts at \(x_0 = 1\), below the threshold \(x = 2\), so it should settle at the refuge \(x^* \approx 0.683\).

title: Budworm: Integration and Time Series
text:
Experiment






Exercise



Once your functions work, explore these questions.

Multiple equilibria. For \(r = 0.5\) and \(k = 10\), how many equilibria exist? Which are stable?
Bistability. Start from \(x_0 = 1\) and \(x_0 = 8\). Do they converge to the same equilibrium?
Outbreak dynamics. Start from a small population, \(x_0 < 2\), with a large carrying capacity, \(k > 10\). Does an outbreak happen?
Critical slowing down. Start at \(x_0 = 2.01\). How long does the population take to leave the neighbourhood of \(x = 2\)? Compare with the time scale \(1/|f'(2)| \approx 7\) and with the rate of change far from equilibrium.
Hysteresis. Increase \(k\) slowly from 5 to 15 and back to 5 with \(r = 0.56\). Does the population return along the same path?
Parameter space. Draw a diagram of the number of equilibria as a function of \(r\) and \(k\). Where do the bifurcations occur?









Solution






There are four equilibria: \(x = 0\) (unstable), \(x_a \approx 0.68\) (stable), \(x_b = 2\) (unstable) and \(x_c \approx 7.32\) (stable).
No. \(x_0 = 1\) goes to the refuge \(x_a\) and \(x_0 = 8\) goes to the outbreak level \(x_c\). The unstable point \(x_b = 2\) separates the two basins.
It depends on how small. For \(r = 0.5\) the threshold \(x_b\) moves down as \(k\) grows: \(x_b \approx 1.79\) for \(k = 12\) and \(x_b \approx 1.63\) for \(k = 15\). So \(x_0 = 1.7\) stays at the refuge for \(k = 12\) but triggers an outbreak for \(k = 15\). A very small population, such as \(x_0 = 1\), still stays at the refuge.
The population needs about 27 time units to move from 2.01 to 2.5, roughly four times \(1/f'(2) \approx 7\), because it must grow by a factor of 50 at rate \(f'(2) = 0.14\): \(\ln(50)/0.14 \approx 28\). Far from equilibrium, \(|dx/dt|\) is much larger and the population moves in a few time units.
No. The population jumps up near \(k \approx 9.94\) and only jumps down near \(k \approx 6.45\). Hysteresis shows the loop.
The number of positive equilibria is three inside a cusp-shaped region of the \((k, r)\) plane and one outside. The two boundary curves are saddle-node bifurcations; Hysteresis plots them with bifurcation_curves from amlab/odes_1d/budworm_analysis.py.


from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

from amlab.odes_1d.spruce_budworm import spruce_budworm

sol = solve_ivp(spruce_budworm, (0, 100), [2.01], args=(0.5, 10.0),
                dense_output=True, rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-12)
t_fine = np.linspace(0, 100, 10001)
t_leave = t_fine[np.argmax(sol.sol(t_fine)[0] > 2.5)]
print(f"time to reach x = 2.5 from x = 2.01: {t_leave:.1f}")
for x0, k in [(1.0, 15.0), (1.7, 12.0), (1.7, 15.0)]:
    end = solve_ivp(spruce_budworm, (0, 300), [x0], args=(0.5, k), rtol=1e-9).y[0, -1]
    print(f"x0 = {x0}, k = {k}: x(300) = {end:.2f}")

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text: This page continues CDIMA: Nullclines and Fixed Points. You decide the stability of the fixed point from the Jacobian and check the Hopf condition \(b_c = 3a/5 - 25/a\) from Hopf Bifurcation (Strogatz 2024, sec. 8.3).

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text:
Prediction






Exercise



For \(a = 10\), which of \(b = 3\) and \(b = 4\) gives a stable fixed point? What should the eigenvalues look like at \(b = 3.5\)?








Solution





\(b_c = 3 \cdot 10/5 - 25/10 = 3.5\). The fixed point is stable for \(b > b_c\), so \(b = 4\) gives a stable spiral and \(b = 3\) an unstable one. At \(b = b_c\) the eigenvalues are a purely imaginary pair: the real part crosses zero while the imaginary part stays nonzero.

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text:
Implementation: the Jacobian
The Jacobian collects the partial derivatives of the right-hand side:
\[
J =
\begin{bmatrix}
\partial f/\partial x & \partial f/\partial y \\
\partial g/\partial x & \partial g/\partial y
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
As in one dimension, a stable equilibrium attracts nearby trajectories and an unstable one repels them. In two dimensions the eigenvalues of \(J\) at the fixed point decide which. You can compute \(J\) analytically or numerically. The numerical route uses central differences and works for any model.






Exercise



Complete the central difference Jacobian. Column \(j\) is the derivative of the right-hand side with respect to variable \(j\).
def numerical_jacobian(func, point, args, h=1e-6):
    jac = np.zeros((2, 2))
    for j in range(2):
        e = np.zeros(2)
        e[j] = h
        jac[:, j] = # TODO: (f(point + e) - f(point - e)) / (2h)
    return jac








Solution





def numerical_jacobian(func, point, args, h=1e-6):
    jac = np.zeros((2, 2))
    for j in range(2):
        e = np.zeros(2)
        e[j] = h
        jac[:, j] = (np.asarray(func(0, point + e, *args))
                     - np.asarray(func(0, point - e, *args))) / (2 * h)
    return jac
amlab.odes_2d.cdima_analysis.numerical_jacobian is the reference version for CDIMA.



Then compute the eigenvalues with np.linalg.eigvals:

both real parts negative: stable (node or spiral);
at least one real part positive: unstable.

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text:
Validation
Compare the numerical Jacobian with the analytical one and check where the real part of the eigenvalues changes sign.

import numpy as np

from amlab.odes_2d.cdima_analysis import (
    cdima_jacobian,
    hopf_b,
    locate_hopf_numerically,
    numerical_jacobian,
)

a = 10.0
for b in [3.0, 3.5, 4.0]:
    ev = np.linalg.eigvals(numerical_jacobian(a, b))
    diff = np.max(np.abs(numerical_jacobian(a, b) - cdima_jacobian(a, b)))
    print(f"b = {b}: eigenvalues {np.round(ev, 4)}, |J_num - J_exact| = {diff:.1e}")

for a in [8.0, 10.0, 15.0]:
    print(f"a = {a}: numerical Hopf b = {locate_hopf_numerically(a):.4f}, formula 3a/5 - 25/a = {hopf_b(a):.4f}")

b = 3.5: eigenvalues [-0.+2.6458j -0.-2.6458j], |J_num - J_exact| = 4.9e-10
b = 4.0: eigenvalues [-0.1+2.8267j -0.1-2.8267j], |J_num - J_exact| = 4.9e-10
a = 8.0: numerical Hopf b = 1.6750, formula 3a/5 - 25/a = 1.6750
a = 10.0: numerical Hopf b = 3.5000, formula 3a/5 - 25/a = 3.5000

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text:
Experiment






Exercise



Run the phase plane from CDIMA: Phase Plane with \(a = 10\) and \(b = 4, 3.6, 3.4, 3\). Where does the limit cycle appear? How does its size change as \(b\) decreases below \(b_c\)?








Solution





For \(b = 4\) and \(b = 3.6\) the oscillations die out (slowly at \(b = 3.6\), where the real part of the eigenvalues is only \(-0.02\)). The limit cycle appears once \(b < b_c = 3.5\). Its amplitude grows as \(b\) decreases: about 0.43 at \(b = 3.4\) and 0.86 at \(b = 3\).

from amlab.odes_2d.cdima_analysis import limit_cycle_amplitude

for b in [4.0, 3.6, 3.4, 3.0]:
    print(f"b = {b}: amplitude of x after transients = {limit_cycle_amplitude(10.0, b, t_end=400.0):.3f}")

b = 4.0: amplitude of x after transients = 0.000
b = 3.6: amplitude of x after transients = 0.000
b = 3.4: amplitude of x after transients = 0.430
b = 3.0: amplitude of x after transients = 0.862

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text:
Interpretation
For \(b > b_c\) the fixed point is a stable spiral and the reaction settles to constant concentrations. For \(b < b_c\) it is an unstable spiral surrounded by a stable limit cycle: the concentrations oscillate. The formula gives the whole stability boundary in the \((a, b)\) plane. Note that \(b_c > 0\) requires \(a > \sqrt{125/3} \approx 6.45\); for smaller \(a\) the fixed point is stable for every \(b > 0\).

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text:
Limitations
The linear analysis says nothing about the size of the limit cycle, nor whether the Hopf bifurcation is supercritical. You answered those questions with simulations in Hopf Bifurcation.

You now have the full phase-plane workflow: trajectories, nullclines, fixed points and their stability. Next you animate the trajectories, then reproduce the same plots for the Van der Pol oscillator and the FitzHugh-Nagumo model.

title: Linear Systems in the Plane
text:
Reading




Compulsory: Strogatz (2024), Chapter 5, Sections 6.1-6.2, Chapter 7 and Section 8.2.
Recommended: (epstein1998introduction?).
In one dimension a trajectory can only move monotonically towards a fixed point or away from it. In two dimensions it can also rotate, and sustained oscillations become possible. The first step is to understand linear systems, because near a fixed point every smooth system looks linear (Strogatz 2024, chap. 5).

title: Linear Systems in the Plane
text:
Eigenvalues from trace and determinant
Consider \(\dot{\mathbf x} = A\mathbf x\) with \(A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\). Let
\[
\tau = \operatorname{tr} A = a + d, \qquad \Delta = \det A = ad - bc .
\]
The eigenvalues are the roots of \(\lambda^2 - \tau\lambda + \Delta = 0\):
\[
\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{\tau \pm \sqrt{\tau^2 - 4\Delta}}{2}, \qquad \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \tau, \quad \lambda_1\lambda_2 = \Delta .
\tag{1}\]
Solutions are combinations of \(e^{\lambda_1 t}\) and \(e^{\lambda_2 t}\), so the signs and the type (real or complex) of the eigenvalues decide the phase portrait (Strogatz 2024, sec. 5.2).

title: Linear Systems in the Plane
text:
Classification

\(\Delta < 0\): real eigenvalues of opposite sign. Saddle point.
\(\Delta > 0\) and \(\tau^2 > 4\Delta\): real eigenvalues of the same sign. Node, stable if \(\tau < 0\) and unstable if \(\tau > 0\).
\(\Delta > 0\) and \(\tau^2 < 4\Delta\): complex eigenvalues \(\tau/2 \pm i\omega\). Spiral, stable if \(\tau < 0\) and unstable if \(\tau > 0\). The frequency is \(\omega = \sqrt{4\Delta - \tau^2}/2\).
\(\Delta > 0\) and \(\tau = 0\): purely imaginary eigenvalues. Center, with closed orbits.
\(\Delta = 0\): at least one zero eigenvalue. Non-isolated fixed points.









Figure 1: Classification of fixed points of linear systems in the (trace, determinant) plane. The parabola is tau^2 = 4 Delta.













Figure 2: Phase portraits of four linear systems: saddle, stable node, stable spiral and center.

title: Linear Systems in the Plane
text:
From linear to nonlinear
For a nonlinear system, the Jacobian at a fixed point plays the role of \(A\). The linear classification carries over to the nonlinear system for saddles, nodes and spirals. Centers and the borderline cases on \(\Delta = 0\) or \(\tau^2 = 4\Delta\) can change type under nonlinear terms (Strogatz 2024, sec. 6.3).






Exercise



Classify the fixed point of \(\dot x = -x + 2y\), \(\dot y = -2x - y\).








Solution





\(\tau = -2\), \(\Delta = 1 + 4 = 5\), \(\tau^2 - 4\Delta = 4 - 20 < 0\). The eigenvalues are \(-1 \pm 2i\): a stable spiral with angular frequency 2.

print(np.linalg.eigvals([[-1, 2], [-2, -1]]))

[-1.+2.j -1.-2.j]

title: The Phase Plane
text:
A planar system
\[
\dot x = f(x, y), \qquad \dot y = g(x, y)
\tag{1}\]
defines a vector field on the \((x, y)\) plane. Each point is a state, and trajectories follow the arrows. You can often understand the whole dynamics from a few geometric objects: nullclines, fixed points and closed orbits (Strogatz 2024, chap. 6 and 7).

title: The Phase Plane
text:
Nullclines
The \(x\)-nullcline is the curve \(f(x, y) = 0\), where the flow is vertical. The \(y\)-nullcline is \(g(x, y) = 0\), where the flow is horizontal. The nullclines divide the plane into regions in which the signs of \(\dot x\) and \(\dot y\) are fixed, so you can sketch the direction of the flow in each region (Strogatz 2024, sec. 6.1).

title: The Phase Plane
text:
Fixed points and the Jacobian
Fixed points are the intersections of the two nullclines. To find their type, linearize: with \(\mathbf u = (x - x^*, y - y^*)\), \(\dot{\mathbf u} \approx J\mathbf u\) with the Jacobian
\[
J = \begin{pmatrix} \partial f/\partial x & \partial f/\partial y \\ \partial g/\partial x & \partial g/\partial y \end{pmatrix}_{(x^*, y^*)} .
\]
Then classify \(J\) by its trace and determinant as in Linear Systems in the Plane. If no eigenvalue has zero real part (a hyperbolic fixed point), the linearization predicts the local phase portrait correctly (Strogatz 2024, sec. 6.3).

title: The Phase Plane
text:
Limit cycles
A limit cycle is an isolated closed trajectory. Nearby trajectories spiral towards it (stable limit cycle) or away from it (unstable). A stable limit cycle is a self-sustained oscillation: its amplitude and period are set by the system, not by the initial condition, and the system returns to it after a small perturbation (Strogatz 2024, chap. 7). Linear systems cannot have limit cycles: their closed orbits, when they exist, come in continuous families.








Figure 1: Phase plane of the Van der Pol oscillator (mu = 1, Lienard form) with nullclines. Two trajectories, one starting inside and one outside, approach the same limit cycle.

title: The Phase Plane
text:
The Poincaré-Bendixson theorem
In the plane, the long-run behaviour of a bounded trajectory is limited.






Theorem (Poincaré-Bendixson)



Let \(R\) be a closed, bounded region of the plane, and let the vector field be continuously differentiable on an open set containing \(R\). If \(R\) contains no fixed points and there is a trajectory that starts in \(R\) and stays in \(R\) for all future time, then that trajectory is a closed orbit or spirals towards a closed orbit as \(t \to \infty\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.3).


In practice you look for a trapping region: a region on whose boundary the vector field points inwards. If you remove a small disc around an unstable fixed point, the remaining annulus contains no fixed point, and the theorem guarantees a closed orbit. A consequence is that chaos is impossible in autonomous planar systems; it requires at least three dimensions, as in the Lorenz system (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.3).






Exercise



For the Van der Pol system in the form \(\dot x = \mu(y - x^3/3 + x)\), \(\dot y = -x/\mu\), find the fixed point and its type for \(\mu = 1\).








Solution





The nullclines \(y = x^3/3 - x\) and \(x = 0\) meet only at the origin. The Jacobian there is \(\begin{pmatrix} \mu & \mu \\ -1/\mu & 0\end{pmatrix}\), with \(\tau = \mu = 1\) and \(\Delta = 1\). Since \(\tau^2 - 4\Delta = -3 < 0\) and \(\tau > 0\), the origin is an unstable spiral. Trajectories leave it and approach the limit cycle in Figure 1.

title: Hysteresis
text: When a system has an S-shaped bifurcation diagram, the state it occupies depends on the direction in which the parameter changes. This is hysteresis: undoing the change in the parameter does not undo the change in the state (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.7 and 3.4).

title: Hysteresis
text:
The loop in k
Take \(r = 0.56\) and let \(k\) grow slowly from 5 to 15, then decrease back to 5. “Slowly” means that the population has time to reach the attracting fixed point for each value of \(k\). Figure 1 shows the result on top of the bifurcation diagram from Saddle-Node Bifurcation.








Figure 1: Hysteresis loop of the budworm model for r = 0.56. Increasing k (blue), the population stays on the refuge branch until the fold near k = 9.94 and then jumps to the outbreak branch. Decreasing k (red), it stays on the outbreak branch until the fold near k = 6.45.





The outbreak starts at \(k \approx 9.94\) but only ends when \(k\) drops below \(6.45\). Between these values the answer to “what is the budworm density for this forest?” depends on history.

title: Hysteresis
text:
The region of bistability
The saddle-node curves from the exercise on the previous page,
\[
r(x) = \frac{2x^3}{(1+x^2)^2}, \qquad k(x) = \frac{2x^3}{x^2 - 1}, \qquad x > 1,
\]
bound the region of the \((k, r)\) plane with three positive fixed points (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.7). The two branches meet at a cusp. Both \(dr/dx\) and \(dk/dx\) vanish at \(x = \sqrt 3\), which gives the cusp point \((k, r) = (3\sqrt 3, 3\sqrt 3/8) \approx (5.20, 0.65)\).








Figure 2: Stability diagram of the budworm model in the (k, r) plane. Inside the shaded region there are two stable fixed points (bistability). The horizontal line r = 0.56 is the path of the loop above.





As \(k \to \infty\) the upper curve approaches \(r = 1/2\). Ludwig et al. used this fact: for a large carrying capacity, outbreaks require \(R > 1/2\) in their notation (ludwig1978qualitative?).

title: Hysteresis
text:
Consequences

An outbreak is triggered by crossing one fold and ended only by crossing the other. Returning the parameter to its value just before the outbreak is not enough.
Near a fold the refuge state loses resilience: the decay rate \(|f'(x^*)|\) tends to zero, so the system recovers more slowly from perturbations. Similar arguments are used for sudden shifts in lakes, coral reefs and forests (scheffer2001catastrophic?).







Exercise



Fix \(k = 10\) and vary \(r\) instead. The folds are at \(r \approx 0.384\) and \(r \approx 0.560\). Describe what happens when \(r\) increases from 0.3 to 0.7 and then decreases back to 0.3.








Solution





Starting on the refuge branch, the population stays low until \(r \approx 0.560\), where the refuge fixed point disappears and the population jumps to the outbreak level. On the way back it stays high until \(r \approx 0.384\), where the outbreak fixed point disappears and it drops to the refuge. Between 0.384 and 0.560 the state depends on the direction of change.









Optional extension



amlab/odes_1d/spruce_budworm_histeresis.py lets \(k\) oscillate in time, \(k(t) = k_0 + A(1 + \sin 2\pi f t)\), and animates \(x\) against \(k\). Run it locally:
from amlab.odes_1d.spruce_budworm_histeresis import make_animation

make_animation()
Change r inside make_animation to 0.56 and k0, amp so that \(k\) spans the interval \([6, 11]\). Does a loop appear? What happens if you increase the frequency freq?

title: Module 1: Low-Dimensional Dynamics
text:
This module covers models with one or two state variables described by ordinary differential equations. You start with a single equation for an insect population and learn to find equilibria, decide their stability and follow them as parameters change. You then apply the same tools to epidemics, fit a model to data, and move to the plane, where oscillations, limit cycles, Hopf bifurcations and excitable systems appear (Strogatz 2024). Lectures and laboratories alternate: each lecture is followed by a session in which you implement the model in Python. Reusable code is in amlab/odes_1d/, amlab/odes_2d/ and amlab/epidemics/.

Session Structure

The Spruce Budworm Model Fixed Points and Stability Bistability

Session 5: Modelling the spread of epidemics: SIR and SIS

Session 6: Laboratory: epidemics and real data
Simulating the SIR Model Simulating the SIS Model Fitting an Epidemic to Data Predicting the Peak
Session 7: Two-dimensional systems: modelling oscillations
Linear Systems in the Plane The Phase Plane Hopf Bifurcation
Session 8: Laboratory: two-dimensional systems
CDIMA: Phase Plane CDIMA: Nullclines and Fixed Points CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point Animations and Interactivity Van der Pol Oscillator Practice: Planar Systems CDIMA: Parameter Map
Session 9: Excitable systems and models of the neuron
Excitability FitzHugh-Nagumo Model Relaxation Oscillations Morris-Lecar Model Bistable Switches
Extra (optional): the Lorenz system
