Pages marked “optional extension” and the practice pages (grey buttons) are ungraded. The graded assignments of the course are in Modules 2 and 4.


Learning Goals

Formulate a model as an ODE, and remove units to reduce the number of parameters.
Find equilibria and decide their stability from the linearization.
Recognize saddle-node and Hopf bifurcations, bistability and hysteresis.
Integrate ODEs with scipy.integrate.solve_ivp, and validate the result against known solutions.
Build interactive tools (Streamlit apps, Matplotlib animations and clickable parameter maps).
Use SIR and SIS models to compute reproduction numbers, herd immunity thresholds and final sizes.
Fit a model to incidence data and explain why the peak of an epidemic is hard to predict.
Read a phase plane: nullclines, fixed points, limit cycles, excitability and relaxation oscillations.








References

Strogatz, Steven H. 2024. Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos: With Applications to Physics, Biology, Chemistry, and Engineering. Chapman; Hall/CRC.

title: Fixed Points and Stability
text: A one-dimensional model \(\dot x = f(x)\) is fully described by the graph of \(f\). This page applies that idea to the budworm model \(f(x) = rx(1 - x/k) - x^2/(1+x^2)\) from The Spruce Budworm Model (Strogatz 2024, chap. 2 and Section 3.7).

title: Fixed Points and Stability
text:
Fixed points
A fixed point (equilibrium) \(x^*\) satisfies \(f(x^*) = 0\). For the budworm, \(x^* = 0\) is always a fixed point. The others satisfy
\[
r\left(1 - \frac{x}{k}\right) = \frac{x}{1 + x^2}.
\tag{1}\]
The left side is the per capita growth rate, a straight line with intercepts \(r\) and \(k\). The right side is the per capita predation rate. Fixed points are the intersections of the two curves, and there can be one, two or three of them (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.7; ludwig1978qualitative?).








Figure 1: Graphical solution of the fixed point equation for k = 10. Small r gives one intersection (refuge), intermediate r gives three, large r gives one (outbreak).

title: Fixed Points and Stability
text:
Linear stability
Write \(x = x^* + \eta\) with \(\eta\) small. A Taylor expansion gives \(\dot\eta \approx f'(x^*)\,\eta\), so the perturbation grows or decays like \(e^{f'(x^*)t}\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 2.4).

\(f'(x^*) < 0\): the fixed point is stable.
\(f'(x^*) > 0\): the fixed point is unstable.
\(f'(x^*) = 0\): linearization is inconclusive; this happens at a bifurcation.

The time scale of the decay or growth is \(1/|f'(x^*)|\). For the budworm,
\[
f'(x) = r\left(1 - \frac{2x}{k}\right) - \frac{2x}{(1 + x^2)^2}.
\]
At \(x^* = 0\), \(f'(0) = r > 0\), so the zero state is always unstable. A small budworm population always grows, because predation vanishes faster than growth as \(x \to 0\) (ludwig1978qualitative?).

title: Fixed Points and Stability
text:
The phase line
You can read stability directly from the sign of \(f\): the flow moves right where \(f > 0\) and left where \(f < 0\). Figure 2 shows the rate for \(r = 0.5\) and \(k = 10\).








Figure 2: Rate dx/dt against x for r = 0.5, k = 10. Blue: stable fixed points. Red: unstable fixed point. The green dashed line marks x = 1.





The positive fixed points for these values can be computed exactly, since Equation 1 is a cubic in \(x\).

from amlab.odes_1d.budworm_analysis import budworm_equilibria, budworm_slope

x_star = budworm_equilibria(r=0.5, k=10.0)
for x in x_star:
    s = budworm_slope(x, 0.5, 10.0)
    print(f"x* = {x:.3f}, f'(x*) = {s:+.3f}, {'stable' if s < 0 else 'unstable'}")

x* = 0.683, f'(x*) = -0.203, stable
x* = 2.000, f'(x*) = +0.140, unstable
x* = 7.317, f'(x*) = -0.237, stable








Exercise



Show that the middle fixed point for \(r = 0.5\), \(k = 10\) is exactly \(x^* = 2\).








Solution





Substitute \(x = 2\) in Equation 1: the left side is \(0.5(1 - 0.2) = 0.4\) and the right side is \(2/5 = 0.4\). The other roots of the cubic \(-(r/k)x^3 + rx^2 - (1 + r/k)x + r = 0\) are \(4 \pm \sqrt{11} \approx 0.683\) and \(7.317\).

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
text:
Reading




Recommended: Strogatz (2024), Chapter 1.
Course material: Syllabus and How the Course Works.
A mathematical model is a deliberate simplification of a real system. You keep a few variables and a few rules that you believe control the behaviour you care about, and you discard the rest. The model then lets you reason about the system with the tools of mathematics and computation.

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
text:
Variables, parameters and rules
Most models in this course have three parts.

State variables describe the system at a given time: a population \(x(t)\), the fractions \(S, I, R\) of an epidemic, two chemical concentrations.
Parameters are numbers that stay fixed during one experiment: a growth rate, a carrying capacity, a transmission rate.
Rules say how the state changes. In Part I of the course the rules are ordinary differential equations \(\dot{\mathbf x} = \mathbf f(\mathbf x; \theta)\) (Strogatz 2024).

The same structure reappears later with random rules (Module 3), spatial rules (Module 4), networks (Module 5) and discrete rules (Module 6).

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
text:
All models are wrong
George Box wrote that “since all models are wrong the scientist cannot obtain a ‘correct’ one by excessive elaboration” (box1976science?). A few years later he titled a section “All models are wrong but some are useful” (box1979robustness?). The point is practical. You cannot make a model true by adding detail, so you should ask whether it is useful for a stated purpose.
Two consequences follow.

A model that fits the data well can still be useless, for example when it has so many parameters that it would fit any data.
A model that gets the numbers wrong can still be useful, for example when it correctly predicts that a system has two stable states.

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
text:
Parsimony
Box also argued for parsimonious models: use the fewest parameters that still capture the effect you study (box1976science?). Each extra parameter must be estimated, and each one makes it harder to see which mechanism produces the behaviour.
The spruce budworm model of Session 2 is a good example. Ludwig, Jones and Holling reduced a detailed forest simulation to three differential equations, and a single equation for the fast variable already explains the outbreak pattern (ludwig1978qualitative?). They state that their conclusions depend on the qualitative shape of the terms, not on their exact form (ludwig1978qualitative?).

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
section: When is a model good enough?
text:
When is a model good enough?
There is no general rule, but you can ask the same questions every time.

Purpose: what question should the model answer? Explanation, prediction and control need different levels of detail.
Assumptions: can you list them? Which one is the weakest?
Sensitivity: does the conclusion survive small changes in the parameters and in the form of the terms?
Data: does the model reproduce the observations it was not fitted to?
Limits: does it give the right answer in simple limiting cases you already understand?







Exercise



Take the logistic model \(\dot N = rN(1 - N/K)\) for a population. List three assumptions it makes about the real population. For each one, name a situation where it fails.








Solution





Possible answers:

The population is large enough to treat \(N\) as a continuous variable. It fails for small or endangered populations, where random births and deaths matter.
The per capita growth rate decreases linearly with \(N\). It fails when individuals need a minimum density to reproduce (Allee effect).
\(r\) and \(K\) are constant. They fail when food supply or climate changes on the same time scale as the population.

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
text:
Next
The next page turns these questions into a workflow you will use in every session.

title: Solving Initial Value Problems
text:
Reading




Recommended: SciPy documentation for solve_ivp; Streamlit documentation.
Course material: Virtanen et al. (2020).
This session builds the numerical workflow you will use in the whole course: define a right-hand side, choose an initial condition, integrate forward in time, and interpret the solution. There is no new mathematics. The core activity is the budworm pipeline in the next three pages.
The workflow has five steps, and you will repeat them in every laboratory:
Once you understand this pipeline, you can reuse it almost unchanged for planar systems, coupled oscillators and PDE reductions later in the course.

title: Solving Initial Value Problems
text:
The initial value problem
The mathematical object is
\[
\dot{\mathbf y} = \mathbf f(t, \mathbf y), \qquad \mathbf y(t_0) = \mathbf y_0 .
\tag{1}\]
In a scalar problem \(\mathbf y(t)\) is one number; in a small system it is a vector. The code does not change.

title: Solving Initial Value Problems
text:
The solve_ivp pipeline
scipy.integrate.solve_ivp takes

fun(t, y, *args): the right-hand side. It must accept t first, even if the model does not depend on time.
t_span = (t0, tf): the integration interval.
y0: the initial state, as a list or array.
t_eval: optional times at which you want the solution stored. Without it, you get the solver’s own steps.
args: a tuple of extra parameters passed to fun.
method: the integrator. The default "RK45" is the explicit Runge-Kutta pair of Dormand and Prince, of order 5 with an embedded order 4 error estimate used to adapt the step size (dormand1980family?).
rtol, atol: relative and absolute error tolerances (defaults 1e-3 and 1e-6).

The default RK45 method is a good first choice for most examples in this module. Later sessions make the choice of method part of the modelling discussion.
The result sol has sol.t (times), sol.y (array of shape (n_variables, n_times)), and sol.success.

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp


def exponential_decay(t, y, lam):
    """Right-hand side of dy/dt = -lam * y."""
    return -lam * y


sol = solve_ivp(
    exponential_decay,
    t_span=(0, 10),
    y0=[2.0],
    t_eval=np.linspace(0, 10, 200),
    args=(0.5,),
)
print(sol.success, sol.y.shape)

True (1, 200)

title: Solving Initial Value Problems
text:
Validation
Always test the solver on a problem with a known answer before you trust it on a new model.

exact = 2.0 * np.exp(-0.5 * sol.t)
for rtol in [1e-3, 1e-6, 1e-9]:
    s = solve_ivp(exponential_decay, (0, 10), [2.0], t_eval=sol.t, args=(0.5,), rtol=rtol, atol=1e-12)
    print(f"rtol = {rtol:.0e}: max error = {np.max(np.abs(s.y[0] - exact)):.1e}")

rtol = 1e-03: max error = 4.2e-04
rtol = 1e-06: max error = 4.6e-07
rtol = 1e-09: max error = 4.0e-10


The error falls as you tighten rtol. If it does not, the right-hand side has a bug or the problem needs a different method.






Exercise



args=(0.5) without the comma raises an error. Explain why.








Solution





(0.5) is just the number 0.5, not a tuple. solve_ivp expects a tuple and unpacks it into fun(t, y, *args). A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma: (0.5,).









Optional extension



Implement the forward Euler method \(y_{n+1} = y_n + \Delta t\, f(t_n, y_n)\) for the decay problem. Halve \(\Delta t\) several times and check that the error at \(t = 10\) halves too (first-order convergence). The reference code in amlab/utils/solver.py contains Euler and Runge-Kutta versions.

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
Optional extension



This page and Sensitivity and Chaos are extra material, not part of the syllabus sessions. They extend the planar systems of Session 7 to three dimensions, where the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem no longer applies and chaos becomes possible (Strogatz 2024, chap. 9).
The Lorenz system is one of the standard examples where a smooth deterministic ODE produces irregular long-term behavior (Lorenz 1963; Strogatz 2024).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot x &= s (y - x), \\
\dot y &= r x - y - x z, \\
\dot z &= x y - b z.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
For the classical Lorenz attractor, the standard parameter choice is
\[
s = 10,
\qquad
r = 28,
\qquad
b = \frac{8}{3}.
\]
Figure 1: Lorenz attractor trajectory (Euler integration).

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
From ODEs to chaos
The earlier sessions studied phase portraits, fixed points and oscillations. The Lorenz system keeps the same ingredients, a deterministic vector field and a time-stepping scheme, but adds a new phenomenon:

trajectories remain bounded;
the system is fully deterministic;
long-term prediction still becomes difficult because nearby initial conditions diverge.

This is the core idea behind deterministic chaos.






Note



The Lorenz attractor is bounded but not periodic. A trajectory keeps moving forever without settling into a fixed point or a simple closed orbit.

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
Implement the vector field
The right-hand side takes one point \((x,y,z)\) and returns the instantaneous velocity in phase space.






Exercise



Complete the Lorenz vector field Equation 1.
def lorenz(xyz, s=10.0, r=28.0, b=8.0 / 3.0):
    x, y, z = xyz
    x_dot = # TODO
    y_dot = # TODO
    z_dot = # TODO
    return np.array([x_dot, y_dot, z_dot])








Solution





def lorenz(xyz, s=10.0, r=28.0, b=8.0 / 3.0):
    x, y, z = xyz
    x_dot = s * (y - x)
    y_dot = r * x - y - x * z
    z_dot = x * y - b * z
    return np.array([x_dot, y_dot, z_dot])

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
Fixed points
Setting the right-hand side equal to zero gives the equilibrium points.
For \(r > 1\), the Lorenz system has three fixed points (Strogatz 2024, sec. 9.2):
\[
(0,0,0),
\qquad
\left(\sqrt{b(r-1)}, \sqrt{b(r-1)}, r-1\right),
\qquad
\left(-\sqrt{b(r-1)}, -\sqrt{b(r-1)}, r-1\right).
\]
For \(s = 10\), \(b = 8/3\) the two nonzero fixed points lose stability in a subcritical Hopf bifurcation at \(r = s(s + b + 3)/(s - b - 1) \approx 24.74\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 9.2). At \(r = 28\) no fixed point is stable, and trajectories keep circling around the two lobes of the attractor.

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
Simulate with Euler
Forward Euler updates the state by
\[
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n + \Delta t\, f(\mathbf{x}_n).
\]
In code, that becomes a simple loop over time steps. Euler is only first-order accurate. It is used here because it is simple enough that you see how time stepping turns a continuous ODE into a computable trajectory. Use solve_ivp for quantitative work.
def simulate_lorenz(initial_state=(0.0, 1.0, 1.05), dt=0.01, num_steps=10000):
    xyzs = np.empty((num_steps + 1, 3))
    xyzs[0] = initial_state

    for i in range(num_steps):
        xyzs[i + 1] = xyzs[i] + lorenz(xyzs[i]) * dt

    return xyzs

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
What to look for

The trajectory stays in a bounded region of phase space.
It alternates between two lobes instead of converging to one point.
The geometry looks structured, but the switching times are hard to predict over long intervals.







Exercise



Change \(r\) to 0.5, 10, 20 and 28, keeping \(s = 10\), \(b = 8/3\) and the initial condition \((0, 1, 1.05)\). Where does the trajectory end up? Then change the initial condition at \(r = 28\).








Solution





For \(r = 0.5 < 1\) the origin is the only fixed point and the trajectory decays to it. For \(r = 10\) and \(r = 20\) it settles on one of the two nonzero fixed points \(\bigl(\pm\sqrt{b(r-1)}, \pm\sqrt{b(r-1)}, r-1\bigr)\). For \(r = 28\) it never settles and keeps switching between the lobes. A new initial condition at \(r = 28\) gives a different path on the same attractor.

from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp


def lorenz_rhs(t, u, r, s=10.0, b=8.0 / 3.0):
    x, y, z = u
    return [s * (y - x), r * x - y - x * z, x * y - b * z]


for r in [0.5, 10, 20, 28]:
    end = solve_ivp(lorenz_rhs, (0, 200), [0.0, 1.0, 1.05], args=(r,), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-12).y[:, -1]
    c = np.sqrt(8 / 3 * (r - 1)) if r > 1 else 0.0
    print(f"r = {r}: state at t = 200 = {np.round(end, 2)}, sqrt(b(r-1)) = {c:.2f}")

r = 0.5: state at t = 200 = [ 0. -0.  0.], sqrt(b(r-1)) = 0.00
r = 10: state at t = 200 = [4.9 4.9 9. ], sqrt(b(r-1)) = 4.90
r = 20: state at t = 200 = [-7.12 -7.12 19.  ], sqrt(b(r-1)) = 7.12
r = 28: state at t = 200 = [-4.32  0.53 28.89], sqrt(b(r-1)) = 8.49





Reference code: amlab/extra/lorenz_attractor.py.

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
The London Millennium Footbridge opened on 10 June 2000. On the opening day it moved sideways, unexpectedly, when crowds crossed it (dallard2001london?). The engineers found that the lateral force from pedestrians depended on the motion of the deck. They concluded that the same effect could occur on any bridge with a lateral frequency below about 1.3 Hz carrying enough pedestrians. The bridge was retrofitted with viscous and tuned mass dampers (dallard2001london?).
Strogatz et al. (2005) explained the onset with a Kuramoto-type model. Bridge wobbling and crowd synchrony are two sides of one instability, and both appear when the crowd exceeds a critical size.

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
Modelling assumptions

The bridge is a single lateral vibration mode, a damped harmonic oscillator.
Each pedestrian is a phase oscillator whose sideways force is periodic in the stepping phase.
Pedestrians do not interact with each other. They interact only through the bridge.

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
Bridge
Let \(X(t)\) be the lateral displacement of the relevant mode. With \(N\) pedestrians,
\[
M\ddot X + B\dot X + KX = G\sum_{i=1}^N \sin\Theta_i,
\qquad
\Omega_0 = \sqrt{K/M}.
\tag{1}\]
\(M\), \(B\) and \(K\) are the modal mass, damping and stiffness, and \(G\) is the maximum lateral force of one pedestrian (Strogatz et al. 2005). Here \(K\) is a stiffness, not the Kuramoto coupling.

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
Pedestrians
Pedestrian \(i\) has natural stepping frequency \(\Omega_i\), drawn from a density \(P(\Omega)\). The bridge perturbs the gait according to
\[
\dot\Theta_i = \Omega_i + C A \sin(\Psi - \Theta_i + \alpha),
\qquad i = 1, \dots, N,
\tag{2}\]
where \(C\) measures the sensitivity to vibrations and \(\alpha\) is a phase lag. The amplitude \(A\) and phase \(\Psi\) of the bridge are defined by
\[
X = A\sin\Psi, \qquad \dot X = A\,\Omega_0\cos\Psi.
\tag{3}\]
Strogatz et al. (2005) call Equation 2 hypothetical but testable. It has the same form as the firefly equation in Phase Locking, with a stimulus whose strength \(CA\) grows with the wobble.

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
Feedback loop
Compare Equation 2 with the mean-field Kuramoto equation in The Order Parameter. The bridge plays the role of the mean field. Crowd coherence is measured with the usual order parameter
\[
R e^{i\Phi} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N e^{i\Theta_j}.
\tag{4}\]
A small wobble nudges some pedestrians into step. Their forces add coherently and drive the bridge harder, which entrains more pedestrians. For small crowds, \(R\) fluctuates at the level \(N^{-1/2}\) and the bridge barely moves (Strogatz et al. 2005).

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
Critical crowd size
For \(\alpha = \pi/2\) and \(P(\Omega)\) symmetric about \(\Omega_0\), Strogatz et al. (2005) obtain
\[
N_c = \frac{4\zeta}{\pi}\,\frac{K}{G\,C\,P(\Omega_0)},
\qquad \zeta = \frac{B}{\sqrt{4MK}},
\tag{5}\]
where \(\zeta\) is the damping ratio. Since \(4\zeta K = 2B\sqrt{K/M} = 2B\Omega_0\), the same result reads
\[
N_c = \frac{2B\,\Omega_0}{\pi\,G\,C\,P(\Omega_0)}.
\tag{6}\]
Compare with \(K_c = 2/(\pi g(0))\) in Critical Coupling. More damping raises the threshold. A narrower spread of gait frequencies (larger \(P(\Omega_0)\)) lowers it. Strogatz et al. (2005) estimated \(C \approx 16\ \text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\) from crowd tests on the bridge. Eckhardt et al. (2007) analyse the model in more detail.






Exercise



Check that Equation 6 is dimensionless. Use \([G] = \text{N}\), \([B] = \text{kg/s}\), \([C] = \text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\) and \([P] = \text{s}\) (a density over angular frequency).








Solution





The numerator \(B\Omega_0\) has units \(\text{kg}\,\text{s}^{-2}\). The denominator \(GCP\) has units \((\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2})(\text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1})(\text{s}) = \text{kg}\,\text{s}^{-2}\). The ratio is dimensionless, as a number of pedestrians should be.









Exercise



Take \(P(\Omega)\) normal with mean \(\Omega_0\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\). Write \(N_c\) in terms of \(\sigma\). How does \(N_c\) change if the damping is doubled?








Solution





\(P(\Omega_0) = 1/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma)\), so \(N_c = 2\sqrt{2\pi}\,B\,\Omega_0\,\sigma/(\pi G C)\). \(N_c\) is proportional to \(B\), so doubling the damping doubles the critical crowd size. This is the reasoning behind adding dampers.



You will simulate this model in the graded Kuramoto Assignment.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Animation
text:
A final snapshot hides how the cluster forms. You can use matplotlib.animation to create an animation of the oscillators moving around the unit circle as they evolve according to the Kuramoto ODE. This will allow you to visualize the process of synchronization in real time.
To create an animation, make sure you are working on a Python script in your local computer (e.g., kuramoto.py) and run it with python kuramoto.py. It is possible to do animations on Jupyter notebooks, but it is more complicated and may not work in all environments.
First, your script should initialize the oscillators and all parameters that you want to control (e.g., coupling strength, number of oscillators, etc.).
# Remember to include / import the following functions
# that you have created earlier:
# initialize_oscillators()
# kuramoto_ode()

coupling_strength = 1.0  # K
num_oscillators = 100  # Number of oscillators
sigma = 1.0  # Standard deviation of the natural frequencies
dt = 0.1  # Time step for the integration time

# Initialize oscillators (phase and natural frequency)
theta, omega = initialize_oscillators(
    num_oscillators,
    sigma=sigma,
    seed=1,
)
t_span = (0, dt)
# For the animation, we use a small time span
# But you can go higher for the static image
# t_span = (0, 100)
Second, create a figure and axes. Every element inside this plot should be named, so that you can update it in real time. Follow this template:
# Initialize the figure and axes
fig, ax_phase = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))

# Define the labels and size of this plot
ax_phase.set_title("Kuramoto Model")
ax_phase.set_xlabel("Cos(theta)")
ax_phase.set_ylabel("Sin(theta)")
ax_phase.set_xlim(-1.1, 1.1)
ax_phase.set_ylim(-1.1, 1.1)
ax_phase.set_aspect("equal")
ax_phase.grid(True)

# Draw unit circle (optional, but it helps to visualize the boundary)
circle = plt.Circle((0, 0), 1, color="lightgray", fill=False)
ax_phase.add_artist(circle)

# Initialize scatter plot for oscillators
scatter = ax_phase.scatter([], [], s=50, color="blue", alpha=0.25)
# [] means we are starting with an empty array of points,
# which you update in the animation loop
# s is the size of the dots, and alpha is the transparency

# Initialize line for the phase centroid (order parameter)
(centroid_line,) = ax_phase.plot([], [], color="red", linewidth=2)
(centroid_point,) = ax_phase.plot([], [], "ro", markersize=8)
# Same idea here:
# we start with empty data and update it in the animation loop
All the block above will initialize the figure and axes, draw the unit circle, and create empty plot elements for the oscillators and the order parameter. The variables scatter, centroid_line, and centroid_point are references to these plot elements, which you update in the animation loop.
Next, define an update function that will be called at each time step of the animation. This function will compute the new positions of the oscillators and the order parameter based on the current state of the system. It should look something like this:
def update_function(frame: int):
    # Access the variables from the outer scope
    global theta

    # Solve the ODE system over one short time interval
    sol = solve_ivp(
        kuramoto_ode,
        (0, dt),
        theta,
        args=(omega, coupling_strength),
    )
    # Update theta with the new values from the solution
    theta = sol.y[:, -1]

    # Keep theta within [0, 2 * pi]
    theta = np.mod(theta, 2 * np.pi)

    # Update scatter plot on the unit circle
    x = np.cos(theta)
    y = np.sin(theta)
    data = np.vstack((x, y)).T
    scatter.set_offsets(data)
    return [scatter]
Finally, create the animation using matplotlib.animation.FuncAnimation:
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

ani = FuncAnimation(
    fig,  # Our figure object
    update_function,  # Updates the plot at each frame
    frames=200, # Number of frames in the animation
    interval=100, # Time between frames in milliseconds
    blit=True, # Optimize rendering by only updating changed elements
    )
plt.show()
You should see an animation of the oscillators moving around the unit circle. You can experiment with different parameters (e.g., coupling strength, number of oscillators, etc.) to see how it affects the synchronization process.






Figure 1: Kuramoto oscillators animation on the unit circle.



Is your order parameter not moving? If you followed the guide, the red line and dot stay empty. The update function never touches centroid_line and centroid_point.






Exercise



Compute the order parameter inside update_function() and update centroid_line and centroid_point, so the red vector follows the centroid of the phases.
def update_function(frame: int):
    global theta
    sol = solve_ivp(kuramoto_ode, (0, dt), theta, args=(omega, coupling_strength))
    theta = np.mod(sol.y[:, -1], 2 * np.pi)
    scatter.set_offsets(np.column_stack((np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta))))

    # TODO: compute the order parameter r exp(i psi)

    # TODO: update centroid_line (from the origin) and centroid_point
    return [scatter, centroid_line, centroid_point]








Hint





z = np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta)) is a complex number. Its real and imaginary parts, z.real and z.imag, are the coordinates of the red dot. Use set_data() on both artists; it expects sequences, so wrap single values in a list.









Solution





def update_function(frame: int):
    global theta
    sol = solve_ivp(kuramoto_ode, (0, dt), theta, args=(omega, coupling_strength))
    theta = np.mod(sol.y[:, -1], 2 * np.pi)
    scatter.set_offsets(np.column_stack((np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta))))

    # Order parameter r exp(i psi)
    z = np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta))
    centroid_line.set_data([0, z.real], [0, z.imag])
    centroid_point.set_data([z.real], [z.imag])
    return [scatter, centroid_line, centroid_point]









Exercise



Run the animation with \(K = 1\), \(K = 1.6\) and \(K = 3\) (normal frequencies, \(\sigma = 1\)). Describe what you see in each case, and relate it to \(K_c \approx 1.60\).








Solution





At \(K = 1\) the dots stay spread out and the red vector jitters near the centre with length of order \(0.1\). At \(K = 1.6\), close to \(K_c\), a loose cluster forms and dissolves; \(r\) fluctuates strongly. At \(K = 3\) a clear cluster forms and rotates slowly (or stays put, since the mean frequency is close to zero). Oscillators with large \(|\omega_i|\) still drift past the cluster, because only those with \(|\omega_i| \le Kr\) lock.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Pairwise vs Mean Field
text:
Optional extension



This page is optional. You can compare the pairwise form of the ODE with the mean-field form. Implement both versions and see how they differ in computational cost and in the resulting dynamics. The mean-field form is much faster for large populations and gives the same trajectories.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Pairwise vs Mean Field
text:
Pairwise form
You can write the right-hand side in two ways (The Kuramoto Model and The Order Parameter):
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + \frac{K}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i)
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + K r \sin(\psi - \theta_i).
\]
The pairwise form is straightforward but expensive for large \(N\). The mean-field form is cheaper and shows how each oscillator responds to the whole population.






Exercise



Write kuramoto_ode_pairwise(), which follows the pairwise form of the model in The Kuramoto Model directly. Rename your first function kuramoto_ode_meanfield(). Check that both return the same derivatives for the same input.
def kuramoto_ode_pairwise(t, theta, omega, coupling_strength=1.0):
    # TODO: build the matrix of phase differences theta_j - theta_i

    # TODO: sum sin(theta_j - theta_i) over j and scale by K / N
    return dtheta_dt








Hint





Broadcasting builds the full matrix of differences in one line: theta[None, :] - theta[:, None] has entry \(\theta_j - \theta_i\) in row \(i\), column \(j\).
Once both functions exist, switching between them is as simple as changing the ODE function in the solve_ivp() call inside the update_function() of Animation:
sol = solve_ivp(
    kuramoto_ode_pairwise, # Change this to the other ODE function
    (0, dt),
    theta,
    args=(omega, coupling_strength),
    )
This is why modularity matters. By keeping your code organized and modular, you can swap out one component (like the ODE function) without rewriting the animation code. A modular structure also saves work in the Kuramoto Assignment, where you implement a different model of coupled oscillators, the Millennium Bridge.









Solution





def kuramoto_ode_pairwise(t, theta, omega, coupling_strength=1.0):
    # Row i, column j holds theta_j - theta_i
    diff = theta[None, :] - theta[:, None]
    dtheta_dt = omega + coupling_strength / len(theta) * np.sin(diff).sum(axis=1)
    return dtheta_dt


theta, omega = initialize_oscillators(100, seed=1)
print(np.allclose(
    kuramoto_ode_pairwise(0, theta, omega, 2.0),
    kuramoto_ode_meanfield(0, theta, omega, 2.0),
))  # True

title: Kuramoto Lab: Pairwise vs Mean Field
text:
Computational cost






Exercise



Time both ODE functions with %timeit (or time.perf_counter()) for \(N = 100\), \(1000\) and \(5000\). How does the cost grow with \(N\) in each case?








Solution





The pairwise version builds an \(N \times N\) matrix of phase differences, so one evaluation costs \(O(N^2)\) time and memory. The mean-field version computes one complex mean, which costs \(O(N)\). Going from \(N = 1000\) to \(N = 5000\) should multiply the pairwise time by roughly 25 and the mean-field time by roughly 5. Both give the same trajectories up to round-off.

title: Vicsek Lab: Order Parameter
text:
The order parameter \(\varphi\) (called \(v_a\) in The Vicsek Model) is defined as the magnitude of the average velocity vector normalized by the speed:
\[
\varphi(t) = \frac{1}{N v_0} \left|\sum_{i=1}^N v_0 \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta_i(t)) \\ \sin(\theta_i(t)) \end{bmatrix}\right| = \frac{1}{N} \left|\sum_{i=1}^N \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta_i(t)) \\ \sin(\theta_i(t)) \end{bmatrix}\right|.
\tag{1}\]
You can compute this at each time step to see how the system evolves. In the disordered phase, \(\varphi \approx 0\) because the headings are random and cancel out. In the ordered phase, \(\varphi \approx 1\) because all particles align in the same direction.






Exercise



Implement Equation 1.
def vicsek_order_parameter(theta: np.ndarray, v0: float = 0.03) -> float:
    # TODO: Compute the order parameter phi based on the headings theta
    return phi








Solution





The speed \(v_0\) cancels, so np.abs(np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta))) gives the same value.
def vicsek_order_parameter(theta: np.ndarray, v0: float = 0.03) -> float:
    """
    Compute the normalized order parameter (mean velocity divided by v0), as in Vicsek et al. (1995).
    """
    vx = v0 * np.cos(theta)
    vy = v0 * np.sin(theta)
    avg_vx = np.mean(vx)
    avg_vy = np.mean(vy)
    return float(np.sqrt(avg_vx**2 + avg_vy**2) / v0)

Solution





The speed \(v_0\) cancels, so np.abs(np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta))) gives the same value.
def vicsek_order_parameter(theta: np.ndarray, v0: float = 0.03) -> float:
    """
    Compute the normalized order parameter (mean velocity divided by v0), as in Vicsek et al. (1995).
    """
    vx = v0 * np.cos(theta)
    vy = v0 * np.sin(theta)
    avg_vx = np.mean(vx)
    avg_vy = np.mean(vy)
    return float(np.sqrt(avg_vx**2 + avg_vy**2) / v0)

title: Vicsek Lab: Order Parameter
text:
Experiment: reproduce Figure 2
Try to reproduce Figure 2 of the original paper (Vicsek et al. 1995), which shows the order parameter \(\varphi\) as a function of noise \(\eta\) and of the density \(\rho = N / L^2\). Run simulations for different values of \(N\), \(L\), and \(\eta\), compute the order parameter at each time step, and then average it over time to get a single value for each combination of parameters.
For reference, here are the parameters used in the original paper for Figure 2(a):

Number of particles \(N\): from 40 up to 10000. Start with the two smallest values, 40 and 100, and try larger ones only if you have time.
Density \(\rho\): constant at 4.0
Box size L: computed from density and number of particles, so \(L = \sqrt{N / \rho}\).
Noise \(\eta\): try several values between 0.0 and 5.0

Figure 1 shows the order parameter as a function of noise for different values of \(N\) at a constant density of \(\rho = 4.0\). This is a small sample of the figure you want to produce. You should see that as noise increases, the order parameter decreases, indicating a transition from an ordered phase to a disordered phase. The larger the number of particles, the sharper this transition should be.








Figure 1: Order parameter against noise for \(N = 40\) and \(N = 100\) at density \(\rho = 4\) (5000 steps, average over the last 1000, one realization).





And here are the parameters for Figure 2(b):

Density \(\rho\): try several values between 0.1 and 10.0. Higher values will take longer to compute, so start with a few values like 0.1, 1.0, and 4.0. In addition, you can distribute the values logarithmically so that you have more points at low densities where they compute faster.
Box size \(L\): constant at 20.
Number of particles \(N\): computed from density and box size, so \(N = \rho L^2\).
Noise \(\eta\): constant. The course uses \(\eta = 2.0\); check the value in the caption of Figure 2(b) of Vicsek et al. (1995).

Figure 2 shows the order parameter as a function of density for different values of \(N\) at a constant noise level. This is a small sample of the figure you want to generate. At low densities the order parameter is small (disordered phase), and at high densities it grows toward one (ordered phase). In a small box it does not reach zero at low density, because few particles give a large noise floor of order \(1/\sqrt{N}\).








Figure 2: Order parameter against density at noise \(\eta = 2\) in a box of side \(L = 5\) (5000 steps, average over the last 1000).











Exercise



Write a function that runs the model and returns the time-averaged order parameter. Use it to draw your versions of Figure 1 and Figure 2 with the parameters above.

    xy, theta = initialize_particles(num_boids, box_size)
    ls_phi = []
    for step in range(steps):
        # TODO: advance one step with vicsek_equations

        # TODO: in the last avg_steps steps, store the order parameter
        pass
    # TODO: return the mean of the stored values








Hint





Start short. With steps=1000 and avg_steps=200 each run of \(N = 100\) takes well under a second with the vectorized update. Increase the number of steps once the curves look right, and check that the result does not change much.









Solution





import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def time_averaged_order(num_boids, box_size, noise, steps=5000, avg_steps=1000):
    xy, theta = initialize_particles(num_boids, box_size)
    ls_phi = []
    for step in range(steps):
        xy, theta = vicsek_equations(xy, theta, noise=noise, box_size=box_size)
        if step >= steps - avg_steps:
            ls_phi.append(vicsek_order_parameter(theta))
    return np.mean(ls_phi)


# Figure 2(a): phi against noise at fixed density
density = 4.0
noises = np.linspace(0.0, 5.0, 10)
for num_boids in [40, 100]:
    box_size = np.sqrt(num_boids / density)
    phi = [time_averaged_order(num_boids, box_size, eta) for eta in noises]
    plt.plot(noises, phi, "o", label=f"N = {num_boids}")
plt.xlabel(r"Noise $\eta$")
plt.ylabel(r"Order parameter $\varphi$")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

# Figure 2(b): phi against density at fixed noise and box size
box_size = 20
densities = np.logspace(-1, np.log10(4.0), 6)
phi = [
    time_averaged_order(int(rho * box_size**2), box_size, noise=2.0)
    for rho in densities
]
plt.plot(densities, phi, "o")
plt.xlabel(r"Density $\rho$")
plt.ylabel(r"Order parameter $\varphi$")
plt.show()
The second part is slow for \(\rho = 4\) (\(N = 1600\)). Lower the number of steps, or use a smaller box as in Figure 2, while you test your code.

title: Vicsek Lab: Order Parameter
text:
Interpretation

Both figures show the two routes to order in Vicsek et al. (1995): less noise, or more density.
The curves for \(N = 40\) and \(N = 100\) are close. With systems this small you cannot tell whether the transition is continuous or discontinuous; that question needed much larger simulations (gregoire2004onset?; chate2008collective?).

title: Kuramoto Lab: Bifurcation Diagram
text: This page is the experiment step. You scan the coupling \(K\), measure the steady-state coherence \(r_\infty\) and compare it with theory. As \(K\) increases, the system moves from incoherence (\(r \approx 0\)) to partial synchrony (\(r > 0\)) (Kuramoto 2003; Strogatz 2000).

title: Kuramoto Lab: Bifurcation Diagram
text:
Theory to compare with
For any symmetric unimodal frequency density \(g(\omega)\), the critical coupling is (Critical Coupling)
\[
K_c = \frac{2}{\pi g(0)}.
\tag{1}\]
For a Cauchy (Lorentzian) distribution with scale parameter \(\gamma\),
\[
g(\omega)=\frac{1}{\pi} \frac{\gamma}{\omega^2+\gamma^2},
\tag{2}\]
so \(g(0)=1/(\pi\gamma)\) and the critical coupling simplifies to
\[
K_c = 2\gamma.
\tag{3}\]
In this case the order parameter has a closed form:
\[
r_\infty(K)=
\begin{cases}
0, & K \le K_c, \\
\sqrt{1-\frac{K_c}{K}}, & K > K_c.
\end{cases}
\tag{4}\]
Warning: Equation 4 holds only for the Cauchy distribution.








Figure 1: Kuramoto diagram: theoretical curve from Equation 4 and empirical points (drawn from a normal distribution). Why is there a mismatch?





For any other smooth symmetric density with \(g''(0) < 0\), the theoretical order parameter near onset is (Strogatz 2000)
\[
r \approx \sqrt{\frac{16}{\pi K_c^3}} \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{-g''(0)}}
\tag{5}\]
where \(\mu\) measures the distance from the critical point (a dimensionless reduced coupling) and \(g''(0)\) is the second derivative of the frequency distribution at \(0\).
\[
\mu = \frac{K - K_c}{K_c}
\tag{6}\]
This formula comes from expanding the self-consistency equation for small \(r\). It captures the square-root growth of \(r\) just above \(K_c\) and fails far from it.
For a normal distribution with standard deviation \(\sigma\):
\[
g(\omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} \exp\left(-\frac{\omega^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
\tag{7}\]
\[
g''(\omega) = \left( \frac{\omega^2}{\sigma^4} - \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \right) g(\omega)
\tag{8}\]

title: Kuramoto Lab: Bifurcation Diagram
text:
Experiment






Exercise



In a new script, draw the theoretical bifurcation diagram Equation 4 for \(0 < K < 5\), with \(\gamma = 1\). On top of it, draw the empirical curve. Use \(N = 1000\) oscillators with normal frequencies, \(\sigma = 1\), integrate up to \(t = 100\), and average \(r(t)\) over the window \(90 \le t \le 100\). Use the final phases for one value of \(K\) as the initial condition for the next. (The figures on this page use \(N = 500\) to render quickly.)

# TODO: theoretical curve from the Cauchy formula, with K_c = 2 gamma

theta, omega = initialize_oscillators(1000, sigma=1.0, seed=1)

    # TODO: integrate kuramoto_ode up to t = 100, evaluating 90 <= t <= 100
    # TODO: compute r(t) in that window and store its mean in r_inf[idx]
    # TODO: continue from the last state
    pass

# TODO: plot r_theory as a line and r_inf as points








Hint





Pass t_eval=np.arange(90, 100, 0.1) to solve_ivp() so that sol.y only holds the times you average over. Then np.abs(np.mean(np.exp(1j * sol.y), axis=0)) gives \(r(t)\) at each of those times.









Solution





import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

k_values = np.linspace(0.0, 5.0, 20)

# Theoretical curve for a Cauchy density with gamma = 1
kc = 2.0
r_theory = np.zeros_like(k_values)
above = k_values > kc
r_theory[above] = np.sqrt(1 - kc / k_values[above])

theta, omega = initialize_oscillators(1000, sigma=1.0, seed=1)
r_inf = np.zeros_like(k_values)
for idx, k in enumerate(k_values):
    sol = solve_ivp(
        kuramoto_ode, (0, 100), theta,
        t_eval=np.arange(90, 100, 0.1), args=(omega, k),
    )
    r_t = np.abs(np.mean(np.exp(1j * sol.y), axis=0))
    r_inf[idx] = r_t.mean()
    theta = sol.y[:, -1]  # continue from the last state

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(k_values, r_theory, color="blue", label="Theoretical (Cauchy)")
ax.plot(k_values, r_inf, "o", color="red", label="Empirical (normal frequencies)")
ax.set_xlabel("Coupling strength (K)")
ax.set_ylabel("Order parameter (r)")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
Your plot should look like Figure 1.









Exercise



Do your two curves match? Figure 1 shows a mismatch. Explain why, and fix it.








Solution





The mismatch occurs because the closed-form theoretical curve Equation 4 is derived for a Cauchy frequency distribution, while the empirical data in Figure 1 is generated from a normal distribution.
To fix this you have two consistent options:

Keep the normal distribution and use a matching theoretical prediction (typically only an approximation near onset, such as Equation 5).
Keep the closed-form curve Equation 4 and generate the empirical data using a Cauchy distribution.









Figure 2: Kuramoto diagram: empirical points (normal frequencies) and a matching theoretical prediction (see Equation 5 for the near-onset scaling).





Alternatively, fix the mismatch by changing the empirical distribution to a Cauchy distribution, which matches the closed-form curve Equation 4.








Figure 3: Kuramoto diagram: theoretical curve Equation 4 and empirical points (Cauchy frequencies).

title: Flows on the Circle
text:
A periodic rhythm can be described by a single angle, the phase \(\theta\). The phase lives on the circle: \(\theta\) and \(\theta + 2\pi\) are the same state. A one-dimensional flow on the circle is
\[
\dot\theta = f(\theta), \qquad f(\theta + 2\pi) = f(\theta).
\tag{1}\]
Unlike a flow on the line, a flow on the circle can return to its starting point. This is the simplest model of an oscillator (Strogatz 2024, sec. 4.1).

title: Flows on the Circle
text:
Uniform oscillator
The simplest choice is a constant speed, \(\dot\theta = \omega\). The solution is \(\theta(t) = \omega t + \theta_0\) and the period is \(T = 2\pi/\omega\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 4.2).

title: Flows on the Circle
text:
Nonuniform oscillator
A phase that speeds up and slows down along the cycle obeys
\[
\dot\theta = \omega - a \sin\theta, \qquad \omega > 0,\; a \ge 0.
\tag{2}\]
This equation appears in the firefly model, in overdamped pendulums and in Josephson junctions (Strogatz 2024, sec. 4.3 to 4.6). Its behaviour depends on the ratio \(a/\omega\).

For \(a < \omega\) there are no fixed points. The phase circulates, slowest near \(\theta = \pi/2\).
At \(a = \omega\) a half-stable fixed point appears at \(\theta = \pi/2\). This is a saddle-node bifurcation on the circle (see Saddle-Node Bifurcation).
For \(a > \omega\) there are two fixed points with \(\sin\theta^* = \omega/a\). One is stable and one is unstable. The oscillation stops.

For \(a < \omega\) the period is
\[
T = \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{d\theta}{\omega - a\sin\theta} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\omega^2 - a^2}}.
\tag{3}\]
As \(a \to \omega^-\) the period diverges like \(T \approx \dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,\pi}{\sqrt{\omega}}\,(\omega - a)^{-1/2}\). The trajectory spends almost all its time in the bottleneck left behind by the fixed points that are about to appear (Strogatz 2024, sec. 4.3).








Figure 1: Nonuniform oscillator with \(\omega = 1\). Left: the vector field \(f(\theta)\) for three values of \(a\). Right: the period from Equation 3 and the square-root scaling near \(a = \omega\).











Exercise



Take \(a > \omega\). Find the two fixed points of Equation 2 in \([0, 2\pi)\) and decide which one is stable.








Solution





The fixed points satisfy \(\sin\theta^* = \omega/a < 1\), so \(\theta_1^* = \arcsin(\omega/a) \in (0, \pi/2)\) and \(\theta_2^* = \pi - \theta_1^*\). The derivative of the vector field is \(f'(\theta) = -a\cos\theta\). At \(\theta_1^*\) the cosine is positive, so \(f' < 0\) and the point is stable. At \(\theta_2^*\) the cosine is negative and the point is unstable.









Exercise



Check Equation 3 numerically for \(\omega = 1\) and \(a = 0.8\). Integrate the ODE with solve_ivp and measure the time it takes \(\theta\) to grow by \(2\pi\).








Solution





The formula gives \(T = 2\pi/\sqrt{1 - 0.64} = 2\pi/0.6 \approx 10.47\).
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

def rhs(t, theta, omega, a):
    return omega - a * np.sin(theta)

def one_turn(t, theta, omega, a):
    return theta[0] - 2 * np.pi

one_turn.terminal = True
sol = solve_ivp(rhs, (0, 100), [0.0], args=(1.0, 0.8), events=one_turn, rtol=1e-10)
print(sol.t_events[0][0])  # about 10.472

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
Optional extension



This page is optional. It combines the Vicsek model with the repulsion rule of the Couzin model.
In the Couzin model, avoidance takes absolute priority: if an individual senses another within its zone of repulsion, it turns away and ignores alignment and attraction (Couzin et al. 2002). You can implement a similar rule in the Vicsek model to simulate predator avoidance (Vicsek et al. 1995). The predator can be a fixed point, a random walker, or even the mouse cursor. In all cases, if a boid senses the predator within a certain radius, it will turn directly away from it.
Below is a guide on how to implement this in your Vicsek animation. You can choose to implement one or more types of predators (static, random walk, mouse-following) and compare their effects on the collective behavior of the particles.

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
Static Predator
The simplest case is a predator fixed at a given position. To implement this:

Set the predator’s position (e.g., xy_pred = np.array([L/2, L/2]) for the center).
In your Vicsek update function, check for boids within the predator radius and set their direction directly away from the predator (as in the Couzin rule).
In your animation, draw the predator as a red circle.

Where to add: - Set xy_pred before the animation loop in your main script. - Pass xy_pred to your Vicsek update at each frame. - Draw the predator in the plotting section (after initializing the axes).






Where to include the code






Set xy_pred before the animation loop: In run_simulation, set xy_pred = np.array([box_size/2, box_size/2]) (or wherever you want the static predator) before entering the animation.
Pass xy_pred to the Vicsek update: In the update_animation function, pass xy_pred as an argument to vicsek_equations.
Draw the predator: After initializing the axes in run_simulation, add the predator circle with circle_predator = plt.Circle(xy_pred, radius_predator, color="red", fill=False) and ax_plane.add_artist(circle_predator).
Update the predator’s position in the plot (if needed): For a static predator, this is only needed once. For moving predators, update circle_predator.set_center(xy_pred) in each animation frame.

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
Random Walk Predator
To make the predator more dynamic, let it perform a random walk:

At each animation frame, update xy_pred by adding a small random displacement (e.g., xy_pred += np.random.normal(0, step_size, 2)).
Apply periodic boundary conditions to keep the predator in the box.
The avoidance rule for boids remains unchanged.

Where to add: - In your animation update function, before updating the boids, update xy_pred with a random walk step. - Pass the new xy_pred to the Vicsek update. - Update the predator’s position in the plot.

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
Mouse-Following Predator
For an interactive experience, let the predator follow the mouse:

Use a mouse event callback to update xy_pred to the mouse position whenever the mouse moves over the plot.
The avoidance rule for boids is the same: those within the predator radius turn directly away.

Where to add:

Register a mouse motion callback (e.g., with fig.canvas.mpl_connect('motion_notify_event', on_mouse_move)).
In the callback, update xy_pred to the mouse coordinates if the mouse is over the main plot.
The animation update function will use the current xy_pred as usual.

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
Integration
In all cases, the predator logic is integrated as follows:

The predator’s position (xy_pred) is set or updated before each Vicsek update.
The Vicsek update function receives xy_pred and applies the Couzin avoidance rule.
The predator is drawn as a red circle in the main plot.
For the mouse-following version, the mouse callback is registered during figure setup.

This modular approach allows you to experiment with different predator behaviors by simply changing how xy_pred is updated, while keeping the avoidance rule and animation structure consistent.

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
Practice
Option B of Practice: Collective Motion asks you to implement this model in a script named vicsek_predator.py. A reference version is in amlab/collective_motion/vicsek_predator.py.

title: Critical Coupling
text: This page summarizes Kuramoto’s self-consistency argument for the limit \(N \to \infty\), following Strogatz (2000, sec. 4). Work in the rotating frame, so \(g\) is symmetric about \(0\).

title: Critical Coupling
text:
Steady states with constant \(r\)
Look for steady solutions in which \(r\) and \(\psi\) are constant. In the rotating frame, with \(g\) symmetric, you can choose the origin of phases so that \(\psi = 0\) (Strogatz 2000). Then the mean-field equation reads
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i - K r \sin\theta_i.
\tag{1}\]
Each oscillator is a nonuniform oscillator (Flows on the Circle) with \(a = Kr\). The population splits in two groups:

Locked oscillators, \(|\omega_i| \le Kr\), sit at a stable fixed point with \(\sin\theta_i = \omega_i/(Kr)\) and \(|\theta_i| \le \pi/2\).
Drifting oscillators, \(|\omega_i| > Kr\), circulate around the circle. Their stationary distribution is symmetric under \(\theta \to \theta + \pi\) together with \(\omega \to -\omega\), so they add nothing to \(r\) (Strogatz 2000).

title: Critical Coupling
text:
Self-consistency
Only the locked oscillators contribute to \(r\). Using \(\omega = Kr\sin\theta\) to change variables,
\[
r = K r \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos^2\theta \; g(Kr\sin\theta)\, d\theta.
\tag{2}\]
\(r = 0\) always solves Equation 2: this is the incoherent state. A partially locked state with \(r > 0\) must satisfy
\[
1 = K \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos^2\theta \; g(Kr\sin\theta)\, d\theta.
\tag{3}\]
Letting \(r \to 0^+\) and using \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta = \pi/2\) gives the threshold where this branch starts:
\[
K_c = \frac{2}{\pi g(0)}.
\tag{4}\]
This is Kuramoto’s formula for the critical coupling (Kuramoto 2003; Strogatz 2000).

title: Critical Coupling
text:
Two cases you will use
Lorentzian frequencies. For \(g(\omega) = \gamma / [\pi(\gamma^2 + \omega^2)]\), Equation 4 gives \(K_c = 2\gamma\) and Equation 3 can be solved exactly:
\[
r = \sqrt{1 - \frac{K_c}{K}}, \qquad K \ge K_c.
\tag{5}\]
Normal frequencies. For a normal density with standard deviation \(\sigma\), \(K_c = 2\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma/\pi = \sqrt{8/\pi}\,\sigma \approx 1.596\,\sigma\). There is no closed form for \(r(K)\), so you solve Equation 3 numerically.

title: Critical Coupling
text:
Square-root onset
For any smooth \(g\) with \(g''(0) < 0\), expanding Equation 3 for small \(r\) gives
\[
r \approx \sqrt{\frac{16}{\pi K_c^3}}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{-g''(0)}}, \qquad \mu = \frac{K - K_c}{K_c},
\tag{6}\]
so \(r\) grows like \(\sqrt{K - K_c}\) just above threshold (Strogatz 2000). The transition from incoherence to partial locking is continuous. The same square-root law appears at a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation.








Figure 1: Order parameter in the limit \(N \to \infty\). Solid: exact Lorentzian result Equation 5 with \(\gamma = 1\) (\(K_c = 2\)). Dashed: near-onset approximation Equation 6 for a normal density with \(\sigma = 1\) (\(K_c \approx 1.60\)), valid only close to \(K_c\).

title: Critical Coupling
section: What the argument does not show
text:
What the argument does not show
Kuramoto’s argument finds the steady states. It does not prove which of them are stable, nor that the population approaches them. These questions were settled only by much later work, which Strogatz (2000) reviews. Finite \(N\) adds fluctuations of order \(N^{-1/2}\) on top of these curves (Finite-Size Effects).






Exercise



Check that Equation 6 agrees with the Lorentzian result Equation 5 near \(K_c\).








Solution





For \(\gamma = 1\), \(g(0) = 1/\pi\), \(K_c = 2\) and \(g''(0) = -2/\pi\). Then Equation 6 gives \(r \approx \sqrt{16/(8\pi)}\,\sqrt{\mu\pi/2} = \sqrt{\mu}\). The exact result is \(r = \sqrt{(K - K_c)/K} = \sqrt{\mu K_c/K}\), which tends to \(\sqrt{\mu}\) as \(K \to K_c\).









Exercise



Your frequencies are normal with \(\sigma = 0.5\). What is \(K_c\)? What happens to \(K_c\) if you double the spread of frequencies?








Solution





\(K_c = \sqrt{8/\pi}\times 0.5 \approx 0.80\). Since \(g(0) \propto 1/\sigma\), \(K_c\) is proportional to \(\sigma\). Doubling the spread doubles \(K_c\): a more diverse population needs stronger coupling to synchronize.

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Reading




Compulsory: Vicsek et al. (1995).
Recommended: Couzin et al. (2002); (helbing1995social?).
The Kuramoto model synchronizes phases in time. The Vicsek model aligns headings in space. It describes \(N\) self-propelled particles that move at constant speed and copy the average heading of their neighbours, with some noise (Vicsek et al. 1995). There is no leader and no global signal, yet the whole group can move in one direction.

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Rules
Each particle \(i\) has a position \(\mathbf{x}_i(t)\) in a square box of side \(L\) with periodic boundaries, and a heading \(\theta_i(t)\). At every time step \(\Delta t\) all particles update at the same time:
\[
\theta_i(t + \Delta t) = \langle \theta(t) \rangle_{r,i} + \Delta\theta_i,
\tag{1}\]
\[
\mathbf{x}_i(t + \Delta t) = \mathbf{x}_i(t) + v_0 \Delta t \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_i(t + \Delta t) \\ \sin\theta_i(t + \Delta t) \end{bmatrix}.
\tag{2}\]

\(\langle \theta \rangle_{r,i}\) is the mean direction of all particles within distance \(r\) of particle \(i\), including \(i\) itself. It is computed as \(\arctan\big(\langle\sin\theta\rangle / \langle\cos\theta\rangle\big)\), using the quadrant of the vector \((\langle\cos\theta\rangle, \langle\sin\theta\rangle)\).
\(\Delta\theta_i\) is drawn uniformly from \([-\eta/2, \eta/2]\). The noise amplitude \(\eta\) runs from \(0\) (no noise) to \(2\pi\) (a random heading every step).
The speed \(v_0\) is the same for all particles.

Vicsek et al. (1995) used \(r = 1\), \(\Delta t = 1\) and \(v_0 = 0.03\). The two control parameters are the noise \(\eta\) and the density \(\rho = N/L^2\).

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Order parameter
Collective motion is measured by the normalized average velocity
\[
v_a = \frac{1}{N v_0}\left|\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{v}_i\right| = \left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N e^{i\theta_i}\right|,
\tag{3}\]
which is the Kuramoto order parameter applied to headings. \(v_a \approx 1\) when all particles move the same way and \(v_a \approx 0\) when headings are random.

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Kinetic phase transition
Vicsek et al. (1995) found that \(v_a\) falls from near \(1\) to near \(0\) as the noise increases, and rises as the density increases. Near the transition they reported the scaling laws
\[
v_a \sim \big(\eta_c(\rho) - \eta\big)^{\beta}, \qquad v_a \sim \big(\rho - \rho_c(\eta)\big)^{\delta},
\]
with \(\beta = 0.45 \pm 0.07\) and \(\delta = 0.35 \pm 0.06\). They interpreted it as a continuous transition. Later simulations of much larger systems by (gregoire2004onset?) and (chate2008collective?) found that the onset of collective motion is discontinuous. Near the threshold, the ordered phase organizes into dense travelling bands. Small simulations like the ones in this course cannot distinguish the two scenarios.






Figure 1: Order parameter against noise at density \(\rho = 4\) for \(N = 40\) and \(N = 100\), one realization each, generated with amlab.collective_motion.vicsek. Compare with Figure 2(a) of Vicsek et al. (1995).









Exercise



In Figure 1, \(v_a\) stays around \(0.1\) to \(0.2\) at the largest noise, instead of going to zero. Why? Use what you know from the Kuramoto model.








Solution





At high noise the headings are close to independent and uniform. Then \(v_a\) is the modulus of the mean of \(N\) random unit vectors, so \(\mathbb{E}[v_a^2] = 1/N\) (The Order Parameter). For \(N = 40\) and \(N = 100\) this gives typical values of \(0.16\) and \(0.1\), which is what the figure shows.









Exercise



Compare the Vicsek model with the mean-field Kuramoto model. Name one analogue of the coupling strength \(K\) and one analogue of the frequency spread \(\sigma\).








Solution





Alignment plays the role of coupling. Its effective strength grows with the number of neighbours inside radius \(r\), so the density \(\rho\) (or \(r\) itself) acts like \(K\). The noise \(\eta\) plays the role of the disorder that opposes alignment, like \(\sigma\). One important difference: in the Vicsek model the neighbours change as particles move, so the interaction network is itself dynamic.

title: The Kuramoto Model
text:
Reading




Compulsory: Strogatz (2000), Sections 1 to 4.
Recommended: Strogatz et al. (2005).
The Kuramoto model describes a large population of coupled oscillators with different natural frequencies. Each oscillator \(i\) has a phase \(\theta_i\) and a natural frequency \(\omega_i\) (kuramoto1975self?; Kuramoto 2003; Strogatz 2000). It is the standard example of how collective synchronization emerges from simple interactions among oscillators that are not identical. Physicists, biologists and engineers use it to study circadian rhythms, synchronized neurons and the stability of power grids (Strogatz 2000).

title: The Kuramoto Model
text:
From limit cycles to phases
For any system of weakly coupled, nearly identical limit-cycle oscillators, the long-term dynamics reduce to phase equations of the form
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + \sum_{j=1}^N \Gamma_{ij} \left( \theta_j - \theta_i \right),\quad i = 1, \dots, N,
\tag{1}\]
where \(\Gamma_{ij}\) is the coupling function that describes how oscillator \(j\) influences oscillator \(i\) through their phase difference (Kuramoto 2003; Strogatz 2000). This reduction keeps the timing of each oscillator and discards its amplitude. (winfree1967biological?) first proposed studying populations in this way.

title: The Kuramoto Model
text:
Kuramoto’s choice
Kuramoto took the simplest case: equally weighted, all-to-all, purely sinusoidal coupling,
\[
\Gamma_{ij}(\theta) = \frac{K}{N} \sin \theta.
\tag{2}\]
Substituting into Equation 1 gives the Kuramoto model:
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + \frac{K}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i), \quad i = 1, \dots, N.
\tag{3}\]

\(K \ge 0\) is the coupling strength.
The factor \(1/N\) keeps the total input to each oscillator finite as \(N\) grows.
The natural frequencies \(\omega_i\) are drawn from a density \(g(\omega)\) that is unimodal and symmetric about its mean \(\Omega\) (Strogatz 2000).

Two oscillators with \(\theta_j\) slightly ahead of \(\theta_i\) give \(\sin(\theta_j - \theta_i) > 0\), so \(i\) speeds up toward \(j\). The coupling always pulls phases together. What competes against it is the spread of natural frequencies.

title: The Kuramoto Model
text:
Rotating frame
Move to a frame that rotates at the mean frequency, \(\theta_i \to \theta_i + \Omega t\). The coupling depends only on phase differences, so Equation 3 keeps its form and the new frequencies have mean zero. From now on you can assume \(g(\omega) = g(-\omega)\) (Strogatz 2000).

title: The Kuramoto Model
section: Frequency densities used in this module
text:
Frequency densities used in this module








Density
\(g(\omega)\)
\(g(0)\)




Normal, standard deviation \(\sigma\)
\(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\, e^{-\omega^2/(2\sigma^2)}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\)


Lorentzian (Cauchy), scale \(\gamma\)
\(\dfrac{\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2 + \omega^2)}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{\pi\gamma}\)



The Lorentzian case gives closed-form results (Critical Coupling). The normal case is the default in the lab. The initial phases are drawn uniformly on \([0, 2\pi)\) unless stated otherwise.






Exercise



Show that Equation 3 with \(N = 2\) reduces to the firefly equation of Phase Locking for the phase difference \(\phi = \theta_2 - \theta_1\). What is the locking condition?








Solution





With \(N = 2\), \(\dot\theta_1 = \omega_1 + \tfrac{K}{2}\sin(\theta_2 - \theta_1)\) and \(\dot\theta_2 = \omega_2 + \tfrac{K}{2}\sin(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\). Subtracting,
\[
\dot\phi = (\omega_2 - \omega_1) - K\sin\phi.
\]
This is the phase-difference equation of Phase Locking with detuning \(\omega_2 - \omega_1\) and strength \(K\). The two oscillators lock when \(|\omega_2 - \omega_1| \le K\).

title: Phase Locking
text: A single firefly can lock its flashing to a periodic light. The model below, from Strogatz (2024, sec. 4.5), is based on (ermentrout1984beyond?). It is the smallest model of synchronization: one oscillator driven by one rhythm.

title: Phase Locking
text:
The model
Let \(\Theta(t)\) be the phase of the stimulus and \(\theta(t)\) the phase of the firefly. A flash happens when a phase passes through \(0\). The stimulus runs at constant frequency \(\Omega\). The firefly has natural frequency \(\omega\) and is pulled toward the stimulus with strength \(A > 0\):
\[
\dot\Theta = \Omega, \qquad \dot\theta = \omega + A\sin(\Theta - \theta).
\tag{1}\]
If the stimulus is ahead (\(0 < \Theta - \theta < \pi\)), the firefly speeds up. If it is behind, the firefly slows down.

title: Phase Locking
text:
Phase difference
The quantity you care about is the phase difference \(\phi = \Theta - \theta\). It obeys
\[
\dot\phi = \Omega - \omega - A\sin\phi.
\tag{2}\]
With the dimensionless time \(\tau = At\) and detuning \(\mu = (\Omega - \omega)/A\), this becomes
\[
\phi' = \mu - \sin\phi,
\tag{3}\]
which is the nonuniform oscillator from Flows on the Circle.

title: Phase Locking
text:
Locking range

If \(|\mu| \le 1\), Equation 3 has a stable fixed point \(\phi^* = \arcsin\mu\). The firefly runs at the stimulus frequency \(\Omega\) with a constant phase lag. This is phase locking, or entrainment.
If \(|\mu| > 1\), there are no fixed points and \(\phi\) keeps increasing. The firefly drifts relative to the stimulus. This is phase drift.

In the original variables the firefly entrains when
\[
\omega - A \le \Omega \le \omega + A.
\tag{4}\]
Outside this range, the time for \(\phi\) to grow by \(2\pi\) is
\[
T_{\text{drift}} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{(\omega - \Omega)^2 - A^2}}.
\tag{5}\]
Both predictions can be tested with a flashing light, because \(\omega\) and the width of the locking range are measurable (Strogatz 2024, sec. 4.5). Real fireflies differ between species. Some can even shift their own natural frequency, which needs an extra adaptation variable (ermentrout1991adaptive?).








Figure 1: Phase difference \(\phi = \Theta - \theta\) for a firefly with \(\omega = 1\) and \(A = 0.2\). Inside the locking range (\(\Omega = 1.15\)) the difference settles to \(\arcsin\mu\). Outside it (\(\Omega = 1.3\)) the difference keeps growing, one turn every \(T_{\text{drift}}\).





Predicted drift period for Omega = 1.3: 28.10








Exercise



Use Figure 1 and the printed value. Measure the drift period in the plot for \(\Omega = 1.3\) and compare it with Equation 5.








Solution





With \(\omega = 1\), \(\Omega = 1.3\) and \(A = 0.2\), Equation 5 gives \(T_{\text{drift}} = 2\pi/\sqrt{0.09 - 0.04} = 2\pi/\sqrt{0.05} \approx 28.1\). In the plot \(\phi\) climbs by about \(2\pi \approx 6.28\) every 28 time units, with slow stretches where \(\phi\) is near \(\pi/2\), the bottleneck.









Exercise



A firefly has a natural period of \(0.9\) s and entrains to stimulus periods between \(0.78\) s and \(1.06\) s. Estimate \(A\).








Solution





Convert periods to angular frequencies with \(\Omega = 2\pi/T\). The extremes of the locking range are \(\Omega_{\max} = 2\pi/0.78 \approx 8.06\) and \(\Omega_{\min} = 2\pi/1.06 \approx 5.93\) rad/s. By Equation 4, \(\Omega_{\max} - \Omega_{\min} = 2A\), so \(A \approx 1.06\) rad/s. The midpoint, \(6.99\) rad/s, is close to \(\omega = 2\pi/0.9 \approx 6.98\) rad/s, which is a consistency check. (These numbers are illustrative, chosen for the exercise.)

title: Phase Locking
text:
From one oscillator to many
Here the stimulus is fixed and does not respond to the firefly. In a swarm every firefly is both a stimulus and a responder. The Kuramoto model in Session 11 treats that case.

title: Vicsek Lab: Initialization
text: In this lab you implement the Vicsek model (Vicsek et al. 1995), validate it, and animate it. The rules are in The Vicsek Model.

title: Vicsek Lab: Initialization
text:
Why not solve_ivp?
In Module 1 you used ODE solvers like scipy.integrate.solve_ivp() for continuous-time systems. The Vicsek model is a discrete-time, agent-based model. At each step all particles update their heading and position from their neighbours and some noise. There is no differential equation to integrate, so you implement it with a loop over time steps.

title: Vicsek Lab: Initialization
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Before you code, write down your expectations.

With noise \(\eta = 0\) and a large interaction radius, what is the order parameter after many steps?
With \(\eta = 2\pi\), what is it for \(N = 100\)?
At fixed noise, does increasing the density help or hurt alignment?









Solution





With no noise and every particle seeing every other, all headings converge to one direction and \(v_a \to 1\). With \(\eta = 2\pi\) every heading is random at every step, so \(v_a\) is of order \(1/\sqrt{N} = 0.1\). Higher density means more neighbours inside the radius, which averages out the noise and helps alignment (Vicsek et al. 1995).

title: Vicsek Lab: Initialization
text:
Initial State






Exercise



Create the initial positions and headings. Positions are uniform on the box \([0, L]^2\) and headings are uniform on \([0, 2\pi)\).

    # Random initial theta, shape (N)
    theta = # TODO

    # Random initial x, y - shape (2, N)
    xy = # TODO
    return xy, theta








Hint





np.random.uniform(low, high, size) accepts a tuple as size. Use size=(2, num_boids) for the positions, so that xy[0] holds the x-coordinates and xy[1] the y-coordinates.









Solution





def initialize_particles(num_boids, box_size):
    theta = np.random.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, num_boids)
    xy = np.random.uniform(0, box_size, (2, num_boids))
    return xy, theta



Try out your function now. Vicsek et al. (1995) used between \(N = 40\) and \(N = 10000\) particles and box sizes between \(L = 3\) and \(L = 50\). The more particles you have, the slower the simulation will be, so start with a small number like \(N=100\) and a box size of \(L=10\).
Figure 1 shows what you are building: after a few steps, nearby particles already point in similar directions.








Figure 1: Vicsek model after 20 steps: \(N = 100\) particles in a box of side \(L = 10\), noise \(\eta = 0.5\). Arrows show headings and grey dots the recent trajectory.

title: Module 2: Synchronization and Collective Behaviour
text:
This module studies how order appears in large groups of interacting units. You start with one oscillator on the circle and one oscillator driven by a rhythm, move to the Kuramoto model of many coupled oscillators and the Millennium Bridge, and end with models of flocks, schools and crowds. The main tools are phase equations, order parameters and agent-based simulation (Steven H. Strogatz 2024; Steven H. Strogatz 2000; Vicsek et al. 1995).

Session Structure
Session 10: Synchronization: from one oscillator to many
Synchronization in Nature Flows on the Circle Phase Locking
Session 11: The Kuramoto model
The Kuramoto Model The Order Parameter Critical Coupling The Millennium Bridge
Session 12: Laboratory: Kuramoto and the Millennium Bridge
Initialization The ODE Pairwise vs Mean Field (optional) Animation Bifurcation Diagram Locating the Threshold Full Simulation (optional) Finite-Size Effects Kuramoto Assignment (graded)

The Vicsek Model The Couzin Model The Social Force Model

Initialization Update Rule Vectorized Update (optional) Order Parameter Validation Animation Interactive Animation (optional) Predator Avoidance (optional) Practice: Collective Motion


Learning Goals
By the end of this module you should be able to:

Describe an oscillator by its phase and analyse flows on the circle, including the saddle-node bifurcation of the nonuniform oscillator.
Derive the locking range of an oscillator driven by a periodic stimulus.
Write the Kuramoto model, rewrite it in mean-field form, and state the critical coupling \(K_c = 2/(\pi g(0))\).
Simulate the Kuramoto model, measure \(r_\infty(K)\), and separate real synchronization from finite-size fluctuations.
Explain the Millennium Bridge instability as a feedback loop between crowd synchrony and bridge motion, and compute the critical crowd size.
Implement the Vicsek model and explain the roles of noise and density in the transition to collective motion.
Compare the rules and the questions of the Vicsek, Couzin and social force models.








References

Strogatz, Steven H. 2024. Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos: With Applications to Physics, Biology, Chemistry, and Engineering. Chapman; Hall/CRC.


Strogatz, Steven H. 2000. “From Kuramoto to Crawford: Exploring the Onset of Synchronization in Populations of Coupled Oscillators.” Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena 143: 1–20.


Vicsek, Tamás, András Czirók, Eshel Ben-Jacob, Inon Cohen, and Ofer Shochet. 1995. “Novel Type of Phase Transition in a System of Self-Driven Particles.” Physical Review Letters 75 (6): 1226.

title: Kuramoto Assignment (Graded)
text:
This is a graded assignment, released in Session 12. It is worth 10% of your final grade.
Your goal is to review the theory of synchronization of weakly coupled oscillators, study the Kuramoto model numerically, and then simulate the Millennium Bridge crowd-bridge synchrony model (Kuramoto 2003; Strogatz 2000; Pikovsky, Rosenblum, and Kurths 2001; Strogatz et al. 2005; Eckhardt et al. 2007). The lab pages of Session 12 give you the building blocks. The theory is in Critical Coupling and The Millennium Bridge.

title: Kuramoto Assignment (Graded)
text:
Kuramoto Model
Start from the basic Kuramoto model with all-to-all symmetric coupling:
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + \frac{K}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j-\theta_i),
\qquad i=1,\dots,N.
\tag{1}\]
Here \(\theta_i \in [0,2\pi)\) is the phase of oscillator \(i\), \(K>0\) is the coupling constant, and the natural frequencies \(\omega_i\) are sampled from a unimodal symmetric distribution \(g(\omega)\).

title: Kuramoto Assignment (Graded)
text:
Numerical Integration
Write a Python script that integrates the Kuramoto equations numerically. Start with the following values:

\(N=100\) oscillators.
\(g(\omega)\) equal to the standard normal distribution.
\(K=7\).

For the initial condition, write a function that assigns phases either randomly over the whole circle, the disperse case, or over a small arc, the concentrated case. For the numerical integration, you may write your own scheme, for instance explicit Euler, or use scipy.integrate. In either case, produce the following outputs:

A graph of \(r(t)\), the order parameter, versus time. In the subcritical case \(K<K_c\), the asymptotic value \(r_\infty\) should be approximately zero up to fluctuations, while for \(K>K_c\) you should observe \(r_\infty \in (0,1)\) for large \(t\). The amplitude of the fluctuations should decrease as \(N\) grows, typically like \(\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})\).
An animation of the oscillators moving on the unit circle. You may also plot the centroid \(re^{i\psi}\).

title: Kuramoto Assignment (Graded)
text:
Critical Coupling
Review Critical Coupling and Sections 3 and 4 of Strogatz (2000) until you are comfortable with the derivation of the critical coupling \(K_c\). For more detail, see Pikovsky, Rosenblum, and Kurths (2001). Then compare the theoretical prediction with the value obtained numerically.

Sample 20 values of \(K\) between \(K_{\min}\) and \(K_{\max}\) such that \(K_{\min}<K_c<K_{\max}\). A reasonable choice is \(K_{\min}=K_c/3\) and \(K_{\max}=3K_c\).
For each sampled value of \(K\), estimate \(r_\infty\) by making sure that \(r(t)\) has reached its saturation regime, then average over a tail window to reduce fluctuations. A reasonable choice is to average over the last 300 time steps. Keep both the mean and standard deviation.
Plot \(r_\infty(K)\) with error bars and identify the approximate value of \(K_c\), comparing it with the theoretical prediction.
Validate your results with different choices of \(g(\omega)\), for instance normal distributions with different variance, and check whether the theoretical prediction for \(K_c\) remains consistent.
Plot the smooth theoretical curve defined implicitly by the self-consistency equation (4.5) of Strogatz (2000) together with your numerical points:

\[
1 = K\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos^2\theta\, g\big(Kr\sin\theta\big)\,d\theta.
\tag{2}\]

If you are not able to solve the implicit equation numerically for a general distribution \(g(\omega)\), include at least the Cauchy case, where the formula is explicit:

\[
g(\omega) = \frac{1}{\pi(1+\omega^2)},
\qquad
r_\infty(K) = \sqrt{1-\frac{K_c}{K}}.
\tag{3}\]
Check that your numerical points approach the theoretical curve more closely as \(N\) becomes large.

title: Kuramoto Assignment (Graded)
text:
Millennium Bridge Crowd Synchrony
Read The Millennium Bridge first. The model couples one lateral bridge mode to \(N\) pedestrian phase oscillators (Strogatz et al. 2005):
\[
M\ddot X + B\dot X + KX = G\sum_{i=1}^N \sin\Theta_i,
\qquad
\dot\Theta_i = \Omega_i + C\,A\sin\big(\Psi-\Theta_i+\alpha\big),
\tag{4}\]
with \(\Omega_0 = \sqrt{K/M}\) and the bridge amplitude and phase given by
\[
A = \sqrt{X^2 + \big(\dot X/\Omega_0\big)^2},
\qquad
\Psi = \operatorname{atan2}\big(X,\ \dot X/\Omega_0\big).
\tag{5}\]
Here \(K\) is the bridge stiffness, not the Kuramoto coupling. Crowd synchrony is measured with \(R e^{i\Phi} = N^{-1}\sum_j e^{i\Theta_j}\).
For \(\alpha = \pi/2\) and a frequency density \(P(\Omega)\) symmetric about \(\Omega_0\), the critical crowd size is
\[
N_c = \frac{2B\,\Omega_0}{\pi\,G\,C\,P(\Omega_0)}.
\tag{6}\]
If \(P\) is normal with mean \(\Omega_0\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), then \(P(\Omega_0) = 1/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma)\).

Use random initial phases \(\Theta_i(0) \sim \mathrm{Unif}[0,2\pi)\) and small initial bridge motion, for instance \(X(0) \approx 0\) and \(\dot X(0) \approx 0\).
Perform the following controlled crowd-ramp experiment:

Start with \(N=N_0\) pedestrians. Every \(\Delta T\) seconds, increase the crowd size by \(\Delta N\), adding new pedestrians with fresh initial phases and natural frequencies, until reaching \(N_{\max}\).
Compute the theoretical value of \(N_c\) using your chosen parameters and frequency distribution.
Define the first time at which the crowd reaches the theoretical threshold,

\[
t_c = \inf\{t : N(t) \ge N_c\}.
\tag{7}\]

Produce three stacked plots, and in each one draw a vertical dashed line at \(t=t_c\) labeled “\(N=N_c\)”:

\(N(t)\) versus \(t\), the crowd-size staircase.
\(A(t)\) versus \(t\), the bridge wobble amplitude.
\(R(t)\) versus \(t\), the degree of synchronization.

Briefly describe what happens before and after \(t_c\), and comment on whether the observed onset of wobbling and synchrony is close to the theoretical prediction.

Reference code is available in amlab/odes_coupled/bridge.py. It uses a different, nondimensional formulation of the bridge-pedestrian coupling, so its parameters do not map one to one onto the equations above. Use it for ideas, but do not copy it.
