title: The Motter-Lai Model
text: Motter and Lai proposed a minimal model of cascades of overload failures on networks (motter2002cascade?). The model has one parameter and one rule. This page states the model. The next page implements it.

title: The Motter-Lai Model
text:
Load
Something travels between every pair of nodes along shortest paths: data packets, goods, or, in a crude picture, power. The load \(L_i\) of node \(i\) is the number of shortest paths between pairs of other nodes that pass through \(i\) (motter2002cascade?). When several shortest paths join the same pair, each one counts with equal weight. This is the betweenness centrality of Network Concepts, without normalization:
\[
L_i = \sum_{s \neq i \neq t} \frac{\sigma_{st}(i)}{\sigma_{st}}.
\]

title: The Motter-Lai Model
text:
Capacity
Operators build some spare capacity into each node. Motter and Lai assume that the capacity is proportional to the initial load \(L_i(0)\) of the intact network (motter2002cascade?):
\[
C_i = (1 + \alpha)\, L_i(0), \qquad \alpha \ge 0.
\]
The tolerance parameter \(\alpha\) is the same for every node. With \(\alpha = 0\) the network runs at full capacity; with large \(\alpha\) every node has plenty of margin.

title: The Motter-Lai Model
text:
Cascade iteration

Start from the intact network and compute \(L_i(0)\) and \(C_i\) for all nodes.
Remove a trigger node.
Recompute the loads \(L_i\) on the remaining network. The shortest paths change, so the load redistributes.
Remove every node with \(L_i > C_i\).
Repeat steps 3 and 4 until no node is overloaded.

The damage is measured by the relative size of the largest connected component after the cascade (motter2002cascade?):
\[
G = \frac{N'}{N},
\]
where \(N\) is the number of nodes of the intact network and \(N'\) the size of its largest component at the end. \(G \approx 1\) means the network survived; \(G \ll 1\) means it broke apart.

title: The Motter-Lai Model
The Motter-Lai Model
text:
A small example
Figure 1 runs one cascade on a Barabási-Albert graph with 40 nodes. The trigger is the node with the largest load and \(\alpha = 0.5\).








Figure 1: One Motter-Lai cascade on a Barabási-Albert graph (N = 40, m = 2, alpha = 0.5). Black: trigger. Red: nodes that fail by overload in the first step. Orange: nodes that fail in the second step. Grey: survivors.





failed per step: [1, 9, 2], G = 0.53


Node size is proportional to the initial load. Most nodes have a small load, and a few hubs carry most shortest paths. Notice that many of the failed nodes had a small initial load: a small load means a small capacity, so a modest increase after the redistribution is enough to overload them.






Exercise



In a star graph with \(N\) nodes, what is the load of the centre and of a leaf? What happens to \(G\) if the centre fails? Does \(\alpha\) matter?








Solution





Every pair of leaves has exactly one shortest path, through the centre, so the centre has load \(\binom{N-1}{2}\) and each leaf has load 0. If the centre fails, no edges remain and \(G = 1/N\). The value of \(\alpha\) does not matter: the network breaks apart through the removal itself, with no overload step.

title: NetworkX Basics
text:
Toolkit page



This page is self-study material for Session 23. Work through it before the network labs.
A graph models pairwise relations between objects. It consists of nodes (also called vertices) and edges (also called links) that connect pairs of nodes (Newman 2018).
This page shows how to build graphs with the networkx library (Hagberg, Schult, and Swart 2008). NetworkX is a Python package for the creation, manipulation and study of the structure, dynamics and functions of complex networks. The examples follow A First Course in Network Science (Menczer, Fortunato, and Davis 2020); see the book’s GitHub repository. The folder references/networkx_indiana of this repository has the matching notebooks. You will learn to:
First, import the library:
Now initialize an empty graph:
G = nx.Graph()

print(G)

Graph with 0 nodes and 0 edges
G is now an empty undirected graph. The next sections add nodes and edges to it.

title: NetworkX Basics
text:
Nodes (Vertices)
Nodes represent the entities in a graph. They can be anything: people in a social network, airports in a flight network, or web pages in the internet.
To add nodes, use the add_node(<id>) method. The <id> can be any hashable Python object. You can see the list of nodes in the graph using the nodes() method.

# Add three nodes to the graph
G.add_node("Spain")
G.add_node("Portugal")
G.add_node("France")

# Show the nodes in the graph
print(G.nodes())

['Spain', 'Portugal', 'France']








What does “hashable” mean?





In Python, a hashable object is an object that has a hash value that remains constant during its lifetime. This means that the object can be used as a key in a dictionary or as an element in a set. Examples of hashable objects include integers, strings, and tuples (as long as they contain only hashable types). Lists and dictionaries are not hashable because they are mutable (their contents can change).




Node Attributes
Each node can have attributes that provide additional information about it. For example, in a social network, a node might represent a person and have attributes like name, age, or location.
NetworkX stores attributes on nodes. Think of G.nodes as a dictionary where the keys are the node IDs and the values are dictionaries of attributes. You can add attributes to a node by accessing it through G.nodes[<id>] and assigning values to the attributes.
For example, add a “population” attribute to the country nodes:

# Add population attribute to the nodes
G.nodes["Spain"]["population"] = 47_000_000
G.nodes["Portugal"]["population"] = 10_000_000
G.nodes["France"]["population"] = 67_000_000

# Show the nodes with their attributes
population = nx.get_node_attributes(G, 'population')
for node, pop in population.items():
    print(f"{node}: {pop} inhabitants")

Spain: 47000000 inhabitants
Portugal: 10000000 inhabitants
France: 67000000 inhabitants


Using get_node_attributes(G, 'population'), you can retrieve the population attribute for all nodes in the graph as a dictionary.
If you are including a new node and want to add attributes at the same time, you can use the add_node() method with keyword arguments. For example:

# Add a new node with attributes
G.add_node("Italy", population=60_000_000)

# Show the nodes with their attributes
population = nx.get_node_attributes(G, 'population')
for node, pop in population.items():
    print(f"{node}: {pop} inhabitants")

Spain: 47000000 inhabitants
Portugal: 10000000 inhabitants
France: 67000000 inhabitants
Italy: 60000000 inhabitants

This page is self-study material for Session 23. It continues Paths in Directed Graphs.
This page computes degree and clustering with networkx (Newman 2018). You will need degree moments in the epidemic lab.
You reuse the two graphs from the previous pages.
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Create an undirected graph
# (foods that go well together)
G_foods = nx.from_edgelist([
    ("bread", "cheese"),
    ("bread", "chocolate"),
    ("bread", "cured ham"),
    ("cheese", "cured ham"),
    ("chocolate", "cookies"),
    ("chocolate", "milk"),
    ("chocolate", "watermelon"),
    ("cookies", "milk"),
    ("cured ham", "watermelon"),
])

# Visualize the graph
pos = nx.circular_layout(G_foods)
nx.draw(G_foods, node_color="lightblue", with_labels=True, pos=pos)
plt.show()
# Create a directed graph
D_food_chain = nx.DiGraph()  # food chain (prey -> predator)
D_food_chain.add_edges_from([
    ("grass", "antelope"),
    ("grass", "zebra"),
    ("antelope", "lion"),
    ("antelope", "hyena"),
    ("zebra", "lion"),
    ("zebra", "hyena"),
    ("hyena", "lion"),
])

# Visualize the graph
pos = nx.spring_layout(D_food_chain)
nx.draw(D_food_chain, node_color="lightgreen", with_labels=True, pos=pos)
plt.show()

title: Degree and Clustering
text:
Degree
The degree \(k\) of a node is the number of edges connected to it. In an undirected graph, the degree of a node is simply the number of neighbors it has.

# Degree of a node
print("Degree of 'bread':", G_foods.degree("bread"))

Degree of 'bread': 3


The average degree of an undirected graph is given by:
\[\langle k \rangle = \frac{2E}{N}\]
where \(E\) is the number of edges and \(N\) is the number of nodes.

# Average degree of the graph
ls_degrees = [G_foods.degree(node) for node in G_foods.nodes()]
avg_degree = sum(ls_degrees) / len(ls_degrees)
print("Average degree:", avg_degree)

Average degree: 2.5714285714285716



Degrees in Directed Graphs
In a directed graph, you distinguish between in-degree (number of incoming edges) and out-degree (number of outgoing edges).

print("In-degree of 'antelope' (number of prey):", D_food_chain.in_degree("antelope"))
print("Out-degree of 'antelope' (number of predators):", D_food_chain.out_degree("antelope"))

In-degree of 'antelope' (number of prey): 1
Out-degree of 'antelope' (number of predators): 2

title: Degree and Clustering
text:
Clustering Coefficient
Many real networks have triangles: if A is connected to B and C, there is a higher-than-random chance that B is also connected to C (Watts and Strogatz 1998; Newman 2018). This tendency is captured by the clustering coefficient.
For an undirected graph, the local clustering coefficient of node \(i\) is:
\[
C_i = \frac{2T_i}{k_i(k_i - 1)}
\]
where \(k_i\) is the degree of node \(i\), and \(T_i\) is the number of triangles that include node \(i\). If \(k_i < 2\), define \(C_i = 0\).
In the food graph, \(C_{\text{bread}} = 1/3\): “bread” has three neighbors, and only one neighbor-pair is connected.
The average clustering coefficient is:
\[
C = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N C_i.
\]
In NetworkX:

nx.clustering(G) returns \(C_i\) for every node.
nx.average_clustering(G) returns the average \(C\).

You will use \(C\) later to compare random vs small-world vs scale-free synthetic networks.

# Local clustering coefficient for each node
clustering = nx.clustering(G_foods)
print("Local clustering:")
for node, c in clustering.items():
    print(f"  {node}: {c:.3f}")

print("Average clustering:", nx.average_clustering(G_foods))

# Another common global measure is transitivity
# (ratio of triangles to connected triples)
print("Transitivity:", nx.transitivity(G_foods))

Local clustering:
  bread: 0.333
  cheese: 1.000
  chocolate: 0.167
  cured ham: 0.333
  cookies: 1.000
  milk: 1.000
  watermelon: 0.000
Average clustering: 0.5476190476190477
Transitivity: 0.375








Exercise



Compute the local clustering coefficient of “chocolate” by hand from the drawing of G_foods. Then check your answer with nx.clustering.








Solution





“chocolate” has four neighbours (bread, cookies, milk and watermelon), so there are \(4 \cdot 3 / 2 = 6\) neighbour pairs. Only cookies and milk are connected, so \(C_{\text{chocolate}} = 1/6 \approx 0.167\).

print(nx.clustering(G_foods, "chocolate"))

0.16666666666666666

title: Centrality in NetworkX
text:
Centrality (Node Importance)
In many real networks, not all nodes play the same role:

in an airport network, some airports are hubs;
in an email network, some people act as bridges between groups.

These ideas are quantified by centrality measures (Newman 2018).

Degree Centrality
The simplest centrality is based on degree. In an undirected graph with \(N\) nodes, the (normalized) degree centrality is (Newman 2018)
\[
\mathrm{deg\_cent}(i) = \frac{k_i}{N-1}.
\]

deg_cent = nx.degree_centrality(G_foods)
print("Degree centrality:")
for node, c in sorted(deg_cent.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True):
    print(f"  {node}: {c:.3f}")

Degree centrality:
  chocolate: 0.667
  bread: 0.500
  cured ham: 0.500
  cheese: 0.333
  cookies: 0.333
  milk: 0.333
  watermelon: 0.333


A higher degree centrality means the node is more “important” in terms of connectivity. In the food graph, “chocolate” has the highest degree centrality, while “bread” and “cured ham” are the next most connected nodes.


Closeness Centrality
Closeness measures how close a node is (on average) to all others via shortest paths (Sabidussi 1966). One common definition is
\[
\mathrm{close}(i) = \frac{N-1}{\sum_{j \neq i} d(i,j)},
\]
where \(d(i,j)\) is the shortest-path distance.
A higher closeness centrality means the node can reach other nodes more quickly. In the food graph, “chocolate” has the highest closeness centrality, followed by “bread”.






Disconnected graphs



If a graph is disconnected, some distances are infinite and closeness becomes tricky. In practice you often compute path-based metrics on the largest connected component.



close_cent = nx.closeness_centrality(G_foods)
print("Closeness centrality:")
for node, c in sorted(close_cent.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True):
    print(f"  {node}: {c:.3f}")

Closeness centrality:
  chocolate: 0.750
  bread: 0.667
  watermelon: 0.600
  cured ham: 0.545
  cheese: 0.500
  cookies: 0.500
  milk: 0.500




Betweenness Centrality
Betweenness identifies bridges: nodes that sit on many shortest paths (Freeman 1977). Formally,
\[
\mathrm{between}(v) = \sum_{s \neq v \neq t} \frac{\sigma_{st}(v)}{\sigma_{st}},
\]
where \(\sigma_{st}\) is the number of shortest paths from \(s\) to \(t\), and \(\sigma_{st}(v)\) is the number of those paths that pass through \(v\).

bc = nx.betweenness_centrality(G_foods)
print("Betweenness centrality:")
for node, c in sorted(bc.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True):
    print(f"  {node}: {c:.3f}")

Betweenness centrality:
  chocolate: 0.567
  bread: 0.300
  cured ham: 0.100
  watermelon: 0.100
  cheese: 0.000
  cookies: 0.000
  milk: 0.000


Higher betweenness centrality means the node acts as a bridge between different parts of the graph. In the food graph, “chocolate” has the highest betweenness centrality, with “bread” as the second most important bridge.


PageRank (Directed Networks)
For directed networks (like the web), PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random walk (“random surfer”) on the graph (Page et al. 1999).

pr = nx.pagerank(D_food_chain, alpha=0.85)
print("PageRank (directed food chain):")
for node, c in sorted(pr.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True):
    print(f"  {node}: {c:.3f}")

PageRank (directed food chain):
  lion: 0.403
  hyena: 0.218
  antelope: 0.140
  zebra: 0.140
  grass: 0.099








Performance note





On large graphs, exact betweenness can be expensive. NetworkX supports approximation (sample \(k\) sources):
nx.betweenness_centrality(G, k=200, seed=SEED)

title: Epidemic Threshold
text: In the well-mixed SIS model of Compartmental Models, an infection persists only if \(R_0 > 1\). On a network, the corresponding condition depends on the degree distribution. This page derives it and states exactly when the threshold vanishes.

title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
Setup
Use the continuous-time SIS model: each S-I edge transmits at rate \(\beta\) and each infected node recovers at rate \(\mu\). The spreading rate is \(\lambda = \beta/\mu\). In the discrete-time simulations of SIS Simulation, \(\lambda \approx \beta/\mu\) when both probabilities are small.

title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
Homogeneous mean field
If every node had exactly \(\langle k \rangle\) neighbours, the infected density \(\rho\) would obey \(\dot\rho = -\rho + \lambda\langle k \rangle \rho(1-\rho)\) (time in units of \(1/\mu\)). The threshold is \(\lambda_c = 1/\langle k \rangle\) (Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015).

title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
Heterogeneous mean field
Now group nodes by degree. Let \(\rho_k\) be the fraction of infected nodes among nodes of degree \(k\). Assume an uncorrelated network: an edge leads to a node of degree \(k'\) with probability \(k' p_{k'}/\langle k \rangle\). Then (pastor2001epidemic?; Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015)
\[
\frac{d\rho_k}{dt} = -\rho_k + \lambda k (1 - \rho_k)\,\Theta, \qquad \Theta = \frac{1}{\langle k \rangle}\sum_{k'} k' p_{k'} \rho_{k'} .
\]
Linearize around \(\rho_k = 0\). Multiply by \(k p_k / \langle k \rangle\) and sum over \(k\): \(\dot\Theta = \left(\lambda \langle k^2 \rangle / \langle k \rangle - 1\right)\Theta\). The disease-free state becomes unstable when
\[
\lambda > \lambda_c = \frac{\langle k \rangle}{\langle k^2 \rangle}.
\]
For a Poisson degree distribution, \(\langle k^2 \rangle = \langle k \rangle^2 + \langle k \rangle\) and \(\lambda_c = 1/(\langle k \rangle + 1)\), close to the homogeneous result. For SIR the analogous result is a critical transmissibility \(T_c = \langle k \rangle / (\langle k^2 \rangle - \langle k \rangle)\) (newman2002spread?).

title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
When does the threshold vanish?
For a scale-free distribution \(p_k \sim k^{-\gamma}\) with \(2 < \gamma \le 3\), \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) diverges as \(N \to \infty\), so \(\lambda_c \to 0\) (pastor2001epidemic?). Read this result with its assumptions:

It is an asymptotic result for an idealized infinite scale-free network with \(2 < \gamma \le 3\).
It relies on the heterogeneous mean-field approximation, which ignores degree correlations and the fixed structure of the contacts.
Every finite network has a largest degree \(k_{\max}\), so \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) is finite and the threshold is small but nonzero (pastor2002finite?). For the Barabási-Albert model, \(\langle k^2 \rangle \approx m(m+1)\ln N\) (see Preferential Attachment), so the formula gives \(\lambda_c \approx 2/\big((m+1)\ln N\big)\), which decreases only logarithmically with \(N\).
Other approximations give other finite-size thresholds. The quenched mean-field theory, which keeps the full adjacency matrix, predicts \(\lambda_c = 1/\Lambda_{\max}\), where \(\Lambda_{\max}\) is the largest eigenvalue of \(A\) (castellano2010thresholds?; Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015).

?@fig-threshold-N computes both predictions on generated graphs.








Figure 1: Epidemic threshold predictions against network size for Barabási-Albert (m = 3) and Erdős-Rényi graphs with the same mean degree. Solid: heterogeneous mean field /<k^2>. Dashed: quenched mean field 1/Lambda_max. One graph per size.





BA HMF: [0.079 0.076 0.062 0.054 0.051]
ER HMF: [0.141 0.144 0.143 0.143 0.143]


For the ER graphs the threshold stays near \(1/(\langle k \rangle + 1) = 1/7 \approx 0.14\). For the BA graphs it decreases slowly with \(N\) but stays well above zero at every size you can simulate.






Exercise



A BA network with \(m = 3\) has \(N = 10^9\) nodes. Estimate \(\lambda_c\) from the heterogeneous mean-field formula. Compare it with an ER graph with the same mean degree.








Solution





\(\lambda_c \approx 2/\big((m+1)\ln N\big) = 2/(4 \times 20.7) \approx 0.024\). The ER graph gives \(\lambda_c = 1/(\langle k \rangle + 1) = 1/7 \approx 0.14\) at any size. Even for a network the size of a large country the BA threshold is small but clearly positive.

title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
Optional extension






Exercise



Use amlab.networks_spreading.run_sis_fast on a BA graph with \(N = 2000\). Fix \(\mu = 0.05\), vary \(\beta\), and plot the long-time prevalence against \(\lambda = \beta/\mu\). Locate the value of \(\lambda\) where the prevalence leaves zero and compare it with both predictions.








Solution





Start from 50 infected nodes, run 1000 steps and average the last 200 steps over 3 runs.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
from amlab.networks_spreading import run_sis_fast

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
G = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(2000, 3, seed=7)
mu = 0.05
lams = np.linspace(0.02, 0.2, 10)
prevalence = [
    np.mean([run_sis_fast(G, lam * mu, mu, steps=1000, initial_infected=50, rng=rng)[-200:].mean() for _ in range(3)])
    for lam in lams
]
k = np.array([d for _, d in G.degree()], dtype=float)
plt.plot(lams, prevalence, "o-")
plt.axvline(k.mean() / (k**2).mean(), color="grey", ls=":", label="<k>/<k²>")
plt.xlabel(r"$\lambda = \beta/\mu$")
plt.ylabel("long-time prevalence")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
For this graph both predictions give \(\lambda_c \approx 0.059\). The simulated prevalence is still zero at \(\lambda = 0.08\) and becomes positive between \(0.08\) and \(0.10\). The mean-field theories ignore dynamical correlations: a newly infected node cannot pass the infection back to the neighbour that infected it while that neighbour is still infected, so part of the infection attempts are wasted and the true threshold is higher. On a finite graph, fluctuations also end outbreaks that are just above threshold within the simulated time.

This page is self-study material for Session 23. It continues NetworkX Basics.
The first chunk rebuilds the country graph of the previous page, with four nodes and a population attribute.
import networkx as nx

G = nx.Graph()
G.add_node("Spain", population=47_000_000)
G.add_node("Portugal", population=10_000_000)
G.add_node("France", population=67_000_000)
G.add_node("Italy", population=60_000_000)

title: Edges and Weights
text:
Edges (Links)
Edges represent the connections between nodes in a graph. To add edges to the graph, you can use the add_edge(<node1>, <node2>) method. This will create an undirected edge between node1 and node2 (you refer to nodes by their IDs). You can see the list of edges in the graph using the edges() method.

# Add edges between the nodes (neighboring countries)
G.add_edge("Spain", "Portugal")
G.add_edge("Spain", "France")
# Show the edges in the graph
print(G.edges())

[('Spain', 'Portugal'), ('Spain', 'France')]


Because you are working on an undirected graph, the connection between two nodes does not have a direction. However, you can also create directed graphs where the edges have a direction (from one node to another) using DiGraph() instead of Graph(). In a directed graph, you use add_edge(<source>, <target>) to specify the direction of the edge.

Edge Attributes
Just like nodes, edges can also have attributes, such as weight, which might represent the strength of the connection. For example, in a social network, an edge might represent a friendship between two people, and the weight could represent how close they are.
You can add attributes to an edge by accessing it through G.edges[<node1>, <node2>] and assigning values to the attributes. For example, add a “distance” (between capitals) attribute to represent the distance between the countries:

# Add distance attribute to the edges
G.edges["Spain", "Portugal"]["distance"] = 600  # distance in kilometers
G.edges["Spain", "France"]["distance"] = 1000  # distance in kilometers

# Show the edges with their attributes
distance = nx.get_edge_attributes(G, 'distance')
for edge, dist in distance.items():
    print(f"{edge}: {dist} km")

('Spain', 'Portugal'): 600 km
('Spain', 'France'): 1000 km


Using get_edge_attributes(<graph>, <attribute>), you can retrieve the distance attribute for all edges in the graph as a dictionary.
Again, you can also add attributes to an edge at the same time as you create it using the add_edge() method with keyword arguments. For example:

# Add a new edge with attributes
G.add_edge("France", "Italy", distance=800)

# Show the edges with their attributes
distance = nx.get_edge_attributes(G, 'distance')
for edge, dist in distance.items():
    print(f"{edge}: {dist} km")

('Spain', 'Portugal'): 600 km
('Spain', 'France'): 1000 km
('France', 'Italy'): 800 km




Adding Nodes and Edges Together
You can also add nodes and edges together using the add_edge() method. If you add an edge between two nodes that do not exist in the graph, networkx will automatically create those nodes. For example:

# Add an edge between two nodes that do not exist
G.add_edge("USA", "Canada", distance=3000)
G.add_edge("Netherlands", "Germany", distance=500)
G.add_edge("Germany", "France", distance=900)

# Add the population attribute for the new nodes separately
G.nodes["USA"]["population"] = 331_000_000
G.nodes["Canada"]["population"] = 38_000_000
G.nodes["Netherlands"]["population"] = 17_000_000
G.nodes["Germany"]["population"] = 83_000_000

# Show the nodes and edges in the graph
print("Nodes:", G.nodes())
print("Edges:", G.edges())

Nodes: ['Spain', 'Portugal', 'France', 'Italy', 'USA', 'Canada', 'Netherlands', 'Germany']
Edges: [('Spain', 'Portugal'), ('Spain', 'France'), ('France', 'Italy'), ('France', 'Germany'), ('USA', 'Canada'), ('Netherlands', 'Germany')]




Weighted Edges
The most common edge attribute is weight, which represents the strength of the connection between two nodes. For example, in a social network, the weight of an edge could represent how close two people are. In a transportation network, the weight could represent the distance or travel time between two locations.
Weight is so common that networkx has a special method to add weighted edges: add_weighted_edges_from(). This method takes a list of tuples, where each tuple contains the source node, target node, and weight of the edge. For example:

# Initialize a directed graph
D_contracts = nx.DiGraph()

# Add weighted edges (contracts between companies with the amount of money as weight)
# Disclaimer: weights are made up
weighted_edges = [
    ("OpenAI", "Microsoft", 100_000_000),
    ("OpenAI", "Oracle", 50_000_000),
    ("Microsoft", "Nvidia", 20_000_000),
    ("Oracle", "Nvidia", 10_000_000),
    ("Nvidia", "OpenAI", 5_000_000),
]
D_contracts.add_weighted_edges_from(weighted_edges)

# Show the edges with their weights
weights = nx.get_edge_attributes(D_contracts, 'weight')
for edge, weight in weights.items():
    print(f"{edge}: ${weight}")

('OpenAI', 'Microsoft'): $100000000
('OpenAI', 'Oracle'): $50000000
('Microsoft', 'Nvidia'): $20000000
('Oracle', 'Nvidia'): $10000000
('Nvidia', 'OpenAI'): $5000000

title: Comparing Graph Models
text:
The three previous pages built one model each. This page puts them side by side with the same summary metrics, so you can check the properties claimed for each model on a small graph:
The definitions and examples are in Paths and Components and Degree and Clustering.

title: Comparing Graph Models
text:
Helper functions

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx

SEED = 7


def summarize_graph(G, name="G"):
    """Print a small summary of common network statistics."""
    n = G.number_of_nodes()
    m = G.number_of_edges()
    avg_k = 2 * m / n if n > 0 else 0
    density = nx.density(G)

    # Connectivity (undirected)
    is_connected = nx.is_connected(G) if n > 0 else False
    n_components = nx.number_connected_components(G) if n > 0 else 0

    # Work on the largest connected component when disconnected
    if n == 0:
        L = float("nan")
        C = float("nan")
    else:
        C = nx.average_clustering(G)
        if is_connected:
            L = nx.average_shortest_path_length(G)
        else:
            largest_cc = max(nx.connected_components(G), key=len)
            H = G.subgraph(largest_cc).copy()
            L = nx.average_shortest_path_length(H)

    print(f"--- {name} ---")
    print(f"N = {n}, E = {m}, <k> = {avg_k:.2f}, density = {density:.4f}")
    print(f"connected = {is_connected}, components = {n_components}")
    print(f"clustering C = {C:.3f}")
    print(f"avg shortest path L = {L:.3f} (largest CC if disconnected)")


def plot_degree_histogram(G, title="Degree distribution"):
    """Plot a histogram of the node degrees, one bar per degree value."""
    degrees = [deg for _, deg in G.degree()]
    plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3))
    plt.hist(degrees, bins=range(min(degrees), max(degrees) + 2), align="left", rwidth=0.9)
    plt.xlabel("Degree k")
    plt.ylabel("Count")
    plt.title(title)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

title: Comparing Graph Models
text:
Random graph

G_random = nx.erdos_renyi_graph(n=80, p=0.06, seed=SEED)
summarize_graph(G_random, name="Random (G(N,p))")
plot_degree_histogram(G_random, title="Random graph: degree distribution")

--- Random (G(N,p)) ---
N = 80, E = 211, <k> = 5.28, density = 0.0668
connected = True, components = 1
clustering C = 0.078
avg shortest path L = 2.766 (largest CC if disconnected)

title: Comparing Graph Models
text:
Small-world graph

G_sw = nx.watts_strogatz_graph(n=80, k=6, p=0.08, seed=SEED)
summarize_graph(G_sw, name="Small-world (Watts-Strogatz)")
plot_degree_histogram(G_sw, title="Small-world: degree distribution")

--- Small-world (Watts-Strogatz) ---
N = 80, E = 240, <k> = 6.00, density = 0.0759
connected = True, components = 1
clustering C = 0.494
avg shortest path L = 3.694 (largest CC if disconnected)









The degree distribution stays narrow: most nodes keep a degree close to \(k = 6\).

title: Comparing Graph Models
text:
Scale-free graph

G_sf = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(n=200, m=2, seed=SEED)
summarize_graph(G_sf, name="Scale-free (Barabási-Albert)")
plot_degree_histogram(G_sf, title="Scale-free: degree distribution")

--- Scale-free (Barabási-Albert) ---
N = 200, E = 396, <k> = 3.96, density = 0.0199
connected = True, components = 1
clustering C = 0.075
avg shortest path L = 3.483 (largest CC if disconnected)









Most nodes have degree \(m = 2\) or \(3\), and a few hubs have a degree several times larger.






Exercise



The three graphs above have different sizes and mean degrees. Build a fair comparison: generate an Erdős-Rényi, a Watts-Strogatz and a Barabási-Albert graph with \(N = 200\) and \(\langle k \rangle = 4\), and run summarize_graph on each. Before you run it, predict which graph has the largest \(C\) and which has the smallest \(L\).
N = 200
G_er = # TODO: Erdős-Rényi with <k> = 4
G_ws = # TODO: Watts-Strogatz with k = 4 and p = 0.08
G_ba = # TODO: Barabási-Albert with <k> close to 4
for G, name in [(G_er, "ER"), (G_ws, "WS"), (G_ba, "BA")]:
    summarize_graph(G, name)








Solution





The mean degree of \(G(N, p)\) is \((N-1)p\), so \(p = 4/199\). A Barabási-Albert graph has \(\langle k \rangle \approx 2m\), so \(m = 2\).

N = 200
G_er = nx.erdos_renyi_graph(N, 4 / (N - 1), seed=SEED)
G_ws = nx.watts_strogatz_graph(N, 4, 0.08, seed=SEED)
G_ba = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(N, 2, seed=SEED)
for G, name in [(G_er, "ER"), (G_ws, "WS"), (G_ba, "BA")]:
    summarize_graph(G, name)

--- ER ---
N = 200, E = 409, <k> = 4.09, density = 0.0206
connected = False, components = 4
clustering C = 0.015
avg shortest path L = 3.834 (largest CC if disconnected)
--- WS ---
N = 200, E = 400, <k> = 4.00, density = 0.0201
connected = True, components = 1
clustering C = 0.419
avg shortest path L = 7.766 (largest CC if disconnected)
--- BA ---
N = 200, E = 396, <k> = 3.96, density = 0.0199
connected = True, components = 1
clustering C = 0.075
avg shortest path L = 3.483 (largest CC if disconnected)


The Watts-Strogatz graph has by far the largest clustering (\(C \approx 0.42\)), but with \(k = 4\) and \(p = 0.08\) its paths are still about twice as long as in the other two graphs. The Barabási-Albert graph has the shortest paths (\(L \approx 3.5\)), because its hubs act as shortcuts. The Erdős-Rényi graph has the lowest clustering and is not connected (4 components here), so its \(L\) refers to the largest component.

title: Stable Distributions
text: The Gaussian is the limit of sums with finite variance. Sums of variables with power-law tails and infinite variance also converge, but to a different family: the Lévy stable laws (gnedenko1954limit?; mantegna2000introduction?).

title: Stable Distributions
text:
Definition
A random variable \(X\) is stable if a sum of independent copies has the same shape as \(X\) itself: for every \(n\) there are constants \(a_n > 0\) and \(b_n\) with
\[
X_1 + \dots + X_n \overset{d}{=} a_n X + b_n .
\]
The scale factor is always \(a_n = n^{1/\alpha}\) for some index \(0 < \alpha \le 2\) (gnedenko1954limit?). A stable law has no closed-form density in general. It is defined through its characteristic function. For the symmetric case centred at zero,
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[e^{ikX}\right] = \exp\left(-|c k|^{\alpha}\right),
\tag{1}\]
with scale \(c > 0\). The general family adds a skewness parameter \(\beta \in [-1, 1]\) and a location (mantegna2000introduction?).

title: Stable Distributions
text:
Key properties

\(\alpha = 2\) gives the Gaussian with variance \(2c^2\). \(\alpha = 1\) gives the Cauchy law, with density \(c / [\pi (c^2 + x^2)]\).
For \(\alpha < 2\) the tails are power laws, \(\Pr(|X| > x) \sim C x^{-\alpha}\) as \(x \to \infty\). The variance is infinite. For \(\alpha \le 1\) the mean does not exist either (mantegna2000introduction?).
Generalized central limit theorem. If i.i.d. variables have tails \(\Pr(|X| > x) \sim C x^{-\alpha}\) with \(0 < \alpha < 2\), their suitably centred sums divided by \(n^{1/\alpha}\) converge to a stable law with the same \(\alpha\). If the variance is finite, the limit is Gaussian (gnedenko1954limit?).
In the power-law notation of Power Laws, where the density decays as \(x^{-\alpha_{\text{pdf}}}\), the stable index is \(\alpha = \alpha_{\text{pdf}} - 1\). Only \(\alpha_{\text{pdf}} < 3\) leads to a non-Gaussian limit.

You can sample symmetric stable variables with the method of (chambers1976method?), implemented in amlab.random_walks.sample_symmetric_stable and in scipy.stats.levy_stable (Virtanen et al. 2020).

title: Stable Distributions
text:
Cauchy against normal sample means
For Gaussian data the sample mean of \(n\) values has width \(\propto n^{-1/2}\). For Cauchy data, \(\alpha = 1\) and \(a_n = n\), so the sample mean \(S_n / n\) has exactly the same Cauchy law as a single observation. Averaging does not help.








Figure 1: Running sample mean of 10000 draws for five independent sequences. Left: standard normal. Right: standard Cauchy (\(\alpha = 1\)). The normal means settle at 0; the Cauchy means keep jumping whenever a very large value arrives.











Exercise



Check the scaling \(a_n = n^{1/\alpha}\) for \(\alpha = 1.5\). Draw 10000 sums of \(n\) symmetric stable variables for \(n = 1, 10, 100, 1000\), and compute the interquartile range (IQR) of each set of sums. Fit the slope of \(\log \text{IQR}\) against \(\log n\). Why do you use the IQR and not the standard deviation?








Solution






rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
ns = np.array([1, 10, 100, 1000])
iqr = []
for m in ns:
    s = sample_symmetric_stable(1.5, (10000, m), rng=rng).sum(axis=1)
    q75, q25 = np.percentile(s, [75, 25])
    iqr.append(q75 - q25)
slope = np.polyfit(np.log(ns), np.log(iqr), 1)[0]
print(f"slope {slope:.3f}, theory 1/alpha = {1 / 1.5:.3f}")

slope 0.670, theory 1/alpha = 0.667


The standard deviation is infinite for \(\alpha < 2\), so its sample value is dominated by the largest draw and does not converge. Quantiles exist for every stable law.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
Reading




Compulsory: (newman2005power?).
Recommended: (mantegna2000introduction?), Chapters 3 and 4.
In The Diffusion Equation the position of a walker became Gaussian after many steps. The central limit theorem (CLT) says this happens for sums of almost any independent steps, provided their variance is finite. This session is about what happens when that proviso fails.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
Statement
Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) be independent and identically distributed with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2 > 0\). Let \(S_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n\). Then, for every real \(z\),
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \Pr\left( \frac{S_n - n\mu}{\sigma \sqrt{n}} \le z \right) = \Phi(z),
\tag{1}\]
where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (gnedenko1954limit?). The width of \(S_n\) grows as \(\sqrt{n}\), the same scaling as the random walk.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
Assumptions

Independence. Strongly correlated terms can change both the scaling and the limit.
Identical distribution. Versions for non-identical terms exist (Lindeberg conditions), but no single term may dominate the sum (gnedenko1954limit?).
Finite variance. This is the assumption that matters in this session. If \(\Pr(|X| > x)\) decays like \(x^{-\alpha}\) with \(0 < \alpha < 2\), the variance is infinite and the limit is not Gaussian (gnedenko1954limit?; mantegna2000introduction?).

The theorem says nothing about how fast convergence happens. The tails of the distribution converge last.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
A simulated check
Exponential variables are skewed, far from Gaussian. The figure standardizes sums of \(n\) of them and compares them with the standard normal density.








Figure 1: Histograms of \((S_n - n)/\sqrt{n}\) for sums of \(n\) exponential variables with mean 1 and variance 1 (20000 samples each). The curve is the standard normal density.











Exercise



Repeat the experiment with Student-t variables with 3 degrees of freedom (finite variance \(3\)) and with 1.5 degrees of freedom (infinite variance). Use rng.standard_t. For \(n = 100\), compare the fraction of standardized sums with \(|z| > 3\) to the Gaussian value \(0.0027\). For the second case, standardize by the sample standard deviation of the sums.








Solution






rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 100
for df in [3.0, 1.5]:
    s = rng.standard_t(df, size=(20000, n)).sum(axis=1)
    z_s = (s - s.mean()) / s.std()
    print(f"df = {df}: fraction |z| > 3 is {np.mean(np.abs(z_s) > 3):.4f}")

df = 3.0: fraction |z| > 3 is 0.0050
df = 1.5: fraction |z| > 3 is 0.0016


With 3 degrees of freedom the fraction is of the same order as the Gaussian value but still larger. The CLT holds, but the tails converge slowly. With 1.5 degrees of freedom the sample standard deviation is dominated by a few huge values; the rescaled sums pile up near zero and do not approach the normal law as \(n\) grows. The next pages explain why.

title: Calibrated KS Test
text:
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test compares a whole distribution function with a model. Used naively with estimated parameters it gives wrong p-values. On this page you see why and build a version calibrated by simulation. You continue from Normality Tests.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

from amlab.finance import load_prices, log_returns

r = log_returns(load_prices()["close"])

WARNING: data/finance/prices.csv not found. Using a SYNTHETIC GARCH(1,1) series with Student-t innovations (seed 2026). These are not market data. See data/finance/README.md.

title: Calibrated KS Test
section: Why the plain KS test is not valid here
text:
Why the plain KS test is not valid here
The KS statistic is the largest distance between the empirical CDF \(F_n\) and a model CDF \(F\):
\[
D = \sup_x |F_n(x) - F(x)| .
\]
Kolmogorov’s null distribution of \(D\), which scipy.stats.kstest uses for its p-value, assumes that \(F\) is fixed before you see the data. Here you do not know \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\); you estimate them from the same returns. The fitted normal is then pulled towards the data, so \(D\) is systematically smaller than under a fixed \(F\). The standard p-values are too large and the test rejects too rarely (lilliefors1967kolmogorov?).
(lilliefors1967kolmogorov?) obtained the correct null distribution by Monte Carlo. The same idea is a parametric bootstrap (efron1979bootstrap?): simulate many normal samples of size \(n\), estimate \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) on each one, recompute \(D\), and compare the observed \(D\) with that simulated distribution. Because the normal is a location-scale family, the null distribution of \(D\) with estimated parameters does not depend on the true \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), so you can simulate from \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\).

title: Calibrated KS Test
section: Core activity: a bootstrap-calibrated KS test
text:
Core activity: a bootstrap-calibrated KS test






Exercise



Complete the two functions. Then apply ks_normal_bootstrap to the returns with 300 bootstrap samples and compare its p-value with the naive one from stats.kstest.
def ks_stat_normal(x):
    """KS distance between x and the normal fitted to x."""
    # TODO: estimate mu and sigma (ddof=1) and call stats.kstest(x, "norm", args=(mu, sigma))
    return ...


def ks_normal_bootstrap(x, n_boot, rng):
    d_obs = ks_stat_normal(x)
    # TODO: for n_boot repetitions, draw a standard normal sample of len(x)
    #       and store ks_stat_normal of it
    d_boot = ...
    # TODO: p-value = (1 + number of d_boot >= d_obs) / (n_boot + 1)
    return d_obs, ...








Solution






def ks_stat_normal(x):
    """KS distance between x and the normal fitted to x."""
    return stats.kstest(x, "norm", args=(x.mean(), x.std(ddof=1))).statistic


def ks_normal_bootstrap(x, n_boot, rng):
    d_obs = ks_stat_normal(x)
    d_boot = np.array([ks_stat_normal(rng.standard_normal(x.size)) for _ in range(n_boot)])
    return d_obs, (1 + np.sum(d_boot >= d_obs)) / (n_boot + 1)


rng = np.random.default_rng(18)
d_obs, p_boot = ks_normal_bootstrap(r, n_boot=300, rng=rng)
p_naive = stats.kstest(r, "norm", args=(r.mean(), r.std(ddof=1))).pvalue
print(f"D = {d_obs:.4f}; naive p = {p_naive:.2e}; bootstrap p = {p_boot:.4f}")

D = 0.0760; naive p = 1.42e-25; bootstrap p = 0.0033


With 300 bootstrap samples the smallest possible p-value is \(1/301 \approx 0.003\). A result at that floor means “smaller than 0.003”. When the departure from normality is this large, both versions reject; the validation below shows where they differ. The function is also available as amlab.finance.ks_normal_bootstrap.

title: Calibrated KS Test
section: Validation: the test on data that are normal
text:
Validation: the test on data that are normal
A valid test at level 5 % rejects 5 % of truly normal samples. Check both versions on 500 normal samples of size 200. The null distribution of \(D\) is the same for all of them, so you simulate it once.

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
m = 200
d_null = np.array([ks_stat_normal(rng.standard_normal(m)) for _ in range(1000)])
p_naive, p_boot = [], []
for _ in range(500):
    x = rng.normal(3.0, 2.0, m)
    d = ks_stat_normal(x)
    p_naive.append(stats.kstest(x, "norm", args=(x.mean(), x.std(ddof=1))).pvalue)
    p_boot.append((1 + np.sum(d_null >= d)) / (d_null.size + 1))
p_naive, p_boot = np.array(p_naive), np.array(p_boot)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.hist([p_naive, p_boot], bins=10, range=(0, 1), label=["naive", "bootstrap"])
ax.set_xlabel("p-value")
ax.set_ylabel("count")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"rejection rate at 5%: naive {np.mean(p_naive < 0.05):.3f}, bootstrap {np.mean(p_boot < 0.05):.3f}")







Figure 1: p-values of the naive KS test (parameters estimated, standard p-value) and of the bootstrap-calibrated test on 500 samples that really are normal. A valid test gives uniformly distributed p-values.





rejection rate at 5%: naive 0.000, bootstrap 0.048


The naive p-values pile up near 1 and almost never fall below 0.05. The bootstrap version rejects close to 5 % of the time, as it should.

title: Calibrated KS Test
text:
Interpretation
The Q-Q plot, the Jarque-Bera test and the KS test ask the same question: are the returns consistent with an i.i.d. normal sample? For market data the answer is usually a clear no, because of the heavy tails you see in the Q-Q plot (cont2001empirical?).

title: Calibrated KS Test
text:
Limitations

Every test here assumes i.i.d. data. Returns with volatility clustering are not i.i.d., so the bootstrap null distribution is only approximate.
With thousands of observations any test rejects even small departures from normality. Rejection says nothing about whether the departure matters for your purpose.
The Jarque-Bera test depends on moments that may not exist for heavy tails.

title: Calibrated KS Test
text:
Optional extension






Exercise



Fit a Student-t distribution to the returns with stats.t.fit(r) and adapt the bootstrap KS test to it. The t family has a shape parameter, so the null distribution now depends on it: simulate from the fitted t and refit all three parameters on every bootstrap sample. Keep n_boot small (about 100) because stats.t.fit is slow.








Solution





The structure is the same as for the normal. Only the fit and the simulation change. A large p-value means the fitted t is consistent with the data at the level of the KS test. It does not remove the i.i.d. assumption.
def ks_stat_t(x):
    """KS distance between x and the Student-t fitted to x."""
    params = stats.t.fit(x)
    return stats.kstest(x, "t", args=params).statistic, params


def ks_t_bootstrap(x, n_boot, rng):
    d_obs, params = ks_stat_t(x)
    d_boot = np.array([
        ks_stat_t(stats.t.rvs(*params, size=x.size, random_state=rng))[0]
        for _ in range(n_boot)
    ])
    return d_obs, params, (1 + np.sum(d_boot >= d_obs)) / (n_boot + 1)


d_t, params_t, p_t = ks_t_bootstrap(r, n_boot=100, rng=np.random.default_rng(19))
print(f"fitted nu = {params_t[0]:.2f}; D = {d_t:.4f}; bootstrap p = {p_t:.3f}")

title: Power Laws
text: A distribution has a fat (heavy) tail when large values are much more likely than under a Gaussian. The simplest example is the power law. This page follows (newman2005power?) and (clauset2009power?).

title: Power Laws
text:
Definition
A continuous power law has density
\[
p(x) = \frac{\alpha - 1}{x_{\min}} \left( \frac{x}{x_{\min}} \right)^{-\alpha}, \qquad x \ge x_{\min},
\tag{1}\]
with \(\alpha > 1\) so that it can be normalized. Its complementary cumulative distribution function (CCDF) is also a power law, with exponent one less:
\[
P(X \ge x) = \left( \frac{x}{x_{\min}} \right)^{-(\alpha - 1)} .
\tag{2}\]
The mean is finite only if \(\alpha > 2\) and the variance only if \(\alpha > 3\) (newman2005power?). For \(1 < \alpha \le 3\) the sample variance never settles, however much data you collect.

title: Power Laws
section: Pareto, Zipf and the same law
text:
Pareto, Zipf and the same law
Pareto’s law is a statement about the CCDF: the fraction of people with wealth above \(x\) decays as a power of \(x\). Zipf’s law is a statement about ranks: the \(r\)-th most frequent word appears with frequency proportional to \(r^{-s}\). A rank plot is the CCDF with the axes swapped, so both are power laws for the same data (newman2005power?).

title: Power Laws
text:
Log-log plots and their pitfalls
On log-log axes Equation 1 is a straight line with slope \(-\alpha\). That suggests fitting a line by least squares. (clauset2009power?) show that this is a poor estimator:

A histogram with linear bins has very few counts in the tail, and its logarithm is noisy and biased.
The least-squares fit has no valid error estimate, because the points are not independent Gaussian errors.
A straight-looking stretch does not prove a power law. A log-normal, for instance, can look straight over several decades.

Plot the CCDF instead, which needs no binning, and estimate \(\alpha\) by maximum likelihood.








Figure 1: The same 5000 samples of a power law with \(\alpha = 2.5\) and \(x_{\min} = 1\). Left: histogram with linear bins on log-log axes. Right: empirical CCDF, with the exact CCDF \(x^{-1.5}\) as a dashed line.

title: Power Laws
text:
The maximum likelihood estimator
Given \(n\) observations \(x_i \ge x_{\min}\), the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\alpha\) is
\[
\hat{\alpha} = 1 + n \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \frac{x_i}{x_{\min}} \right]^{-1},
\qquad
\sigma_{\hat{\alpha}} = \frac{\hat{\alpha} - 1}{\sqrt{n}},
\tag{3}\]
(newman2005power?; clauset2009power?). In practice \(x_{\min}\) is unknown. (clauset2009power?) choose it by minimizing the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the data above \(x_{\min}\) and the fitted law, and then test the fit with a bootstrap. You meet the same estimator again as the Hill estimator in the lab.

alpha_hat, err = mle_power_law_exponent(x, xmin=1.0)
print(f"MLE: alpha = {alpha_hat:.3f} +/- {err:.3f}  (true 2.5)")

MLE: alpha = 2.503 +/- 0.021  (true 2.5)








Exercise



Estimate \(\alpha\) by a least-squares line through the log-log histogram of the left panel (use only bins with counts). Repeat for 200 independent samples of size 5000 and compare the mean and spread of the least-squares and MLE estimates.








Solution






rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
ls, ml = [], []
for _ in range(200):
    s = sample_pareto(5000, 2.5, 1.0, rng)
    c, e = np.histogram(s, bins=200)
    m = 0.5 * (e[1:] + e[:-1])
    keep = c > 0
    ls.append(-np.polyfit(np.log(m[keep]), np.log(c[keep]), 1)[0])
    ml.append(mle_power_law_exponent(s, 1.0)[0])
print(f"least squares: {np.mean(ls):.3f} +/- {np.std(ls):.3f}")
print(f"MLE:           {np.mean(ml):.3f} +/- {np.std(ml):.3f}")

least squares: 1.599 +/- 0.171
MLE:           2.499 +/- 0.020


The least-squares estimate is strongly biased because the sparse tail bins, many with a single count, flatten the line. The MLE is centred on 2.5 with a spread close to \((\alpha - 1)/\sqrt{n} \approx 0.02\).

title: Mean Squared Displacement
text: The mean squared displacement (MSD) measures how far a random walker spreads. It is the standard quantity you compute from tracked particles, cells or animals.

title: Mean Squared Displacement
text:
Definition
For an ensemble of walkers that start at the origin,
\[
\mathrm{MSD}(t) = \langle |\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{x}(0)|^2 \rangle ,
\]
where \(\langle \cdot \rangle\) is the average over walkers. For the unbiased 1D lattice walk you found \(\langle x^2(n) \rangle = n\delta^2\) in The Random Walk.

title: Mean Squared Displacement
text:
Diffusive scaling
A walker that takes one step every \(\tau\) seconds has made \(n = t/\tau\) steps at time \(t\). Then \(\langle x^2 \rangle = (t/\tau)\,\delta^2\). (berg1993random?, Eqs. 1.9 to 1.11) defines the diffusion coefficient
\[
D = \frac{\delta^2}{2\tau}
\tag{1}\]
and obtains
\[
\langle x^2(t) \rangle = 2Dt .
\tag{2}\]
Motions along different axes are independent, so each coordinate contributes \(2Dt\). In \(d\) dimensions
\[
\langle r^2(t) \rangle = 2dDt ,
\tag{3}\]
which gives \(4Dt\) in the plane and \(6Dt\) in space (berg1993random?, Eqs. 1.13 and 1.14). The root-mean-square distance grows as \(\sqrt{t}\). To go twice as far, a diffusing particle needs four times as long.

title: Mean Squared Displacement
text:
A simulated check
The figure uses 2000 planar walkers with independent Gaussian steps of standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\) per coordinate and \(\tau = 1\). Each coordinate has step variance \(\sigma^2\), so \(D = \sigma^2 / (2\tau) = 1/2\) and Equation 3 predicts \(\mathrm{MSD} = 4Dt = 2t\).








Figure 1: Simulated MSD of 2000 planar Gaussian walkers (dots) and the prediction \(4Dt\) with \(D = 1/2\) (line). On log-log axes a slope of 1 is the signature of normal diffusion.

title: Mean Squared Displacement
text:
Anomalous diffusion
Many experiments find \(\mathrm{MSD} \propto t^{\gamma}\) with \(\gamma \neq 1\). The case \(\gamma < 1\) is subdiffusion and \(\gamma > 1\) is superdiffusion (metzler2000random?). Such behaviour requires that one of the random walk assumptions fails: steps are correlated, waiting times have no finite mean, or step lengths have no finite variance. You see the last case in Lévy flights.






Exercise



Estimate \(D\) from the simulation by fitting a straight line to \(\mathrm{MSD}(t)\) through the origin. How close is your estimate to \(1/2\)? Then fit the exponent \(\gamma\) as the slope of \(\log \mathrm{MSD}\) against \(\log t\).








Solution





The least-squares slope through the origin is \(\sum t\,\mathrm{MSD} / \sum t^2\), and \(D\) is that slope divided by \(2d = 4\).

slope = np.sum(t * msd) / np.sum(t**2)
gamma = np.polyfit(np.log(t[1:]), np.log(msd[1:]), 1)[0]
print(f"D estimate: {slope / 4:.3f}  (theory 0.5)")
print(f"exponent gamma: {gamma:.3f}  (theory 1)")

D estimate: 0.504  (theory 0.5)
exponent gamma: 1.007  (theory 1)

title: Tail Exponent
text:
The normality tests told you that returns are not Gaussian. This page measures how heavy the tail is. You estimate the tail index \(\alpha\) in \(\Pr(|r| > x) \sim C x^{-\alpha}\) with the Hill estimator, and you compare it with the Gaussian (\(\alpha = \infty\)), with stable laws (\(\alpha < 2\)) and with the range \(2 < \alpha < 5\) reported by (cont2001empirical?).
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from amlab.finance import load_prices, log_returns

r = log_returns(load_prices()["close"])
a = np.abs(r - r.mean())

WARNING: data/finance/prices.csv not found. Using a SYNTHETIC GARCH(1,1) series with Student-t innovations (seed 2026). These are not market data. See data/finance/README.md.

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Mandelbrot’s stable model predicts \(\alpha < 2\) (mandelbrot1963variation?). A Gaussian has no power-law tail at all. Which value do you expect for your series? Write it down before you estimate it.








Solution





For market returns expect a value between 2 and 5, often close to 3 (cont2001empirical?; gopikrishnan1998inverse?). That is heavier than a Gaussian but lighter than a stable law. Compare your estimate with this range in the Interpretation section.

title: Tail Exponent
text:
The Hill estimator
Sort the positive data in decreasing order, \(X_{(1)} \ge X_{(2)} \ge \dots\). Using only the \(k\) largest values,
\[
\hat{\alpha}_k = \left[ \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \ln \frac{X_{(i)}}{X_{(k+1)}} \right]^{-1}
\tag{1}\]
(hill1975simple?). This is the power-law maximum likelihood estimator of Power Laws with \(x_{\min} = X_{(k+1)}\), written for the CCDF exponent \(\alpha = \alpha_{\text{pdf}} - 1\). For i.i.d. data with an exact power-law tail its standard error is approximately \(\hat{\alpha}_k / \sqrt{k}\).
The choice of \(k\) is a trade-off. Small \(k\) uses few points and gives a noisy estimate. Large \(k\) reaches into the centre of the distribution, where the power law does not hold, and biases the estimate. The usual tool is the Hill plot, \(\hat{\alpha}_k\) against \(k\): you look for a range of \(k\) where it is roughly flat.

title: Tail Exponent
section: Core activity: implement and apply the estimator
text:
Core activity: implement and apply the estimator






Exercise



Implement Equation 1. Then apply it to the absolute returns a with \(k = 100\).
def hill(x, k):
    """Hill estimate of the tail index from the k largest values of x > 0."""
    xs = # TODO: sort x in decreasing order
    # TODO: return 1 / mean(log(xs[:k] / xs[k]))
    return ...








Solution






def hill(x, k):
    """Hill estimate of the tail index from the k largest values of x > 0."""
    xs = np.sort(x)[::-1]
    return 1.0 / np.mean(np.log(xs[:k] / xs[k]))


print(f"k = 100: alpha = {hill(a, 100):.2f}")

k = 100: alpha = 3.28


A vectorized version that accepts an array of k values is amlab.finance.hill_estimator.

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Validation on known tails
Before you trust the estimator on returns, apply it to samples whose tail index you know. A Student-t variable with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom has \(\Pr(|X| > x) \sim C x^{-\nu}\).

from amlab.finance import hill_estimator

rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
for nu in [2, 3, 4]:
    x = np.abs(rng.standard_t(nu, size=a.size))
    print(f"Student-t nu = {nu}: Hill (k = 100) = {hill_estimator(x, 100):.2f}")

Student-t nu = 2: Hill (k = 100) = 2.31
Student-t nu = 3: Hill (k = 100) = 3.01
Student-t nu = 4: Hill (k = 100) = 3.20


The estimates are close to \(\nu\) but not equal. The Student-t tail is a power law only asymptotically, and the deviation grows with \(\nu\). Keep this bias in mind when you read the value for returns.

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Experiment: Hill plot

ks = np.arange(20, a.size // 5)
alpha_r = hill_estimator(a, ks)
gauss = np.abs(rng.normal(0.0, a.std(), a.size))
alpha_g = hill_estimator(gauss, ks)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
ax.plot(ks, alpha_r, label="returns")
ax.fill_between(ks, alpha_r * (1 - 1 / np.sqrt(ks)), alpha_r * (1 + 1 / np.sqrt(ks)), alpha=0.2)
ax.plot(ks, alpha_g, label="Gaussian sample")
ax.axhspan(2, 5, color="grey", alpha=0.1, label="range in Cont (2001)")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("number of upper order statistics $k$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\hat{\alpha}_k$")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Hill plot of the absolute log returns and of a Gaussian sample of the same size and standard deviation. The shaded band is plus or minus one standard error \(\hat{\alpha}_k/\sqrt{k}\) for the returns.

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Interpretation
For heavy-tailed data the Hill plot has a plateau at small to intermediate \(k\). For the Gaussian sample \(\hat{\alpha}_k\) keeps growing as \(k\) shrinks, because the true tail index is infinite: the estimator always returns a finite number, so the shape of the Hill plot matters more than any single value.
For market returns (cont2001empirical?) reports tail indices between 2 and 5, and (gopikrishnan1998inverse?) report values close to 3 for US stocks. A value above 2 means finite variance. Such a tail is heavy, but it is not the tail of a Lévy stable law with \(\alpha < 2\).

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Limitations

The standard error \(\hat{\alpha}_k/\sqrt{k}\) assumes i.i.d. data. Volatility clustering makes the effective sample size smaller, so the real uncertainty is larger (cont2001empirical?).
A power law holds only asymptotically. A slowly varying correction, such as a logarithm, changes the estimate at every finite \(k\) (cont2001empirical?).
There is no automatic rule for \(k\) in this lab. Report the range of \(k\) you used and show the Hill plot.

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Optional extension






Exercise



Estimate the tail index separately for losses (\(r < 0\)) and gains (\(r > 0\)). Is there evidence for the gain/loss asymmetry listed by (cont2001empirical?)? Use the standard errors to judge whether the difference is larger than the noise.








Solution





Use the same \(k\) for both tails. The standard error of the difference of two independent estimates is \(\sqrt{s_1^2 + s_2^2}\). A smaller \(\alpha\) for losses means a heavier loss tail. Call the asymmetry real only if the difference is about two standard errors or more, and check that it holds over a range of \(k\).
rc = r - r.mean()
losses, gains = -rc[rc < 0], rc[rc > 0]
k = 100
a_loss, a_gain = hill_estimator(losses, k), hill_estimator(gains, k)
se = np.hypot(a_loss / np.sqrt(k), a_gain / np.sqrt(k))
print(f"losses {a_loss:.2f}, gains {a_gain:.2f}, difference {a_loss - a_gain:.2f} +/- {se:.2f}")

title: Module 3: Modelling with Randomness
text:
This module adds randomness to your models. You start from the random walk and derive diffusion, the law behind the spread of molecules in a cell. You then see what happens when rare, very large steps dominate: fat tails, stable laws and Lévy flights. Finally you apply these ideas to financial prices and test the random walk model on a daily price series in the laboratory. Reusable code is in amlab.random_walks and amlab.finance.

Session Structure
Session 15: From random walks to diffusion
The Random Walk Mean Squared Displacement The Diffusion Equation Diffusion in Biology
Session 16: When the bell curve fails: fat tails and anomalous diffusion
The Central Limit Theorem Power Laws Stable Distributions Lévy Flights
Session 17: Modelling financial markets
Returns and Efficient Markets Stylized Facts of Returns Scaling of Returns
Session 18: Laboratory: financial time series
Loading Prices and Computing Returns Normality Tests Calibrated KS Test Tail Exponent Scaling of Returns in Data



Learning Goals
After this module you can:

Derive the mean and variance of a lattice random walk and the relation \(\langle x^2 \rangle = 2Dt\).
Obtain the diffusion equation as the continuum limit of a random walk, with \(D = \delta^2 / (2\tau)\).
State the central limit theorem, its assumptions, and the generalized version for infinite variance.
Estimate a power-law exponent by maximum likelihood and explain why a least-squares fit on a log-log histogram is biased.
Describe stable laws with index \(0 < \alpha \le 2\) and simulate Lévy flights.
Compute log returns, test them for normality with a correctly calibrated Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, and estimate their tail index.
Compare real or synthetic return data with the random walk model and with the stylized facts of financial markets.

title: Loading Prices and Computing Returns
text: In this laboratory you test the random walk model of Returns and Efficient Markets on a daily price series. The lab has five pages: this one (returns and autocorrelation), Normality Tests, Calibrated KS Test, Tail Exponent and Scaling of Returns in Data.

title: Loading Prices and Computing Returns
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Before you run any code, write down your answers:

What order of magnitude do you expect for the standard deviation of daily log returns of a stock index: 0.01 %, 1 % or 10 %?
If the market is weak-form efficient, what should the autocorrelation of \(r_t\) at lag 1 be?
Should the autocorrelation of \(|r_t|\) at lag 1 be zero too?









Solution






About 1 %. A typical stock index moves by roughly one percent on an ordinary day.
Close to zero. A clear linear correlation would let you forecast tomorrow’s return from today’s.
No. Efficiency says nothing about the size of the moves. Large moves tend to follow large moves (volatility clustering), so the autocorrelation of \(|r_t|\) is positive (cont2001empirical?). You check both answers below.

Exercise



Write a function that returns the log returns \(r_t = \ln(P_t / P_{t-1})\) of a price array.
def log_returns(prices):

def log_returns(prices):

prices = df["close"].to_numpy()

section: Experiment: autocorrelation of returns and absolute returns
text:
Experiment: autocorrelation of returns and absolute returns
Under the null hypothesis of i.i.d. returns, sample autocorrelations are approximately normal with standard deviation \(1/\sqrt{n}\), so values outside \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n}\) are unusual.






Exercise



Complete the function below. Then compute the sample autocorrelation of \(r_t\) and of \(|r_t|\) for lags 1 to 50 and plot both with the \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n}\) band.
def autocorrelation(x, max_lag):
    """Sample autocorrelation at lags 0..max_lag."""
    x = x - x.mean()
    # TODO: for each lag k, compute sum(x[:-k] * x[k:]) / sum(x * x)
    return ...








Solution





Lag 0 needs care, because x[:-0] is empty. Slice with x[: x.size - k] instead.
def autocorrelation(x, max_lag):
    """Sample autocorrelation at lags 0..max_lag."""
    x = x - x.mean()
    return np.array([np.sum(x[: x.size - k] * x[k:]) / np.sum(x * x) for k in range(max_lag + 1)])
The same function is available as amlab.finance.autocorrelation, which the plot below uses.

from amlab.finance import autocorrelation

lags = np.arange(1, 51)
acf_r = autocorrelation(r, 50)[1:]
acf_abs = autocorrelation(np.abs(r), 50)[1:]
band = 2 / np.sqrt(r.size)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.plot(lags, acf_r, "o-", ms=3, label="$r_t$")
ax.plot(lags, acf_abs, "s-", ms=3, label="$|r_t|$")
ax.axhline(band, ls="--", c="k", lw=0.8)
ax.axhline(-band, ls="--", c="k", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("lag (days)")
ax.set_ylabel("autocorrelation")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"lag 1: r {acf_r[0]:.3f}, |r| {acf_abs[0]:.3f}, band {band:.3f}")







Figure 2: Sample autocorrelation of log returns and of absolute log returns. The dashed lines are \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n}\).





lag 1: r -0.024, |r| 0.166, band 0.028

title: Loading Prices and Computing Returns
text:
Interpretation
Compare with your predictions. For market data (cont2001empirical?) reports insignificant linear autocorrelation of daily returns and a positive, slowly decaying autocorrelation of absolute returns. If your plot shows the same pattern, the returns are close to uncorrelated but they are not independent. The strong form of the random walk hypothesis, i.i.d. returns, fails.

title: Loading Prices and Computing Returns
text:
Limitations

The \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n}\) band assumes i.i.d. data. With volatility clustering the true spread of the sample autocorrelation of \(r_t\) is wider, so a few crossings are not strong evidence (cont2001empirical?).
Closing prices that are not adjusted for dividends and splits create artificial jumps. Check the source of the frozen file.
Weekends and holidays are skipped, so a “daily” return sometimes covers three or more calendar days.

Optional extension

Compute a 60-day rolling standard deviation of \(r_t\) with pandas.Series(r).rolling(60).std() and plot it. Mark the periods with the highest volatility. Do large returns cluster in those periods?








Solution





Shade the days where the rolling volatility is in its top 10 % and overlay the largest 1 % of absolute returns. If most of the large returns fall inside the shaded periods, they cluster.
import pandas as pd

vol = pd.Series(r).rolling(60).std().to_numpy()
