print(f"share of the largest returns in high-volatility periods: {np.mean(high[big]):.2f} (about 0.10 without clustering)")

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Reading




Compulsory: (boccara2010modeling?), Chapter 6.
Recommended: Wolfram (1983).
A cellular automaton (CA) is a dynamical system in which space, time and state are all discrete. Each cell of a lattice holds one of finitely many states, and all cells update at the same time with the same local rule (Wolfram 1983; boccara2010modeling?).

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Definition
A cellular automaton has four ingredients:

a lattice of cells, here \(\mathbb{Z}\) or a ring of \(N\) cells;
a finite state set, here \(\{0, 1\}\);
a neighbourhood, the cells whose states determine the next state of a cell;
a local rule \(f\) that maps each neighbourhood configuration to a new state.

For a one-dimensional CA with radius \(r\), the update is
\[
x_i^{t+1} = f\big(x_{i-r}^t, \ldots, x_i^t, \ldots, x_{i+r}^t\big),
\]
applied to every \(i\) at the same time. This synchronous update is what separates a CA from a model where cells change one at a time.

title: Cellular Automata
text:
From fields to cells
In Module 4 you updated each grid point of a reaction-diffusion model with a local stencil and explicit time stepping (Laplacian in 2D). A CA keeps the same local-update mindset, but changes the mathematical object:

A field value becomes a discrete state, usually 0 or 1.
A finite-difference stencil becomes a lookup rule on a small neighbourhood.
A PDE time step becomes one synchronous rule application across the whole lattice.

The main idea stays the same. Local interactions create global structure.

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Neighbourhoods

One dimension, radius 1: the cell and its two nearest neighbours. These are the elementary cellular automata (Wolfram 1983).
Two dimensions, von Neumann neighbourhood: the cell and its four orthogonal neighbours.
Two dimensions, Moore neighbourhood: the cell and its eight surrounding cells. The Game of Life uses it (gardner1970life?).

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Rule numbering
An elementary rule assigns a new state to each of the \(2^3 = 8\) neighbourhoods. So there are \(2^8 = 256\) elementary rules. Wolfram lists the neighbourhoods from 111 down to 000, writes the eight outputs as a binary number, and uses its decimal value as the rule number (Wolfram 1983).



Table 1: Rule table of Rule 30. The outputs, read from left to right, form 00011110 in binary, which is 30.





Neighbourhood
111
110
101
100
011
010
001
000




New state
0
0
0
1
1
1
1
0












Exercise



Write the rule table of Rule 90. Then show that Rule 90 sets the new state of a cell to the sum of its two neighbours modulo 2.








Solution





\(90 = 01011010_2\), so the outputs for 111, 110, 101, 100, 011, 010, 001, 000 are 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0. The output is 1 exactly when the left and right cells differ, whatever the centre cell is. So \(x_i^{t+1} = (x_{i-1}^t + x_{i+1}^t) \bmod 2\).



Reflection (swap left and right) and complement (swap 0 and 1) map rules to rules with the same behaviour up to symmetry. The chunk below counts the resulting equivalence classes.

from amlab.cellular_automata.elementary import equivalence_class

classes = {min(equivalence_class(rule)) for rule in range(256)}
print("Inequivalent elementary rules:", len(classes))
print("Rule 110 is equivalent to", sorted(equivalence_class(110)))

Inequivalent elementary rules: 88
Rule 110 is equivalent to [110, 124, 137, 193]

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Initial conditions
Two initial conditions are standard (Wolfram 1983):

a single seed, one cell in state 1 and all others 0, which shows how a local perturbation grows;
a random row, each cell 1 with probability \(1/2\), which shows the typical long-run behaviour of the rule.

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Boundary conditions
A computer can only store a finite lattice, so you must decide what happens at the edges.

Periodic: cell \(N\) is the left neighbour of cell \(1\), and the lattice is a ring.
Fixed: ghost cells beyond the edges hold a constant state, usually 0.

On a finite lattice with periodic boundaries there are only \(2^N\) configurations. Every orbit is therefore eventually periodic. The lab page Boundary Conditions measures this.

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Why no ODE solver
A cellular automaton is not a discretization of a differential equation. It is defined directly by the local rule, so you do not need scipy.integrate.solve_ivp or any other ODE solver. The numerical method is exact: a loop over time steps that applies \(f\) to every cell.

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
This is ungraded practice. It collects the lab of Session 30 into one short study that you can use to check your understanding: encode the rule, update the row synchronously, build a space-time diagram, and compare outcomes across experiments (Wolfram 1983).
You can follow the guide here:
1D Cellular Automata Space-Time Diagrams Rule Exploration Boundary Conditions Game of Life Random Soups

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
Goals
The practice checks three skills:

Translate a rule number into a working local update.
Simulate repeated synchronous updates on a one-dimensional lattice.
Interpret how rule choice, initial condition and boundary shape the global pattern.

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
Core tasks

Implement apply_rule() and a reusable simulate_ca() function.
Reproduce a space-time diagram for Rule 30 starting from a single occupied cell at the centre.
Compare at least three rules from the set {30, 90, 110, 184} using the same initial condition.
For one chosen rule, compare two different initial conditions, one single-seed row and one random row.
Write a short paragraph that explains which features are controlled by the rule and which depend strongly on the initial condition.

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
Questions to answer

Which rule in your experiments produced the most regular pattern?
Which rule was most sensitive to the initial condition? Support your answer with the Hamming distance after a single flip.
Did you find one rule that already looks like transport or directed motion? Explain why.







Optional extensions




Implement periodic boundary conditions and compare the result with fixed-zero edges.
Add a stochastic flip rule, for example flipping a cell with small probability after each update.
Track the density of occupied cells over time for one rule and interpret the trend.
Add interactivity to the initial row, either in a notebook or with the reference script.
Find a Game of Life pattern of at most 5 cells that grows for more than 100 generations before it settles.

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
Tips

Test apply_rule() on a short row before you run a long simulation.
Print the rule table once so you know which output corresponds to each neighbourhood.
Keep the first experiments small enough that you can inspect the pattern visually.
Reuse the same plotting code when you compare rules so the differences are easier to see.

Reference code: amlab/cellular_automata/cellular.py, amlab/cellular_automata/elementary.py and amlab/cellular_automata/life.py.

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
Exit question






Exercise



On a ring of 100 cells, you run Rule 30 for 1000 steps and see no repetition. A classmate concludes that Rule 30 is aperiodic on this ring. Is the conclusion correct?








Solution





No. A ring of 100 cells has \(2^{100}\) configurations, so every orbit is eventually periodic. The period can be far longer than 1000 steps, which is why you see no repetition. What you observe is a long transient or a long cycle of a finite system, not true aperiodicity.

title: Space-Time Diagrams
text:
On the page 1D Cellular Automata you wrote apply_rule() and simulate_ca(). Here you test them against an exact result and use them to draw space-time diagrams.
The chunks on this page use the reference apply_rule(). Replace it by your own version to test your code.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from amlab.cellular_automata.cellular import apply_rule

title: Space-Time Diagrams
text:
Validation
Rule 90 has an exact solution: from a single seed, row \(t\) is Pascal’s triangle modulo 2 (see Special Rules). Use it as a test. The chunk below runs the check with the reference apply_rule.

from math import comb


def simulate_ca(initial_state, rule_number, steps):
    rule_bin = np.array([int(bit) for bit in f"{rule_number:08b}"])
    grid = np.zeros((steps, len(initial_state)), dtype=int)
    grid[0] = initial_state
    for t in range(1, steps):
        grid[t] = apply_rule(grid[t - 1], rule_bin)
    return grid


width, steps = 81, 40
seed_row = np.zeros(width, dtype=int)
seed_row[width // 2] = 1
g = simulate_ca(seed_row, 90, steps)
ok = all(g[t, width // 2 - t + 2 * k] == comb(t, k) % 2 for t in range(steps) for k in range(t + 1))
print("Rule 90 matches Pascal's triangle mod 2:", ok)

Rule 90 matches Pascal's triangle mod 2: True


Keep the lattice wider than \(2 \times\) steps so the pattern never reaches the edges during the test.

title: Space-Time Diagrams
text:
Experiment: the space-time diagram
iterations = 80
grid_size = 121

initial_state = np.zeros(grid_size, dtype=int)
initial_state[grid_size // 2] = 1

grid = simulate_ca(initial_state, rule_number=30, steps=iterations)

plt.imshow(grid, cmap="binary", interpolation="nearest", aspect="auto")
plt.xlabel("Cell index")
plt.ylabel("Time")
plt.show()

title: Space-Time Diagrams
text:
Interpretation

Compare the diagram with your prediction on 1D Cellular Automata: the growth speed and the broken symmetry.
Do you see long diagonal structures, nested triangles, or irregular texture? Rule 30 shows all three: a regular left edge, triangles of many sizes and an irregular right part.







Exercise



Add a second occupied cell at grid_size // 2 - 5 in the first row. Count, at every time step, the number of cells in which the two runs differ. Does the effect of the change stay local or spread through the whole diagram?








Solution





The difference spreads. It starts at 1 cell and grows to about 50 cells after 60 steps, roughly one new cell per step. Rule 30 is sensitive to small changes in the initial row.

changed = np.zeros(121, dtype=int)
changed[60] = 1
changed[55] = 1
single = np.zeros(121, dtype=int)
single[60] = 1

diff = (simulate_ca(single, 30, 60) != simulate_ca(changed, 30, 60)).sum(axis=1)
print("Differing cells at t = 0, 10, 30, 59:", diff[[0, 10, 30, 59]])

Differing cells at t = 0, 10, 30, 59: [ 1 11 30 51]

title: Space-Time Diagrams
text:
Limitations

The loop in apply_rule() is slow for large lattices. The vectorized version in amlab/cellular_automata/elementary.py computes all neighbourhood indices at once.
Fixed-zero edges are a modelling choice. Once the pattern reaches them, the result depends on the edges.







Optional extension: interactive initial row



The script amlab/cellular_automata/cellular.py lets you click on the first row, toggle cells, and recompute the automaton immediately. Run it locally, not in the notes:
from amlab.cellular_automata.cellular import main

main(rule_number=30, grid_size=101, iterations=50)

title: Space-Time Diagrams
text: Next

title: Flow and Congestion
text: Once the simulator works, the next step is to extract macroscopic observables. In traffic modelling the most important one is the fundamental diagram, the relationship between density and average flow (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). The theory is on the page The Fundamental Diagram.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Sketch \(q(\rho)\) for p_slow = 0 before you run anything. Where is the maximum? How should the curve change for p_slow = 0.3?








Solution





For p_slow = 0 the curve is the triangle \(q = \min(5\rho,\ 1 - \rho)\). It rises with slope \(v_{\max} = 5\), peaks at \(\rho = 1/6 \approx 0.17\) with \(q = 5/6 \approx 0.83\), and falls linearly to \(q = 0\) at \(\rho = 1\). For p_slow = 0.3 the free-flow slope drops to about \(v_{\max} - p = 4.7\), the peak is rounded and much lower, about \(q \approx 0.5\) near \(\rho \approx 0.1\) on a ring of 400 cells, and the congested branch lies below \(1 - \rho\). Compare with the figure on The Fundamental Diagram.











Figure 1: Estimated fundamental diagram for two slowdown probabilities.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Measure density and flow
Two standard macroscopic quantities are
\[
\rho = \frac{N_{\mathrm{cars}}}{L},
\qquad
q(t) = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{i \in \mathrm{cars}} v_i(t).
\]
Here \(\rho\) is the density and \(q(t)\) is the instantaneous flow, measured as the mean number of cells traveled per road cell and per time step.
To estimate stationary behavior, average \(q(t)\) after a burn-in window.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Record flow during one run
The simplest extension of the simulator is to track the flow after each update.
def simulate_with_flow(steps, length, density, vmax, p_slow, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    occupied, speeds = initialize_road(length=length, density=density, vmax=vmax, rng=rng)

    flow_history = np.zeros(steps)
    flow_history[0] = speeds[occupied].sum() / length

    for t in range(1, steps):
        occupied, speeds = step(
            occupied,
            speeds,
            vmax=vmax,
            p_slow=p_slow,
            rng=rng,
        )
        flow_history[t] = speeds[occupied].sum() / length

    return flow_history

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Sweep the density
Now repeat the experiment for many densities.
densities = np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 19)
mean_flows = []

for density in densities:
    flow_history = simulate_with_flow(
        steps=300,
        length=100,
        density=density,
        vmax=5,
        p_slow=0.3,
        seed=7,
    )
    mean_flows.append(flow_history[100:].mean())
Plotting mean_flows against densities gives the fundamental diagram.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Validation
For p_slow = 0 the stationary flow is \(q = \min(\rho\, v_{\max},\ 1 - \rho)\) (chowdhury2000statistical?). Compare your sweep with this line before you trust the curves for p_slow > 0.

# initialize_road() draws the occupancy at random, so measure the actual density
actual = np.array([
    initialize_road(length=100, density=d, vmax=5, rng=np.random.default_rng(7))[0].mean()
    for d in densities
])
exact = np.minimum(actual * 5, 1 - actual)
sim = np.array([simulate_with_flow(density=d, p_slow=0.0, seed=7)[burn_in:].mean() for d in densities])
print("Largest deviation from the exact p = 0 result:", np.round(np.abs(sim - exact).max(), 3))

Largest deviation from the exact p = 0 result: 0.0


Use the measured density \(N/L\), not the target value: on a road of 100 cells the random initialization can differ from the target by several cars.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Compare slowdown probabilities
The most informative parameter to vary is p_slow.

At small density, cars rarely interact and the flow grows roughly linearly with density.
At intermediate density, the flow reaches a maximum.
At high density, braking dominates and the flow drops because congestion limits motion.

Increasing p_slow usually lowers the peak flow and shifts the congested regime earlier.






Practical tip



Use several seeds if you want smoother curves. For example, estimate the mean flow for each density with 5 to 10 trials and then average the stationary values.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Interpretation

A space-time diagram in a free-flow regime and one in a congested regime show the microscopic picture.
The flow-density curve shows the macroscopic picture: where the maximum flow occurs and how noise changes it.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Limitations

initialize_road() draws the occupancy at random, so the number of cars fluctuates around density * length. Use the measured density \(N/L\) on the horizontal axis for precise work.
One seed per density gives noisy curves near the maximum.

title: Boundary Conditions
text: Every simulation runs on a finite lattice, so you must decide what the edge cells see. This page compares periodic and fixed boundaries and shows how the finite size shapes the long-run behaviour. The reference code is amlab/cellular_automata/elementary.py.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Before you code, answer two questions. On a ring of \(N\) cells there are \(2^N\) possible rows. What does this imply for the long-run behaviour of any rule? Which rule, 90 or 184, will be affected more by fixed-zero edges?








Solution





After at most \(2^N\) steps some row must repeat, and from then on the evolution cycles. So every orbit on a ring is eventually periodic, whatever the rule. Both rules change once the pattern reaches the edges, but Rule 184 changes qualitatively: it conserves the number of 1s on a ring, and fixed-zero edges let the 1s leave at the right end, so the road empties. The experiments below show both effects.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Implementation
With periodic boundaries the left neighbour of cell 0 is cell \(N-1\). np.roll gives both neighbours of every cell in one line, and the three bits give the index into the rule table.






Exercise



Complete step() so that it supports periodic and fixed-zero boundaries.
def step(state, rule, boundary="periodic"):
    table = np.array([(rule >> n) & 1 for n in range(8)])  # entry n: output for neighbourhood n
    if boundary == "periodic":
        left, right = # TODO: use np.roll
    else:
        padded = # TODO: add one ghost cell with value 0 at each end
        left, right = padded[:-2], padded[2:]
    return table[4 * left + 2 * state + right]








Solution





def step(state, rule, boundary="periodic"):
    table = np.array([(rule >> n) & 1 for n in range(8)])
    if boundary == "periodic":
        left, right = np.roll(state, 1), np.roll(state, -1)
    else:
        padded = np.concatenate(([0], state, [0]))
        left, right = padded[:-2], padded[2:]
    return table[4 * left + 2 * state + right]
This is step_eca() in the reference module.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Validation
Far from the edges, the two boundary choices must give the same rows. Check it on a wide lattice where the pattern never reaches the edges:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from amlab.cellular_automata.elementary import simulate_eca, single_seed, random_row, transient_and_period

a = simulate_eca(single_seed(201), 30, 80, boundary="periodic")
b = simulate_eca(single_seed(201), 30, 80, boundary="fixed")
print("Identical while the pattern is far from the edges:", np.array_equal(a, b))

Identical while the pattern is far from the edges: True

title: Boundary Conditions
section: Experiment: patterns that reach the edge
text:
Experiment: patterns that reach the edge








Figure 1: Rule 90 from a single seed on 41 cells for 120 steps. Left: periodic, the two fronts meet on the other side of the ring. Right: fixed zero edges.













Figure 2: Number of occupied cells under Rule 184, from the same random row of 100 cells with density 0.4.





With fixed-zero edges, Rule 184 moves particles out through the right edge and brings in nothing at the left, so the road empties. With periodic edges the count is conserved. For a traffic model the boundary decides whether you model a closed ring road or an open road segment.

title: Boundary Conditions
section: Experiment: every orbit on a ring is periodic
text:
Experiment: every orbit on a ring is periodic
A ring of \(N\) cells has \(2^N\) configurations. After at most \(2^N\) steps some row must repeat, and from then on the evolution cycles. transient_and_period() records every row until the first repeat.








Figure 3: Period of the orbit that starts from a single seed on a ring of N cells. Logarithmic vertical axis. The dashed line is the bound 2^N.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Interpretation

Any finite simulation is eventually periodic. For Rule 30 the period grows quickly with \(N\), so on a lattice of a few hundred cells you never see the repeat. The class 3 behaviour you observe is a transient of a finite system.
Rule 90 has short periods, and for some sizes the seed dies out completely. Find the sizes where the period is 1 in the output of transient_and_period().
A boundary is part of the model. Report it together with the rule and the lattice size.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Limitations

The period depends on the initial row, not only on the rule and \(N\). The figure uses a single seed.
Storing every row limits transient_and_period() to rings of about 20 cells.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Optional extension






Exercise



Optional. Replace the ghost value 0 by 1, or use reflecting edges (the ghost copies the edge cell). Track the number of occupied cells for Rules 184, 90 and 30. Which rules change their long-run behaviour?








Solution





Rule 184 is the rule that changes most. With ghost value 1 the left ghost feeds new 1s into the lattice, the right ghost blocks the exit, and the row fills up completely. With reflecting edges no 1 can leave or enter, so the count is conserved and all 1s pile up at the right end as one jam. Rules 90 and 30 keep an irregular pattern whose number of occupied cells fluctuates from step to step, for every boundary choice. The single values printed below are snapshots of these fluctuations, not steady states.

from amlab.cellular_automata.elementary import rule_table, step_eca


def step_reflect(state, rule):
    table = rule_table(rule)
    padded = np.concatenate((state[:1], state, state[-1:]))
    return table[4 * padded[:-2] + 2 * state + padded[2:]]


updates = {
    "ghost 0": lambda s, r: step_eca(s, r, boundary="fixed", fixed_value=0),
    "ghost 1": lambda s, r: step_eca(s, r, boundary="fixed", fixed_value=1),
    "reflecting": step_reflect,
}
row = random_row(100, 0.4, seed=2)
for rule in (184, 90, 30):
    for name, update in updates.items():
        state = row.copy()
        for t in range(300):
            state = update(state, rule)
        print(f"Rule {rule:3d}, {name:10s}: {int(state.sum()):3d} occupied cells after 300 steps")

Rule 184, ghost 0   :   0 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule 184, ghost 1   : 100 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule 184, reflecting:  40 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  90, ghost 0   :  47 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  90, ghost 1   :  47 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  90, reflecting:  50 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  30, ghost 0   :  50 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  30, ghost 1   :  49 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  30, reflecting:  35 occupied cells after 300 steps

title: Traffic Extensions
text: The Nagel-Schreckenberg model is a minimal model. This page adds three extensions from the literature and asks one question for each: does it change the fundamental diagram qualitatively, or only shift the numbers? The code is in amlab/cellular_automata/traffic_models.py, which stores only car positions and speeds and runs much faster than the cell-based lab code.

title: Traffic Extensions
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Before you run the code, write down for each extension whether you expect a new feature in \(q(\rho)\) (a new branch, a jump, a change of slope) or only a lower or higher curve.








Solution





Slow-to-start adds a new feature: a second, metastable high-flow branch and hysteresis. Slow vehicles on one lane change the slope of the free-flow branch to roughly the speed of the slowest cars. Two lanes with identical cars only give a curve close to the single-lane one, per lane. The table under Interpretation summarizes the results, and the figures below show them.

title: Traffic Extensions
text:
Slow-to-start rule
In the velocity-dependent randomization (VDR) model, a car that was stopped in the previous step brakes randomly with probability \(p_0\), and a moving car with the usual probability \(p\) (barlovic1998metastable?). With \(p_0 > p\), cars leave a jam more slowly than they drive in free flow. This is one of the slow-to-start rules.
In nasch_step() this is one extra line: build the vector of randomization probabilities from the speeds before acceleration.
prob = np.full(x.size, p)
prob[v == 0] = p0          # stopped cars start with a delay
Barlovic et al. show that this rule produces metastable high-flow states and hysteresis in the fundamental diagram (barlovic1998metastable?). To see it, start from two initial conditions at every density: evenly spaced moving cars (homogeneous) and one compact jam.








Figure 1: Fundamental diagram from a homogeneous start (circles) and a compact jam (crosses). Ring of 1000 cells, v_max = 5, p = 0.01, 1000 steps averaged after 1000 burn-in steps. Left: standard model (p0 = p). Right: slow-to-start (p0 = 0.75).





In the standard model both starts give the same curve. With slow-to-start there is a density range where the homogeneous start keeps a high flow and the jammed start stays at a low flow. The high-flow state is metastable: a large enough perturbation sends it to the jammed branch. This changes the diagram qualitatively: the flow is no longer a function of density alone, it also depends on history.

title: Traffic Extensions
text:
Slow vehicles
Give a fraction \(f\) of the cars a lower maximum speed \(v_{\max}^{\text{slow}}\). On a single lane nobody can overtake, so at low density every fast car ends up behind a slow one and the cars form platoons (knospe1999disorder?).








Figure 2: Single lane with a fraction f of slow cars (v_max = 2 instead of 5), p = 0.1, ring of 400 cells.





Even a small fraction of slow cars sets the slope of the free-flow branch to roughly \(v_{\max}^{\text{slow}} - p\), the speed of the slowest car. At high density the curves merge, because the gaps limit every car. This also changes the diagram qualitatively at low density.






Optional extension: two lanes



Add a second lane and a symmetric lane-changing rule, as in Rickert et al. (rickert1996two?). In two_lane_step() a car changes lane when its gap ahead is shorter than \(v+1\), the other lane offers a longer gap, the target cell is free, and the gap behind in the other lane is at least \(v_{\max}\). Then each lane applies the Nagel-Schreckenberg rules.








Figure 3: Flow per lane on one lane and on two lanes, with and without 10% slow cars (v_max = 2), p = 0.1, ring of 300 cells per lane.





With identical cars, the flow per lane on two lanes stays close to the single-lane curve: a second lane mostly doubles the road, it does not change the shape of the diagram. With slow cars, overtaking is possible, but lane changes need a free gap in the other lane. Knospe et al. found that even a small number of slow cars can still create platoons at low density on two lanes (knospe1999disorder?). In the figure, overtaking restores most of the free flow at the lowest densities, but already at \(\rho \approx 0.1\) the two-lane flow falls towards the one-lane curve with slow cars. Check this with several seeds before you draw conclusions.

title: Traffic Extensions
text:
Interpretation







Extension
Qualitative change of \(q(\rho)\)?




Slow-to-start (\(p_0 > p\))
Yes: metastable high-flow branch and hysteresis


Fraction of slow vehicles, one lane
Yes: free-flow slope set by the slowest cars, platoons


Two lanes, identical cars
No: flow per lane close to the single-lane curve

title: Traffic Extensions
text:
Limitations

Each point is one run with one seed. Near the edges of the hysteresis range, the result depends on the seed and on the run length, because metastable states decay at random times.
The lane-changing rule here is a simplified symmetric rule. Rickert et al. show that the details of lane changing affect the shape of the diagram (rickert1996two?).

title: Traffic Extensions
text:
Optional extension: an open road






Exercise



Optional. Replace the ring by an open road of 200 cells: when cell 0 is empty, a car enters there with probability \(\alpha\) per step, and cars that pass the last cell leave. Measure the flow as the number of cars that leave per step, and plot it as a function of \(\alpha\) for \(v_{\max} = 5\) and \(p = 0.3\).








Solution





Store the positions in increasing order, so that the last entry is the front car. The front car sees a free road ahead.

def open_road_flow(alpha, length=200, steps=2000, burn_in=500, vmax=5, p=0.3, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x = np.array([], dtype=int)    # positions, increasing
    v = np.array([], dtype=int)
    exits = 0
    for t in range(steps):
        if (x.size == 0 or x[0] > 0) and rng.random() < alpha:
            x = np.concatenate(([0], x))      # a new car enters at cell 0
            v = np.concatenate(([vmax], v))
        gaps = np.append(np.diff(x) - 1, vmax)  # the front car sees a free road
        v = np.minimum(np.minimum(v + 1, vmax), gaps)
        slow = rng.random(x.size) < p
        v = np.where(slow, np.maximum(v - 1, 0), v)
        x = x + v
        out = x >= length                     # cars that pass the last cell leave
        if t >= burn_in:
            exits += out.sum()
        x, v = x[~out], v[~out]
    return exits / (steps - burn_in)


alphas = np.linspace(0.05, 1.0, 12)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.plot(alphas, [open_road_flow(a) for a in alphas], marker="o")
ax.set_xlabel(r"Entry probability $\alpha$")
ax.set_ylabel("Cars leaving per step")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








At small \(\alpha\) almost every car that enters also leaves, so the flow is close to \(\alpha\). The flow levels off at about 0.45 near \(\alpha \approx 0.5\) to \(0.7\) and drops slightly, to about 0.40, at \(\alpha = 1\). In that limit a new car enters as soon as cell 0 is free, right behind the previous car, so a dense queue forms near the entrance, and the flow is limited by the rate at which cars leave that queue. Both values stay below the maximum flow of about 0.5 on a ring with the same \(p\). Check the numbers with several seeds.

title: 1D Cellular Automata
text:
Elementary cellular automata are one of the cleanest examples of emergence in a discrete system. Each cell stores a binary state, each update only depends on the three-cell neighbourhood, and repeated rule application creates nontrivial large-scale patterns (Wolfram 1983). In this lab you build the simulator yourself. The definitions are on the page Cellular Automata.
Figure 1: Rule 30 space-time diagram.

title: 1D Cellular Automata
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Rule 30 starts from a single occupied cell. Before you code, predict: how fast can the occupied region grow, in cells per step? Will the pattern stay symmetric or break symmetry quickly? Write down your answer.








Solution





The occupied region grows by at most one cell per step on each side, because each cell only sees its nearest neighbours. The figure above reaches this bound: the left and right edges move one cell per step. The pattern is not symmetric, because Rule 30 is not equal to its own reflection (the reflection is Rule 86).

title: 1D Cellular Automata
text:
What you need

numpy stores the lattice, builds the rule table and updates rows.
matplotlib.pyplot plots space-time diagrams and rule comparisons.
matplotlib.backend_bases handles mouse clicks in the optional interactive script on Space-Time Diagrams.







Scripts or notebooks?



Use a notebook when you want to compare several rules, inspect arrays, or save snapshots. Use a script when you want quick interaction, such as clicking on the first row and recomputing the full diagram.

title: 1D Cellular Automata
text:
Local state and neighbourhood
Let \(x_i^t \in \{0,1\}\) be the state of cell \(i\) at time \(t\). An elementary cellular automaton updates the row through a local rule
\[
x_i^{t+1} = f\big(x_{i-1}^t, x_i^t, x_{i+1}^t\big).
\]
Because each neighbourhood has three binary entries, there are only \(2^3 = 8\) possible patterns. A rule is therefore an 8-entry lookup table.

title: 1D Cellular Automata
text:
Encode the rule table
By convention we order the neighbourhoods from 111 down to 000.
rule_number = 30
rule_bin = np.array([int(bit) for bit in f"{rule_number:08b}"])
For Rule 30 this produces the binary table 00011110, which tells you the output for each of the eight neighbourhoods.

title: 1D Cellular Automata
text:
Implement the local update






Exercise



Complete apply_rule(). It returns the next row, with the two edge cells kept at zero.
def apply_rule(state, rule_bin):
    new_state = np.zeros_like(state)
    for i in range(1, len(state) - 1):
        neighborhood = state[i - 1 : i + 2]
        # TODO: convert the three bits to an integer n between 0 and 7
        # TODO: look up the output (rule_bin is ordered from 111 down to 000)
        new_state[i] = # TODO
    return new_state








Hint





int("".join(neighborhood.astype(str)), 2) turns the bits [1, 1, 0] into the integer 6. Because rule_bin[0] is the output for 111 (n = 7), the output for neighbourhood n sits at index 7 - n.









Solution





def apply_rule(state, rule_bin):
    new_state = np.zeros_like(state)
    for i in range(1, len(state) - 1):
        neighborhood = state[i - 1 : i + 2]
        index = 7 - int("".join(neighborhood.astype(str)), 2)
        new_state[i] = rule_bin[index]
    return new_state



This first version keeps the boundary cells at zero because the loop only updates indices 1 through len(state) - 2. The page Boundary Conditions treats the edges properly.

title: 1D Cellular Automata
text:
Simulate many time steps






Exercise



Wrap the update in a reusable simulator that stores every row in a 2D array.
def simulate_ca(initial_state, rule_number, steps):
    rule_bin = np.array([int(bit) for bit in f"{rule_number:08b}"])
    grid = np.zeros((steps, len(initial_state)), dtype=int)
    grid[0] = initial_state

    for t in range(1, steps):
        grid[t] = # TODO: apply the rule to the previous row

    return grid








Solution





def simulate_ca(initial_state, rule_number, steps):
    rule_bin = np.array([int(bit) for bit in f"{rule_number:08b}"])
    grid = np.zeros((steps, len(initial_state)), dtype=int)
    grid[0] = initial_state
    for t in range(1, steps):
        grid[t] = apply_rule(grid[t - 1], rule_bin)
    return grid

title: Rule Exploration
text: Once one simulator works, the interesting question is what changes when only the local rule changes. In this lab you keep the simulator fixed and vary the rule and the initial condition.

title: Rule Exploration
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Before you run the code, use the rule tables to predict: which of the four rules conserve the number of occupied cells? Which rule gives a pattern that is symmetric about the seed?








Solution





Only Rule 184 conserves the number of 1s on a ring: each 1 either stays or moves one cell to the right into an empty cell. Only Rule 90 gives a symmetric pattern, because it equals its own reflection. The Validation section below checks the first claim. The chunk here checks both on a ring of 121 cells.

from amlab.cellular_automata.elementary import random_row, simulate_eca, single_seed

for rule in (30, 90, 110, 184):
    g = simulate_eca(random_row(121, 0.5, seed=7), rule, 80, boundary="periodic")
    s = simulate_eca(single_seed(121), rule, 40)
    conserved = bool((g.sum(axis=1) == g[0].sum()).all())
    symmetric = bool((s == s[:, ::-1]).all())
    print(f"Rule {rule:3d}: conserves 1s {conserved}, symmetric {symmetric}")

Rule  30: conserves 1s False, symmetric False
Rule  90: conserves 1s False, symmetric True
Rule 110: conserves 1s False, symmetric False
Rule 184: conserves 1s True, symmetric False













Figure 1: Four elementary rules started from the same single-seed initial condition.

title: Rule Exploration
text:
Build a reusable simulator
The core function should take three inputs: an initial row, a rule number, and the number of time steps.
def simulate_ca(initial_state, rule_number, steps):
    rule_bin = np.array([int(bit) for bit in f"{rule_number:08b}"])
    grid = np.zeros((steps, len(initial_state)), dtype=int)
    grid[0] = initial_state

    for t in range(1, steps):
        grid[t] = apply_rule(grid[t - 1], rule_bin)

    return grid
With this wrapper in place, changing the experiment only means changing the inputs.

title: Rule Exploration
text:
Compare several rules
Rules 30, 90, 110, and 184 are a good first comparison because they already show very different behavior.

Rule 90 creates a highly regular, symmetric pattern.
Rule 30 quickly becomes irregular and looks almost random.
Rule 110 shows localized structures and interacting motifs.
Rule 184 transports occupied sites to the right and is a useful bridge to traffic models.

rules = [30, 90, 110, 184]

for rule_number in rules:
    grid = simulate_ca(initial_state, rule_number, steps=80)
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    plt.imshow(grid, cmap="binary", interpolation="nearest", aspect="auto")
    plt.title(f"Rule {rule_number}")
    plt.xlabel("Cell index")
    plt.ylabel("Time")
    plt.show()

title: Rule Exploration
text:
Change the initial condition
The second important experiment is to keep the rule fixed and change only the first row.
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
initial_state = (rng.random(121) < 0.5).astype(int)

grid = simulate_ca(initial_state, rule_number=110, steps=80)
plt.imshow(grid, cmap="binary", interpolation="nearest", aspect="auto")
plt.show()
This lets you separate two effects:

what is imposed by the rule itself,
and what is inherited from the initial data.

title: Rule Exploration
text:
Validation
Rule 184 moves each occupied cell one step to the right when the cell ahead is empty, so it conserves the number of 1s on a ring. Check it with the vectorized reference code, which uses periodic boundaries:

g184 = simulate_eca(random_row(121, 0.4, seed=7), 184, 80, boundary="periodic")
print("Occupied cells over time (first 5 steps):", g184.sum(axis=1)[:5])
print("Conserved on the whole run:", bool((g184.sum(axis=1) == g184[0].sum()).all()))

Occupied cells over time (first 5 steps): [48 48 48 48 48]
Conserved on the whole run: True


With the fixed-zero edges of apply_rule(), occupied cells leave at the right edge, so the count drops. That is a property of the boundary, not of the rule.

title: Rule Exploration
text:
Optional extension: stochastic flips
You can add noise after each update. For example, flip each cell with a small probability p_flip.
def noisy_update(state, rule_bin, p_flip=0.01, rng=None):
    if rng is None:
        rng = np.random.default_rng()

    new_state = apply_rule(state, rule_bin)
    flips = rng.random(len(new_state)) < p_flip
    new_state[flips] = 1 - new_state[flips]
    return new_state
That changes the model from a deterministic rule system into a stochastic one.






Exercise



Optional. Run Rule 184 on a ring of 200 cells from a random row with density 0.2, for 500 steps, with p_flip = 0 and with p_flip = 0.01. Plot the density of occupied cells over time. Use step_eca(state, 184, boundary="periodic") from amlab.cellular_automata.elementary in place of apply_rule(), so that the edges do not remove cells.








Solution





Without noise the density stays at its initial value, because Rule 184 conserves the 1s. With noise it drifts to about 1/2: a flip turns a 1 into a 0 at rate p_flip times the density and a 0 into a 1 at rate p_flip times one minus the density, and the two rates balance at density 1/2.

from amlab.cellular_automata.elementary import step_eca

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
for p_flip in (0.0, 0.01):
    state = random_row(200, 0.2, seed=1)
    density = []
    for t in range(500):
        state = step_eca(state, 184, boundary="periodic")
        flips = rng.random(state.size) < p_flip
        state[flips] = 1 - state[flips]
        density.append(state.mean())
    ax.plot(density, label=f"p_flip = {p_flip}")
ax.set_xlabel("Time")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Rule Exploration
text:
Interpretation

Which rule preserves symmetry most clearly? Rule 90 is equal to its own reflection, so its diagram from a single seed is symmetric.
Which rule seems most sensitive to tiny changes in the first row? Measure it with the Hamming distance, as on Wolfram Classes.
Which rule looks most like transport or directed motion? Rule 184 is the simplest traffic model: it is the Nagel-Schreckenberg model with maximum speed 1 and no random braking (chowdhury2000statistical?).

title: Rule Exploration
text:
Limitations

A few runs of one lattice size do not prove a class assignment. Try other seeds and sizes.
A random row with density \(1/2\) is only one choice. Rule 184, for example, behaves differently above and below density \(1/2\).

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
This is ungraded practice. You now have the core ingredients of an agent-based traffic model: local update rules, a reproducible simulator, a space-time diagram, and macroscopic observables such as density and flow (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992; Wilensky and Rand 2015). This page combines them into one short traffic study.
You can follow the guide here:
Traffic Model Flow and Congestion Traffic Extensions

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
Goals
The practice checks three skills:

Build a correct agent-based traffic simulator.
Connect microscopic update rules with macroscopic observables.
Explain when and why congestion appears.

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
Core tasks

Implement initialize_road(), step(), and simulate() for the Nagel-Schreckenberg model.
Produce space-time diagrams for at least three densities: one low-density regime, one intermediate regime, and one congested regime.
Estimate the fundamental diagram \(q(\rho)\) using at least 10 density values and a burn-in period before you average the flow.
Validate the result for p_slow = 0 against \(q = \min(\rho\, v_{\max},\ 1 - \rho)\).
Compare the flow-density curve for at least two values of p_slow, and describe where the maximum flow occurs and how the onset of congestion changes when p_slow increases.

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
Questions to answer

At what density does free flow begin to break down in your experiments?
Does higher random slowdown mostly change the peak flow, the jam onset, or both?
Which figure best explains the transition from microscopic rules to macroscopic congestion?







Optional extensions




Add sliders for density, p_slow, or vmax.
Compare random initial conditions with a localized dense cluster of cars.
Introduce a small fraction of slow vehicles and study the effect on the flow curve.
Replace the periodic road by open boundaries with inflow and outflow.

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
Tips

Test one update step on a short road before you launch long runs.
Fix the seed when you debug.
Discard an initial burn-in window when you estimate stationary flow.
Keep the plotting code separate from the simulation code so repeated experiments stay simple.

Reference code: amlab/cellular_automata/traffic.py and amlab/cellular_automata/traffic_models.py.

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
Exit question






Exercise



On a ring road you measure the same density twice and get two clearly different mean flows. Your code has no bug. Name one model feature from this session that can explain it.








Solution





A slow-to-start rule (\(p_0 > p\)). It creates a density range with a metastable high-flow state and a jammed state, so the flow depends on the initial condition and not only on the density (barlovic1998metastable?). A run that is too short, so that the burn-in has not removed the transient, can give the same symptom.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
One Repository, Many Contributors
This session turns version control into a team workflow. The goal is not only to push code, but to make changes traceable, reviewable, and easy to merge.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Set Up the Shared Repository



Host the repo

Create the repository, fill in the basics, and decide who owns the remote.



Add collaborators

Invite teammates first. Review only works if the right people can see and comment on the code.



Clone locally

Work in VS Code or the terminal from a local clone, not by editing files in the browser.



First shared commit

Create a simple README or starter file once, then push it so everyone starts from the same baseline.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Branch-Based Workflow
git clone <repo-url>
git checkout -b feature/short-task-name
git add .
git commit -m "Implement the first draft"
git push -u origin feature/short-task-name

Do not work directly on main. Each branch should map to one small task so the review is focused and conflicts stay manageable.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Pull Request Anatomy



Base and compare

The base branch should be main. The compare branch should be the feature branch you just pushed.



Title and description

The title states the change. The description explains the intent, what changed, and what needs review.



Assignee and reviewer

Assign the person doing the work and the person who will review it.



Work in progress

Use [WIP] in the title when the branch is not ready for review yet.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Review and Merge



Files changed

Review only the diff against main, not the whole repository.



Line comments

Comment directly on the lines that need clarification or revision.



Review outcome

Choose comment, approve, or request changes based on the actual state of the branch.



Merge only when ready

Once comments are resolved and the team agrees, merge and stop working on that branch.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Issues Keep the Team Organized



Issue

Describe one task or bug clearly and assign it to one person.



Branch

Create a dedicated branch to address that issue only.



Pull request

Open a PR from that branch and mention the issue number in the description.



Merge and close

After the PR is merged, the issue becomes the record of why the change happened.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Team Working Agreement



Do


keep PRs small,
write descriptive branch names,
review before merging,
update main locally after a merge.




Avoid


committing directly to main,
asking for review on unfinished work,
mixing unrelated tasks in one branch,
ignoring review comments.






Applied Math Lab

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
From State Vectors to Fields
The key change in the PDE session is spatial structure. The state is no longer a short vector of variables. It is a field sampled on a grid.



Mathematical object

u(x, t)
The unknown is now a field over space, not a short ODE state vector.



Coupling mechanism

Diffusion enters through the Laplacian, which links each location to its neighbors.



Lecture goal

Turn the theory they already saw into concrete calculations for Gierer-Meinhardt and the later Gray-Scott transition.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Flow for This Session



Boundary conditions

Implement Neumann, Dirichlet, and periodic conditions on Cartesian grids.



Laplacian

Write the centered finite-difference stencil with vectorized shifts.



Explicit Euler

Advance the full field with a direct time-stepping loop.



Turing application

Compute the equilibrium, the Jacobian, the mode matrix, and the unstable-mode list.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Boundary Conditions on Cartesian Grids
The same implementation logic works in 1D and on rectangles.



Neumann

Zero flux means copy the nearest interior value.
u[0] = u[1], u[-1] = u[-2]



Dirichlet

Fix the value at the boundary after every Euler step.
u[0] = u_left, u[-1] = u_right



Periodic

Wrap one edge onto the other. With np.roll(), the stencil already does it.


On a rectangle, the zero-flux pattern is
uv[:, 0, :] = uv[:, 1, :]
uv[:, -1, :] = uv[:, -2, :]
uv[:, :, 0] = uv[:, :, 1]
uv[:, :, -1] = uv[:, :, -2]

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Vectorized Laplacian



1D stencil

\[
\Delta u(x) \approx \frac{u(x+\Delta x) - 2u(x) + u(x-\Delta x)}{\Delta x^2}
\]
lap_u = np.roll(u, 1) - 2 * u + np.roll(u, -1)
lap_u = lap_u / dx**2



2D preview

\[
\Delta u \approx u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4u_{i,j}
\]
The same np.roll() idea extends later to rectangular grids.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Explicit Euler Closes the Solver
Once the right-hand side is available, the PDE update is just
\[
U^{n+1} = U^n + \Delta t\,G(U^n).
\]
du_dt, dv_dt = gierer_meinhardt_pde(0, uv, dx=dx)
uv[0] = uv[0] + dt * du_dt
uv[1] = uv[1] + dt * dv_dt
uv[:, 0] = uv[:, 1]
uv[:, -1] = uv[:, -2]
The order matters. First apply Euler, then reimpose the boundary data.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Gierer-Meinhardt Is the Working Example
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \Delta u + \gamma \left(a - b u + \frac{u^2}{v}\right),
\qquad
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = d\,\Delta v + \gamma (u^2 - v)
\]
This is the model we use to turn the Turing theory into concrete calculations.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Compute the Homogeneous Equilibrium
Set the reaction terms to zero:
\[
f(u, v) = a - bu + \frac{u^2}{v} = 0,
\qquad
g(u, v) = u^2 - v = 0.
\]
From \(g(u_*, v_*) = 0\),
\[
v_* = u_*^2.
\]
Substitute into \(f = 0\):
\[
a - bu_* + 1 = 0
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
u_* = \frac{a+1}{b},
\qquad
v_* = \left(\frac{a+1}{b}\right)^2.
\]
For \(a = 0.4\) and \(b = 1\),
\[
u_* = 1.4,
\qquad
v_* = 1.96.
\]

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
section: Compute the Jacobian at the Equilibrium
text:
Compute the Jacobian at the Equilibrium
At a general point \((u, v)\),
\[
J(u, v) =
\begin{pmatrix}
-b + 2u/v & -u^2/v^2 \\
2u & -1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
At \((u_*, v_*)\) this becomes
\[
J_* =
\begin{pmatrix}
2b/(a+1) - b & -\left(b/(a+1)\right)^2 \\
2(a+1)/b & -1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For \(a = 0.4\) and \(b = 1\),
\[
J_* =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.4286 & -0.5102 \\
2.8 & -1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
section: Turing Conditions Define the Parameter Window
text:
Turing Conditions Define the Parameter Window
\[
f_u + g_v < 0,
\qquad
f_u g_v - f_v g_u > 0,
\qquad
g_v + d f_u > 2\sqrt{d(f_u g_v - f_v g_u)}
\]



Interpretation

The homogeneous equilibrium is stable without spatial variation, but some spatial mode can grow.



Worked comparison

At \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\), the point \(d = 30\) is inside the Turing window, while \(d = 20\) is outside.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
section: Spatial Modes on a Finite Interval
text:
Spatial Modes on a Finite Interval
For Neumann boundary conditions on \([0, L]\),
\[
\phi_n(x) = \cos\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right),
\qquad
\lambda_n = -\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}\right)^2,
\qquad
n = 0, 1, 2, \dots
\]
This is the step the professor emphasized. The spatial part is solved by hand, and those \(\lambda_n\) are what enter the temporal calculation.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
From \(\lambda_n\) to \(A_n\) and \(\sigma_n\)
For each mode \(n\),
\[
A_n = J + \lambda_n D,
\qquad
D = \operatorname{diag}(1, d).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
A_n = J - k_n^2 D,
\qquad
k_n = \frac{n\pi}{L}.
\]
The temporal eigenvalues of mode \(n\) are the roots of
\[
\det\left(A_n - \sigma^{(n)} I\right) = 0.
\]
Positive \(\sigma^{(n)}\) means that spatial mode is unstable.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
section: Code Turns the Theory into a Mode List
text:
Code Turns the Theory into a Mode List
unstable_modes = []
for n in range(1, num_modes):
    lambda_n = -(n * np.pi / length) ** 2
    A_n = J + lambda_n * D
    growth_rate = np.max(np.linalg.eigvals(A_n).real)
    if growth_rate > 0:
        unstable_modes.append((n, growth_rate))

unstable_modes.sort(key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
This list does two things.

It tells you which modes are unstable.
Its first entry predicts the dominant early wavelength.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Worked Example with \(L = 40\)
Take \(\gamma = 1\), \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\).



Case A

\(d = 30\)

Turing conditions satisfied
Unstable 1D modes: \(n = 5, 6\)
Growth rates: \(\sigma^{(5)} \approx 0.0214\), \(\sigma^{(6)} \approx 0.0206\)
Dominant mode: \(n = 5\)




Case B

\(d = 20\)

Third Turing condition fails
No unstable 1D modes
Perturbations decay back to the homogeneous state

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Same Checklist for Gray-Scott
The pipeline does not change.

Compute the homogeneous equilibrium.
Compute the Jacobian.
Compute the Laplacian eigenvalues.
Build \(A_n = J + \lambda_n D\).
Compute the temporal eigenvalues \(\sigma_n\).

The conceptual change is the boundary condition.

Gierer-Meinhardt usually uses Neumann boundaries.
Gray-Scott usually uses periodic boundaries.

At the usual Gray-Scott base state \((u, v) = (1, 0)\), the linearized system is damped, so the classical Turing calculation becomes interesting only at a nontrivial homogeneous equilibrium when one exists.

title: Collective Motion
text:
Local Rules, Global Order
Collective motion is the first session where the main model is not a continuous-time ODE. The dynamics come from a repeated update rule applied to many agents at once.

title: Collective Motion
text:
Session Arc



Base rule

Start with Vicsek alignment, noise, constant speed, and periodic boundaries.



Observable

Measure the transition with the order parameter instead of relying on animation alone.



Extensions

Then ask what changes when you add repulsion, predators, or richer decision rules.

title: Collective Motion
section: Why This Is Not an ODE Session
text:
Why This Is Not an ODE Session



Previous sessions

State changes came from derivatives and continuous-time rate laws.



This session

Each time step updates headings and positions directly from neighbor information, so a simulation loop is more natural than solve_ivp().

title: Collective Motion
text:
Vicsek Update Rule
\[
\theta_i(t + \Delta t) = \langle \theta_j(t) \rangle_{j \in \mathcal N_i} + \frac{\eta}{2} \xi_i
\]
\[
\mathbf x_i(t + \Delta t) = \mathbf x_i(t) + v_0 \Delta t (\cos \theta_i, \sin \theta_i)
\]

At each step, every boid aligns with neighbors inside a radius \(r\), adds noise, moves at constant speed, and wraps back into the box with periodic boundary conditions.

title: Collective Motion
text:
What Moves the Transition



Noise \(\eta\)

Higher noise breaks alignment and pushes the system toward disorder.



Density

More local contacts make alignment easier.



Interaction radius \(r\)

This sets who can influence whom at each step.



Speed \(v_0\)

This controls how quickly local alignment propagates through the box.

title: Collective Motion
section: The Order Parameter Is the Summary Statistic
text:
The Order Parameter Is the Summary Statistic





Order parameter versus noise






Average velocity versus density





Use the average normalized velocity to quantify how ordered the flock is. The interesting part is the transition, not just the animation.

title: Collective Motion
section: The Session Extends in Two Directions
text:
The Session Extends in Two Directions



Couzin model

Add a repulsion zone so agents avoid collisions instead of only aligning.



Predator extension

Add an escape rule, then decide whether the predator is passive, autonomous, or includes eating-spawning dynamics.

title: Collective Motion
text:
Minimal Simulation Loop
for step in range(num_steps):
    theta = update_angles(xy, theta, radius=r, noise=eta)
    xy = xy + speed * dt * np.vstack((np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)))
    xy = xy % box_size
    order[step] = compute_order_parameter(theta)
This is the discrete-time analogue of the solver loop from the ODE sessions.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Geometry Enters the Picture
The solver workflow is still the same, but now the state has two components and the right picture is a trajectory in the phase plane, not just a time series.
\[
\dot x = f(x, y; \theta), \qquad \dot y = g(x, y; \theta)
\]

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Session Arc



CDIMA reaction

Use one worked chemical system to build the language of nullclines and fixed points.



Van der Pol

See how nonlinear damping creates a stable limit cycle.



FitzHugh-Nagumo

Compare oscillation with excitability in a fast-slow system.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Phase-Plane Workflow



Integrate

Use solve_ivp() exactly as before, but now the state vector is (x, y).



Plot

Show trajectories directly in the phase plane.



Analyze

Find the curves where \(\dot x = 0\) and \(\dot y = 0\).



Classify

Use the Jacobian to distinguish stable points, saddles, and oscillatory behavior.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Nullclines, Fixed Points, Stability



Nullclines

Solve
\[
f(x, y; \theta) = 0, \qquad g(x, y; \theta) = 0
\]
to find where the vector field changes direction.



Fixed point

Intersections of the nullclines are the equilibrium candidates.



Linear test

Evaluate the Jacobian near the equilibrium and inspect its eigenvalues.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
CDIMA Is the Template
\[
\dot x = a - x - \frac{4xy}{1 + x^2}, \qquad
\dot y = b x \left(1 - \frac{y}{1 + x^2}\right)
\]



Why it matters

This model has all the ingredients you need for the rest of the session: nullclines, fixed points, stability, and trajectory comparison.



Classroom target

Start here before you move to Van der Pol or FitzHugh-Nagumo. It is the cleanest worked example in the module.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Two Signatures to Compare



Van der Pol oscillator

\[
\dot x = \mu (y - f(x)), \qquad
\dot y = -\frac{x}{\mu}, \qquad
f(x) = \frac{x^3}{3} - x
\]
Look for a self-sustained stable limit cycle.



FitzHugh-Nagumo

\[
\epsilon \dot v = f(v) - w + I_{\mathrm{app}}, \qquad
\dot w = v - \gamma w
\]
Look for excitable transients and timescale separation.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Animation and Interaction
ani = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, animate, fargs=(sol.y,), interval=20, blit=True)


def mouse_click(event):
    if event.inaxes is ax:
        x0, y0 = event.xdata, event.ydata
        # restart solve_ivp with the new initial state
This turns the phase plane into an experiment. Students can click a new initial condition and immediately see whether the system returns to equilibrium, spirals, or converges to a cycle.

\dot S = -\beta S I, \quad
\dot I = \beta S I - \gamma I, \quad

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
When Many Oscillators Talk
The main question in this session is no longer what one trajectory does, but when a whole population of oscillators starts moving coherently.

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
Ingredients of the Kuramoto Model



State

Each oscillator carries a phase \(\theta_i(t)\) on the unit circle.



Heterogeneity

Each oscillator has a natural frequency \(\omega_i\) drawn from a distribution.



Coupling

All-to-all sinusoidal interaction tries to align phases when \(K > 0\).


\[
\dot \theta_i = \omega_i + \sum_{j=1}^N \frac{K}{N} \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i)
\]

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
The Macroscopic Observable
\[
r e^{i \Psi} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^N e^{i \theta_j}
\]



Order parameter \(r\)

\(r \approx 0\) means incoherence. \(r \approx 1\) means strong phase alignment.



Mean phase \(\Psi\)

The average direction tells you where the synchronized pack is located on the circle.

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
Mean-Field Interpretation
\[
\dot \theta_i = \omega_i + K r \sin(\Psi - \theta_i)
\]



Positive feedback

If a small amount of coherence appears, the effective coupling \(K r\) grows and recruits more oscillators.



Critical onset

Synchronization appears when the coupling becomes strong enough relative to the spread of natural frequencies.

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
From Theory to Bifurcation Diagram



What we plot

Draw the long-time average of \(r\) against the coupling strength \(K\).



Common mistake

Do not compare empirical data from one frequency distribution against the exact theory for another. The deck now makes that warning explicit instead of hiding it in a later slide.

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
What the Full Simulation Shows



Visual cues to look for


points clustering on the unit circle,
growth of the order parameter,
sensitivity to \(K\), \(N\), and the frequency distribution,
mismatch between finite-\(N\) simulations and asymptotic theory.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
section: From an Interval to a Rectangle
text:
From an Interval to a Rectangle
The 1D solver already gives the full workflow. In 2D, the ideas stay the same but the geometry becomes richer.



Data shape

A field on \([0, L_x] \times [0, L_y]\) becomes a matrix.



Diffusion stencil

The second derivative becomes the 5-point Laplacian.



Visible payoff

Mode pairs generate spots, stripes, fronts, and labyrinths.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Rectangular Grid and 5-Point Stencil
\[
\Delta u(x,y) \approx \frac{u(x+dx,y) + u(x-dx,y) + u(x,y+dx) + u(x,y-dx) - 4u(x,y)}{dx^2}
\]
lap = -4 * field
lap += np.roll(field, 1, axis=0)
lap += np.roll(field, -1, axis=0)
lap += np.roll(field, 1, axis=1)
lap += np.roll(field, -1, axis=1)
lap = lap / dx**2
This is still the same vectorized idea from session 6, now applied along two axes.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Boundary Conditions in 2D



Neumann

Copy the nearest interior row or column.



Dirichlet

Pin the edge to a prescribed value.



Periodic

Keep the np.roll() wrapping and do not overwrite the edges.


For zero flux on a rectangle,
uv[:, 0, :] = uv[:, 1, :]
uv[:, -1, :] = uv[:, -2, :]
uv[:, :, 0] = uv[:, :, 1]
uv[:, :, -1] = uv[:, :, -2]

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Gierer-Meinhardt in 2D Uses Mode Pairs
With Neumann boundaries on \([0, L_x] \times [0, L_y]\),
\[
\lambda_{n_x,n_y} = -\left(\frac{n_x\pi}{L_x}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{n_y\pi}{L_y}\right)^2.
\]
The temporal matrix is still
\[
A_{n_x,n_y} = J + \lambda_{n_x,n_y} D.
\]
So the 1D workflow survives intact. The only change is that one mode number becomes a pair.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
section: Domain Geometry Changes the Leading Pattern
text:
Domain Geometry Changes the Leading Pattern
Take \(L_x = 20\), \(L_y = 50\), \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\), \(\gamma = 1\).



Case A

\(d = 30\)

Turing unstable

Case B

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Gray-Scott Reuses the Same Solver
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = d_1 \Delta u - u v^2 + f(1-u),
\qquad
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = d_2 \Delta v + u v^2 - (f+k)v
\]
The numerical recipe is nearly unchanged.

Same rectangular grid
Same 5-point stencil
Same explicit Euler update
Different reaction term
Periodic boundaries instead of Neumann

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Periodic Boundaries Change the Spectrum
For periodic boundaries on a rectangle,
\[
\lambda_{m,n} = -\left(\frac{2\pi m}{L_x}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{2\pi n}{L_y}\right)^2.
\]
That is the main conceptual bridge from Gierer-Meinhardt to Gray-Scott.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
The Core 2D Update Loop
for _ in range(num_steps):
    lap_u = np.roll(u, 1, axis=0) + np.roll(u, -1, axis=0)
    lap_u += np.roll(u, 1, axis=1) + np.roll(u, -1, axis=1) - 4 * u
    lap_v = np.roll(v, 1, axis=0) + np.roll(v, -1, axis=0)
    lap_v += np.roll(v, 1, axis=1) + np.roll(v, -1, axis=1) - 4 * v
    u += dt * (d1 * lap_u - u * v**2 + f * (1 - u))
    v += dt * (d2 * lap_v + u * v**2 - (f + k) * v)
With periodic boundaries, this loop is complete. With Neumann or Dirichlet data, the edge values must be overwritten after each Euler step.

title: Random Soups
text:
A random initial grid in the Game of Life is called a soup. This page follows one soup for 300 generations and then changes the birth and survival rules. You need life_step() from the page Game of Life.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from amlab.cellular_automata.life import life_step

title: Random Soups
text:
Experiment: a random soup
Start from a random grid and track the fraction of live cells.








Figure 1: Random initial grid (128 x 128, periodic, 30% live cells). Left: the grid after 300 generations. Right: fraction of live cells over time.

title: Random Soups
text:
Interpretation

After a brief jump in the first generation, the density falls quickly over about 50 generations and then decays slowly. The snapshot shows mostly still lifes and blinkers, plus a few regions that are still active.

title: Random Soups
text:
Limitations

A finite periodic grid can only show a finite part of the Game of Life. Patterns that grow without bound need a larger or adaptive grid.
The density curve depends on the initial fraction of live cells and on the seed. Average over several seeds before you draw conclusions.

title: Random Soups
text:
Optional extension






Exercise



Optional. Change the rule to B36/S23 or to B2/S (birth with 2 neighbours, no survival) by editing the birth and survival masks. Repeat the random-soup experiment and compare the density curves.








Solution





B36/S23 (HighLife) adds birth with 6 neighbours. Its density curve stays above the Game of Life for the first 100 generations or so and then decays to a similar low value. B2/S (Seeds) behaves differently: every live cell dies after one generation, yet the density settles near 0.21 and the grid stays active everywhere.

from amlab.cellular_automata.life import count_neighbours


def life_like_step(grid, birth, survive):
    n = count_neighbours(grid)
    born = (grid == 0) & np.isin(n, birth)
    stay = (grid == 1) & np.isin(n, survive)
    return (born | stay).astype(grid.dtype)


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
for name, birth, survive in (("B3/S23", [3], [2, 3]), ("B36/S23", [3, 6], [2, 3]), ("B2/S", [2], [])):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
    g = (rng.random((128, 128)) < 0.3).astype(np.uint8)
    density = []
    for t in range(300):
        density.append(g.mean())
        g = life_like_step(g, birth, survive)
    ax.plot(density, label=name)
ax.set_xlabel("Generation")
ax.set_ylabel("Fraction of live cells")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Special Rules and Theorems
text: A few elementary rules and a few theorems appear again and again in the cellular automata literature. This page collects them briefly.

title: Special Rules and Theorems
text:
Rule 90 and Pascal’s triangle
Rule 90 sets each cell to the sum of its two neighbours modulo 2,
\[
x_i^{t+1} = \big(x_{i-1}^t + x_{i+1}^t\big) \bmod 2 .
\]
The rule is additive: the evolution of the sum (mod 2) of two initial rows is the sum of their evolutions (Wolfram 1983). Started from a single seed at cell 0, the state at time \(t\) and position \(i = 2k - t\) is \(\binom{t}{k} \bmod 2\), the rows of Pascal’s triangle modulo 2. The pattern is self-similar, with fractal dimension \(\log_2 3 \approx 1.585\) (Wolfram 1983).








Figure 1: Rule 90 from a single seed, 64 steps. The pattern equals Pascal’s triangle modulo 2.





The assert in the code checks the Pascal identity for every cell of the figure.

title: Special Rules and Theorems
text:
Rule 110 is universal
Rule 110 belongs to class 4. Cook proved that it can emulate a cyclic tag system, and therefore any Turing machine. This settled a conjecture of Wolfram (cook2004universality?). The proof needs an infinite lattice with a periodic background pattern and specific localized structures on it.
A consequence is that some questions about the long-run behaviour of Rule 110, such as whether a given pattern ever appears, are undecidable in general.

title: Special Rules and Theorems
text:
Langton’s lambda
Pick one state as quiescent, here 0. Langton’s parameter \(\lambda\) is the fraction of neighbourhood configurations that the rule maps to a non-quiescent state (langton1990computation?). For an elementary rule, \(\lambda\) is the number of 1s in the rule table divided by 8.
Langton studied larger rule spaces (more states and larger neighbourhoods). As \(\lambda\) increases from 0, typical rules move from fixed-point behaviour, through periodic behaviour, to chaotic behaviour, and the complex rules concentrate near the transition between ordered and chaotic regimes (langton1990computation?). With only 256 rules and 9 possible values of \(\lambda\), the elementary rules are too few to show this cleanly. The output below shows that rules 108 (class 2), 30 and 90 (class 3) all have \(\lambda = 1/2\).

from amlab.cellular_automata.elementary import langton_lambda

for rule in (32, 108, 30, 90, 110):
    print(f"Rule {rule:3d}: lambda = {langton_lambda(rule):.3f}")

Rule  32: lambda = 0.125
Rule 108: lambda = 0.500
Rule  30: lambda = 0.500
Rule  90: lambda = 0.500
Rule 110: lambda = 0.625

title: Special Rules and Theorems
text:
Garden-of-Eden configurations
A Garden-of-Eden configuration has no predecessor: no configuration evolves into it in one step. Such configurations can only appear as initial conditions.
Two configurations are mutually erasable if they differ on a finite set of cells and have the same successor. Moore showed that a cellular automaton with mutually erasable configurations has Garden-of-Eden configurations (moore1962machine?). Myhill proved the converse (myhill1963converse?). Together:

Garden-of-Eden theorem. A cellular automaton on \(\mathbb{Z}^d\) has a Garden-of-Eden configuration if and only if it has two mutually erasable configurations.

In other words, the global map is surjective exactly when it is injective on configurations that differ in finitely many cells.






Exercise



Find two configurations of a ring of \(N = 4\) cells that Rule 184 maps to the same successor. Explain why this implies that some configurations of the ring have no predecessor.








Solution






import itertools
import numpy as np
from amlab.cellular_automata.elementary import step_eca

successors = {}
for bits in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=4):
    key = "".join(map(str, step_eca(np.array(bits), 184)))
    successors.setdefault(key, []).append("".join(map(str, bits)))
for image, preimages in successors.items():
    if len(preimages) > 1:
        print(image, "<-", preimages)

1010 <- ['0011', '0101', '1100']
0101 <- ['0110', '1001', '1010']


For example 1100 and 0101 both map to 1010 on a ring of 4 cells. A map from the finite set of \(2^N\) configurations to itself that is not injective is not surjective either, so some configurations on the ring have no predecessor.

Encode an elementary cellular automaton rule as an 8-entry lookup table and simulate it with synchronous updates.
Build and interpret space-time diagrams, and compare how rule choice and initial condition affect long-run behaviour.
Classify space-time diagrams with the four Wolfram classes and discuss the limits of that classification.
Explain how boundary conditions and finite lattice size shape long-run behaviour.
Implement the Game of Life and identify still lifes, oscillators and gliders.
Represent traffic with occupancy and speed arrays, and implement the Nagel-Schreckenberg rules.
Measure density and flow, estimate the fundamental diagram, and explain how local agent behaviour creates stop-and-go waves and jams.
Decide which model extensions change the fundamental diagram qualitatively.








References

Nagel, Kai, and Michael Schreckenberg. 1992. “A Cellular Automaton Model for Freeway Traffic.” Journal de Physique I 2 (12): 2221–29. https://doi.org/10.1051/jp1:1992277.


Wolfram, Stephen. 1983. “Statistical Mechanics of Cellular Automata.” Reviews of Modern Physics 55 (3): 601–44. https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.55.601.

Assessment criteria
The syllabus asks you to explain what is modelled, state the assumptions, and add an extension, test or criticism of your own, within ten minutes. The syllabus lists no further criteria, so prepare against these three content items and the time limit.







Exercise



Pick one explorable from Complexity Explorables that you do not plan to present. Write one sentence for each content item: what is modelled, one assumption, and one extension, test or criticism.








Solution





There is no single answer. A good answer is specific. For example, for a model of flocking: the model represents birds as points that align with neighbours within a fixed radius; one assumption is that every bird sees all neighbours within that radius, with no blind angle; one test is to vary the noise level and check whether the order parameter drops as the noise grows (Vicsek et al. 1995). Compare with the Vicsek model in Module 2.

title: Game of Life
text:
Conway’s Game of Life is a two-dimensional cellular automaton on a square lattice with the Moore neighbourhood of eight cells. Martin Gardner introduced it to a wide audience in 1970 (gardner1970life?). The rules are:
In the notation for “life-like” rules this is B3/S23. Berlekamp, Conway and Guy outlined a proof that the Game of Life can simulate a universal computer (berlekamp1982winning?). Reference code: amlab/cellular_automata/life.py.

title: Game of Life
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Before you code, take a horizontal row of three live cells (the blinker). Apply the rules by hand for two generations. What do you get?








Solution





The two end cells have one live neighbour each, so they die. The centre cell has two and survives. The cells directly above and below the centre have three live neighbours, so they are born. After one generation you get a vertical row of three cells. The same argument turned by 90 degrees gives the horizontal row back after two generations. The blinker is an oscillator with period 2.

title: Game of Life
Game of Life
text:
Validation
A blinker has period 2. A glider returns to its shape after 4 generations, shifted by one cell diagonally (gardner1970life?). period_and_shift() checks both.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from amlab.cellular_automata.life import PATTERNS, place, life_step, simulate_life, period_and_shift

for name in PATTERNS:
    period, shift = period_and_shift(place((24, 24), name, 10, 10))
    kind = "spaceship" if shift != (0, 0) else ("still life" if period == 1 else "oscillator")
    print(f"{name:8s} period {period}, shift {shift}: {kind}")

block    period 1, shift (0, 0): still life
beehive  period 1, shift (0, 0): still life

text:
Interpretation

Gliders move at one cell every four generations along a diagonal. On a periodic grid a glider can come back and collide with debris, so the final state depends on the grid size.







Exercise



Place two gliders on a \(40 \times 40\) periodic grid so that they collide. Simulate 200 generations. What remains after the collision?








Solution






glider = PATTERNS["glider"]
g = np.zeros((40, 40), dtype=np.uint8)
g[5:8, 5:8] = glider                      # moves down and right
g[5:8, 25:28] = glider[:, ::-1]           # mirrored: moves down and left

print("Live cells after 200 generations:", int(final.sum()))
