title: The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model
text:
Reading




Compulsory: Nagel and Schreckenberg (1992).
Recommended: (boccara2010modeling?), Chapter 6.
Nagel and Schreckenberg proposed a cellular automaton for single-lane freeway traffic (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). The road is a ring of \(L\) cells. Each cell is empty or holds one car. Each car \(n\) has a position \(x_n\) and an integer speed \(v_n \in \{0, 1, \ldots, v_{\max}\}\), measured in cells per time step. The model is agent-based: every car carries its own state and reacts to the car in front.

title: The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model
text:
From cellular automata to agents
In an elementary cellular automaton every cell follows the same binary rule. The traffic model keeps discrete time and a one-dimensional road, but enriches the state (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992; Wilensky and Rand 2015):

Occupied cells correspond to cars.
Each car stores a speed.
The update depends on the gap ahead and on a random slowdown.

The update is still local. It is more expressive, because agents now carry internal state.
Why call this agent-based if the road is still a grid? Because each occupied cell corresponds to an individual car with its own speed. You write the update from the point of view of each car and its local environment, not as an equation for a global density field.
The road is periodic: the first and last cells are neighbours. This removes boundary effects and makes the congestion dynamics easier to interpret. The page Boundary Conditions shows what an open edge does to Rule 184.

title: The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model
text:
The four rules
Let \(d_n\) be the number of empty cells between car \(n\) and the car ahead. At every time step, all cars apply the following rules in this order, in parallel (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992):

Acceleration. \(v_n \leftarrow \min(v_n + 1,\ v_{\max})\).
Braking. \(v_n \leftarrow \min(v_n,\ d_n)\).
Randomization. With probability \(p\), \(v_n \leftarrow \max(v_n - 1,\ 0)\).
Motion. \(x_n \leftarrow x_n + v_n\).

Rule 2 guarantees that cars never collide. Cars never overtake, so their order on the ring never changes. The number of cars is conserved on the ring, and the density is \(\rho = N/L\).

title: The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model
section: The role of the randomization step
text:
The role of the randomization step
Without rule 3 (\(p = 0\)) the model is deterministic. From a random start it reaches a stationary state with flow
\[
q(\rho) = \min\big(\rho\, v_{\max},\ 1 - \rho\big),
\]
so every car moves at \(v_{\max}\) for \(\rho < 1/(v_{\max}+1)\) and jams only appear above that density (chowdhury2000statistical?).
With \(p > 0\) three things change (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992; chowdhury2000statistical?):

drivers fluctuate in speed, even on an empty road;
a car that brakes randomly forces the car behind to brake, which can start a jam in free traffic, with no external cause;
jams move backwards, against the direction of traffic.

With \(v_{\max} = 1\) and \(p = 0\) the model reduces to the elementary Rule 184 (chowdhury2000statistical?).








Figure 1: Space-time diagrams on a ring of 200 cells at density 0.15, v_max = 5. Left: p = 0, all cars move freely after a transient. Right: p = 0.3, jams form spontaneously and travel backwards. Cars move to the right; time runs downward.

title: The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model
text:
Scales
In the original interpretation one cell corresponds to 7.5 m, the space a car occupies in a jam, and one time step to about 1 s. Then \(v_{\max} = 5\) corresponds to \(5 \times 7.5\) m/s \(= 135\) km/h (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992).






Exercise



Why must the braking rule come before the randomization rule? What could go wrong if you apply randomization first and braking second?








Solution





If randomization comes first, a car whose speed is limited by the gap (\(d_n < v_n - 1\)) brakes to \(d_n\) anyway, so the random slowdown has no effect on it. Fluctuations would then only act on cars with enough free road ahead, and cars in dense traffic would move deterministically. In the original order the random slowdown acts after braking, on every car, including cars that follow closely. This is what lets one random slowdown propagate backwards as a jam. Test it: swap the two rules in your code and compare the space-time diagrams.

title: Traffic Model
text: Traffic flow is a natural agent-based model. Each car moves according to simple local rules, but repeated interactions create stop-and-go waves, jams, and a transition between free flow and congestion (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). The rules are on the page The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model. In this lab you implement them.

title: Traffic Model
text:
Prediction






Exercise



With \(v_{\max} = 5\) and \(p = 0\), below which density should every car end up moving at \(v_{\max}\)? What changes in the space-time diagram when you switch on \(p = 0.3\)?








Solution





A car at \(v_{\max} = 5\) needs 5 empty cells ahead, so each car uses 6 cells. Below \(\rho = 1/(v_{\max}+1) = 1/6 \approx 0.17\) there is room for every car, and with \(p = 0\) all cars reach \(v_{\max}\) after a transient. With \(p = 0.3\) random slowdowns start jams even below that density. In the diagram they appear as dense, nearly horizontal bands that drift to the left, against the traffic.

title: Traffic Model
text:
What you need

numpy stores the occupancy pattern, the speed of each car and the experimental results.
matplotlib.pyplot plots space-time diagrams and flow-density curves.







Scripts or notebooks?



Use a notebook for density sweeps, repeated trials and parameter scans. Use a script if you want a faster interactive visualization or plan to add widgets later.










Figure 1: Traffic CA space-time diagram (cars as black pixels).

title: Traffic Model
text:
Represent the road state
We store the system with two arrays of length length:

occupied[i] tells us whether cell i contains a car.
speeds[i] stores the speed of that car, measured in cells per step.

This lets the road stay discrete while each agent still has its own internal state.

title: Traffic Model
text:
Initialize the agents
The initialization function samples an occupancy pattern and assigns a random speed to each occupied cell.
occupied, speeds = initialize_road(length=100, density=0.2, vmax=5)
The density is
\[
\rho = \frac{\text{number of cars}}{\text{road length}}.
\]

title: Traffic Model
text:
Implement one synchronous update
At each time step, every car follows the same four rules:

Accelerate up to \(v_{\max}\).
Brake so it does not collide with the next car.
Slow down randomly with probability \(p_{\text{slow}}\).
Move forward by its new speed.

The key point is that all cars update synchronously.






Exercise



Complete step(). It returns the new occupancy and speed arrays after one synchronous update of all cars on a periodic road.
def step(occupied, speeds, vmax=5, p_slow=0.3, rng=None):
    if rng is None:
        rng = np.random.default_rng()

    # TODO: accelerate
    # TODO: brake to avoid collisions
    # TODO: random slowdown
    # TODO: move cars
    return new_occupied, new_speeds








Hint





Work with the car positions positions = np.where(occupied)[0], which are sorted along the road. The gap of a car is the number of empty cells up to the next car, (next_pos - pos - 1) % length. The next car of the last car in the list is the first car, because the road is a ring. Write all new speeds first and move the cars only at the end, so that every car sees the old configuration.









Solution





def step(occupied, speeds, vmax=5, p_slow=0.3, rng=None):
    if rng is None:
        rng = np.random.default_rng()

    length = len(occupied)
    positions = np.where(occupied)[0]
    speeds_new = speeds.copy()

    speeds_new[positions] = np.minimum(speeds_new[positions] + 1, vmax)

    gaps = np.zeros_like(positions)
    for idx, pos in enumerate(positions):
        next_pos = positions[(idx + 1) % len(positions)]
        gaps[idx] = (next_pos - pos - 1) % length
    speeds_new[positions] = np.minimum(speeds_new[positions], gaps)

    slow_mask = rng.random(len(positions)) < p_slow
    speeds_new[positions[slow_mask]] = np.maximum(
        speeds_new[positions[slow_mask]] - 1, 0
    )

    new_occupied = np.zeros_like(occupied)
    new_speeds = np.zeros_like(speeds)
    new_positions = (positions + speeds_new[positions]) % length
    new_occupied[new_positions] = True
    new_speeds[new_positions] = speeds_new[positions]

    return new_occupied, new_speeds

title: Traffic Model
text:
Validation
Three checks catch most bugs:

the number of cars stays constant;
no two cars ever occupy the same cell (the occupancy array keeps the same number of True entries);
for \(p = 0\) and density below \(1/(v_{\max}+1)\), every car reaches \(v_{\max}\) after a transient.


import numpy as np
from amlab.cellular_automata.traffic import initialize_road, step

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
occupied, speeds = initialize_road(length=120, density=0.1, vmax=5, rng=rng)
n_cars = occupied.sum()
for t in range(200):
    occupied, speeds = step(occupied, speeds, vmax=5, p_slow=0.0, rng=rng)
    assert occupied.sum() == n_cars, "a car was lost or two cars collided"
print("Cars:", n_cars, "| speeds after 200 steps:", np.unique(speeds[occupied]))

Cars: 15 | speeds after 200 steps: [5]

Wrap the update in a loop and save the occupancy pattern at every time step.

title: Traffic Model
text:
What the dark bands mean
In the diagram, black cells are occupied sites. When dense diagonal bands become nearly horizontal, cars are moving slowly and congestion is forming. When the pattern is sparse and diagonal, cars are advancing freely.

title: Traffic Model
text:
Interpretation
A jam is not imposed externally. It emerges from repeated local braking and stochastic slowdown. Jams in the diagram drift to the left while cars move to the right: the jam front moves against the traffic.

title: Traffic Model
text:
Limitations

The road is a ring with one lane, identical cars and identical drivers.
The cell-based loop over cars in step() is slow for long roads. The vectorized version in amlab/cellular_automata/traffic_models.py stores only the car positions.

Full reference: amlab/cellular_automata/traffic.py.

title: The Fundamental Diagram
text: The fundamental diagram is the relation between traffic density and traffic flow in the stationary state. It is the main macroscopic observable of a traffic model and the one you compare with road measurements (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992; chowdhury2000statistical?).

title: The Fundamental Diagram
text:
Density, flow and speed
On a ring of \(L\) cells with \(N\) cars:
\[
\rho = \frac{N}{L}, \qquad
\bar v = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N v_n, \qquad
q = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{n=1}^N v_n = \rho\, \bar v .
\]
The flow \(q\) is the number of cars that pass a fixed point per time step, averaged over the ring. In simulations you average \(q\) over time after discarding a burn-in period.

title: The Fundamental Diagram
text:
Free flow and congested branches

Free flow. At low density cars rarely interact. Each car moves at about \(v_{\max} - p\) on average, so \(q \approx \rho\,(v_{\max} - p)\) grows linearly with \(\rho\) (chowdhury2000statistical?).
Congested branch. At high density the gaps limit the speeds and \(q\) decreases with \(\rho\). At \(\rho = 1\) nothing moves.
Maximum flow. Between the two branches the flow reaches a maximum, the capacity of the road. Randomization lowers the capacity and moves it to lower density.

For \(p = 0\) the diagram is the exact triangle \(q = \min(\rho\, v_{\max},\ 1 - \rho)\) with its maximum at \(\rho = 1/(v_{\max} + 1)\) (chowdhury2000statistical?).








Figure 1: Simulated fundamental diagram (ring of 400 cells, v_max = 5, 400 steps after 200 burn-in steps, random initial positions). The dashed line is the exact result for p = 0. Left: flow. Right: mean speed.





The simulation for \(p = 0\) lies on the exact triangle, which validates the code. For \(p > 0\) the peak is lower and rounded.

title: The Fundamental Diagram
text:
Empirical evidence: jams without bottlenecks
Sugiyama and co-workers asked 22 drivers to drive around a circular track of 230 m, starting from a uniform configuration. A stop-and-go wave formed spontaneously and travelled backwards, with no bottleneck on the track (sugiyama2008traffic?). They interpret the jam as a collective instability of free flow that appears when the density exceeds a critical value.
This is the phenomenon that the randomization step produces in the Nagel-Schreckenberg model: jams on a homogeneous ring, triggered by fluctuations. The experiment does not test the specific rules of the model. It shows that a model of homogeneous traffic on a ring must be able to produce such jams.






Exercise



Use the free-flow approximation \(q \approx \rho (v_{\max} - p)\) and the congested branch \(q \approx 1 - \rho\) of the deterministic model to estimate where the maximum flow occurs for \(v_{\max} = 5\) and \(p = 0.3\). Compare with the figure.








Solution





The two lines cross at \(\rho (v_{\max} - p) = 1 - \rho\), so \(\rho^* = 1/(v_{\max} - p + 1) = 1/5.7 \approx 0.175\) and \(q^* \approx 0.82\). The simulated curve for \(p = 0.3\) peaks near \(\rho \approx 0.1\) with \(q\) below 0.5, so at lower density and much lower flow. Randomization also lowers the congested branch below \(1 - \rho\), because stopped cars restart with a delay. The crossing of the two straight lines is only an upper estimate.

title: Wolfram Classes
text: Wolfram studied the long-run behaviour of one-dimensional cellular automata started from random initial rows. He proposed that almost all rules fall into four qualitative classes (wolfram1984universality?).

title: Wolfram Classes
text:
The four classes

Class 1. Evolution leads to a homogeneous state, for example all cells 0.
Class 2. Evolution leads to a set of separated simple structures that are stable or periodic.
Class 3. Evolution leads to an aperiodic, chaotic pattern.
Class 4. Evolution leads to complex localized structures, sometimes long-lived.

Wolfram related the first three classes to limit points, limit cycles and chaotic attractors of continuous dynamical systems, and conjectured that class 4 rules can support universal computation (wolfram1984universality?).








Figure 1: Space-time diagrams of one representative rule per class, started from the same random row (200 cells, periodic boundaries, time runs downward). Rule 32 (class 1), rule 108 (class 2), rule 30 (class 3) and rule 110 (class 4).

title: Wolfram Classes
text:
How to read the diagrams

In rule 32 every cell is 0 after a few steps.
In rule 108 isolated stripes remain fixed or blink with a short period. A change in the initial row only affects nearby stripes.
In rule 30 the pattern looks random, and a single-cell change in the initial row spreads through a growing region.
In rule 110 moving localized structures travel over a periodic background and collide.

title: Wolfram Classes
text:
Sensitivity to a single flip
A quantitative way to separate class 2 from class 3 is to flip one cell of the initial row and track the Hamming distance, the number of cells in which the two runs differ.








Figure 2: Number of cells that differ between two runs whose initial rows differ in one cell (400 cells, periodic boundaries).





For rule 30 the distance grows roughly linearly, because the perturbed region spreads at a finite speed of at most one cell per step on each side.

title: Wolfram Classes
text:
Limits of the classification
The classes are defined by visual inspection of typical runs, not by a formal test. Some rules show different behaviour for different initial conditions, and later work proposed measures such as Langton’s \(\lambda\) to organize the rule space (langton1990computation?). Treat the classes as a first vocabulary, not as a theorem.






Exercise



Run rule 184 from a random row with density \(0.3\) and with density \(0.7\). Which class would you assign? Does your answer depend on the density?








Solution






fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3), sharey=True)
for ax, rho in zip(axes, (0.3, 0.7)):
    ax.imshow(simulate_eca(random_row(200, rho, seed=1), 184, 100), cmap="binary", aspect="auto")
    ax.set_title(f"Rule 184, density {rho}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Rule 184 conserves the number of 1s. At density \(0.3\) all particles end up moving freely to the right; at \(0.7\) the holes move freely to the left. Both look like class 2 after a short transient, so the answer does not depend on the density here. You will meet rule 184 again as the simplest traffic model.

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
In Scaling of Returns you saw the prediction \(p_{\Delta t}(0) \propto \Delta t^{-1/\alpha}\) and the result \(\alpha \approx 1.4\) of (mantegna1995scaling?) for minute data. Here you aggregate daily returns over longer horizons and test how the distribution changes with \(\Delta t\).
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

from amlab.finance import load_prices, log_returns

r = log_returns(load_prices()["close"])
r = r - r.mean()
horizons = np.array([1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100])

WARNING: data/finance/prices.csv not found. Using a SYNTHETIC GARCH(1,1) series with Student-t innovations (seed 2026). These are not market data. See data/finance/README.md.

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Prediction






Exercise



For each model below, predict how the standard deviation of \(r(\Delta t)\) and its excess kurtosis change with \(\Delta t\):

i.i.d. Gaussian returns;
i.i.d. returns with finite variance but fat tails;
returns that are uncorrelated but show volatility clustering.









Solution





In all three cases the standard deviation grows as \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\), because the variances of uncorrelated terms add. The kurtosis tells the models apart:

i.i.d. Gaussian: the excess kurtosis is 0 at every horizon.
i.i.d. with fat tails (finite fourth moment): it starts positive and falls as \(K_1 / \Delta t\).
Volatility clustering: it starts positive and falls more slowly than \(K_1 / \Delta t\), because days in a calm or a turbulent period are not independent.

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Core activity: aggregate the returns
The log return over \(\Delta t\) days is the sum of \(\Delta t\) daily log returns. Use non-overlapping blocks, so that different aggregated returns do not share days.






Exercise



Complete aggregate_returns. Then compute the standard deviation, the excess kurtosis and the density at zero of \(r(\Delta t)\) for every horizon in horizons.
def aggregate_returns(r, horizon):
    """Sum r over non-overlapping blocks of length horizon."""
    m = # TODO: number of complete blocks
    # TODO: reshape r[: m * horizon] to (m, horizon) and sum along axis 1
    return ...








Solution






def aggregate_returns(r, horizon):
    """Sum r over non-overlapping blocks of length horizon."""
    m = r.size // horizon
    return r[: m * horizon].reshape(m, horizon).sum(axis=1)


def p_zero(x):
    """Density at 0, estimated in a window of one tenth of the IQR."""
    q75, q25 = np.percentile(x, [75, 25])
    eps = 0.1 * (q75 - q25)
    return np.mean(np.abs(x) < eps / 2) / eps


def scaling_table(r):
    """Standard deviation, excess kurtosis and p(0) at every horizon."""
    rows = []
    for h in horizons:
        x = aggregate_returns(r, h)
        rows.append((x.std(), stats.kurtosis(x), p_zero(x)))
    return np.array(rows)


table = scaling_table(r)
for h, (sd, kurt, p0) in zip(horizons, table):
    print(f"dt = {h:3d}: blocks {r.size // h:5d}, std {sd:.4f}, kurtosis {kurt:6.2f}, p(0) {p0:7.2f}")

dt =   1: blocks  5000, std 0.0091, kurtosis  11.97, p(0)   59.46
dt =   2: blocks  2500, std 0.0127, kurtosis   8.86, p(0)   45.14
dt =   5: blocks  1000, std 0.0206, kurtosis   4.24, p(0)   24.77
dt =  10: blocks   500, std 0.0294, kurtosis   5.64, p(0)   16.92
dt =  20: blocks   250, std 0.0396, kurtosis   1.31, p(0)   12.45
dt =  50: blocks   100, std 0.0697, kurtosis   1.03, p(0)    6.05

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Validation: a shuffled series
Shuffling the returns in time keeps their distribution and destroys all dependence. The shuffled series is i.i.d. with the same fat tails. For it, the standard deviation must grow as \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\) and, when the fourth moment is finite, the excess kurtosis of a sum of \(\Delta t\) i.i.d. terms is the one-day value divided by \(\Delta t\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(32)
table_shuffled = scaling_table(rng.permutation(r))
slope_sd = np.polyfit(np.log(horizons), np.log(table_shuffled[:, 0]), 1)[0]
print(f"shuffled: slope of log std vs log dt = {slope_sd:.3f} (theory 0.5)")

shuffled: slope of log std vs log dt = 0.497 (theory 0.5)

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Experiment: three scaling plots

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.5))
for tab, label, marker in [(table, "original", "o"), (table_shuffled, "shuffled", "s")]:
    axes[0].loglog(horizons, tab[:, 0], marker, label=label)
    axes[1].semilogx(horizons, tab[:, 1], marker, label=label)
    axes[2].loglog(horizons, tab[:, 2], marker, label=label)
axes[0].loglog(horizons, table[0, 0] * np.sqrt(horizons), "k-", lw=0.8)
axes[1].semilogx(horizons, table[0, 1] / horizons, "k-", lw=0.8)
axes[2].loglog(horizons, table[0, 2] / np.sqrt(horizons), "k-", lw=0.8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("std of $r(\\Delta t)$")
axes[1].set_ylabel("excess kurtosis")
axes[2].set_ylabel("$p_{\\Delta t}(0)$")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("$\\Delta t$ (days)")
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

slope_p0 = np.polyfit(np.log(horizons), np.log(table[:, 2]), 1)[0]
print(f"p(0) slope, original data: {slope_p0:.3f}  ->  effective alpha = {-1 / slope_p0:.2f}")







Figure 1: Scaling with the horizon \(\Delta t\) for the original and the shuffled returns. Left: standard deviation, with slope 1/2. Centre: excess kurtosis, with the i.i.d. prediction \(K_1/\Delta t\). Right: density at zero, with slope \(-1/2\).





p(0) slope, original data: -0.616  ->  effective alpha = 1.62

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Interpretation

The standard deviation grows close to \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\) because daily returns are nearly uncorrelated. This is the part of the random walk model that survives.
The excess kurtosis falls with \(\Delta t\): the distribution becomes more Gaussian at longer horizons, which is the aggregational Gaussianity of (cont2001empirical?). If it falls more slowly for the original data than for the shuffled data, the difference comes from volatility clustering, since that is the only thing the shuffle removed.
The effective \(\alpha\) from \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) tells you whether the centre of the distribution rescales like a Lévy law or like a Gaussian over these horizons. (mantegna1995scaling?) found \(\alpha \approx 1.4\) for horizons of 1 to 1000 minutes on the S&P 500; daily and longer horizons are a different regime.

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Limitations

At \(\Delta t = 100\) days a 20-year series gives only about 50 blocks. The kurtosis and \(p(0)\) at long horizons are very noisy. Report them with that caveat or use overlapping blocks and account for the dependence they introduce.
The sample kurtosis is unreliable for heavy tails (cont2001empirical?). Use it to compare series, not as a precise value.
The \(p(0)\) estimate depends on the window width. Try a few widths and check that your conclusion does not change.

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Optional extension






Exercise



Plot the histograms of \(r(\Delta t)/\Delta t^{1/2}\) for \(\Delta t = 1, 5, 20\) on one log-density axis. If the returns scaled like a Gaussian random walk, the curves would collapse onto one. Repeat with \(\Delta t^{1/1.4}\) and compare which rescaling collapses the centre better, as in (mantegna1995scaling?).








Solution





Loop over the two exponents and draw one panel for each. Judge the collapse near zero, not in the tails, where the long horizons have few points.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5), sharey=True)
for ax, alpha in zip(axes, [2.0, 1.4]):
    for h in [1, 5, 20]:
        x = aggregate_returns(r, h) / h ** (1 / alpha)
        dens, edges = np.histogram(x, bins=40, density=True)
        ax.semilogy(0.5 * (edges[1:] + edges[:-1]), dens, ".-", label=f"dt = {h}")
    ax.set_title(f"rescaled by dt^(1/{alpha})")
    ax.set_xlabel("rescaled return")
axes[0].set_ylabel("density")
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Exit question






Exercise



Suppose that on the same daily series the \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) method gives an effective \(\alpha\) below 2 while the Hill estimator of Tail Exponent gives about 3. Is that a contradiction?








Solution





No. The two methods look at different parts of the distribution. The Hill estimator measures the far tail of one-day returns. The \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) method measures how the height of the centre changes under aggregation, which depends on the whole distribution and on the dependence between days. (mantegna1995scaling?) found exactly this combination for the S&P 500: a Lévy-like centre with \(\alpha \approx 1.4\) and tails that fall off faster than a Lévy law, so the variance is finite. The truncated Lévy flight of (mantegna1994stochastic?) is one model with both properties.

title: Returns and Efficient Markets
text:
Reading




Compulsory: (mantegna2000introduction?), Chapters 1 to 3.
Recommended: (mandelbrot1963variation?); (mantegna1995scaling?).
The first random walk model of prices is older than Einstein’s theory of Brownian motion. Bachelier modelled price changes on the Paris exchange as independent Gaussian increments in his 1900 thesis (bachelier1900theorie?). This session asks how well that model describes real markets.

title: Returns and Efficient Markets
text:
Prices and returns
Let \(P_t\) be the closing price on day \(t\). The simple return and the log return are
\[
R_t = \frac{P_t - P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}}, \qquad r_t = \ln \frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}} = \ln(1 + R_t).
\tag{1}\]
For daily data \(|R_t|\) is usually small and \(r_t \approx R_t\). Log returns have one property that makes them the natural variable for modelling: they add over time. The log return over \(\Delta t\) days is
\[
r_t(\Delta t) = \ln \frac{P_t}{P_{t - \Delta t}} = \sum_{i=0}^{\Delta t - 1} r_{t-i} .
\tag{2}\]
So \(\ln P_t\) is a random walk whose steps are the daily log returns, and everything from The Random Walk and Stable Distributions applies to it.

title: Returns and Efficient Markets
text:
The random walk hypothesis
The simplest model assumes that daily log returns are independent and identically distributed, often Gaussian with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\):
\[
\ln P_t = \ln P_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{t} r_i, \qquad r_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2).
\tag{3}\]
Then \(\operatorname{Var}[r_t(\Delta t)] = \sigma^2 \Delta t\), the financial version of \(\mathrm{MSD} = 2Dt\). Bachelier’s original model used price changes instead of log returns (bachelier1900theorie?).

title: Returns and Efficient Markets
text:
Efficient markets
(fama1970efficient?) calls a market efficient when prices “fully reflect” the available information. He distinguishes three forms by the information set: past prices (weak form), all public information (semi-strong form), and all information, including private information (strong form). Fama also notes that the independence assumed in Equation 3 is stronger than what efficiency requires. In a “fair game” model the deviations of returns from their expected values cannot be predicted from the information set, but they need not be independent or identically distributed (fama1970efficient?).
The practical consequence you test in the lab: under weak-form efficiency, past returns should carry no linear information about future returns.








Figure 1: Five simulated price paths from the geometric random walk with \(P_0 = 100\), \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 0.01\) per day over 1000 days. All paths come from the same model; the apparent trends are chance.











Exercise



A price goes from 100 to 150 and then back to 100. Compute the two simple returns and the two log returns. Which of them sum to the total return over the two days?








Solution






p = np.array([100.0, 150.0, 100.0])
R = np.diff(p) / p[:-1]
r = np.diff(np.log(p))
print("simple returns:", R, "sum", R.sum())
print("log returns:   ", r.round(4), "sum", r.sum().round(12))

simple returns: [ 0.5        -0.33333333] sum 0.16666666666666669
log returns:    [ 0.4055 -0.4055] sum 0.0


The simple returns are \(+50\%\) and \(-33.3\%\); their sum, \(+16.7\%\), is not the true total return of \(0\). The log returns are \(\pm 0.405\) and sum to exactly \(0\).

title: The Diffusion Equation
text: A single walker is unpredictable. The density of many walkers obeys a deterministic partial differential equation. This page derives it from the lattice walk, following the idea of (berg1993random?).

title: The Diffusion Equation
section: From the walk to a PDE
text:
From the walk to a PDE
Let \(P(x, t)\) be the probability that a walker is at site \(x\) at time \(t\). An unbiased walker at \(x\) at time \(t + \tau\) came from \(x - \delta\) or from \(x + \delta\), each with probability \(1/2\):
\[
P(x, t + \tau) = \tfrac{1}{2} P(x - \delta, t) + \tfrac{1}{2} P(x + \delta, t).
\]
Expand the left side to first order in \(\tau\) and the right side to second order in \(\delta\):
\[
\tau \frac{\partial P}{\partial t} = \frac{\delta^2}{2} \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x^2} + O(\delta^4) + O(\tau^2).
\]
Now let \(\delta \to 0\) and \(\tau \to 0\) while the ratio \(D = \delta^2 / (2\tau)\) stays fixed. The result is the diffusion equation
\[
\frac{\partial P}{\partial t} = D \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x^2} .
\tag{1}\]
The limit only makes sense with \(\delta^2 \propto \tau\). If you scale \(\delta \propto \tau\) instead, the right side vanishes and nothing spreads. This is the continuum version of the \(\sqrt{t}\) law from Mean Squared Displacement. The same equation, written for a concentration, is Fick’s second law (berg1993random?).

title: The Diffusion Equation
text:
The heat kernel
For walkers that all start at \(x = 0\), \(P(x, 0) = \delta_{\text{Dirac}}(x)\), the solution on the whole line is
\[
P(x, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi D t}} \exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{4Dt}\right),
\tag{2}\]
a Gaussian with mean zero and variance \(2Dt\) (berg1993random?, Eq. 1.22). Its variance reproduces \(\langle x^2 \rangle = 2Dt\). The same Gaussian also follows from the binomial distribution of the walk when the number of steps is large, which is a special case of the central limit theorem.








Figure 1: Positions of 20000 lattice walkers (\(\delta = \tau = 1\), so \(D = 1/2\)) after 25, 100 and 400 steps, compared with the heat kernel. Bins have width \(2\delta\) because a walker after \(n\) steps sits only on sites with the parity of \(n\).

title: The Diffusion Equation
text:
Assumptions to remember
Equation 1 needs independent steps with finite variance and no bias. A bias adds a drift term, which gives diffusion with drift (berg1993random?). If the step variance is infinite, the limit is not a Gaussian at all; see Stable Distributions. In Module 4 the same Laplacian term appears in reaction-diffusion models.






Exercise



Check numerically that Equation 2 solves Equation 1. Evaluate heat_kernel on a grid at \(t = 10\) with \(D = 0.5\), approximate \(\partial_t P\) with a centred difference in time and \(\partial_{xx} P\) with the three-point stencil, and report the largest difference between the two sides.








Solution






from amlab.random_walks import heat_kernel

D, t, h, dt = 0.5, 10.0, 0.01, 1e-4
xg = np.arange(-10, 10, h)
dPdt = (heat_kernel(xg, t + dt, D) - heat_kernel(xg, t - dt, D)) / (2 * dt)
P = heat_kernel(xg, t, D)
d2Pdx2 = (P[2:] - 2 * P[1:-1] + P[:-2]) / h**2
print(f"max |dP/dt - D d2P/dx2| = {np.max(np.abs(dPdt[1:-1] - D * d2Pdx2)):.2e}")
print(f"max |dP/dt| = {np.max(np.abs(dPdt)):.2e}")

max |dP/dt - D d2P/dx2| = 1.58e-08
max |dP/dt| = 6.31e-03


The residual is several orders of magnitude smaller than the terms themselves, as expected from discretization error alone.

title: Scaling of Returns
text: If log returns are independent draws from one stable law, their distribution at every time horizon is a rescaled copy of the one-step distribution. (mantegna1995scaling?) tested this idea on the S&P 500 index. This page states the prediction and their result.

title: Scaling of Returns
text:
The scaling prediction
Let the one-step log returns be i.i.d. symmetric stable with index \(\alpha\) and density \(p_1\). By Stable Distributions, the return over \(\Delta t\) steps, \(r(\Delta t)\), is stable with the same \(\alpha\) and a scale multiplied by \(\Delta t^{1/\alpha}\). Its density is
\[
p_{\Delta t}(x) = \Delta t^{-1/\alpha}\, p_1\!\left( x\, \Delta t^{-1/\alpha} \right).
\tag{1}\]
At \(x = 0\) this gives the probability of return to the origin
\[
p_{\Delta t}(0) = p_1(0)\, \Delta t^{-1/\alpha} .
\tag{2}\]
On log-log axes \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) against \(\Delta t\) is a straight line with slope \(-1/\alpha\). For Gaussian returns \(\alpha = 2\) and the slope is \(-1/2\). The peak of the distribution is well sampled, so Equation 2 is easier to measure than the tail.

title: Scaling of Returns
text:
What Mantegna and Stanley found
(mantegna1995scaling?) used S&P 500 index values sampled every minute from 1984 to 1989. They report that:

\(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) follows Equation 2 for \(\Delta t\) from 1 to 1000 minutes, three orders of magnitude.
The slope is about \(-0.71\), which gives \(\alpha \approx 1.4\) (\(1.40 \pm 0.05\) in the paper). The exponent is stable over the six years of data.
After rescaling with Equation 1, the central part of the distributions at different \(\Delta t\) matches a Lévy stable law.
The far tails fall off faster than a Lévy law, approximately exponentially, so the variance is finite.

The last point led to the truncated Lévy flight: a Lévy flight whose largest steps are cut off. Sums of such steps look stable for a long range of \(n\) and only converge to a Gaussian after very many steps (mantegna1994stochastic?). Later work on the tails of individual US stocks found a power-law tail exponent close to 3, outside the stable range \(0 < \alpha \le 2\) (gopikrishnan1998inverse?). This is consistent with the heavy-tail and aggregational Gaussianity facts of Stylized Facts of Returns.

title: Scaling of Returns
text:
A simulated check
The figure applies the \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) method to two synthetic series of \(10^6\) i.i.d. returns: symmetric stable with \(\alpha = 1.4\) and Gaussian. The density at zero is estimated as the fraction of aggregated returns in a window \(|r| < \varepsilon/2\) divided by \(\varepsilon\), with \(\varepsilon\) equal to one tenth of the interquartile range at that horizon.








Figure 1: Estimated probability of return to the origin against horizon for i.i.d. stable (\(\alpha = 1.4\)) and Gaussian returns. Lines have slopes \(-1/1.4\) and \(-1/2\).











Exercise



Fit the slope of \(\log p_{\Delta t}(0)\) against \(\log \Delta t\) for both series and convert it to an estimate of \(\alpha\). Then repeat the fit for the stable series using only \(\Delta t \ge 100\). Why does the estimate get noisier?








Solution






for label, r in series.items():
    p0 = np.array([p_zero(aggregate_returns(r, h)) for h in horizons])
    s_all = np.polyfit(np.log(horizons), np.log(p0), 1)[0]
    big = horizons >= 100
    s_big = np.polyfit(np.log(horizons[big]), np.log(p0[big]), 1)[0]
    name = label.replace("$", "").replace("\\alpha", "alpha")
    print(f"{name:18s} alpha (all) = {-1 / s_all:.2f}, alpha (dt >= 100) = {-1 / s_big:.2f}")

stable, alpha = 1.4 alpha (all) = 1.37, alpha (dt >= 100) = 1.15
Gaussian           alpha (all) = 2.08, alpha (dt >= 100) = 2.52


With \(10^6\) returns there are only 2000 non-overlapping blocks at \(\Delta t = 500\), and few of them fall inside the small window around zero. Long horizons cost data, which is why (mantegna1995scaling?) needed minute-by-minute prices to span three decades of \(\Delta t\).

title: The Random Walk
text:
Reading




Compulsory: (berg1993random?), Chapters 1 and 2.
Recommended: (britton2003essential?), Chapter 5 (Biological Motion).
A random walk is a sequence of positions in which each step is random and independent of the previous ones. Karl Pearson named the problem in a letter to Nature (pearson1905problem?). In the same year Einstein’s theory of Brownian motion described a suspended particle through many independent displacements (einstein1905bewegung?). In this module you use random walks to model diffusing molecules, heavy-tailed fluctuations and prices.

title: The Random Walk
text:
The one-dimensional lattice walk
Follow (berg1993random?). A particle starts at \(x = 0\) at time \(t = 0\) and obeys three rules:

Every \(\tau\) seconds it steps a distance \(\delta\) to the right or to the left.
It steps right with probability \(p\) and left with probability \(q = 1 - p\), independently of earlier steps.
Different particles move independently of each other.

After \(n\) steps the position is a sum of independent steps \(\xi_i \in \{+\delta, -\delta\}\):
\[
x(n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \xi_i .
\tag{1}\]

title: The Random Walk
text:
Mean and variance
Each step has mean \((p - q)\delta\) and variance \(4pq\,\delta^2\). Means and variances of independent variables add, so
\[
\langle x(n) \rangle = n (p - q)\,\delta, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}[x(n)] = 4 n p q\, \delta^2 .
\tag{2}\]
This agrees with the binomial derivation in (berg1993random?, Eqs. 1.15 to 1.20). For the unbiased walk, \(p = q = 1/2\), the mean stays at zero and \(\langle x^2(n) \rangle = n\delta^2\). The typical distance from the origin grows as \(\sqrt{n}\), not as \(n\).








Figure 1: Twenty unbiased lattice walks with \(\delta = 1\). The dashed curves are \(\pm\sqrt{n}\), one standard deviation of \(x(n)\).











Exercise



Simulate 5000 walkers for 400 steps with \(p = 0.6\) and \(\delta = 1\) using simulate_lattice_walk. Compare the sample mean and variance of \(x(400)\) with Equation 2.








Solution





The theory gives \(\langle x \rangle = 400 \cdot 0.2 = 80\) and \(\operatorname{Var} = 4 \cdot 400 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.4 = 384\).

from amlab.random_walks import simulate_lattice_walk

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = simulate_lattice_walk(5000, 400, p=0.6, rng=rng)
print(f"mean     {x[:, -1].mean():7.2f}  (theory 80)")
print(f"variance {x[:, -1].var():7.2f}  (theory 384)")

mean       79.92  (theory 80)
variance  394.05  (theory 384)

title: The Random Walk
text:
What the model leaves out
The lattice walk ignores inertia: successive steps are uncorrelated. (berg1993random?) estimates that a protein such as lysozyme in water takes about \(10^{12}\) such steps per second, so the memory of each step is lost almost at once. Walks with memory or with long jumps behave differently; you meet one kind in Lévy flights.

title: Lévy Flights
text: A Lévy flight is a random walk whose step lengths have a power-law distribution with infinite variance. The walk is dominated by rare long jumps, and it spreads faster than ordinary diffusion.

title: Lévy Flights
text:
The model
In the plane, draw each step with a uniformly random direction and a length \(\ell\) with density
\[
p(\ell) \propto \ell^{-\mu}, \qquad \ell \ge \ell_{\min},
\]
the parametrization used by (viswanathan1999optimizing?). Three regimes follow from Power Laws and Stable Distributions:

\(\mu \le 1\): the density cannot be normalized.
\(1 < \mu < 3\): the step variance is infinite. The position after \(n\) steps is a sum in the domain of attraction of a stable law with index \(\alpha = \mu - 1\), so its typical size grows as \(n^{1/\alpha} = n^{1/(\mu - 1)}\). This is faster than \(n^{1/2}\).
\(\mu > 3\): the variance is finite, the CLT applies, and you recover normal diffusion.

The mean squared displacement of a Lévy flight is infinite at every time, because a single step already has infinite variance. You measure the spreading with a quantile, such as the median distance, instead. Models that give each jump a finite speed, called Lévy walks, have a finite MSD growing as \(t^{\gamma}\) with \(\gamma > 1\) (superdiffusion) (metzler2000random?).

title: Lévy Flights
text:
Trajectories








Figure 1: Two planar walks of 2000 steps with \(\ell_{\min} = 1\). Left: \(\mu = 10\), finite variance, a Brownian-like path. Right: \(\mu = 2\), a Lévy flight made of clusters of short steps joined by rare long jumps. Note the different axis scales.

title: Lévy Flights
text:
Why it matters
(viswanathan1999optimizing?) studied a searcher looking for randomly placed targets. When targets are sparse and can be revisited, the optimal choice is \(\mu \approx 2\). (metzler2000random?) review the mathematics of anomalous diffusion, including Lévy flights and walks. In finance, (mandelbrot1963variation?) proposed that price changes are stable with \(\alpha < 2\), which makes the logarithm of the price a one-dimensional Lévy flight. You test that idea in Modelling Financial Markets.






Exercise



Simulate 1000 flights of 1000 steps for \(\mu = 2.5\) and for \(\mu = 10\). Compute the median distance from the origin at each step and fit the exponent \(\nu\) in \(\text{median} \propto n^{\nu}\) over \(n \in [10, 1000]\). Compare with \(1/(\mu - 1)\) and \(1/2\).








Solution






rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n = np.arange(10, 1001)
for mu, theory in [(2.5, 1 / 1.5), (10.0, 0.5)]:
    paths = np.array([levy_flight_2d(1000, mu=mu, rng=rng) for _ in range(1000)])
    med = np.median(np.linalg.norm(paths, axis=2), axis=0)
    nu = np.polyfit(np.log(n), np.log(med[n]), 1)[0]
    print(f"mu = {mu:4}: nu = {nu:.3f}, theory {theory:.3f}")

mu =  2.5: nu = 0.677, theory 0.667
mu = 10.0: nu = 0.501, theory 0.500


The Lévy flight spreads with \(\nu \approx 2/3\), the finite-variance walk with \(\nu \approx 1/2\). Convergence to the asymptotic exponent is slow, so expect a small deviation at these sizes.

title: Diffusion in Biology
text: The relation \(\langle x^2 \rangle = 2Dt\) has a direct consequence for living cells: diffusion is fast over short distances and very slow over long ones. The numbers on this page come from (berg1993random?).

title: Diffusion in Biology
text:
Time to diffuse a distance
Invert \(\langle x^2 \rangle = 2Dt\) from Mean Squared Displacement to get the typical time to cover a distance \(x\) along one axis:
\[
t \approx \frac{x^2}{2D}.
\]
(berg1993random?) uses \(D = 10^{-5}\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\) for a small molecule in water at room temperature. The code below reproduces his two examples: the width of a bacterium (\(10^{-4}\) cm) and the width of a test tube (1 cm).

D = 1e-5  # cm^2/s, small molecule in water (Berg 1993, Chapter 1)

for label, x_cm in [("bacterium, 1 micrometre", 1e-4), ("test tube, 1 cm", 1.0)]:
    t = x_cm**2 / (2 * D)
    print(f"{label:25s} t = {t:9.2e} s = {t / 3600:8.2e} h")

bacterium, 1 micrometre   t =  5.00e-04 s = 1.39e-07 h
test tube, 1 cm           t =  5.00e+04 s = 1.39e+01 h


The first time is about half a millisecond and the second about 14 hours, as in (berg1993random?). The distance grew by \(10^4\) and the time by \(10^8\).

title: Diffusion in Biology
text:
Consequences

There is no “diffusion velocity”. The ratio \(\sqrt{\langle x^2 \rangle}/t = \sqrt{2D/t}\) depends on the observation time (berg1993random?).
Over micrometres diffusion moves small molecules within milliseconds. Over centimetres it takes hours, so transport over large distances needs flow or active mechanisms. Berg’s example is perfume: with \(D \approx 10^{-1}\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\) in air, diffusion alone would take about a month to cross a crowded room, so convection does the work (berg1993random?).
A random walker explores a small region thoroughly and returns to the same points many times before it wanders off (berg1993random?). Chapter 3 of the same book computes how fast molecules diffuse to a receptor or a cell (“diffusion to capture”).
Swimming bacteria are self-propelled random walkers. Their motion is treated in (berg1993random?).

(britton2003essential?) covers biological motion from the modelling side, including taxis and travelling waves.






Exercise



A protein such as lysozyme has \(D \approx 10^{-6}\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\) in water (berg1993random?). Estimate the time it needs to cross a cell of diameter \(10\ \mu\text{m}\) and to travel along a nerve axon of length 1 m. What does the second number tell you about how neurons must transport proteins?








Solution






D = 1e-6  # cm^2/s
for label, x_cm in [("cell, 10 micrometres", 1e-3), ("axon, 1 m", 100.0)]:
    t = x_cm**2 / (2 * D)
    print(f"{label:22s} t = {t:9.2e} s = {t / (3600 * 24 * 365):8.2e} years")

cell, 10 micrometres   t =  5.00e-01 s = 1.59e-08 years
axon, 1 m              t =  5.00e+09 s = 1.59e+02 years


Crossing the cell takes about half a second. Diffusing along a 1 m axon would take over a century, so axons must use active transport. This is an order-of-magnitude argument; it ignores crowding and binding, which slow diffusion further.

title: Stylized Facts of Returns
text: A stylized fact is a statistical property that appears in many markets, instruments and periods. (cont2001empirical?) lists eleven. Any model of prices should reproduce at least the first few. This page quotes the ones you test in the lab.

title: Stylized Facts of Returns
section: The facts you test in the lab
text:
The facts you test in the lab
From (cont2001empirical?):

Absence of autocorrelations. Linear autocorrelations of returns are often insignificant, except at very small intraday time scales (about 20 minutes).
Heavy tails. The unconditional distribution of returns has a power-law or Pareto-like tail, with a tail index that is finite, higher than two and less than five for most data sets. This excludes both the normal distribution and stable laws with infinite variance.
Aggregational Gaussianity. As the time scale \(\Delta t\) of the returns grows, their distribution looks more and more normal. The shape of the distribution is therefore not the same at different time scales.
Volatility clustering. Measures of volatility have positive autocorrelation over several days: large changes tend to be followed by large changes, of either sign.
Slow decay of autocorrelation in absolute returns. The autocorrelation of \(|r_t|\) decays roughly as a power law of the lag with an exponent between 0.2 and 0.4.

The list also contains gain/loss asymmetry, intermittency, conditional heavy tails, the leverage effect, volume/volatility correlation and asymmetry in time scales (cont2001empirical?).

title: Stylized Facts of Returns
section: What this does to the random walk model
text:
What this does to the random walk model
The first fact supports the random walk hypothesis of Returns and Efficient Markets. The others reject its strong form. Uncorrelated is not the same as independent: \(|r_t|\) is predictable from \(|r_{t-1}|\) even when \(r_t\) is not predictable from \(r_{t-1}\) (cont2001empirical?). The heavy-tail fact also rejects Mandelbrot’s stable model with \(\alpha < 2\) (mandelbrot1963variation?) for the far tail, since a tail index above two means finite variance.

title: Stylized Facts of Returns
section: A model that reproduces some of them
text:
A model that reproduces some of them
The ARCH model of (engle1982autoregressive?) and its generalization GARCH(1,1) by (bollerslev1986generalized?) let the variance depend on the past:
\[
r_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad \sigma_t^2 = \omega + a\, r_{t-1}^2 + b\, \sigma_{t-1}^2 ,
\tag{1}\]
with \(z_t\) independent, zero mean and unit variance, and \(a + b < 1\) for a finite unconditional variance \(\omega / (1 - a - b)\). A large return raises tomorrow’s variance, which produces volatility clustering while \(r_t\) stays uncorrelated. See also (mantegna2000introduction?).
The figure compares i.i.d. Gaussian returns with a GARCH(1,1) series with Student-t innovations, the synthetic fallback of the lab (amlab.finance.synthetic_garch_prices). The GARCH series is built to show these facts, so the figure illustrates the definitions; it is not evidence about markets.








Figure 1: Top: 2000 days of i.i.d. Gaussian returns and of a synthetic GARCH(1,1) series with the same unconditional standard deviation (1% per day). Bottom: autocorrelation of \(r_t\) and of \(|r_t|\) for the GARCH series. The dashed band is \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n}\).











Exercise



Compute the excess kurtosis (scipy.stats.kurtosis) of the Gaussian and GARCH returns above. Then shuffle the GARCH returns in time with rng.permutation and recompute the autocorrelation of \(|r_t|\) at lag 1. Which property survives the shuffle, and which one disappears?








Solution






from scipy import stats

shuffled = rng.permutation(r_garch)
print(f"excess kurtosis, Gaussian: {stats.kurtosis(r_iid):.2f}")
print(f"excess kurtosis, GARCH:    {stats.kurtosis(r_garch):.2f}")
print(f"lag-1 ACF of |r|, GARCH:    {autocorrelation(np.abs(r_garch), 1)[1]:.3f}")
print(f"lag-1 ACF of |r|, shuffled: {autocorrelation(np.abs(shuffled), 1)[1]:.3f}")

excess kurtosis, Gaussian: 0.07
excess kurtosis, GARCH:    11.97
lag-1 ACF of |r|, GARCH:    0.166
lag-1 ACF of |r|, shuffled: -0.014


Shuffling keeps the distribution, so the fat tails (large kurtosis) survive. It destroys the time order, so volatility clustering disappears. Heavy tails and clustering are separate facts, and a model can have one without the other.

title: Normality Tests
text:
The Gaussian random walk model predicts normal log returns. On this page you test that prediction graphically and with the Jarque-Bera test. On the next page, Calibrated KS Test, you add a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test with a correctly computed p-value. You continue from Loading Prices and Computing Returns.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

from amlab.finance import load_prices, log_returns

r = log_returns(load_prices()["close"])
z = (r - r.mean()) / r.std(ddof=1)  # standardized returns
n = r.size

WARNING: data/finance/prices.csv not found. Using a SYNTHETIC GARCH(1,1) series with Student-t innovations (seed 2026). These are not market data. See data/finance/README.md.

title: Normality Tests
text:
Prediction






Exercise



If returns were normal, what fraction of days would have \(|z| > 4\)? Write the number down. Then count them in the data.








Solution





For a standard normal, \(\Pr(|Z| > 4) = 2\,\Pr(Z > 4) \approx 6 \times 10^{-5}\), about one day in 16 000. Real returns exceed this by a large factor.

print(f"normal prediction: {2 * stats.norm.sf(4):.1e}")
print(f"observed:          {np.mean(np.abs(z) > 4):.1e}")

normal prediction: 6.3e-05
observed:          5.8e-03

title: Normality Tests
section: Graphical checks: histogram and Q-Q plot
text:
Graphical checks: histogram and Q-Q plot
A histogram on a logarithmic density axis shows the tails. A quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot shows the sorted standardized returns against the quantiles of the standard normal at probabilities \((i - 0.5)/n\). Normal data lie on the diagonal.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.8))
grid = np.linspace(-8, 8, 400)
axes[0].hist(z, bins=80, range=(-8, 8), density=True, alpha=0.6)
axes[0].semilogy(grid, stats.norm.pdf(grid), "k-")
axes[0].set_ylim(1e-5, 1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("standardized return")
axes[0].set_ylabel("density")

theoretical = stats.norm.ppf((np.arange(1, n + 1) - 0.5) / n)
axes[1].plot(theoretical, np.sort(z), ".", ms=2)
axes[1].plot([-4, 4], [-4, 4], "k--")
axes[1].set_xlabel("normal quantile")
axes[1].set_ylabel("sample quantile")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Left: histogram of standardized log returns with the standard normal density, on a log scale. Right: normal Q-Q plot. Points above the diagonal on the right and below it on the left indicate heavier tails than the normal.

title: Normality Tests
text:
The Jarque-Bera test
With sample skewness \(S\) and sample excess kurtosis \(K\), the Jarque-Bera statistic is
\[
JB = \frac{n}{6} \left( S^2 + \frac{K^2}{4} \right),
\]
which is asymptotically \(\chi^2\) with 2 degrees of freedom under normality (jarque1980efficient?).

jb = stats.jarque_bera(r)
print(f"skewness {stats.skew(r):.2f}, excess kurtosis {stats.kurtosis(r):.2f}")
print(f"JB = {jb.statistic:.1f}, p-value = {jb.pvalue:.2e}")

skewness -0.33, excess kurtosis 11.97
JB = 29942.3, p-value = 0.00e+00


The test depends on the fourth moment. For heavy-tailed returns the sample kurtosis fluctuates wildly between samples (cont2001empirical?), so read \(K\) as “far from 0”, not as a precise number.

title: Normality Tests
text:
Interpretation so far
The Q-Q plot shows how the data depart from the normal, which a p-value does not. The Jarque-Bera test gives a p-value but relies on moments that may not exist for heavy tails. Next you build a test based on the whole distribution function: Calibrated KS Test.

title: Comparing Networks under SIS
Comparing Networks under SIS
text:
Compare Network Types
With \(\beta = 0.2\) and \(\langle k \rangle \approx 6\) every network ends up with most nodes infected, so the structure hardly matters. The differences show up closer to the epidemic threshold, so Figure 1 uses \(\beta = 0.02\).






Exercise



Run 12 simulations for each graph type with \(N = 150\) and \(\beta = 0.02\), and plot the average infected fraction over time on the same axes. Use SEED + r for both the graph and the dynamics of run r.










Figure 1: Mean infected fraction over time for three network models with N = 150 and mean degree close to 6 (beta = 0.02, mu = 0.1, 12 runs each).











Solution





models = ["random", "small-world", "scale-free"]
N = 150
runs = 12
beta_compare = 0.02

for model in models:
    trajectories = []
    for r in range(runs):
        seed_run = SEED + r
        Gm = make_graph(model, n=N, seed=seed_run)
        counts = run_sis(Gm, beta=beta_compare, mu=mu, steps=steps,
                         initial_infected=initial_infected, seed=seed_run)
        trajectories.append(np.array(counts) / N)
    plt.plot(np.mean(trajectories, axis=0), label=model)

plt.xlabel("Time step")
plt.ylabel("Mean infected fraction")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

title: Comparing Networks under SIS
text:
Interpretation






Exercise



Compare Figure 1 with your prediction on SIS Model on Networks:

Which network type sustains infection longer at the same \((\beta, \mu)\)?
Do hubs (scale-free) make persistence easier? Why?
How does clustering (small-world) change local outbreaks vs global spread?
If you increase \(N\) but keep average degree similar, what do you expect to happen?









Solution






The scale-free graph. At \(\beta = 0.02\) it keeps close to 20% of its nodes infected, the random graph a few percent and the small-world graph almost none.
Yes. A hub has many neighbours, so it is reinfected soon after it recovers, and while infected it exposes many susceptible nodes. This is why the threshold \(\langle k \rangle / \langle k^2 \rangle\) of Epidemic Threshold is lower on heterogeneous networks.
In the small-world graph most neighbours of an infected node are also neighbours of each other. Many infection attempts hit nodes that are already infected, and the outbreak stays local for longer. Only the few rewired shortcuts carry it across the ring.
With 5 initial infected nodes, a larger \(N\) starts from a smaller infected fraction, so the curves take longer to rise. The long-time prevalence depends on the threshold. For the random and small-world graphs the threshold does not depend on \(N\) at fixed mean degree. For the Barabási-Albert graph \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) grows like \(\ln N\), so its threshold decreases slowly and persistence becomes easier.

title: Comparing Networks under SIS
text:
Limitations

Time is discrete and all nodes update at once. The continuous-time SIS model used in the theory of Epidemic Threshold has rates instead of probabilities; for small \(\beta\) and \(\mu\) the two are close.
The contact network is static. Real contacts change over time.
Every node has the same \(\beta\) and \(\mu\).
With \(N = 150\) and 12 runs the curves are noisy, and on a finite network SIS always dies out eventually, although this can take extremely long above the threshold.

title: Comparing Networks under SIS
text:
Optional extension






Exercise



Replace your loop-based simulator by amlab.networks_spreading.run_sis_fast, which uses a sparse adjacency matrix. Use it to plot the long-time prevalence against \(\beta\) for the three models with \(N = 1000\).








Solution





run_sis_fast returns the infected fraction at every step. Average the last 100 steps of a 500-step run to estimate the long-time prevalence.
from amlab.networks_spreading import run_sis_fast

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
betas = np.linspace(0.005, 0.06, 12)
for model in ["random", "small-world", "scale-free"]:
    G = make_graph(model, n=1000)
    prevalence = [
        np.mean(run_sis_fast(G, b, mu, steps=500, initial_infected=20, rng=rng)[-100:])
        for b in betas
    ]
    plt.plot(betas, prevalence, "o-", label=model)
plt.xlabel("beta")
plt.ylabel("long-time prevalence")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
With \(\mu = 0.1\) the scale-free graph already has a positive prevalence at \(\beta = 0.01\). The random graph needs \(\beta \approx 0.02\) and the small-world graph \(\beta \approx 0.025\). Above \(\beta \approx 0.04\) the three curves are close.

What’s Next?
Try the SIR model and compare how permanent immunity changes the outcome.
SIR on Networks

title: Vaccination Strategies
text: You have a limited number of vaccine doses. Which nodes should get them? On a heterogeneous network the answer matters much more than on a well-mixed population.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Three strategies

Random immunization. Vaccinate a fraction \(g\) of nodes chosen uniformly at random. In the heterogeneous mean-field picture this rescales the spreading rate to \(\lambda(1-g)\), so the epidemic stops when \(g > g_c = 1 - \lambda_c/\lambda\). For an infinite scale-free network with \(2 < \gamma \le 3\), \(\lambda_c \to 0\) and therefore \(g_c \to 1\): random vaccination would have to reach almost everyone (pastor2002immunization?).
Targeted immunization. Vaccinate the nodes with the highest degree. Removing hubs cuts \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) sharply, and a small fraction \(g\) is enough to restore a finite threshold (pastor2002immunization?). This needs the degree of every node, which you rarely know for a real population.
Acquaintance immunization. Pick a random node and vaccinate one of its random neighbours. A random neighbour has degree \(k\) with probability \(k p_k / \langle k \rangle\), so the method favours hubs without any global knowledge (cohen2003efficient?).

The three selection rules are in amlab.networks_spreading.






Core activity



Implement acquaintance immunization, then compare the final SIR epidemic size under the three strategies on a Barabási-Albert graph.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Rank the three strategies by the final epidemic size you expect at \(g = 0.1\). Where do you expect acquaintance immunization to fall?








Solution





Targeted immunization should give the smallest epidemic and random immunization the largest. Acquaintance immunization should fall in between: it reaches hubs more often than random selection, but less reliably than a list of the highest degrees. Figure 1 below confirms this ranking.

title: Vaccination Strategies
Vaccination Strategies
text:
Validation
Check the mean degree of the vaccinated nodes. Random selection should match the network mean up to sampling noise (with 100 nodes and a broad degree distribution, the noise is about \(\pm 0.6\)). Acquaintance selection should give a clearly higher value, and targeted selection the highest.

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

from amlab.networks_spreading import (
    acquaintance_immunization, random_immunization, run_sir_fast, targeted_immunization,
)

SEED = 7
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
G = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(1000, 3, seed=SEED)
deg = dict(G.degree())
print(f"network mean degree: {np.mean(list(deg.values())):.2f}")
for name, chosen in [
    ("random", random_immunization(G, 0.1, rng)),
    ("acquaintance", acquaintance_immunization(G, 0.1, rng)),
    ("targeted", targeted_immunization(G, 0.1)),
]:
    print(f"{name:>12}: mean degree of vaccinated nodes = {np.mean([deg[v] for v in chosen]):.2f}")

network mean degree: 5.98
      random: mean degree of vaccinated nodes = 7.35
acquaintance: mean degree of vaccinated nodes = 13.12
    targeted: mean degree of vaccinated nodes = 20.59

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Experiment
Figure 1 runs the discrete-time SIR model (\(\beta = 0.05\), \(\mu = 0.1\), 5 initial infected nodes) for each strategy and each coverage \(g\).








Figure 1: Mean final epidemic size (fraction of all nodes ever infected) against vaccination coverage g on a Barabási-Albert graph (N = 1000, m = 3). 20 runs per point.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Interpretation






Exercise



Read Figure 1 and answer:

How large must \(g\) be for each strategy to reduce the final size below 5%?
Acquaintance immunization uses only local information. How close does it get to the targeted strategy?
Is random vaccination useless on this network? Compare with the asymptotic statement \(g_c \to 1\) and remember that this graph is finite.









Solution






Targeted immunization needs \(g = 0.1\) (final size about 3%). Acquaintance immunization needs between \(g = 0.25\) and \(g = 0.3\). Random immunization never gets below 5% in the plotted range: at \(g = 0.3\) the final size is still about 40%.
It needs about two and a half to three times as many doses as the targeted strategy for the same effect, but it is far better than random selection at every coverage.
No. The final size falls steadily with \(g\), from about 73% to about 40% at \(g = 0.3\). On a finite graph \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) is finite, so \(g_c\) is below 1. It is still large, so random vaccination is the most expensive way to stop the epidemic.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Limitations

The graph is a model network with \(N = 1000\), not a real contact network.
Vaccination is perfect and permanent, and every vaccinated node is removed from the spreading process.
Targeted immunization assumes you know every degree exactly.
20 runs per point leave visible noise, especially near the threshold.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Optional extension






Exercise




Repeat the experiment on an Erdős-Rényi graph with the same mean degree. Does the choice of strategy still matter?
Target by betweenness instead of degree. Compare with the Motter-Lai trigger choice in Cascade Simulation.









Solution





Reuse G, rng, gs and strategies from the page. Swap the graph for an ER graph with \(p = 6/(N-1)\), and add a betweenness strategy.
G_er = nx.erdos_renyi_graph(1000, 6 / 999, seed=SEED)


def betweenness_ranking(G):
    """Nodes sorted by decreasing betweenness (approximate, 200 sources)."""
    bc = nx.betweenness_centrality(G, k=200, seed=SEED)
    return sorted(bc, key=bc.get, reverse=True)


for graph, label in [(G, "BA"), (G_er, "ER")]:
    ranking = betweenness_ranking(graph)
    selectors = {
        "random": lambda g: random_immunization(graph, g, rng),
        "acquaintance": lambda g: acquaintance_immunization(graph, g, rng),
        "targeted": lambda g: targeted_immunization(graph, g),
        "betweenness": lambda g: ranking[: int(round(g * graph.number_of_nodes()))],
    }
    for name, select in selectors.items():
        sizes = [
            np.mean([run_sir_fast(graph, 0.05, 0.1, initial_infected=5, immune=select(g), rng=rng) for _ in range(20)])
            for g in gs
        ]
        print(label, name, np.round(sizes, 2))

On the ER graph the strategies are much closer. The degrees are nearly all similar, so there are no hubs to target. Targeted immunization still wins, but it needs \(g \approx 0.25\) to push the final size to about 5%, against \(g = 0.1\) on the BA graph. Acquaintance immunization is barely better than random selection.
On the BA graph the betweenness ranking performs almost as well as the degree ranking, because the hubs are also the nodes with the largest betweenness. The same overlap explains why the highest-load and highest-degree triggers give the same cascade on the BA graph of Cascade Simulation. On the ER graph degree and betweenness rankings differ more, and the degree ranking is the better choice here.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Exit question






Exercise



A health agency cannot map the contact network but can ask people to name one contact. Which strategy from this page can it implement, and why does it work better than vaccinating the people it first reaches?








Solution





Acquaintance immunization. It vaccinates the named contacts, not the people first reached. A named contact is a random neighbour, and random neighbours have degree \(k\) with probability proportional to \(k p_k\), so they are more often hubs (cohen2003efficient?). Vaccinating hubs lowers \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) and raises the epidemic threshold.

title: SIR Simulation
SIR Simulation
text:
Implement the SIR Dynamics
The update is synchronous: compute all changes from the old state, then apply them.






Exercise



Write step_sir(G, beta, mu), one synchronous step of the SIR update. It differs from step_sis in one place: an infected node that recovers moves to “R”, and “R” nodes never change.
def step_sir(G, beta, mu):
    # TODO: read current states from G.nodes[u]["state"]
    # TODO: build new_state dict with values in {"S","I","R"}
    # TODO: write new_state back via nx.set_node_attributes
    return G








Solution






def step_sir(G, beta, mu):
    current = {u: G.nodes[u]["state"] for u in G.nodes()}
    new_state = current.copy()

    for u in G.nodes():
        if current[u] == "S":
            m = sum(1 for v in G.neighbors(u) if current[v] == "I")
            if m > 0:
                p_infect = 1 - (1 - beta) ** m
                if np.random.random() < p_infect:
                    new_state[u] = "I"

        elif current[u] == "I":
            if np.random.random() < mu:
                new_state[u] = "R"

        else:
            # "R" stays "R"
            pass

    nx.set_node_attributes(G, new_state, "state")
    return G










Exercise



Wrap step_sir into a simulator. Compared to SIS, you track all three counts: \(S(t), I(t), R(t)\). Stop early when no node is infected, since nothing can change after that.
def run_sir(G, beta, mu, steps=100, initial_infected=5, seed=SEED):
    # TODO
    return S_counts, I_counts, R_counts








Solution






def run_sir(G, beta, mu, steps=100, initial_infected=5, seed=SEED):
    H = G.copy()

    # Make the whole run reproducible (step_sir uses np.random.random)
    np.random.seed(seed)

    initialize_state(H, initial_infected=initial_infected, seed=seed)

    def counts(H):
        S = sum(H.nodes[u]["state"] == "S" for u in H.nodes())
        I = sum(H.nodes[u]["state"] == "I" for u in H.nodes())
        R = sum(H.nodes[u]["state"] == "R" for u in H.nodes())
        return S, I, R

    S0, I0, R0 = counts(H)
    S_counts = [S0]
    I_counts = [I0]
    R_counts = [R0]

    for _ in range(steps):
        if I_counts[-1] == 0:
            break
        step_sir(H, beta=beta, mu=mu)
        S, I, R = counts(H)
        S_counts.append(S)
        I_counts.append(I)
        R_counts.append(R)

    return S_counts, I_counts, R_counts

title: SIR Simulation
text:
Run and Visualize
The “epidemic curve” in SIR typically shows a single peak in \(I(t)\) and then decay to zero.








Figure 1: SIR epidemic curve (fractions of S, I, R over time) on one network realization.

title: SIR Simulation
text:
Key Questions to Answer
Here are two precise, testable questions that are specific to SIR:

Can the network become fully infected? That is, does there exist a time \(t\) such that \(I(t)=N\)?
Can the network become fully “healed”? That is, does there exist a time \(t\) such that \(I(t)=0\)?

In SIR, the second question has a clean answer:

Yes. For a finite graph with \(\mu>0\), you eventually reach \(I(t)=0\) and then you are stuck forever (absorbing state).

The first question depends on \((\beta,\mu)\) and the network. It can happen transiently, but it is not an absorbing state.






Exercise



Answer these questions, using Figure 1 and your own runs:

In SIR, is “fully healed” the same as “everyone is susceptible again”? Why not?
What does “final epidemic size” mean here? (Hint: look at \(R(\infty)\).)
Can you have an epidemic with a large peak but small final size? Or vice versa?
Compare two graphs with the same \(N\) and similar average degree: which features (hubs, clustering, path length) do you expect to increase \(R(\infty)\)?









Solution






No. When \(I = 0\) every node is either S or R. The recovered nodes stay immune, so the network does not return to its initial state. In SIS, by contrast, \(I = 0\) means everyone is susceptible again.
The final epidemic size is \(R(\infty)/N\), the fraction of nodes that were ever infected, including the initial ones. You read it from the last value of the R curve once \(I = 0\).
A large peak with a small final size is impossible: every node that is infected at the peak ends in R, so \(R(\infty) \ge \max_t I(t)\). The reverse is possible. On a ring or a lattice with few shortcuts the infection travels as a slow front: only a few nodes are infected at any time, but the front can eventually reach most of the network.
Hubs and short paths increase \(R(\infty)\). The SIR threshold \(T_c = \langle k \rangle / (\langle k^2 \rangle - \langle k \rangle)\) decreases when the degree distribution is broader (newman2002spread?), and short paths let the outbreak reach distant parts of the network before it dies out. High clustering tends to decrease \(R(\infty)\), because many infection attempts hit neighbours that are already infected or recovered.

title: SIR Simulation
text:
What’s Next?
Compare SIS and SIR: how does permanent immunity change the long-run outcome? The next page asks when an epidemic can spread at all.
Epidemic Threshold

title: Module 5: Complex Networks
text:
This module replaces the well-mixed populations of Modules 1 and 2 by networks: who interacts with whom is now given by a graph. You will measure the structure of networks, build the classical models of network growth, and study three processes whose outcome depends on that structure: percolation under node removal, cascades of overload failures, and epidemic spreading (newman2003structure?; Newman 2018). The code uses networkx (Hagberg, Schult, and Swart 2008). Reusable functions are in amlab/networks_cascades/ and amlab/networks_spreading/.

Session Structure
Session 23: Networks: fundamental concepts
Network Concepts Robustness and Percolation
Toolkit (self-study before the labs):
NetworkX Basics Drawing Graphs Paths and Components Centrality in NetworkX
Session 24: Laboratory: cascading failures in power grids
The Iberian Blackout The Motter-Lai Model Cascade Simulation Swing Equation
Session 25: Models of network growth
Erdős-Rényi Random Graphs Small-World Networks Preferential Attachment
Session 26: Laboratory: spreading processes on networks
SIS Model on Networks SIS Simulation SIR on Networks Epidemic Threshold Vaccination Strategies
Practice: Real Networks



Learning Goals
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

Represent a real system as a graph and load network data with networkx.
Compute and interpret degree distributions, path lengths, clustering, centrality and communities.
Apply the Molloy-Reed criterion to predict when a network keeps a giant component under random failure, and explain why targeted attacks are more damaging on heterogeneous networks.
Implement the Motter-Lai cascade model, validate it, and explain what it leaves out compared with a real power grid event.
Generate Erdős-Rényi, Watts-Strogatz and Barabási-Albert networks and relate their properties to the model rules.
Simulate SIS and SIR on networks with reproducible seeds, derive the threshold \(\lambda_c = \langle k \rangle / \langle k^2 \rangle\), and state the assumptions behind the vanishing threshold of scale-free networks.
Compare random, targeted and acquaintance vaccination.








References

Hagberg, Aric A., Daniel A. Schult, and Pieter J. Swart. 2008. “Exploring Network Structure, Dynamics, and Function Using NetworkX.” In Proceedings of the 7th Python in Science Conference (SciPy 2008), 11–15.


Newman, Mark. 2018. Networks. 2nd ed. Oxford University Press.

title: Paths in Directed Graphs
text:
Toolkit page



This page is self-study material for Session 23. It continues Paths and Components.
Start with a small directed graph: a food chain where each edge points from prey to predator.
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Create a directed graph
D_food_chain = nx.DiGraph()  # food chain (prey -> predator)
D_food_chain.add_edges_from([
    ("grass", "antelope"),
    ("grass", "zebra"),
    ("antelope", "lion"),
    ("antelope", "hyena"),
    ("zebra", "lion"),
    ("zebra", "hyena"),
    ("hyena", "lion"),
])

# Visualize the graph
pos = nx.spring_layout(D_food_chain)
nx.draw(D_food_chain, node_color="lightgreen", with_labels=True, pos=pos)

title: Paths in Directed Graphs
text:
Connectivity in Directed Graphs
Connectivity in directed graphs is more complex than in undirected graphs, because you have to consider the direction of the edges. In a directed graph, you can have strongly connected components and weakly connected components.

Paths in Directed Graphs
In a directed graph, a path must follow the direction of the edges. For example, in the directed food chain graph D_food_chain, is there a path from “grass” to “lion”?

# Draw the graph
pos = nx.spring_layout(D_food_chain)
nx.draw(D_food_chain, node_color="lightgreen", with_labels=True, pos=pos)
plt.show()








You can check for the existence of a path in a directed graph using the same has_path(<graph>, <node1>, <node2>) function:

print("Is there a path from 'grass' to 'lion'?", nx.has_path(D_food_chain, "grass", "lion"))   
print("Is there a path from 'lion' to 'grass'?", nx.has_path(D_food_chain, "lion", "grass"))

Is there a path from 'grass' to 'lion'? True
Is there a path from 'lion' to 'grass'? False




Strongly Connected Components
A strongly connected component is a subgraph in which there is a directed path from any node to any other node. A directed graph is strongly connected if it has only one strongly connected component.

print("Is strongly connected:", nx.is_strongly_connected(D_food_chain))
print("Strongly connected components:", list(nx.strongly_connected_components(D_food_chain)))

Is strongly connected: False
Strongly connected components: [{'lion'}, {'hyena'}, {'antelope'}, {'zebra'}, {'grass'}]




Weakly Connected Components
A weakly connected component is a subgraph in which there is an undirected path from any node to any other node. A directed graph is weakly connected if it has only one weakly connected component.

print("Is weakly connected:", nx.is_weakly_connected(D_food_chain))
print("Weakly connected components:", list(nx.weakly_connected_components(D_food_chain)))

Is weakly connected: True
Weakly connected components: [{'hyena', 'antelope', 'lion', 'zebra', 'grass'}]








Exercise



How can you turn D_food_chain into a strongly connected graph? Add as few edges as possible.








Solution





To make D_food_chain strongly connected, you need to ensure that there is a directed path from every node to every other node. One way to achieve this is to add edges that create cycles between the nodes. This example is a tough one, as food chains are typically acyclic. Still, you can take note from “The Lion King”:

“When we die, our bodies become the grass, and the antelope eat the grass. And so, we are all connected in the great Circle of Life.” - Mufasa (lion)


# When a predator dies, it returns to the food chain as prey for the grass
D_food_chain.add_edges_from([
    ("lion", "grass"),
])

# Visualize the new graph
pos = nx.spring_layout(D_food_chain)
nx.draw(D_food_chain, node_color="lightgreen", with_labels=True, pos=pos)
plt.show()









print("Is strongly connected:", nx.is_strongly_connected(D_food_chain))
print("Strongly connected components:", list(nx.strongly_connected_components(D_food_chain)))

Is strongly connected: True
Strongly connected components: [{'hyena', 'antelope', 'lion', 'zebra', 'grass'}]







Diameter and Average Path Length in Directed Graphs
The diameter and average path length in directed graphs are calculated based on the shortest paths that follow the direction of the edges. If the graph is not strongly connected, you can only calculate these metrics for the largest strongly connected component.

# Get the largest strongly connected component
largest_scc = max(nx.strongly_connected_components(D_food_chain), key=len)
subgraph = D_food_chain.subgraph(largest_scc)
print("Diameter of the largest strongly connected component:", nx.diameter(subgraph))
print("Average shortest path length of the largest strongly connected component:", nx.average_shortest_path_length(subgraph))

Diameter of the largest strongly connected component: 3
Average shortest path length of the largest strongly connected component: 1.85
