title: SIS Initial State
SIS Initial State
text:
Initialize States
Store the state of each individual directly on the graph as a node attribute called state.
For example, start with everyone susceptible: create the attribute “state” and set it to “S” for all nodes:

nx.set_node_attributes(G, "S", "state")

print("Node 0:", G.nodes[0])  # node attributes are stored in a dictionary

Node 0: {'state': 'S'}


To infect node 20:

node_20 = G.nodes[20]
node_20["state"] = "I"

print("Node 20:", G.nodes[20])  # now node 20 has state "I"

Node 20: {'state': 'I'}


Alternatively, use a dictionary to set the states of multiple nodes at once:

# Infect nodes 20, 35, and 50
# The rest will be susceptible by default
state_dict = {node: "I" if node in [20, 35, 50] else "S" for node in G.nodes()}
nx.set_node_attributes(G, state_dict, "state")

print("Node 20:", G.nodes[20])  # node 20 is infected
print("Node 21:", G.nodes[21])  # node 21 is susceptible

Node 20: {'state': 'I'}
Node 21: {'state': 'S'}








Exercise



Create a function initialize_state(<graph>) that sets all nodes to “S” and then randomly picks a few nodes to set to “I” (the initial infected). Use a seeded random number generator (np.random.default_rng(seed)) to pick the nodes.
def initialize_state(G, initial_infected=5, seed=SEED):
    # TODO: start everyone as 'S' using node attributes
    # TODO: randomly pick initial_infected nodes and set their node attribute to 'I'
    # Optional: return G (mutated) for convenience
    return G








Solution





The optional rng argument lets a whole simulation share one generator; you will need it on the next page.

def initialize_state(G, initial_infected=5, seed=SEED, rng=None):
    if rng is None:
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    # Start everyone susceptible
    nx.set_node_attributes(G, "S", "state")

    # Infect a random subset
    infected = rng.choice(list(G.nodes()), size=initial_infected, replace=False)
    for node in infected:
        G.nodes[node]["state"] = "I"

    return G




Always validate your functions. Here, check that the number of infected nodes is correct:

initialize_state(G, initial_infected=initial_infected, seed=SEED)
print(
    "Initially infected:",
    sum(G.nodes[node]["state"] == "I" for node in G.nodes()),
)

Initially infected: 5

title: Drawing Attributes
text:
Visualizing Attributes

Node Attributes
You can also visualize the attributes of nodes and edges by using different colors or sizes. For example, you can color the nodes based on their population attribute:

# Get the population attribute for each node
population = nx.get_node_attributes(G, 'population')
# Draw the graph with node sizes proportional to population
node_sizes = [population[node] / 1_000_000 for node in G.nodes()]  # scale down for visualization

pos = nx.circular_layout(G)

nx.draw(
    G,
    pos=pos,
    with_labels=True,
    node_color='lightblue',
    edge_color='gray',
    node_size=node_sizes,  # size of the nodes (vertices) proportional to population
    font_size=12,
    )
plt.show()














What happens if a node is missing an attribute?





In this case, the population dictionary will not have an entry for that node, and trying to access it will raise a KeyError. To avoid this, you can use the get() method of the dictionary, which lets you specify a default value if the key is not found. For example:

# Add a new node without the population attribute
G.add_edge("Denmark", "Germany", distance=400)
# Get the population attribute for each node, using 0 as default if not found
population = nx.get_node_attributes(G, 'population')
# Draw the graph with node sizes proportional to population
node_sizes = [population.get(node, 0) / 1_000_000 for node in G.nodes()]  # scale down for visualization

pos = nx.circular_layout(G)

nx.draw(
    G,
    pos=pos,
    with_labels=True,
    node_color='lightblue',
    edge_color='gray',
    node_size=node_sizes,  # size of the nodes (vertices) proportional to population
    font_size=12,
    )
plt.show()

















Exercise



Add a new attribute to the nodes, called “visited”, which is a boolean that indicates whether you have visited that country or not. Then, visualize the graph by coloring the nodes differently based on whether you have visited them or not: use blue for visited countries and red for unvisited countries.
G.nodes["Spain"]["visited"] = True
# TODO: set "visited" for the other countries

visited = nx.get_node_attributes(G, "visited")
node_colors = # TODO: one colour per node, "blue" if visited, else "red"
nx.draw(G, pos=nx.circular_layout(G), with_labels=True, node_color=node_colors)
plt.show()








Solution





Nodes without the attribute (here Netherlands, Germany and Denmark) count as not visited, thanks to visited.get(node, False).

# Add the "visited" attribute to the nodes
G.nodes["Spain"]["visited"] = True
G.nodes["Portugal"]["visited"] = True

title: Small-World Networks
text: A random graph has short paths but almost no clustering. A regular lattice has high clustering but long paths. Watts and Strogatz built a one-parameter model that interpolates between the two (Watts and Strogatz 1998).

title: Small-World Networks
text:
The model

Place \(N\) nodes on a ring and join each node to its \(k\) nearest neighbours (\(k/2\) on each side, \(k\) even).
Visit every edge \((u, v)\). With probability \(p\), replace it by \((u, w)\), where \(w\) is chosen uniformly among the nodes that are not already neighbours of \(u\).

At \(p = 0\) you have the ring lattice. At \(p = 1\) you have a graph close to a random graph with the same number of edges. The degree distribution stays narrow for every \(p\): every node keeps at least \(k/2\) edges.

title: Small-World Networks
text:
Key result
For the ring lattice, the clustering coefficient is \(C(0) = \frac{3(k-2)}{4(k-1)}\), which tends to \(3/4\) for large \(k\), and the average path length grows linearly with \(N\) (newman2003structure?). Watts and Strogatz found a wide range of small \(p\) in which \(L(p)\) has already dropped close to its random-graph value while \(C(p)\) is still close to \(C(0)\) (Watts and Strogatz 1998). A few random shortcuts are enough to shorten distances across the ring, while they destroy only a few triangles. Networks in this regime are called small-world networks. Watts and Strogatz reported the small-world property in a film actor collaboration network, the power grid of the western United States and the neural network of C. elegans (Watts and Strogatz 1998).
Figure 1 reproduces the shape of their Figure 2 on a smaller graph.








Figure 1: Watts-Strogatz model with N = 300 and k = 6. Average clustering C(p) and average path length L(p), both divided by their values at p = 0, averaged over 3 graphs per value of p.





C(0) = 0.600, formula 3(k-2)/(4(k-1)) = 0.600

title: Small-World Networks
text:
Implementation
In NetworkX, nx.watts_strogatz_graph(n, k, p) generates the model. The variant nx.connected_watts_strogatz_graph retries until the graph is connected, which you need to compute path lengths.

SEED = 7

G_sw = nx.watts_strogatz_graph(n=80, k=6, p=0.08, seed=SEED)
pos = nx.circular_layout(G_sw)
nx.draw(G_sw, pos=pos, node_size=40, node_color="lightblue", edge_color="gray")
plt.title("Watts-Strogatz graph, N = 80, k = 6, p = 0.08")
plt.show()

degrees = [d for _, d in G_sw.degree()]
print("degree range:", min(degrees), "to", max(degrees))
print(f"C = {nx.average_clustering(G_sw):.3f}")








degree range: 4 to 7
C = 0.494


The circular layout keeps the ring visible, so you can spot the rewired shortcuts.






Exercise



Compute \(C\) and \(L\) for nx.watts_strogatz_graph(80, 6, p) with \(p = 0\), \(p = 0.08\) and \(p = 1\). Which value of \(p\) gives a small-world network?








Solution





for p in [0, 0.08, 1]:
    G = nx.connected_watts_strogatz_graph(80, 6, p, seed=SEED)
    print(p, round(nx.average_clustering(G), 3), round(nx.average_shortest_path_length(G), 2))
At \(p = 0.08\) the clustering is still close to the lattice value (\(C(0) = 0.6\)), while \(L\) has dropped well below its lattice value. At \(p = 1\) both are close to random-graph values.



The model explains short paths together with high clustering. It does not produce hubs: for that you need preferential attachment.

title: SIS Model on Networks
text:
Reading




Compulsory: (pastor2001epidemic?).
Recommended: Pastor-Satorras et al. (2015); (newman2002spread?).
In Module 1 you wrote the SIS model as an ODE for a well-mixed population. Here every individual is a node, and infection travels only along edges (Keeling and Rohani 2008; Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015). You will implement SIS on networks with NetworkX and measure how network structure (random, small-world, scale-free) changes the spread.

title: SIS Model on Networks
text:
What is the SIS Model?

States: each node is Susceptible (S) or Infected (I).
Transitions:

\(S \to I\): infection through contacts (controlled by \(\beta\)).
\(I \to S\): recovery (controlled by \(\mu\)).

No permanent immunity: recovered nodes can be reinfected.


Discrete-Time Update Rule
You simulate in discrete time steps \(t = 0, 1, 2, \dots\).
A susceptible node with \(m\) infected neighbors becomes infected with probability (Keeling and Rohani 2008):
\[
\mathbb{P}(S \to I) = 1 - (1 - \beta)^m.
\]






Why \(1 - (1-\beta)^m\)?





If each infected neighbor independently infects you with probability \(\beta\), then the probability you avoid infection from all \(m\) neighbors is \((1-\beta)^m\). So the probability of at least one successful infection is \(1-(1-\beta)^m\).



On the other hand, if a node is infected, it recovers with probability:
\[
\mathbb{P}(I \to S) = \mu.
\]

title: SIS Model on Networks
text:
Prediction
You will compare random (Erdős-Rényi), small-world (Watts-Strogatz) and scale-free (Barabási-Albert) graphs. Try sizes such as \(N \in \{50, 100, 300\}\), run 10 to 30 repetitions for each case and plot the average infected fraction over time.






Exercise



Answer these questions before you write any code:

Take a random graph and a scale-free graph with the same \(N\) and the same mean degree. With the same \((\beta, \mu)\), which one do you expect to sustain more infection?
What should happen to the infected fraction when \(\beta = 0\)?









Solution






The scale-free graph. Its hubs have many neighbours, so they are infected early and often, and each infected hub exposes many susceptible nodes. In the language of Epidemic Threshold, its larger \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) lowers the threshold.
Nobody can be infected, so the infected nodes only recover. Each one stays infected with probability \(1 - \mu\) per step, and the expected number of infected nodes decays as \(I(0)(1-\mu)^t\). You will use this case to validate your code.

title: SIS Model on Networks
text:
Imports and Parameters

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

These are the parameters you can tune:

SEED = 7

# Model parameters
beta = 0.20  # infection probability per infected neighbor (per step)
mu = 0.10    # recovery probability (per step)

# Simulation parameters
steps = 120  # number of time steps to simulate
initial_infected = 5  # should always be < N
N = 100  # number of nodes in the graph







About SEED (why you fix it)



There are two sources of randomness in this activity:

the graph you generate (e.g., which edges appear in Erdős-Rényi), and
the stochastic SIS dynamics (who gets infected / recovers at each step).

You fix SEED so results are reproducible: rerunning the page gives the same plots, which makes debugging and reporting possible.
When you run many repetitions, you use SEED + r so repetition r is a different random trial (new graph + new random infection events) but still reproducible. If you reused the same SEED in every repetition, you would repeat the same realization and your “average over runs” would be meaningless.

title: SIS Model on Networks
text:
Choose a Network
You will compare several models. Start by picking one. The three models are described in Erdős-Rényi Random Graphs, Small-World Networks and Preferential Attachment.






Example of Baseline Graph





G = nx.erdos_renyi_graph(n=N, p=0.08, seed=SEED)
# where p is the probability of edge creation



To make the comparison fair, all three graphs should have about the same mean degree, here \(\langle k \rangle \approx 6\).






Exercise



Implement a helper function make_graph(<model>, <n>), where <model> is a string specifying the type of graph (“random”, “small-world” or “scale-free”) and <n> is the number of nodes. Choose the parameters so that the mean degree is close to 6.
def make_graph(model: str, n: int, seed: int = SEED):
    """Create a graph model with mean degree close to 6: 'random', 'small-world', or 'scale-free'."""
    # TODO
    return G








Solution





The mean degree is \((n-1)p\) for \(G(n, p)\), \(k\) for Watts-Strogatz and about \(2m\) for Barabási-Albert.

def make_graph(model: str, n: int, seed: int = SEED):
    if model == "random":
        return nx.erdos_renyi_graph(n=n, p=6 / (n - 1), seed=seed)
    if model == "small-world":
        return nx.watts_strogatz_graph(n=n, k=6, p=0.08, seed=seed)
    if model == "scale-free":
        return nx.barabasi_albert_graph(n=n, m=3, seed=seed)
    raise ValueError("model must be one of: 'random', 'small-world', 'scale-free'")




Now you can easily create different graph types:

G = make_graph("random", n=100)
print("N, E =", G.number_of_nodes(), G.number_of_edges())

N, E = 100 317


Optional quick visualization:

pos = nx.spring_layout(G)
nx.draw(G, pos=pos, node_size=50, edge_color="gray")
plt.title("Baseline network")
plt.show()

    Returns G_ratio = (largest component after the cascade) / N.
    """

    capacity = # TODO: (1 + alpha) * initial load, for every node
    H = G.copy()
    H.remove_node(trigger)
    while True:

Solved: node_loads() and run_cascade()





def node_loads(G):
    return nx.betweenness_centrality(G, normalized=False)


def run_cascade(G, trigger, alpha, tol=1e-9):
    loads0 = node_loads(G)
    capacity = {v: (1 + alpha) * load for v, load in loads0.items()}
    H = G.copy()
    H.remove_node(trigger)
    while True:
        loads = node_loads(H)
        overloaded = [v for v, load in loads.items() if load > capacity[v] + tol]
        if not overloaded:
            break
        H.remove_nodes_from(overloaded)
    largest = max(nx.connected_components(H), key=len) if len(H) else set()
    return len(largest) / G.number_of_nodes()
The small tolerance tol protects the test load > capacity from rounding errors: with \(\alpha = 0\) an unchanged load must not count as an overload.

title: Cascade Simulation
text:
Validation
Check your code on cases with a known answer before you trust any plot. The chunk below uses the amlab version; run the same checks on yours.

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

from amlab.networks_cascades import run_cascade, select_trigger, cascade_curve

# A cycle has equal loads everywhere. Removing one node turns it into a path.
C = nx.cycle_graph(12)
print("cycle, alpha = 10:", run_cascade(C, 0, alpha=10).G_ratio, "expected", 11 / 12)

# The centre of a star carries every shortest path.
S = nx.star_graph(10)
print("star, centre removed:", run_cascade(S, 0, alpha=1).G_ratio, "expected", 1 / 11)

# Very large alpha: only the trigger is lost on a well-connected graph.
G = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(100, 3, seed=1)
r = run_cascade(G, select_trigger(G, "load"), alpha=100)
print("BA, alpha = 100: failed per step", r.failed_per_step)

cycle, alpha = 10: 0.9166666666666666 expected 0.9166666666666666
star, centre removed: 0.09090909090909091 expected 0.09090909090909091
BA, alpha = 100: failed per step [1]








Exercise



Explain the output for the cycle with \(\alpha = 10\). Then predict what happens on the same cycle with \(\alpha = 0\) and check it.








Solution





After the removal the cycle becomes a path of 11 nodes. Loads grow near the middle of the path, but with \(\alpha = 10\) no node exceeds its capacity, so \(G = 11/12\). With \(\alpha = 0\) the nodes near the middle of the path carry more shortest paths than before, so they fail and the cascade cuts the path into pieces. Run run_cascade(C, 0, alpha=0) to see the final value.

title: Cascade Simulation
text:
Experiment
Now sweep \(\alpha\). For random triggers, average over several trials. The graphs have \(N = 150\) nodes and the same number of edges, so the executed chunk stays fast.








Figure 1: Relative size G of the largest component after a Motter-Lai cascade, as a function of the tolerance alpha. Barabási-Albert (BA) and Erdős-Rényi (ER) graphs with N = 150 and the same number of edges. Random triggers are averaged over 5 trials.

title: Cascade Simulation
text:
Interpretation
Compare Figure 1 with your predictions:

For which graph and which trigger does the cascade stay small at small \(\alpha\)?
How large must \(\alpha\) be before the highest-load trigger stops causing a large cascade on the BA graph?
Motter and Lai found that heterogeneous networks are fragile to load-based attacks (motter2002cascade?). Does your plot agree? With a single graph realization of 150 nodes, which features of the curves would you trust and which not?

title: Cascade Simulation
text:
Limitations

Load follows shortest paths. Electric power follows Kirchhoff’s laws and spreads over all parallel paths.
The model has no time: the redistribution is instantaneous. (schafer2018dynamically?) show that transient dynamics of a few seconds matter for real grid cascades.
Every node has the same relative margin \(\alpha\). Real equipment has heterogeneous limits and protection settings.
A node fails deterministically as soon as \(L_i > C_i\).
A single BA graph with \(N = 150\) gives noisy curves. Average over several graphs before you draw conclusions.







Optional extension




Average the curves over 10 graph realizations and add error bars.
Replace the trigger “highest load” with “highest degree” (select_trigger(G, "degree")). Do the two rankings give the same cascade?
Load a real network from data/ (for example the USA flights graph) and repeat the sweep on its largest component. Use nx.betweenness_centrality(G, k=..., seed=...) if the exact computation is too slow.

title: SIR on Networks
text:
The SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered) model adds permanent immunity to SIS: once a node recovers, it cannot be infected again (Kermack and McKendrick 1927; Keeling and Rohani 2008). You met its ODE version in Compartmental Models. On a network, the final size of an SIR outbreak is closely related to bond percolation, and the mapping is exact when every infected node stays infectious for the same time (newman2002spread?). This links the page to Robustness and Percolation.
This page reuses the graph models and node attributes of the SIS pages and focuses on what is new:

title: SIR on Networks
text:
What is the SIR Model?

States: Each node can be Susceptible (S), Infected (I), or Recovered (R).
Transitions:

\(S \to I\): a susceptible node becomes infected through infected neighbors.
\(I \to R\): an infected node recovers and becomes permanently immune.

Permanent immunity: \(R\) is an absorbing state (once recovered, always recovered).


Discrete-Time Update Rule
You simulate in discrete time steps \(t = 0, 1, 2, \dots\).
If a susceptible node has \(m\) infected neighbors, use the same “independent trials” rule as SIS (Keeling and Rohani 2008):
\[
\mathbb{P}(S \to I) = 1 - (1 - \beta)^m.
\]
If a node is infected, it recovers with probability:
\[
\mathbb{P}(I \to R) = \mu.
\]
Recovered nodes stay recovered:
\[
\mathbb{P}(R \to R) = 1.
\]






What changes compared to SIS?





In SIS, \(I \to S\) (you become susceptible again). In SIR, \(I \to R\) (you become immune). That single change alters the long-term behaviour.





Related Rumor Model
If you want one extra reference beyond SIR, a classical rumor counterpart is the Daley-Kendall model (Ignorant -> Spreader -> Stifler), where spreaders become stiflers after contact with spreaders/stiflers (Daley and Kendall 1965).

title: SIR on Networks
text:
Absorbing States
On a finite graph with \(\mu > 0\), the process reaches a time \(T\) such that there are no infected nodes (\(I(T)=0\)), and after that nothing can ever change (Keeling and Rohani 2008; Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015).
Each node can become infected at most once (because \(R\) is permanent), so there can be at most \(N\) infection events. Since recovery happens with positive probability, infections cannot persist forever.
This means SIR always ends in a “frozen” configuration containing only \(S\) and \(R\) nodes.

title: Robustness and Percolation
text: How much of a network can you remove before it falls apart? You measure the answer with the giant component: the largest connected component, when its size is a finite fraction of \(N\). Let \(S(f)\) be the fraction of the original nodes that stay in the largest component after you remove a fraction \(f\) of the nodes. Removing nodes and asking whether a giant component survives is a site percolation problem (callaway2000network?; newman2003structure?).

title: Robustness and Percolation
text:
The Molloy-Reed criterion
Consider a random graph with a given degree distribution \(p_k\) and no other structure (the configuration model). Molloy and Reed proved that, as \(N \to \infty\), a giant component exists almost surely when
\[
\sum_k k(k-2)\, p_k > 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \kappa \equiv \frac{\langle k^2 \rangle}{\langle k \rangle} > 2,
\]
and does not exist when the sum is negative (molloy1995critical?). The intuition: follow a random edge to a node. That node has on average \(\kappa - 1\) further edges. The branching process started this way keeps growing when \(\kappa - 1 > 1\).

title: Robustness and Percolation
text:
Random failure
Remove each node independently with probability \(f\). Cohen et al. applied the criterion to the diluted graph and found the critical fraction (cohen2000resilience?)
\[
f_c = 1 - \frac{1}{\kappa_0 - 1}, \qquad \kappa_0 = \frac{\langle k^2 \rangle}{\langle k \rangle} \text{ of the intact network.}
\]

For an Erdős-Rényi graph, \(p_k\) is Poisson, \(\kappa_0 = \langle k \rangle + 1\), and \(f_c = 1 - 1/\langle k \rangle\).
For a scale-free distribution \(p_k \sim k^{-\gamma}\) with \(2 < \gamma \le 3\), \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) diverges as \(N \to \infty\), so \(f_c \to 1\). An infinite network of this type keeps a giant component under almost any rate of random failure. A finite network has a finite \(\kappa_0\) and a threshold \(f_c < 1\) (cohen2000resilience?).

title: Robustness and Percolation
text:
Targeted attack
Now remove the nodes with the highest degree first. Albert, Jeong and Barabási showed in simulations that scale-free networks are tolerant to random failure but fragile under this attack: removing a few hubs breaks them apart much faster than an Erdős-Rényi graph with the same \(N\) and \(E\) (albert2000error?). Callaway et al. derived the same behaviour analytically for degree-dependent removal (callaway2000network?).

title: Robustness and Percolation
text:
Generated example
Figure 1 compares a Barabási-Albert graph with an Erdős-Rényi graph that has the same number of nodes and edges. The attack uses the degree ranking of the intact graph.


BA: <k> = 3.99, kappa0 = 11.13, predicted f_c (random) = 0.90
ER: <k> = 3.99, kappa0 = 4.92, predicted f_c (random) = 0.75








Figure 1: Fraction of nodes in the largest component after removing a fraction f of nodes, at random (circles) or by decreasing degree (squares). N = 1000,  close to 4. Dashed lines: the Cohen et al. prediction f_c for random failure, computed from the degree sequence of each graph.





The prediction assumes an uncorrelated configuration model with \(N \to \infty\). The ER curve reaches zero close to its dashed line. The BA curve drops earlier than predicted, since the formula ignores finite-size effects and the degree correlations of the BA model. The qualitative result survives: under attack, the BA graph breaks apart after the removal of about 20% of its nodes, far earlier than under random failure.






Exercise



Use the formula for \(f_c\) to predict the random-failure threshold of an Erdős-Rényi graph with \(\langle k \rangle = 2\) and with \(\langle k \rangle = 10\).








Solution





\(f_c = 1 - 1/\langle k \rangle\) gives \(f_c = 0.5\) for \(\langle k \rangle = 2\) and \(f_c = 0.9\) for \(\langle k \rangle = 10\). A denser random graph survives the removal of a larger fraction of nodes. At \(\langle k \rangle = 1\) the intact graph is already at its percolation threshold.

title: Preferential Attachment
text: Neither the random graph nor the small-world model produces hubs. Many real networks have heavy-tailed degree distributions, sometimes close to a power law \(p_k \sim k^{-\gamma}\) (Barabasi and Albert 1999; newman2003structure?). Barabási and Albert proposed that two ingredients generate such a distribution: growth and preferential attachment (Barabasi and Albert 1999).

title: Preferential Attachment
text:
The Barabási-Albert model

Start with a small network of \(m_0 \ge m\) nodes.
At each step add one new node with \(m\) edges.
Each new edge goes to an existing node \(i\) with probability proportional to its degree, \[
\Pi(k_i) = \frac{k_i}{\sum_j k_j}.
\]
Repeat until the network has \(N\) nodes.

The mean degree tends to \(\langle k \rangle = 2m\).

title: Preferential Attachment
text:
Key results

In the limit of large \(N\), the degree distribution is \[
p_k = \frac{2m(m+1)}{k(k+1)(k+2)} \sim k^{-3}, \qquad k \ge m,
\] so the exponent is \(\gamma = 3\) (newman2003structure?; Newman 2018).
The degrees of the oldest nodes grow like \(\sqrt{t}\), so the largest degree grows like \(k_{\max} \sim m\sqrt{N}\) (Barabasi and Albert 1999; Newman 2018).
With \(\gamma = 3\) the second moment diverges logarithmically. Summing \(k^2 p_k\) up to \(k_{\max}\) gives \(\langle k^2 \rangle \approx m(m+1)\ln N\) for large \(N\). The degree variance \(\langle k^2 \rangle - \langle k \rangle^2\) therefore grows without bound as \(N\) grows, even though the mean stays at \(2m\).
The average path length is small, and the clustering is low and decreases with \(N\) (newman2003structure?).

The divergence of \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) drives two results of this module: the robustness to random failure in Robustness and Percolation and the vanishing epidemic threshold in Epidemic Threshold. Keep in mind that the divergence is slow: at realistic sizes \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) is large but finite.

title: Preferential Attachment
text:
Implementation
In NetworkX, nx.barabasi_albert_graph(n, m) adds nodes one at a time, each with m edges attached by preferential attachment.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

SEED = 7

G_sf = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(n=200, m=2, seed=SEED)
pos = nx.spring_layout(G_sf, seed=SEED)
size = [5 * d for _, d in G_sf.degree()]
nx.draw(G_sf, pos=pos, node_size=size, node_color="lightgreen", edge_color="gray", alpha=0.8)
plt.title("Barabási-Albert graph, N = 200, m = 2")
plt.show()

title: Preferential Attachment
text:
Degree distribution and second moment
Figure 1 compares the empirical distribution with the exact formula. Use logarithmic bins or the complementary cumulative distribution for real data; here the formula lets you compare point by point.








Figure 1: Left: degree distribution of one Barabási-Albert graph (N = 20000, m = 2) against p_k = 2m(m+1)/(k(k+1)(k+2)). Right: second moment of the degree against N, with the approximation m(m+1) ln N (dashed).





The approximation \(m(m+1)\ln N\) follows the simulated values closely over two decades of \(N\). The small deviations come from the approximations in the sum (the lower limit \(k = m\) and the cutoff at \(k_{\max}\)) and from fluctuations of the largest degrees.






Exercise



Compute the mean and the variance of the degree for nx.barabasi_albert_graph(N, 2) with \(N = 10^3\) and \(N = 10^4\). Which one changes?








Solution





for N in [1_000, 10_000]:
    k = np.array([d for _, d in nx.barabasi_albert_graph(N, 2, seed=SEED).degree()])
    print(N, k.mean().round(2), k.var().round(1))
The mean stays close to \(2m = 4\). The variance grows with \(N\), as the logarithmic divergence of \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) predicts.









Other scale-free generators in NetworkX






nx.powerlaw_cluster_graph(n, m, p, seed=...) adds a triangle-closing step to preferential attachment, which raises the clustering.
nx.scale_free_graph(n, seed=...) returns a directed multigraph.
nx.configuration_model(degree_sequence, seed=...) builds a random graph with any degree sequence you choose.

For this course, nx.barabasi_albert_graph is usually the best starting point.

    d1 = slider_d1.val
    d2 = slider_d2.val
    f = slider_f.val
    k = slider_k.val

title: Gray-Scott: Sliders
text:
Put It Together
Inside your animation callback, respect the pause flag before advancing the PDE.
def update_frame(_):
    nonlocal uv
    if pause:
        return [im]

    for _ in range(anim_speed):
        uv = uv + gray_scott_pde(0, uv, d1=d1, d2=d2, f=f, k=k) * dt

    im.set_array(uv[1])
    return [im]
This setup is enough to create your own Gray-Scott experiments. Try drawing thin lines, large blobs, or repeated point sources and see which parameter sets erase the perturbation and which ones amplify it.

title: Gray-Scott: Sliders
text:
Exit question






Exercise



You move the slider for \(d_1\) from \(0.1\) to \(0.2\) while keeping \(dx = 1\) and \(dt = 2\). What happens to the simulation, and why?








Solution





It blows up. The 2D explicit Euler bound is \(dt \le dx^2/(4 d_1)\), which drops from \(2.5\) to \(1.25\), so \(dt = 2\) is now unstable and a grid-scale checkerboard grows. Reduce \(dt\) below \(1.25\) when you increase \(d_1\) (Time-Step Stability).

title: Time-Step Stability
text: Explicit Euler is simple, but it is only conditionally stable for diffusion. If \(dt\) is too large for the grid, the simulation produces a pattern that is not in the PDE and then overflows. This page derives the bound, shows the artefact, and gives a convergence check you should run before trusting any reaction-diffusion figure (leveque2007finite?).

title: Time-Step Stability
text:
The Stability Bound in 1D
Apply explicit Euler and the 3-point Laplacian to pure diffusion \(u_t = D\,u_{xx}\):
\[
u_j^{n+1} = u_j^n + r\left(u_{j+1}^n - 2u_j^n + u_{j-1}^n\right), \qquad r = \frac{D\,dt}{dx^2}.
\]
Insert a Fourier mode \(u_j^n = G^n e^{i k j\,dx}\) (von Neumann analysis). The amplification factor per step is
\[
G(k) = 1 - 4r\sin^2\left(\frac{k\,dx}{2}\right).
\tag{1}\]
The scheme is stable when \(|G| \le 1\) for every \(k\). The worst case is the grid-scale sawtooth \(k = \pi/dx\), where \(G = 1 - 4r\). Requiring \(1 - 4r \ge -1\) gives
\[
dt \le \frac{dx^2}{2D} \quad \text{(1D)}.
\tag{2}\]

title: Time-Step Stability
text:
The Bound in 2D
With the 5-point stencil, the same argument gives \(G = 1 - 4r\left[\sin^2(k_x dx/2) + \sin^2(k_y dx/2)\right]\). The worst mode is the checkerboard, with \(G = 1 - 8r\), so
\[
dt \le \frac{dx^2}{4D} \quad \text{(2D, 5-point stencil)}.
\tag{3}\]
For a system, use the largest diffusion coefficient. In the Gierer-Meinhardt scaling that is \(d\). The reaction terms add a further, usually weaker, restriction (leveque2007finite?).

from amlab.turing import euler_dt_max

settings = [
    ("GM 1D, d = 30, dx = 1", 1.0, 30.0, 1, 0.01),
    ("GM 1D, d = 30, dx = 0.5", 0.5, 30.0, 1, 0.001),
    ("GM 2D, d = 30, dx = 1", 1.0, 30.0, 2, 0.005),
    ("Gray-Scott 2D, D1 = 0.1, dx = 1", 1.0, 0.1, 2, 2.0),
]
for label, dx, diff, ndim, dt in settings:
    bound = euler_dt_max(dx, diff, ndim)
    print(f"{label:34s} bound = {bound:.5f}   dt used = {dt:<6} ok: {dt <= bound}")

GM 1D, d = 30, dx = 1              bound = 0.01667   dt used = 0.01   ok: True
GM 1D, d = 30, dx = 0.5            bound = 0.00417   dt used = 0.001  ok: True
GM 2D, d = 30, dx = 1              bound = 0.00833   dt used = 0.005  ok: True
Gray-Scott 2D, D1 = 0.1, dx = 1    bound = 2.50000   dt used = 2.0    ok: True

title: Time-Step Stability
text:
A Numerical Artefact
Figure 1 runs Case A (\(d = 30\), \(dx = 1\)), where the bound is \(1/60 \approx 0.0167\), with \(dt = 0.016\) and \(dt = 0.018\).








Figure 1: Left: maximum deviation from the steady state for two time steps. Right: profile of \(v\) for \(dt = 0.018\) after 25 steps, showing the grid-scale sawtooth that the PDE does not contain.





With \(dt = 0.016\) the noise decays within a few time units and the deviation then stays small. The Turing mode grows only at rate \(\sigma \approx 0.02\), so it becomes visible on longer runs. With \(dt = 0.018\) the deviation grows by a fixed factor per step, close to \(|1 - 4r| = 1.16\), and the profile alternates up and down between neighbouring points. That sawtooth is the signature of a violated stability bound. Do not interpret it as a pattern.

title: Time-Step Stability
text:
A Convergence Check
A stable run can still be inaccurate. To check, refine the grid and compare. The Laplacian error is \(\mathcal{O}(dx^2)\) and the Euler error is \(\mathcal{O}(dt)\).
Refining is subtle: if you halve \(dx\) and only halve \(dt\), the ratio \(dt/dx^2\) doubles and you can cross the bound. Starting from \(dx = 1\), \(dt = 0.01\), halving both gives \(dt = 0.005 > 0.25/60\), which is unstable. Divide \(dt\) by four whenever you halve \(dx\).
The check below uses periodic boundaries and a smooth initial perturbation, so the coarse grid points are a subset of the fine ones. It compares successive refinements \(e_1 = \max|w_h - w_{h/2}|\) and \(e_2 = \max|w_{h/2} - w_{h/4}|\) at \(t = 50\). The observed order is \(p = \log_2(e_1/e_2)\).

import numpy as np

from amlab.turing import simulate_gm_1d


def smooth_start(x, length=40.0):
    mode3 = np.cos(6 * np.pi * x / length)
    return 0.01 * np.array([mode3 + 0.5 * np.cos(10 * np.pi * x / length), mode3])


def run(dx, dt):
    return simulate_gm_1d(d=30.0, dx=dx, dt=dt, t_end=50.0, bc="periodic", initial=smooth_start)[1]


space = [run(1.0, 0.01), run(0.5, 0.0025), run(0.25, 0.000625)]
e1 = np.max(np.abs(space[0] - space[1][:, ::2]))
e2 = np.max(np.abs(space[1] - space[2][:, ::2]))
print(f"space and time (dx halved, dt / 4): e1 = {e1:.2e}, e2 = {e2:.2e}, p = {np.log2(e1 / e2):.2f}")

time = [run(1.0, 0.01), run(1.0, 0.005), run(1.0, 0.0025)]
e1 = np.max(np.abs(time[0] - time[1]))
e2 = np.max(np.abs(time[1] - time[2]))
print(f"time only (dx = 1, dt halved):     e1 = {e1:.2e}, e2 = {e2:.2e}, p = {np.log2(e1 / e2):.2f}")

space and time (dx halved, dt / 4): e1 = 1.53e-03, e2 = 3.91e-04, p = 1.97
time only (dx = 1, dt halved):     e1 = 2.23e-06, e2 = 1.11e-06, p = 1.00


The first line gives \(p \approx 2\), the expected second order. The second gives \(p \approx 1\), the order of explicit Euler. The time error at \(dt = 0.01\) is much smaller than the space error at \(dx = 1\), so for this problem \(dx\) controls the accuracy. In your own work, report both checks.






Exercise



You run Gierer-Meinhardt in 2D with \(d = 30\) and \(dx = 1\). What is the largest stable \(dt\)? Would \(dt = 0.01\), which is safe in 1D, work?








Solution





The 2D bound is \(dx^2/(4d) = 1/120 \approx 0.0083\). So \(dt = 0.01\) is unstable in 2D, even though it is stable in 1D. The 2D solver page uses \(dt = 0.005\) and \(dt = 0.008\).

title: Boundary Conditions
text: In the ODE sessions the solver handled all the bookkeeping. In a PDE the boundary conditions are part of the model, and they decide which spatial modes exist (Laplacian Eigenmodes). With explicit Euler you enforce them by hand after every update.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Three Common Choices








Condition
Meaning
Implementation after each Euler step




Periodic
The ends are identified, \(u(0) = u(L)\)
Nothing: np.roll already wraps


Neumann (zero flux)
No material crosses the boundary, \(u_x = 0\)
Copy the nearest interior value onto the edge


Dirichlet (fixed value)
The boundary is held at a prescribed value
Overwrite the edge with that value




Neumann boundary conditions
Zero flux means zero slope at the boundary. A simple implementation copies the nearest interior value:
\[
u_0 = u_1, \qquad u_{N-1} = u_{N-2}.
\tag{1}\]
This sets the difference \((u_1 - u_0)/dx\) to zero. As an approximation of \(u_x = 0\) at \(x_0\) it is only first order in \(dx\). As a centered difference it is second order at the midpoint \(x_0 + dx/2\), so in effect the zero-flux boundaries sit halfway between the first two and the last two grid points. The effective domain length is \((N-2)\,dx\), not \(N\,dx\). It is the scheme used in the course package and in the assignment. Ghost-point schemes that place the boundary exactly exist (leveque2007finite?).
On a fine grid the difference in length is small. On a coarse grid it can shift a mode into or out of the unstable band (see the optional extension on Animal Coat Patterns).


Periodic boundary conditions
The left and right endpoints are neighbours. The rolled Laplacian from Laplacian in 1D is already correct, so no extra step is needed.


Dirichlet boundary conditions
You prescribe fixed values, for example the steady state \((u_*, v_*)\), and write them into the edges.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Implement a Boundary Helper






Exercise



Write one helper that applies any of the three conditions to a (2, N) array after each Euler step.
def apply_boundary_conditions_1d(uv, bc="neumann", dirichlet_values=(1.4, 1.96)):
    # TODO: periodic: return uv unchanged
    # TODO: neumann: copy index 1 onto 0 and index -2 onto -1, for both species
    # TODO: dirichlet: write dirichlet_values into both ends
    return uv








Solution





def apply_boundary_conditions_1d(uv, bc="neumann", dirichlet_values=(1.4, 1.96)):
    if bc == "periodic":
        return uv
    if bc == "neumann":
        uv[:, 0] = uv[:, 1]
        uv[:, -1] = uv[:, -2]
        return uv
    if bc == "dirichlet":
        for species, value in enumerate(dirichlet_values):
            uv[species, 0] = value
            uv[species, -1] = value
        return uv
    raise ValueError("bc must be 'periodic', 'neumann', or 'dirichlet'")

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Why the Choice Matters
The boundary condition changes the admissible wavenumbers. On \((0, 40)\) the Neumann modes are \(k_n = n\pi/40\), while periodic modes are \(k_n = 2n\pi/40\), so the periodic spectrum is twice as sparse.

from amlab.turing import unstable_modes_1d

for bc in ("neumann", "periodic"):
    print(bc, unstable_modes_1d(a=0.40, b=1.00, d=30.0, length=40.0, bc=bc))

neumann [(5, 0.021415536663643042), (6, 0.020554871787465512)]
periodic [(3, 0.020554871787465512)]


With Neumann conditions modes \(5\) and \(6\) grow. With periodic conditions only mode \(3\) (wavenumber \(6\pi/40 \approx 0.47\)) is unstable, which equals the Neumann mode \(6\).






Warning



The periodic option of amlab.pdes_1d.find_unstable_spatial_modes uses the wavenumbers \((n+1)\pi/L\), which are the Neumann wavenumbers shifted by one index, not the periodic ones \(2n\pi/L\). Use amlab.turing.unstable_modes_1d(..., bc="periodic") when you need the periodic spectrum.








Exercise



Dirichlet conditions with \(u = u_*\), \(v = v_*\) at both ends allow only \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) modes with \(n \ge 1\). For Case A on \(L = 40\), which modes are unstable?








Solution





The Dirichlet wavenumbers are the same \(n\pi/L\) as the Neumann ones, without \(n = 0\). So modes \(5\) and \(6\) are unstable, but the eigenfunctions are sines, which vanish at the boundary instead of having zero slope there.

title: Dispersion Relation
text: The Turing conditions tell you whether some mode grows. The dispersion relation tells you which modes grow and how fast (murray2003mathematical? and 2.6).

title: Dispersion Relation
text:
Growth Rate Versus Wavenumber
For each wavenumber \(k\), the growth rates are the roots of
\[
\sigma^2 - \operatorname{tr}A(k^2)\,\sigma + h(k^2) = 0, \qquad A(k^2) = \gamma J - k^2\operatorname{diag}(1, d),
\tag{1}\]
with \(h(k^2) = \det A(k^2) = d\,k^4 - \gamma (d f_u + g_v) k^2 + \gamma^2 \det J\), as on the Turing Conditions page. The function \(k \mapsto \operatorname{Re}\sigma(k^2)\), taking the larger root, is the dispersion relation.

title: Dispersion Relation
text:
The Unstable Band
\(\sigma > 0\) exactly when \(h(k^2) < 0\). The roots of \(h\) give the band
\[
k_1^2 < k^2 < k_2^2, \qquad
k_{1,2}^2 = \frac{\gamma}{2d}\left[(d f_u + g_v) \mp \sqrt{(d f_u + g_v)^2 - 4 d \det J}\right].
\tag{2}\]
The band has width proportional to \(\gamma\) in \(k^2\). At \(d = d_c\) it shrinks to the single value \(k_c^2 = \gamma (d_c f_u + g_v)/(2 d_c)\) (murray2003mathematical?).

title: Dispersion Relation
text:
The Fastest-Growing Mode
The fastest-growing wavenumber \(k_{\max}\) maximizes \(\operatorname{Re}\sigma(k^2)\). Near onset it is close to \(k_m\), the minimizer of \(h\), but the two are not equal in general, because \(\sigma\) also depends on the trace. You find \(k_{\max}\) numerically. The corresponding wavelength \(2\pi/k_{\max}\) predicts the spacing of the first visible pattern. Nonlinear effects can change the spacing later (murray2003mathematical?).
On a finite domain only discrete wavenumbers exist. With Neumann conditions on \((0, L)\), \(k_n = n\pi/L\). The mode that grows fastest is the admissible \(k_n\) with the largest \(\sigma\). If no \(k_n\) falls into the band, the uniform state stays stable even when the Turing conditions hold.








Figure 1: Dispersion relation of Gierer-Meinhardt with \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\), \(\gamma = 1\). Dots mark the Neumann modes \(k_n = n\pi/L\) for \(L = 40\).





For \(d = 20\) every mode decays. At \(d = d_c \approx 26.24\) the curve touches zero. For \(d = 30\) a band of modes grows.

import numpy as np

from amlab.turing import dispersion_relation, gierer_meinhardt_jacobian, unstable_band

jac = gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(0.40, 1.00)
d = 30
k1_sq, k2_sq = unstable_band(*jac, d)
k = np.linspace(np.sqrt(k1_sq), np.sqrt(k2_sq), 2001)
k_max = k[np.argmax(dispersion_relation(k**2, *jac, d))]

print(f"unstable band: {np.sqrt(k1_sq):.3f} < k < {np.sqrt(k2_sq):.3f}")
print(f"fastest-growing k = {k_max:.3f}, wavelength = {2 * np.pi / k_max:.1f}")
print(f"closest Neumann mode on L = 40: n = {k_max * 40 / np.pi:.2f}")

unstable band: 0.349 < k < 0.523
fastest-growing k = 0.429, wavelength = 14.6
closest Neumann mode on L = 40: n = 5.46


The fastest wavenumber \(k_{\max} \approx 0.43\) corresponds to a wavelength of about \(14.6\), which lies between the Neumann modes \(n = 5\) and \(n = 6\) on \(L = 40\). Both modes grow, at almost the same rate, and mode \(5\) is slightly faster. The laboratory checks which one the simulation selects.






Exercise



Keep \(d = 30\) and \(\gamma = 1\) with Neumann conditions. Mode \(n\) is unstable when \(k_1 < n\pi/L < k_2\). For which domain lengths \(L < 20\) is no mode \(n \ge 1\) unstable?








Solution





The code above gives \(k_1 \approx 0.349\) and \(k_2 \approx 0.523\). Mode \(n\) is unstable for \(n\pi/k_2 < L < n\pi/k_1\):

\(n = 1\): \(6.01 < L < 8.99\),
\(n = 2\): \(12.02 < L < 17.99\),
\(n = 3\): \(18.03 < L < 26.98\).

No mode is unstable for \(L \le 6.01\), for \(8.99 \le L \le 12.02\), and in the narrow gap \(17.99 \le L \le 18.03\). Beyond that the intervals overlap. Small domains and some intermediate sizes stay uniform even though the Turing conditions hold (murray2003mathematical?).

title: Module 4: Space and Pattern Formation
text: This module adds space to the dynamics of Modules 1 to 3. You study reaction-diffusion equations, derive the conditions under which diffusion destabilizes a uniform state (Turing 1952; murray2003mathematical?), and build finite-difference solvers for the Gierer-Meinhardt and Gray-Scott models in one and two dimensions (Gierer and Meinhardt 1972; Pearson 1993). Every simulation is checked against the linear theory and against the stability and convergence limits of the numerical scheme.

title: Module 4: Space and Pattern Formation
text:
Why Not scipy.integrate.solve_ivp?
In Modules 1 and 2, solve_ivp() handled the time integration because the state was a short ODE vector. Here the main numerical work is different. You discretize space first, update every grid point at every step, and enforce the boundary conditions yourself after each step. That is why this module uses explicit Euler loops.






Scripts or notebooks?



Use notebooks to test stencils, plot snapshots, or inspect intermediate arrays. Use Python scripts for smooth animations. If your 1D solver still feels shaky, fix it before you start the 2D pages: the 2D code is much easier once the 1D stencil and Euler update are routine.








Note



Explicit Euler is simple and transparent, but it is only conditionally stable. If a simulation explodes immediately, reduce dt, increase dx, or test on a smaller grid first (Time-Step Stability).

title: Gray-Scott Parameters
text:
The feed rate \(f\) and kill rate \(k\) decide what the Gray-Scott solver produces. Pearson (1993) mapped this \((f, k)\) plane with forward Euler on a periodic \(256 \times 256\) grid of physical size \(2.5 \times 2.5\), time step \(1\), and diffusion coefficients \(d_1 = 2 \times 10^{-5}\), \(d_2 = 10^{-5}\). He started from \((1, 0)\) with a central \(20 \times 20\) square set to \((1/2, 1/4)\) plus 1% noise. The course values \(d_1 = 0.1\), \(d_2 = 0.05\) in grid units (\(dx = 1\)) keep his ratio \(d_1/d_2 = 2\) but are not the same scaling, so compare patterns qualitatively.
Pearson (1993) also reports three facts about the kinetics that you should keep in mind:

title: Gray-Scott Parameters
text:
Connection Back to Turing Analysis
The steady-state, Jacobian, and mode-matrix pipeline from Turing Numerics still applies. Only the spectrum changes: with periodic boundaries the wavenumbers are \(2\pi n/L\).
The trivial state \((u, v) = (1, 0)\) has Jacobian \(\operatorname{diag}(-f, -(f+k))\), so it is linearly stable for every mode. The patterns in Figure 1 therefore start from the finite-amplitude square, not from a Turing instability of \((1, 0)\) (Pearson 1993). Most of Pearson’s patterns occur where no nontrivial uniform state exists at all.
The nontrivial homogeneous equilibria satisfy \(u_* v_* = f + k\). Substituting into \(u_* v_*^2 = f(1 - u_*)\) gives
\[
u_* = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 \pm \sqrt{1 - \frac{4(f+k)^2}{f}}\right), \qquad v_* = \frac{f+k}{u_*},
\tag{1}\]
which exist when \(4(f+k)^2 \le f\). The Jacobian at any homogeneous equilibrium is
\[
J_{\mathrm{GS}} =
\begin{pmatrix}
-v_*^2 - f & -2u_*v_* \\
v_*^2 & 2u_*v_* - (f+k)
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{2}\]






Exercise



Implement both helpers. Keep only equilibria with \(u_* > 0\).
import numpy as np

def gray_scott_equilibria(f=0.040, k=0.060):
    equilibria = [(1.0, 0.0)]
    discriminant = 1 - 4 * (f + k) ** 2 / f
    if discriminant >= 0:
        root = np.sqrt(discriminant)
        for sign in (+1, -1):
            u_star = 0.5 * (1 + sign * root)
            # TODO: append the nontrivial equilibrium (u_star, v_star)
    return equilibria


def gray_scott_jacobian(u_star, v_star, f=0.040, k=0.060):
    # TODO: return the 2x2 Jacobian array
    pass








Solution





def gray_scott_equilibria(f=0.040, k=0.060):
    equilibria = [(1.0, 0.0)]
    discriminant = 1 - 4 * (f + k) ** 2 / f
    if discriminant >= 0:
        root = np.sqrt(discriminant)
        for sign in (+1, -1):
            u_star = 0.5 * (1 + sign * root)
            if u_star > 0:
                equilibria.append((u_star, (f + k) / u_star))
    return equilibria


def gray_scott_jacobian(u_star, v_star, f=0.040, k=0.060):
    return np.array(
        [
            [-v_star**2 - f, -2 * u_star * v_star],
            [v_star**2, 2 * u_star * v_star - (f + k)],
        ]
    )









Exercise



For Type A (\(f = 0.040\), \(k = 0.060\)), do nontrivial equilibria exist? What about Type C?








Solution





Type A: \(4(f+k)^2/f = 4 \cdot 0.01 / 0.04 = 1\), so the discriminant is \(0\) and the two nontrivial equilibria merge at \(u_* = 0.5\), \(v_* = 0.2\), a saddle-node point. In floating point the discriminant comes out as about \(-2 \times 10^{-16}\), so the code above returns only \((1, 0)\). Type C: \(4 \cdot 0.127^2 / 0.062 \approx 1.04 > 1\), so only \((1, 0)\) exists. In both cases the pattern cannot come from a Turing instability of a nontrivial uniform state that is stable without diffusion.



Once both helpers work, reuse find_unstable_modes_2d from Unstable Modes in 2D. Swap in gray_scott_jacobian, use \(D = \operatorname{diag}(d_1, d_2)\) with no \(\gamma\), and replace \(\pi/L\) by \(2\pi/L\) for the periodic spectrum.






Exercise



Type D (\(f = 0.078\), \(k = 0.061\)) has nontrivial equilibria. List them, compute \(\operatorname{tr} J\) and \(\det J\) at each one, and scan the periodic modes on \(L = 250\) with \(d_1 = 0.1\), \(d_2 = 0.05\). Is any of them Turing unstable?
def find_unstable_modes_gs(u_star, v_star, f, k, d1=0.1, d2=0.05, length=250.0, num_modes=60):
    jac = gray_scott_jacobian(u_star, v_star, f, k)
    diffusion = np.diag([d1, d2])
    unstable_modes = []
    # TODO: loop over (n, m), including (0, 0), with k2 = (2 pi / L)**2 (n**2 + m**2)
    # TODO: store ((n, m), growth_rate) when the growth rate is positive
    return unstable_modes








Solution





There are three equilibria. \((1, 0)\) is stable, with \(\det J > 0\) and \(\operatorname{tr} J < 0\), and no mode grows. The upper state \(u_* \approx 0.548\), \(v_* \approx 0.254\) has \(\det J < 0\): it is a saddle, unstable already without diffusion, so the flat mode \((0, 0)\) grows too. The lower state \(u_* \approx 0.452\), \(v_* \approx 0.307\) is stable without diffusion and no mode grows for \(d_1/d_2 = 2\). So none of them shows a Turing instability, in line with Pearson (1993).
def find_unstable_modes_gs(u_star, v_star, f, k, d1=0.1, d2=0.05, length=250.0, num_modes=60):
    jac = gray_scott_jacobian(u_star, v_star, f, k)
    diffusion = np.diag([d1, d2])
    unstable_modes = []
    for n in range(num_modes):
        for m in range(num_modes):
            k2 = (2 * np.pi / length) ** 2 * (n**2 + m**2)
            growth_rate = np.max(np.linalg.eigvals(jac - k2 * diffusion).real)
            if growth_rate > 0:
                unstable_modes.append(((n, m), growth_rate))
    unstable_modes.sort(key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
    return unstable_modes


f, k = 0.078, 0.061
for u_star, v_star in gray_scott_equilibria(f, k):
    jac = gray_scott_jacobian(u_star, v_star, f, k)
    modes = find_unstable_modes_gs(u_star, v_star, f, k)
    print(f"({u_star:.3f}, {v_star:.3f})  tr = {np.trace(jac):.4f}  det = {np.linalg.det(jac):.5f}  unstable modes: {len(modes)}")

title: Laplacian in 2D
text:
Reading




Compulsory: Pearson (1993).
Recommended: (murray2003mathematical?), Section 2.5 (scale and geometry effects).
This laboratory lifts the 1D workflow to a rectangle. The main change is the Laplacian. The Euler loop, the boundary logic, and the validation steps stay the same. If your 1D code was modular, you mostly change the array shape.

title: Laplacian in 2D
text:
Rectangular Domains
You work on \([0, L_x] \times [0, L_y]\). After discretization each field becomes a matrix.

The row index stores the \(x\) position, the column index the \(y\) position.
The full state has shape (2, num_x, num_y), one matrix for \(u\) and one for \(v\).

num_x = int(length_x / dx)
num_y = int(length_y / dx)
uv = np.ones((2, num_x, num_y))
You still update the whole matrix at once. Shift it up, down, left, and right, and combine the shifted copies.

title: Laplacian in 2D
text:
The 5-Point Stencil
\[
\Delta u = \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}
\approx \frac{u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4u_{i,j}}{dx^2}.
\tag{1}\]
Applying the 1D centered difference in each direction gives this stencil, with error \(\mathcal{O}(dx^2)\) (leveque2007finite?).






Exercise



Implement the stencil with np.roll(). Each call shifts the whole matrix by one grid cell along one direction.
import numpy as np

def laplacian_2d(field, dx):
    # TODO: combine the four nearest neighbours and the centre point with np.roll
    lap =
    return lap / dx**2








Solution





def laplacian_2d(field, dx):
    lap = -4 * field
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=1, axis=0)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=-1, axis=0)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=1, axis=1)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=-1, axis=1)
    return lap / dx**2

title: Laplacian in 2D
text:
Boundary Conditions on a Rectangle
The same three options as in Boundary Conditions, now on four edges.

Periodic: leave the array unchanged; np.roll already wraps each side onto the opposite one.
Neumann: copy the nearest interior row or column onto each edge.
Dirichlet: overwrite each edge with prescribed values.

def apply_boundary_conditions(uv, bc="neumann", dirichlet_values=(1.4, 1.96)):
    if bc == "periodic":
        return uv
    if bc == "neumann":
        uv[:, 0, :] = uv[:, 1, :]
        uv[:, -1, :] = uv[:, -2, :]
        uv[:, :, 0] = uv[:, :, 1]
        uv[:, :, -1] = uv[:, :, -2]
        return uv
    if bc == "dirichlet":
        for species, value in enumerate(dirichlet_values):
            uv[species, 0, :] = value
            uv[species, -1, :] = value
            uv[species, :, 0] = value
            uv[species, :, -1] = value
        return uv
    raise ValueError("bc must be 'periodic', 'neumann', or 'dirichlet'")

title: Laplacian in 2D
text:
Validate the Stencil
Test on \(u = \cos(2\pi x/L_x)\cos(4\pi y/L_y)\) with periodic wrapping, where \(\Delta u = -\left[(2\pi/L_x)^2 + (4\pi/L_y)^2\right] u\).

import numpy as np


def laplacian_2d(field, dx):
    lap = -4 * field
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=1, axis=0)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=-1, axis=0)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=1, axis=1)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=-1, axis=1)
    return lap / dx**2


length_x, length_y = 20.0, 50.0
for dx in (1.0, 0.5, 0.25):
    x = np.arange(int(length_x / dx)) * dx
    y = np.arange(int(length_y / dx)) * dx
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(x, y, indexing="ij")
    u = np.cos(2 * np.pi * xx / length_x) * np.cos(4 * np.pi * yy / length_y)
    exact = -((2 * np.pi / length_x) ** 2 + (4 * np.pi / length_y) ** 2) * u
    print(f"dx = {dx:.2f}   max error = {np.max(np.abs(laplacian_2d(u, dx) - exact)):.2e}")

dx = 1.00   max error = 1.14e-03
dx = 0.50   max error = 2.86e-04
dx = 0.25   max error = 7.15e-05


The error again drops by four for each halving of \(dx\).






Stability in 2D



The 5-point stencil halves the stable time step: \(dt \le dx^2/(4D)\) instead of \(dx^2/(2D)\). With \(d = 30\) and \(dx = 1\) that is \(dt \le 0.0083\), so the 1D choice \(dt = 0.01\) fails in 2D (Time-Step Stability).








Optional extension



A 9-point stencil that also uses the diagonal neighbours gives a more isotropic Laplacian. amlab.pdes_2d.gray_scott.laplacian_9pt implements one. Compare the two stencils on the test function above.

title: Unstable Modes in 2D
text: In 1D you scanned the Neumann modes \(n\). On a rectangle the modes are pairs \((n, m)\) (murray2003mathematical?). This page extends the scan and compares it with the 2D simulation.

title: Unstable Modes in 2D
text:
Modes on a Rectangle
With Neumann boundaries on \([0, L_x] \times [0, L_y]\) (see Laplacian Eigenmodes),
\[
k_{n,m}^2 = \left(\frac{n\pi}{L_x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{m\pi}{L_y}\right)^2, \qquad
A_{n,m} = \gamma J - k_{n,m}^2\,\mathrm{diag}(1, d).
\tag{1}\]
Mode \((n, 0)\) varies only in \(x\) and \((0, m)\) only in \(y\); both are stripes. Modes with \(n, m \ge 1\) are checkerboards of spots. For periodic boundaries replace \(\pi/L\) by \(2\pi/L\).

Solution





def find_unstable_modes_2d(a=0.40, b=1.00, d=30.0, gamma=1.0, length_x=20.0, length_y=50.0, num_modes=12):
    jac = np.array(gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(a, b)).reshape(2, 2)
    diffusion = np.diag([1.0, d])
    unstable_modes = []

    for n in range(num_modes):
        for m in range(num_modes):
            if n == 0 and m == 0:
                continue
            k2 = (n * np.pi / length_x) ** 2 + (m * np.pi / length_y) ** 2
            a_nm = gamma * jac - k2 * diffusion
            growth_rate = np.max(np.linalg.eigvals(a_nm).real)
            if growth_rate > 0:
                unstable_modes.append(((n, m), growth_rate))

    unstable_modes.sort(key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
    return unstable_modes

Linear theory alone cannot tell you which one wins. In the simulation on Gierer-Meinhardt Solver in 2D, the nonlinear terms select spots. Exercise



Estimate the spot spacing from the growth-rate peak. The fastest continuous wavenumber for Case A is \(k_{\max} \approx 0.43\). What wavelength does that give, and how does it compare with the distance between neighbouring spots in the simulation?








Solution





The wavelength is \(2\pi/0.43 \approx 14.6\). In the snapshot neighbouring spots in the same row are about \(28\) apart along \(y\), and rows are offset by half that distance, so nearest neighbours sit at a distance of roughly \(16\) to \(18\), slightly above the linear wavelength. The spacing is close to the linear wavelength even though the arrangement is chosen by the nonlinear terms.

title: Gierer-Meinhardt Solver in 2D
text:
The reaction terms are those of the 1D laboratory (Gierer and Meinhardt 1972). Only the Laplacian and the array shape change:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} &= \Delta u + \gamma \left(a - b u + \frac{u^2}{v}\right), \\
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} &= d\,\Delta v + \gamma \left(u^2 - v\right),
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
with \(u\) and \(v\) now functions of \((x, y, t)\).

Solution





def gierer_meinhardt_pde_2d(t, uv, gamma=1, a=0.40, b=1.00, d=30, dx=1.0):
    u, v = uv
    lu = laplacian_2d(u, dx)
    lv = laplacian_2d(v, dx)

    f = a - b * u + (u**2) / v
    g = u**2 - v
    du_dt = lu + gamma * f
    dv_dt = d * lv + gamma * g
    return np.array([du_dt, dv_dt])

title: Gierer-Meinhardt Solver in 2D
text:
Time Step with Euler’s Method
Once the right-hand side is available, the full update is explicit Euler applied to the whole array,
\[
UV^{n+1} = UV^n + dt\,G(UV^n),
\]
followed by one boundary update. The order matters. First compute the Euler step, then reapply the edge values, so the next stencil evaluation sees data consistent with the boundary condition. Validate with a long loop and one snapshot before you animate.

    # TODO: Euler update of uv
    # TODO: reapply Neumann boundary conditions
    pass








Solution





for _ in range(num_iter):
    uv = uv + dt * gierer_meinhardt_pde_2d(0, uv, d=30, dx=dx)
    uv = apply_boundary_conditions(uv, bc="neumann")

title: Laplacian Eigenmodes
text: The linearized system \(\partial_t \eta = D\,\Delta\eta + \gamma J\eta\) couples every point to its neighbours. You decouple it by expanding \(\eta\) in eigenfunctions of the Laplacian, which depend on the domain and the boundary conditions (murray2003mathematical?; britton2003essential?).

title: Laplacian Eigenmodes
text:
The Eigenvalue Problem
Look for functions \(\phi\) and numbers \(k^2 \ge 0\) with
\[
\Delta \phi + k^2 \phi = 0 \quad \text{in } \Omega,
\tag{1}\]
plus the boundary condition of the model. The eigenvalue of \(\Delta\) is \(\lambda = -k^2\), and \(k\) is the wavenumber. The wavelength of the mode is \(2\pi / k\).

title: Laplacian Eigenmodes
text:
On an Interval \((0, L)\)









Boundary condition
Condition
Eigenfunctions
Wavenumbers




Neumann (zero flux)
\(\phi'(0) = \phi'(L) = 0\)
\(\cos(n\pi x / L)\)
\(k_n = n\pi/L\), \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\)


Dirichlet (fixed value)
\(\phi(0) = \phi(L) = 0\)
\(\sin(n\pi x / L)\)
\(k_n = n\pi/L\), \(n = 1, 2, \dots\)


Periodic
\(\phi(0) = \phi(L)\), \(\phi'(0) = \phi'(L)\)
\(\cos(2n\pi x/L)\), \(\sin(2n\pi x/L)\)
\(k_n = 2n\pi/L\), \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\)



Mode \(n\) with Neumann conditions fits \(n\) half-wavelengths into the interval. Mode \(0\) is the flat perturbation. For periodic conditions each \(n \ge 1\) has two independent eigenfunctions with the same \(k_n\).








Figure 1: First four Neumann eigenfunctions \(\cos(n\pi x/L)\) on \((0, L)\).

title: Laplacian Eigenmodes
text:
On a Rectangle \((0, L_x) \times (0, L_y)\)
Separation of variables gives products of the 1D eigenfunctions. With Neumann conditions on all four edges,
\[
\phi_{n,m}(x, y) = \cos\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L_x}\right)\cos\left(\frac{m\pi y}{L_y}\right), \qquad
k_{n,m}^2 = \left(\frac{n\pi}{L_x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{m\pi}{L_y}\right)^2.
\tag{2}\]
For Dirichlet conditions replace cosines by sines and start at \(n, m \ge 1\). For periodic conditions replace \(\pi/L\) by \(2\pi/L\). Different pairs \((n, m)\) can share almost the same \(k^2\). That is why 2D domains can select stripes, spots, or mixtures (murray2003mathematical?).

title: Laplacian Eigenmodes
text:
Mode Decomposition
Expand the perturbation as
\[
\eta(x, t) = \sum_n c_n(t)\,\phi_n(x), \qquad c_n(t) \in \mathbb{R}^2.
\]
Because \(\Delta \phi_n = -k_n^2 \phi_n\), the modes separate and each coefficient solves a \(2 \times 2\) linear ODE:
\[
\dot c_n = A_n c_n, \qquad A_n = \gamma J - k_n^2 D.
\tag{3}\]
So \(c_n(t) \propto e^{\sigma t}\), where \(\sigma\) is an eigenvalue of \(A_n\). The uniform state is linearly stable when every admissible mode has \(\operatorname{Re}\sigma < 0\). The next session turns this into the Turing conditions and the dispersion relation.






Exercise



On \((0, 40)\) with Neumann conditions, which mode \(n\) has wavenumber closest to \(k = 0.4\)? How many half-wavelengths does it fit into the domain?








Solution





\(k_n = n\pi/40\), so \(n = 40k/\pi \approx 5.09\). The closest mode is \(n = 5\), with five half-wavelengths, which is two and a half full wavelengths.



Next session: Turing Conditions.

title: Reaction-Diffusion Equations
text:
Reading




Compulsory: (murray2002mathematical?), Chapter 11 (Reaction Diffusion, Chemotaxis, and Nonlocal Mechanisms).
Recommended: (britton2003essential?), Chapter 5 (Biological Motion) and Chapter 7 (Pattern Formation).
In Module 3 you derived the diffusion equation \(\partial_t c = D\,\partial_{xx} c\) as the continuum limit of a random walk (From random walks to diffusion). A reaction-diffusion equation adds local production and decay to that transport term (murray2002mathematical?).

title: Reaction-Diffusion Equations
text:
The General Form
For \(m\) species with concentrations \(w = (w_1, \dots, w_m)\) on a domain \(\Omega\),
\[
\partial_t w = D\,\Delta w + R(w), \qquad D = \operatorname{diag}(D_1, \dots, D_m).
\tag{1}\]

\(\Delta\) is the Laplacian, \(\partial_{xx}\) in 1D and \(\partial_{xx} + \partial_{yy}\) in 2D.
\(D_i > 0\) is the diffusion coefficient of species \(i\).
\(R(w)\) collects the reaction kinetics. With \(D = 0\) you recover an ODE system at every point, as in Module 1.

The model is incomplete without an initial condition \(w(x, 0)\) and boundary conditions on \(\partial\Omega\). You will meet Neumann (zero flux), Dirichlet (fixed value), and periodic conditions on the page Laplacian Eigenmodes.

title: Reaction-Diffusion Equations
section: The Scaling Used in This Module
text:
The Scaling Used in This Module
For two species \(u\) and \(v\) we use the nondimensional form of (murray2003mathematical?):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_t u &= \Delta u + \gamma f(u, v), \\
\partial_t v &= d\,\Delta v + \gamma g(u, v).
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]
Here \(d = D_v / D_u\) is the ratio of diffusion coefficients and \(\gamma\) measures the strength of the reactions relative to diffusion. In Murray’s scaling \(\gamma\) is proportional to the square of the domain length, so increasing \(\gamma\) at fixed domain is equivalent to enlarging the domain (murray2003mathematical?). The Gierer-Meinhardt code in amlab.pdes_1d and amlab.pdes_2d uses exactly these symbols.

title: Reaction-Diffusion Equations
text:
Examples

Fisher-KPP equation. One species, logistic growth plus diffusion: \(\partial_t u = D\,\partial_{xx} u + r u(1-u)\). It was proposed for the spread of an advantageous gene (fisher1937wave?). It has travelling fronts with minimal speed \(c = 2\sqrt{rD}\) (murray2002mathematical?).
Gierer-Meinhardt model. An activator \(u\) and an inhibitor \(v\) with \(f = a - bu + u^2/v\) and \(g = u^2 - v\) (Gierer and Meinhardt 1972). It forms stationary patterns and is the main example of this module.
Gray-Scott model. An autocatalytic reaction with feed and removal (Gray and Scott 1984). Its 2D simulations produce spots, stripes and self-replicating spots (Pearson 1993).
Chemical experiments. Stationary Turing patterns were first observed experimentally in the CIMA reaction (castets1990experimental?).

title: Reaction-Diffusion Equations
text:
A First Simulation
Figure 1 shows a Fisher-KPP front with \(D = r = 1\). The dashed lines move at the predicted speed \(c = 2\).








Figure 1: Fisher-KPP front with \(D = r = 1\), explicit Euler with \(dx = 0.5\), \(dt = 0.05\). Dashed lines mark positions moving at speed \(c = 2\sqrt{rD} = 2\) from the front at \(t = 10\).





For an initial condition with compact support the front speed tends to the minimal speed \(c = 2\sqrt{rD}\) as \(t \to \infty\) (murray2002mathematical?).






Exercise



Set \(D = 0\) in Equation 1. What happens to a spatial profile \(u(x, 0)\) under Fisher-KPP kinetics, and why can no front move?








Solution





Each point solves the logistic ODE \(\dot u = r u (1-u)\) independently. Points with \(u(x,0) > 0\) grow to \(1\) and points with \(u(x,0) = 0\) stay at \(0\). Without diffusion no point can influence its neighbours, so the region with \(u = 0\) never becomes invaded.

title: Linearization
text: A pattern starts as a small perturbation of a spatially uniform state. To decide whether that perturbation grows, you linearize the reaction-diffusion system around the uniform state (murray2003mathematical?).

title: Linearization
text:
Homogeneous Steady States
Take the scaled two-species system
\[
\partial_t w = D\,\Delta w + \gamma R(w), \qquad w = \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix}, \quad D = \operatorname{diag}(1, d), \quad R = \begin{pmatrix} f \\ g \end{pmatrix}.
\]
A homogeneous steady state is a constant \(w_* = (u_*, v_*)\) with \(R(w_*) = 0\). Since \(\Delta w_* = 0\), it solves the PDE for every choice of Neumann or periodic boundary conditions.

title: Linearization
text:
The Linearized System
Write \(w = w_* + \eta\) with \(\eta\) small and keep only linear terms:
\[
\partial_t \eta = D\,\Delta \eta + \gamma J \eta,
\tag{1}\]
where
\[
J =
\begin{pmatrix}
f_u & f_v \\
g_u & g_v
\end{pmatrix}_{(u_*, v_*)}
\tag{2}\]
is the Jacobian of the kinetics at the steady state. Two limits are worth keeping in mind.

Without diffusion, \(\dot\eta = \gamma J\eta\). Stability is decided by \(\operatorname{tr} J\) and \(\det J\), as for the 2D systems of Module 1.
With diffusion, the Laplacian couples neighbouring points. The page Laplacian Eigenmodes shows how to decouple it.

title: Linearization
text:
The Gierer-Meinhardt Steady State
For the Gierer-Meinhardt kinetics (Gierer and Meinhardt 1972),
\[
f(u, v) = a - b u + \frac{u^2}{v}, \qquad g(u, v) = u^2 - v, \qquad a, b > 0.
\]
From \(g = 0\) you get \(v_* = u_*^2\). Substituting into \(f = 0\) gives \(a - b u_* + 1 = 0\), so
\[
u_* = \frac{a+1}{b}, \qquad v_* = \left(\frac{a+1}{b}\right)^2.
\tag{3}\]
At a general point the Jacobian is
\[
J(u, v) =
\begin{pmatrix}
-b + 2u/v & -u^2/v^2 \\
2u & -1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
At \((u_*, v_*)\) this becomes
\[
f_u = \frac{b(1-a)}{1+a}, \qquad f_v = -\frac{b^2}{(1+a)^2}, \qquad g_u = \frac{2(1+a)}{b}, \qquad g_v = -1.
\tag{4}\]






Exercise



Compute \(\operatorname{tr} J\) and \(\det J\) at the Gierer-Meinhardt steady state. For which \(a\) is the steady state stable without diffusion when \(b = 1\)?








Solution





\(\det J = f_u g_v - f_v g_u = -\frac{b(1-a)}{1+a} + \frac{2b}{1+a} = b > 0\).
\(\operatorname{tr} J = \frac{b(1-a)}{1+a} - 1\). For \(b = 1\) this equals \(-\frac{2a}{1+a}\), which is negative for every \(a > 0\). So with \(b = 1\) the steady state is a stable node or focus of the kinetics for all \(a > 0\).

title: Linearization
text:
Checking the Algebra Numerically
The helper amlab.turing.gierer_meinhardt_jacobian implements Equation 4. A finite-difference Jacobian of the kinetics gives the same entries.

import numpy as np

from amlab.turing import gierer_meinhardt_jacobian, gierer_meinhardt_steady_state

a, b = 0.40, 1.00
u_s, v_s = gierer_meinhardt_steady_state(a, b)


def kinetics(u, v):
    return np.array([a - b * u + u**2 / v, u**2 - v])


h = 1e-6
jac_fd = np.column_stack(
    [
        (kinetics(u_s + h, v_s) - kinetics(u_s - h, v_s)) / (2 * h),
        (kinetics(u_s, v_s + h) - kinetics(u_s, v_s - h)) / (2 * h),
    ]
)
jac_exact = np.array(gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(a, b)).reshape(2, 2)
print("steady state:", (u_s, v_s))
print("max difference:", np.abs(jac_fd - jac_exact).max())
print("det J =", np.linalg.det(jac_exact))

steady state: (1.4, 1.9599999999999997)
max difference: 2.525508691064715e-10
det J = 1.0000000000000002

title: Kuramoto Lab: Locating the Threshold
text:
This page is the interpretation step. You compare the transition in your Bifurcation Diagram with the critical coupling \(K_c = 2/(\pi g(0))\) from Critical Coupling.
In your animation script from Animation, set the coupling strength just below and just above the critical value to see the difference in the dynamics. Below \(K_c\) the oscillators remain incoherent. Above \(K_c\) they start to synchronize and form a cluster on the unit circle, as in Figure 1.








Figure 1: Comparison between the theoretical critical coupling \(K_c\) and the empirical transition point observed in simulations. Individual oscillators are blue dots and the order parameter is the red vector.











Exercise



Find \(K_c\) from \(K_c = 2/(\pi g(0))\) for your normal frequencies with \(\sigma = 1\). Estimate the empirical transition point from your points: the value of \(K\) where \(r\) starts to rise clearly above zero. Alternatively, fit the near-onset scaling \(r \approx \sqrt{16/(\pi K_c^3)}\,\sqrt{\mu/(-g''(0))}\) of Bifurcation Diagram to the points just above the transition. Do the two estimates agree?








Solution





For a normal density \(g(0) = 1/\sqrt{2\pi}\), so \(K_c = 2\sqrt{2\pi}/\pi = \sqrt{8/\pi} \approx 1.60\). With \(N = 1000\) and 20 values of \(K\) between 0 and 5, \(r_\infty\) stays below about \(0.1\) up to \(K \approx 1.3\) and jumps to about \(0.6\) between \(K \approx 1.6\) and \(K \approx 1.8\). The grid spacing is about \(0.26\), so the empirical threshold agrees with \(K_c\) within one grid step. The exact \(K\) of the jump moves with the seed, because each sample of frequencies differs from \(g\) (Finite-Size Effects).









Exercise



The empirical points in the normal case lie close to zero for \(K < K_c\) but not exactly at zero. Give two reasons.








Solution





First, a finite population has \(r\) of order \(N^{-1/2}\) even when incoherent (about \(0.045\) for the \(N = 500\) figures of Bifurcation Diagram, \(0.03\) for \(N = 1000\)). Second, the time window may be too short for \(r(t)\) to settle near \(K_c\), where the approach to the steady state is slow. Finite-Size Effects studies the first effect.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Initialization
text: In this lab you implement the Kuramoto model, animate it, and measure the transition to synchrony. You follow the course workflow: prediction, implementation, validation, experiment, interpretation and limitations. The theory is in The Kuramoto Model, The Order Parameter and Critical Coupling.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Initialization
text:
Prediction






Exercise



Before writing code, answer these questions on paper. You will check them later.

Take \(N = 100\) oscillators with normal frequencies, \(\sigma = 1\). What is \(K_c\)?
What value of \(r\) do you expect at \(t = 0\) for uniform random phases? (The Order Parameter has an exercise on this.)
For \(K = 10\) and for \(K = 0.1\), sketch what the phases on the circle will look like at \(t = 10\).









Solution





\(K_c = 2/(\pi g(0)) = \sqrt{8/\pi} \approx 1.60\). At \(t = 0\), \(r\) is of order \(1/\sqrt{N} = 0.1\). For \(K = 10 \gg K_c\) most phases gather in a tight cluster. For \(K = 0.1 \ll K_c\) they stay spread around the circle.

Initialize Oscillators
The phases \(\theta_i\) are sampled uniformly on \([0, 2\pi)\) and the natural frequencies \(\omega_i\) from a normal distribution with standard deviation \(\sigma\) (Kuramoto 2003; Strogatz 2000).






Exercise

    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # Assign a random initial phase to each oscillator
    theta = # TODO: draw from a uniform distribution on [0, 2 pi)

    # Assign a random natural frequency to each oscillator
    omega = # TODO: draw from a normal distribution with standard deviation sigma
    return theta, omega








Hint





A NumPy random generator rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) has methods for sampling:

Uniform distribution: rng.uniform(low=0.0, high=2 * np.pi, size=num_oscillators)
Normal distribution: rng.normal(loc=0.0, scale=sigma, size=num_oscillators)

A fixed seed makes your runs reproducible.









Solution





Remember to import NumPy first.
import numpy as np


def initialize_oscillators(num_oscillators: int, sigma: float = 1.0, seed: int = None):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # Assign a random initial phase to each oscillator
    theta = rng.uniform(low=0.0, high=2 * np.pi, size=num_oscillators)

    # Assign a random natural frequency to each oscillator
    omega = rng.normal(loc=0.0, scale=sigma, size=num_oscillators)
    return theta, omega

text:
Draw Particles
To show the movement of the particles, draw them to look like “tadpoles”: a big head with a smaller tail. In practice, you plot their current position as the “head”, using a bigger marker, and their recent trajectory as the “tail”, using many small points. This will show the direction of movement and give a better sense of the dynamics. You use two artists:

one for the tail (many tiny points),
one for the current positions (bigger markers).

Translating this to code, you will - create xy_tail with shape (2, N, TAIL_LEN), and - create the two Line2D artists with ax_plane.plot(...).
def init_particles_plot(ax_plane: Axes, xy: np.ndarray, box_size: float, tail_len: int):
    # build a tail tensor by repeating xy across a third axis
    xy_tail = np.repeat(xy[:, :, np.newaxis], tail_len, axis=2)

    # tail (small grey points)
    (plt_particles,) = ax_plane.plot(
        xy_tail[0].flatten(), xy_tail[1].flatten(),
        linestyle="", marker=".", markersize=2, color="grey"
    )

    # current positions (bigger black circles)
    (plt_current,) = ax_plane.plot(
        xy[0], xy[1],
        linestyle="", marker="o", markersize=3, color="black"
    )

    # set plot limits
    ax_plane.set_xlim(0, box_size)
    ax_plane.set_ylim(0, box_size)
    ax_plane.set_aspect("equal")

    return xy_tail, plt_particles, plt_current

Solution: Full update_animation()





def update_animation(frame: int):
    nonlocal \
        xy, \
        xy_tail, \
        theta, \
        noise_eta, \
        v0, \
        radius_interaction, \
        box_size, \
        dict_noise, \
        ls_order_param
    xy, theta = vicsek_equations(
        xy,
        theta,
        v0=v0,
        dt=dt,
        radius_interaction=radius_interaction,
        box_size=box_size,
        noise=noise_eta,
    )

    # Update tails
    xy_tail = np.roll(xy_tail, shift=-1, axis=2)
    xy_tail[:, :, -1] = xy
    plt_particles.set_data(xy_tail[0].flatten(), xy_tail[1].flatten())
    plt_current.set_data(xy[0], xy[1])

    # Update order parameter
    ls_order_param.append(vicsek_order_parameter(theta))
    ls_order_param = ls_order_param[-ORDER_WINDOW:]
    x_vals = np.arange(len(ls_order_param))
    line_order_param.set_data(x_vals, ls_order_param)

    # Average the last ORDER_WINDOW//3 values to get the order parameter (similar to Couzin)
    order_param = np.mean(ls_order_param[-ORDER_WINDOW // 3 :])
    dict_noise[noise_eta] = order_param
    dict_noise = dict(sorted(dict_noise.items()))
    if dict_noise:
        line_noise.set_data(*zip(*dict_noise.items()))
    else:
        line_noise.set_data([], [])
    return (plt_particles, plt_current, line_order_param, line_noise)
