title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text: The formulas in Critical Coupling hold in the limit \(N \to \infty\). Your simulations use finite \(N\). This page covers the last two steps of the workflow: interpretation and limitations.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text:
Two finite-\(N\) effects

Noise floor. For incoherent phases, \(\mathbb{E}[r^2] = 1/N\) (The Order Parameter). Below \(K_c\) you measure \(r_\infty\) of order \(N^{-1/2}\), not zero.
Sampling of frequencies. With \(N\) random draws, the empirical frequency distribution differs from \(g\). The transition point of one sample moves around \(K_c\), and the sharp corner of the \(N \to \infty\) curve is rounded off.

Simulations and physical arguments suggest that the fluctuations of \(r(t)\) are of order \(N^{-1/2}\), except very close to \(K_c\) where they may be amplified. As of 2000 there were no rigorous convergence results for finite \(N\) (Strogatz 2000, sec. 5.1). Both effects shrink as \(N\) grows. Figure 1 shows them with a normal frequency density, \(\sigma = 1\), so \(K_c \approx 1.60\).








Figure 1: Time-averaged order parameter against \(K\) for three population sizes (normal frequencies, \(\sigma = 1\), one random sample each, RK4 with \(\Delta t = 0.1\) up to \(t = 80\), average over \(40 \le t \le 80\)). Error bars show the standard deviation of \(r(t)\) in that window. Dotted lines mark \(K_c\) and the noise floors \(N^{-1/2}\).

title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text:
Interpretation

Below \(K_c\), each curve sits near its own floor \(N^{-1/2}\): about \(0.14\), \(0.07\) and \(0.03\).
Near \(K_c\) the fluctuations of \(r(t)\) are largest. The transition is sharpest for the largest \(N\).
The \(N = 50\) sample rises before \(K_c\). Its 50 frequencies have a sample standard deviation of about \(0.88\), smaller than \(\sigma = 1\), so this particular population is easier to synchronize. A different seed would move its curve.
Well above \(K_c\), the three curves agree. Most oscillators are locked and sampling details matter little.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text:
Limitations

One sample of frequencies per \(N\) is not enough to separate the two finite-size effects. Average over several seeds if you need error bars on \(r_\infty\) itself, not just on \(r(t)\).
Close to \(K_c\), \(r(t)\) settles slowly. A fixed time window can stop too early.
The mean-field model has all-to-all coupling. Real oscillators often interact through a network, which changes the threshold. Module 5 returns to this with the swing equation for power grids.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text:
Averaging over samples
This part is optional.






Exercise



Repeat Figure 1 with 10 seeds for each \(N\) and plot the mean of \(r_\infty\) over seeds. Then plot \(r_\infty\sqrt{N}\) against \(K\). Below \(K_c\) the curves for different \(N\) should collapse onto a single curve. Where does the collapse fail?








Solution





At \(K = 0\) all three curves start at \(r_\infty\sqrt{N} \approx 0.89\), the mean of \(\sqrt{N}\,r\) for independent uniform phases (\(\sqrt{\pi}/2\)). Up to \(K \approx 1\) they stay together and rise slowly, to about \(1.6\): coupling below threshold enhances the fluctuations but keeps them of order \(N^{-1/2}\). Close to \(K_c\) the curves separate: \(r_\infty\) no longer scales like \(N^{-1/2}\), and the largest population departs first. The run takes about 15 seconds.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from amlab.synchronization.kuramoto_sweep import critical_coupling, order_parameter_sweep

sigma = 1.0
kc = critical_coupling(1 / (np.sqrt(2 * np.pi) * sigma))
k_values = np.linspace(0, 4, 17)
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4))
for n in [50, 200, 1000]:
    r_seeds = []
    for seed in range(10):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        omega = rng.normal(0, sigma, n)
        theta0 = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n)
        r_mean, _ = order_parameter_sweep(k_values, omega, theta0, t_end=80, dt=0.1, t_average=40)
        r_seeds.append(r_mean)
    r_avg = np.mean(r_seeds, axis=0)
    axs[0].plot(k_values, r_avg, "o-", label=f"N = {n}")
    axs[1].plot(k_values, r_avg * np.sqrt(n), "o-", label=f"N = {n}")
for ax in axs:
    ax.axvline(kc, color="black", linestyle=":")
    ax.set_xlabel("Coupling strength K")
    ax.legend()
axs[0].set_ylabel(r"mean of $r_\infty$ over seeds")
axs[1].set_ylabel(r"$r_\infty \sqrt{N}$")
axs[1].set_xlim(0, kc)
axs[1].set_ylim(0, 5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text:
Exit question






Exercise



You run a simulation with \(N = 400\) and \(K = 1.0\) (normal frequencies, \(\sigma = 1\)) and find \(r_\infty \approx 0.05\). A classmate says this shows weak partial synchronization. Is that right?








Solution





No. \(K = 1.0\) is below \(K_c \approx 1.60\), so the \(N \to \infty\) prediction is \(r_\infty = 0\). The measured value is consistent with the incoherent noise floor \(N^{-1/2} = 0.05\). To claim partial synchrony you would need \(r_\infty\) well above \(N^{-1/2}\) and a value that does not decrease as you increase \(N\).



The graded Kuramoto Assignment is released in this session.

title: Practice: Collective Motion
text:
Exit question






Exercise



In the Vicsek model you double both \(N\) and \(L^2\), keeping the density and the noise fixed. Which features of the order parameter curve \(\varphi(\eta)\) should stay the same, and which should change?








Solution





The density \(\rho = N/L^2\) is unchanged, so in the ordered phase \(\varphi\) should be about the same. At high noise, \(\varphi\) is set by the finite-size floor of order \(1/\sqrt{N}\), which decreases by a factor \(\sqrt{2}\). The transition region should become sharper. This is the pattern in Figure 2(a) of Vicsek et al. (1995).

title: Vicsek Lab: Vectorized Update
text:
Optional extension



This page is optional. Loops are slow in Python: the double loop of Update Rule costs \(O(N^2)\) interpreted operations per step. You can compute all neighbor averages at once with a distance matrix. The amlab code uses this version.

title: Vicsek Lab: Vectorized Update
text:
Vectorized version






Exercise



Rewrite vicsek_equations() without loops. Build the matrix of pairwise distances, turn it into a boolean neighbor matrix, and compute all average directions with matrix products.
def vicsek_equations(
    xy: np.ndarray,
    theta: np.ndarray,
    noise: float = 0.1,
    box_size: float = 25,
    dt: float = 1,
    radius_interaction: float = 1,
    v0: float = 0.03,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    # TODO: Compute distance matrix and neighbor matrix
    # Useful functions:
    # scipy.spatial.distance.pdist
    # scipy.spatial.distance.squareform
    
    # TODO: Vectorized computation of average direction of neighbors (including itself)
    # Useful functions: np.sin, np.cos, np.arctan2

    # TODO: Add noise to the average heading
    # Useful function: np.random.uniform

    # TODO: Update position based on new headings
    # Useful functions: np.cos, np.sin

    return xy_new, theta_new








Hint





If neighbors is the boolean \(N \times N\) matrix with entry True when \(|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j| \le r\), then neighbors @ np.sin(theta) sums \(\sin\theta_j\) over the neighbors of every particle at once. The diagonal is True, so each particle counts itself.









Solution





import numpy as np
import scipy.spatial


def vicsek_equations(
    xy: np.ndarray,
    theta: np.ndarray,
    noise: float = 0.1,
    box_size: float = 25,
    dt: float = 1,
    radius_interaction: float = 1,
    v0: float = 0.03,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """
    Update the state of the particles based on the Vicsek model.

    Parameters
    ----------
    xy : np.ndarray
        Position of the particles.
    theta : np.ndarray
        Angle of the particles.
    noise : float, optional
        Noise parameter, eta, default is 0.1.
    box_size : float, optional
        Dimension of the space, L, default is 25.
    dt : float, optional
        Time step, default is 1 [Vicsek1995]
    radius_interaction : float, optional
        Interaction radius, default is 1 [Vicsek1995]
    v0 : float, optional
        Speed of the particles, default is 0.03 [Vicsek1995]

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Updated position of the particles.
    np.ndarray
        Updated angle of the particles.
    """
    # Compute distance matrix and neighbor matrix
    d_matrix = scipy.spatial.distance.pdist(xy.T)
    d_matrix = scipy.spatial.distance.squareform(d_matrix)
    neighbors = d_matrix <= radius_interaction
    # Vectorized computation of average direction of neighbors (including itself)
    num_boids = xy.shape[1]
    sin_theta = np.sin(theta)
    cos_theta = np.cos(theta)
    # neighbors is (N, N), sin_theta/cos_theta is (N,)
    # Matrix-vector product: (N, N) @ (N,) -> (N,)
    sum_sin = neighbors @ sin_theta  # (N,)
    sum_cos = neighbors @ cos_theta  # (N,)
    count = neighbors.sum(axis=1)  # (N,)
    mean_sin = sum_sin / count
    mean_cos = sum_cos / count
    theta_avg = np.arctan2(mean_sin, mean_cos)
    # Add noise: uniform in [-noise/2, noise/2]
    noise_arr = noise * (np.random.uniform(size=num_boids) - 0.5)
    theta_new = theta_avg + noise_arr
    theta_new = np.mod(theta_new, 2 * np.pi)

    # Update position
    v = v0 * np.array([np.cos(theta_new), np.sin(theta_new)])
    xy_new = xy + dt * v
    # Periodic boundary conditions
    xy_new = np.mod(xy_new, box_size)

    return xy_new, theta_new

title: Vicsek Lab: Vectorized Update
text:
Limitations of this implementation
The distance in these functions is the plain Euclidean distance. With periodic boundaries, two particles near opposite edges are close to each other, but the code does not see them as neighbors. For small \(r\) compared with \(L\) the effect is limited to particles near the edges.

title: Vicsek Lab: Vectorized Update
text:
Minimum-image distance






Exercise



Fix the limitation. Replace the displacement \(\Delta\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{x}_i\) by dx - box_size * np.round(dx / box_size) in each coordinate before computing the norm. Compare the time-averaged order parameter with and without this correction for \(N = 100\), \(L = 5\).
def vicsek_equations_periodic(xy, theta, noise=0.1, box_size=25, dt=1, radius_interaction=1, v0=0.03):
    # TODO: displacements between all pairs, shape (2, N, N)

    # TODO: apply the minimum-image correction and compute the distances

    # TODO: same steps as the vectorized version from here on
    return xy_new, theta_new








Hint





Broadcasting gives all displacements at once: xy[:, :, None] - xy[:, None, :] has shape (2, N, N). np.round(dx / box_size) is \(\pm 1\) exactly when the direct displacement is longer than half the box, so the correction picks the nearest periodic copy.









Solution





With \(L = 5\) and \(r = 1\), a large fraction of the box lies within \(r\) of an edge, so the correction matters. Averaged over the last 1000 of 3000 steps, it raises \(\varphi\) from about \(0.76\) to \(0.82\) at \(\eta = 2\) and from about \(0.25\) to \(0.32\) at \(\eta = 4\). Without the correction, particles near the edges have fewer neighbours and align less.
import numpy as np
from amlab.collective_motion.vicsek import initialize_particles, vicsek_equations


def vicsek_equations_periodic(xy, theta, noise=0.1, box_size=25, dt=1, radius_interaction=1, v0=0.03):
    # Displacements between all pairs, shape (2, N, N)
    dx = xy[:, :, None] - xy[:, None, :]
    # Minimum-image convention: use the nearest periodic copy
    dx = dx - box_size * np.round(dx / box_size)
    dist = np.sqrt((dx**2).sum(axis=0))
    neighbors = dist <= radius_interaction
    # Average direction of neighbors, including the particle itself
    theta_avg = np.arctan2(neighbors @ np.sin(theta), neighbors @ np.cos(theta))
    theta_new = theta_avg + noise * (np.random.uniform(size=theta.size) - 0.5)
    theta_new = np.mod(theta_new, 2 * np.pi)
    v = v0 * np.array([np.cos(theta_new), np.sin(theta_new)])
    xy_new = np.mod(xy + dt * v, box_size)
    return xy_new, theta_new


def mean_order(update, noise, steps=3000, avg_steps=1000, seed=0):
    np.random.seed(seed)
    xy, theta = initialize_particles(100, box_size=5)
    phi = []
    for step in range(steps):
        xy, theta = update(xy, theta, noise=noise, box_size=5)
        if step >= steps - avg_steps:
            phi.append(np.abs(np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta))))
    return np.mean(phi)


for noise in [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]:
    print(noise, round(mean_order(vicsek_equations, noise), 3), round(mean_order(vicsek_equations_periodic, noise), 3))


for noise in [2.0, 4.0]:
    print(noise, mean_order(vicsek_equations, noise), mean_order(vicsek_equations_periodic, noise))

title: Vicsek Lab: Validation
text:
Before animating the Vicsek model, validate your implementation in limits where you know the answer (Vicsek et al. 1995). Here you use static plots to see how the interaction radius \(r\) affects alignment. With \(r = 0\) each particle only sees itself, so the headings perform independent random walks. With \(r = L\) every particle sees every other (up to the edges, see the limitation in Vectorized Update), so the model becomes a mean-field alignment.
You will run the Vicsek model for a few time steps and visualize the headings of all particles for different values of \(r\). This will help you see the transition from random motion to local and global alignment as the interaction radius increases.






Exercise



Run the code below with three interaction radii: \(r = 0\), \(r = L / 10\), and \(r = L\), where \(L\) is the box size. What do you observe? How does the interaction radius affect the alignment of the particles?
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Initialize parameters
num_particles = 100
box_size = 10 # L
interaction_radius = 1.0 # r
noise_strength = 0.1 # eta
v0 = 0.03 # speed of particles

# Initialize particle positions and headings
xy, theta = initialize_particles(num_particles, box_size)

# Update positions and headings for a few time steps
for t in range(10):
    xy, theta = vicsek_equations(
    xy=xy,
    theta=theta,
    noise=noise_strength,
    box_size=box_size,
    radius_interaction=interaction_radius,
    v0=v0,
    )

# Plot the headings of the particles
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6))
plt.quiver(
    xy[0],
    xy[1],
    np.cos(theta),
    np.sin(theta),
    angles='xy',
    scale_units='xy',
    scale=2,  # bigger scale means smaller arrows
)
# Limit the plot to the box size
plt.xlim(0, box_size)
plt.ylim(0, box_size)
plt.title('Particle headings after 10 time steps')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('y')
plt.grid()
plt.show()








Solution





Radius \(r = 0\). For \(r = 0\), there is no interaction between particles, so they will move in random directions based on their initial headings and noise. The plot will show a random distribution of arrows with no clear alignment.





Particle headings for \(r = 0\)




Radius \(r = L / 10\). For \(r = L / 10\), particles will interact with others within a radius of one-tenth of the box size. This means that each particle will have a limited chance to align with nearby particles, leading to small local clusters of aligned particles. The plot will show groups of arrows pointing in similar directions, indicating partial alignment.





Particle headings for \(r = L / 10\)




Radius \(r = L\). For \(r = L\), particles will interact with all other particles in the box. This means that each particle will tend to align with the average direction of all particles, leading to global alignment. The plot will show arrows mostly pointing in the same direction, indicating strong alignment.





Particle headings for \(r = L\)













Exercise



Add a quantitative check. For \(r = L\) and \(\eta = 0.1\), print the order parameter after 10 and after 100 steps. For \(r = 0\), do the same. Which values do you expect?
for radius in [0.0, box_size]:
    xy, theta = initialize_particles(num_particles, box_size)
    for t in range(100):
        # TODO: advance one step with radius_interaction=radius

        # TODO: print the order parameter after 10 and after 100 steps
        pass








Solution





For \(r = L\) (and \(L = 10\)) almost every pair is within the radius, so after a few steps all headings are close to the common mean and \(\varphi\) is close to \(1\), reduced slightly by the noise. For \(r = 0\) the headings do not interact and \(\varphi\) stays of order \(1/\sqrt{N} = 0.1\) at all times. If your code gives something else, check the neighbor search and the angle average.
for radius in [0.0, box_size]:
    xy, theta = initialize_particles(num_particles, box_size)
    for t in range(100):
        xy, theta = vicsek_equations(
            xy=xy, theta=theta, noise=noise_strength, box_size=box_size,
            radius_interaction=radius, v0=v0,
        )
        if t + 1 in (10, 100):
            print(f"r = {radius}, step {t + 1}: phi = {vicsek_order_parameter(theta):.3f}")









References

Vicsek, Tamás, András Czirók, Eshel Ben-Jacob, Inon Cohen, and Ofer Shochet. 1995. “Novel Type of Phase Transition in a System of Self-Driven Particles.” Physical Review Letters 75 (6): 1226.

title: Synchronization in Nature
text:
Reading




Compulsory: Steven H. Strogatz (2024), Chapter 4, especially Section 4.5.
Recommended: (strogatz2003sync?).
Synchronization is the adjustment of the rhythms of self-sustained oscillators due to a weak interaction between them (Pikovsky, Rosenblum, and Kurths 2001). Two ingredients matter. Each unit oscillates on its own, with its own natural frequency. The units interact, and the interaction changes their timing, not their existence. This module models both ingredients with phase variables.

title: Synchronization in Nature
text:
Three classical examples

Fireflies
Males of some Southeast Asian firefly species, such as Pteroptyx malaccae, gather in trees and flash in unison. (buck1988synchronous?) reviews the field and laboratory evidence. A single firefly can also entrain to a periodic flashing light, which is the experiment behind the model in Phase Locking (ermentrout1984beyond?; ermentrout1991adaptive?).


Metronomes on a moving base
Place two or more metronomes on a light board that rests on two cans. The board moves slightly with each swing, and this motion couples the pendulums. (pantaleone2002synchronization?) shows that the metronomes usually end up swinging in phase, with antiphase motion only under special conditions. He also shows that the system is a mechanical realization of the Kuramoto model you study in Session 11.


Cardiac pacemaker cells
The sinoatrial node sets the heartbeat. (michaels1987mechanisms?) simulated two-dimensional arrays of electrically coupled sinus node cells with different intrinsic periods. The activation maps looked like a wave spreading from a single leading pacemaker, yet the pattern came from the mutual entrainment of all the spontaneously beating cells.

title: Synchronization in Nature
text:
Modelling choices
The examples share a structure, and the models in this module keep only that structure.








Example
Oscillator
Coupling




Fireflies
Flash cycle of one insect
Light from the other insects


Metronomes
Pendulum with escapement
Motion of the common base


Pacemaker cells
Membrane potential cycle
Electrical current between cells


Millennium Bridge
Gait of one pedestrian
Lateral motion of the deck (Steven H. Strogatz et al. 2005)



(winfree1967biological?) proposed describing each unit by a phase alone and studying large populations of such phase oscillators. (kuramoto1975self?) simplified Winfree’s model into the solvable form that now carries his name (Steven H. Strogatz 2000). A different route treats the interaction as short pulses, as in the integrate-and-fire model of (mirollo1990synchronization?).






Exercise



Pick the metronome example. Name the state variable of one oscillator, the physical quantity that carries the coupling, and one parameter that you expect to control whether synchronization happens.








Solution





The state of one metronome is the angle of its pendulum, which you can reduce to a phase on the circle. The coupling is carried by the horizontal displacement of the base. A natural control parameter is the mass of the base relative to the pendulums: a heavier base moves less and couples the metronomes more weakly. The spread of natural frequencies (the tempo settings) matters too. (pantaleone2002synchronization?) analyses both.

title: Synchronization in Nature
text:
Where this module goes

Phase Locking couples one oscillator to a periodic stimulus.
The Kuramoto Model couples many oscillators to each other.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Full Simulation
text:
Order Parameter






Exercise



Complete the function that computes the order parameter. It returns \(r\), \(\psi\) and the two coordinates \(r\cos\psi\) and \(r\sin\psi\) of the red dot.
def kuramoto_order_parameter(theta: np.ndarray) -> tuple:
    # TODO: compute r * exp(i * phi)
    order_param =  # replace this line
    r = np.abs(order_param)
    phi = np.angle(order_param)
    rcosphi = np.real(order_param)
    rsinphi = np.imag(order_param)
    return r, phi, rcosphi, rsinphi








Solution





axis=0 averages over oscillators, so the same function also works on the 2D array sol.y and returns \(r(t)\).
def kuramoto_order_parameter(theta: np.ndarray) -> tuple:
    order_param = np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta), axis=0)
    r = np.abs(order_param)
    phi = np.angle(order_param)
    rcosphi = np.real(order_param)
    rsinphi = np.imag(order_param)
    return r, phi, rcosphi, rsinphi

title: The Social Force Model
text: (helbing1995social?) model pedestrians as if they were subject to “social forces”. These forces are not physical. They measure the motivation of a pedestrian to change velocity in response to a goal, to other people and to walls. Unlike the Vicsek and Couzin models, this is a continuous-time model with acceleration, so speeds can change.

title: The Social Force Model
text:
Equation of motion
Pedestrian \(\alpha\) wants to walk in the direction \(\mathbf{e}_\alpha\) of its next target at desired speed \(v^0_\alpha\). Deviations from the desired velocity relax on a time scale \(\tau_\alpha\):
\[
\mathbf{F}^0_\alpha = \frac{1}{\tau_\alpha}\left(v^0_\alpha \mathbf{e}_\alpha - \mathbf{v}_\alpha\right).
\tag{1}\]
The total social force adds repulsion from other pedestrians \(\beta\), repulsion from borders \(B\) and optional attractions \(i\) (helbing1995social?):
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{w}_\alpha}{dt} = \mathbf{F}^0_\alpha + \sum_\beta \mathbf{F}_{\alpha\beta} + \sum_B \mathbf{F}_{\alpha B} + \sum_i \mathbf{F}_{\alpha i} + \text{fluctuations},
\tag{2}\]
where \(\mathbf{w}_\alpha\) is the preferred velocity. The actual velocity equals \(\mathbf{w}_\alpha\), capped at a maximum speed \(v^{\max}_\alpha\).

title: The Social Force Model
text:
Repulsion
The repulsion from pedestrian \(\beta\) is the gradient of a potential, \(\mathbf{f}_{\alpha\beta} = -\nabla_{\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta}} V_{\alpha\beta}[b(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta})]\), with \(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta} = \mathbf{r}_\alpha - \mathbf{r}_\beta\). The equipotential lines are ellipses stretched in the walking direction of \(\beta\), because \(\beta\) needs room for its next step:
\[
2b = \sqrt{\left(|\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta}| + |\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta} - v_\beta \Delta t\, \mathbf{e}_\beta|\right)^2 - (v_\beta \Delta t)^2}.
\tag{3}\]
Forces from behind count less. A situation outside the angle of sight \(2\varphi\) is weighted by a factor \(c\) with \(0 < c < 1\).
In their simulations (helbing1995social?) used \(V_{\alpha\beta}(b) = V^0 e^{-b/\sigma}\) and \(U_{\alpha B}(d) = U^0 e^{-d/R}\) with \(V^0 = 2.1\ \text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}\), \(\sigma = 0.3\) m, \(U^0 = 10\ \text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}\), \(R = 0.2\) m, \(\Delta t = 2\) s, \(\tau_\alpha = 0.5\) s, \(2\varphi = 200^\circ\) and \(c = 0.5\). Desired speeds were normal with mean \(1.34\) m/s and standard deviation \(0.26\) m/s.








Figure 1: Magnitude of the repulsive social force from a standing pedestrian (\(v_\beta = 0\), so \(b = |\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta}|\)) and from a wall, with the parameters of (helbing1995social?).

title: The Social Force Model
text:
Collective effects
With only these local rules, simulations reproduced two effects seen in real crowds (helbing1995social?):

Lane formation in counterflowing crowds: people walking in the same direction form lanes.
Oscillations at bottlenecks: at a narrow door, the passing direction switches back and forth between the two groups.







Exercise



A pedestrian walks at \(1.0\) m/s and wants \(1.34\) m/s. What acceleration does Equation 1 give with \(\tau = 0.5\) s? How long does it take to close most of the gap?








Solution





The acceleration is \((1.34 - 1.0)/0.5 = 0.68\ \text{m s}^{-2}\). Without other forces, the gap decays like \(e^{-t/\tau}\), so after about \(3\tau = 1.5\) s only \(5\%\) of it is left.









Exercise



Name one difference between the social force model and the Vicsek model, in the rules and in the question each model answers.








Solution





In the rules: Vicsek particles have fixed speed and only turn; social force pedestrians accelerate and decelerate, and each has its own goal. In the question: Vicsek asks when a group with no goal starts moving together. The social force model asks how people with goals share space, which is why (helbing1995social?) propose it as a tool for planning pedestrian areas.

title: The Couzin Model
text: The Vicsek model has alignment only. Its groups spread out and have no boundary. Couzin et al. (2002) added two behaviours that real animal groups show: individuals avoid collisions, and they are attracted to others so they are not left alone. The model was built for fish schools and bird flocks in three dimensions. The course uses a two-dimensional version.

title: The Couzin Model
The Couzin Model
text:
Rules
Repulsion has priority. Individuals try to keep a minimum distance from others at all times, a behaviour often observed in animals. You can read the zone of repulsion as personal space, or as collision avoidance. If \(n_r > 0\) neighbours are in the zor, the desired direction is
\[
\mathbf{d}_i(t+\tau) = -\sum_{j \ne i}^{n_r} \mathbf{r}_{ij}(t).
\tag{1}\]
Otherwise, orientation and attraction. With \(n_o\) neighbours in the zoo and \(n_a\) in the zoa,
\[
\mathbf{d}_o(t+\tau) = \sum_{j=1}^{n_o} \frac{\mathbf{v}_j(t)}{|\mathbf{v}_j(t)|},
\qquad
\mathbf{d}_a(t+\tau) = \sum_{j \ne i}^{n_a} \mathbf{r}_{ij}(t).
\tag{2}\]
If only the zoo has neighbours, \(\mathbf{d}_i = \mathbf{d}_o\). If only the zoa has neighbours, \(\mathbf{d}_i = \mathbf{d}_a\). If both do, \(\mathbf{d}_i = \tfrac12(\mathbf{d}_o + \mathbf{d}_a)\). If the result is the zero vector, or no neighbour is detected, the individual keeps its direction, \(\mathbf{d}_i = \mathbf{v}_i\).
Noise. Decisions in animals are affected by sensory and movement errors. To model this, the desired direction is rotated by a random angle from a wrapped Gaussian with standard deviation \(\sigma\).
Limited turning. After every individual has computed \(\mathbf{d}_i\), all of them turn toward it with turning rate \(\theta\). If the angle between \(\mathbf{v}_i(t)\) and \(\mathbf{d}_i(t+\tau)\) is less than the maximum turning angle \(\theta\tau\), then \(\mathbf{v}_i(t+\tau) = \mathbf{d}_i(t+\tau)\). Otherwise the individual rotates by \(\theta\tau\) toward the desired direction. They move at constant speed \(s\).

title: The Couzin Model
text:
Collective states
Couzin et al. (2002) measure two quantities, the group polarization and the group angular momentum:
\[
p_{\text{group}} = \frac{1}{N}\left|\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{v}_i\right|,
\qquad
m_{\text{group}} = \frac{1}{N}\left|\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{r}_{ic} \times \mathbf{v}_i\right|,
\tag{3}\]
where \(\mathbf{r}_{ic}\) is the unit vector from the group centroid \(\mathbf{c}_{\text{group}} = N^{-1}\sum_i \mathbf{c}_i\) to individual \(i\). Both lie in \([0, 1]\). Varying the widths \(\Delta r_o = r_o - r_r\) and \(\Delta r_a = r_a - r_o\), they found four states:



State
\(p_{\text{group}}\)
\(m_{\text{group}}\)




Swarm
low
low


Torus (milling)
low
high


Dynamic parallel group
high
low


Highly parallel group
very high
low



They also found collective memory: for the same parameters, the group state depends on the path taken through parameter space (Couzin et al. 2002). This is hysteresis, as in the spruce budworm model of Module 1 (Hysteresis).






Exercise



Set \(\Delta r_o = 0\) in the Couzin model. Which rules remain, and which collective state do you expect?








Solution





With no zone of orientation there is no alignment, only repulsion and attraction. Individuals stay together but do not align, so you expect a swarm: low \(p_{\text{group}}\) and low \(m_{\text{group}}\). This matches the swarm region of Couzin et al. (2002).



The code for this model is in amlab/collective_motion/couzin.py and the animation in amlab/collective_motion/couzin_animation.py. Implementing it is Option A of Practice: Collective Motion.
To explore the model before you code it, try the interactive Flock’n Roll explorable, which is based on Couzin et al. (2002).

title: Kuramoto Lab: The ODE
text: This page covers the implementation and validation steps. You write the right-hand side of the Kuramoto model and check it in two regimes where you know the answer.

title: Kuramoto Lab: The ODE
text:
Implementation: define the ODE
Choose between the pairwise form of the Kuramoto model and the mean-field form. They are mathematically identical (The Order Parameter). The mean field approximation is often more efficient for large populations, as it avoids computing pairwise interactions.
The right-hand side only uses \(\sin\) and \(e^{i\theta}\), which are \(2\pi\)-periodic, so the dynamics do not need the phases to stay in \([0, 2\pi)\). Wrapping with np.mod(theta, 2 * np.pi) is still useful before plotting.






Exercise



Define the ODE function for the Kuramoto model and call it kuramoto_ode(). It computes the derivatives \(\dot\theta_i\) from the current phases \(\theta_i\), the natural frequencies \(\omega_i\) and the coupling strength \(K\). Follow the general template that solve_ivp() expects:
def ode(t, state, *params):
    # state represents the current values of the variables (e.g., x, y)

    # params are any additional parameters needed to compute the derivatives
    # each of them is separated by commas

    return dstate_dt  # this should be a sequence of the same length as `state`
Remember: solve_ivp() requires the time argument even if it is not used.
def kuramoto_ode(t, theta, omega, coupling_strength=1.0):
    # TODO: compute the order parameter r * exp(i * psi)

    # TODO: compute dtheta_dt with the mean-field form
    return dtheta_dt








Solution





The function below uses the mean-field form, which is cheaper than computing pairwise interactions. It computes the order parameter at each call and uses it to calculate the derivatives.
def kuramoto_ode(t, theta, omega, coupling_strength=1.0):
    # Wrapping is optional: sin and exp are 2 pi-periodic
    theta = np.mod(theta, 2 * np.pi)
    order_param = np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta))
    r = np.abs(order_param)
    phi = np.angle(order_param)
    dtheta_dt = omega + coupling_strength * r * np.sin(phi - theta)
    return dtheta_dt

title: Kuramoto Lab: The ODE
text:

title: The Order Parameter
text:
To visualize the Kuramoto model, picture each phase \(\theta_j\) as a point \(e^{i\theta_j}\) running around the unit circle in the complex plane (Strogatz 2000).
Figure 1: Oscillators (blue dots) on the unit circle. The order parameter (red) points towards the centroid of the phases.

title: The Order Parameter
text:
Definition
The complex order parameter is the centroid of these points:
\[
r e^{i\psi} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^N e^{i\theta_j}.
\tag{1}\]

\(r \in [0, 1]\) is the coherence. \(r = 1\) when all phases coincide. \(r \approx 0\) when the phases are spread around the circle.
\(\psi\) is the mean phase, the phase of the collective rhythm.

In Figure 1 the initial phases cover only part of the circle, so the red vector has a clear length and direction. To see the vector move as the phases evolve, run the script amlab/odes_coupled/kuramoto.py. You build the same animation yourself in Animation.

title: The Order Parameter
text:
Mean-field form
Multiply Equation 1 by \(e^{-i\theta_i}\) and take the imaginary part:
\[
r\sin(\psi - \theta_i) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i).
\]
The Kuramoto model therefore becomes
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + K r \sin(\psi - \theta_i),\quad i = 1, \dots, N.
\tag{2}\]
This rewriting is exact for every \(N\) (Strogatz 2000). Each oscillator no longer sees the others one by one. It sees only the mean field: it is pulled toward the mean phase \(\psi\) with effective strength \(Kr\). Computing \(r\) and \(\psi\) costs \(O(N)\) operations per step, while the double sum in the pairwise form costs \(O(N^2)\).

title: The Order Parameter
text:
Feedback between coherence and coupling
Equation 2 shows why synchronization can appear spontaneously (Strogatz 2000):

Oscillators are pulled toward \(\psi\) with strength \(Kr\).
If more of them cluster, \(r\) grows.
A larger \(r\) increases the pull \(Kr\), which recruits more oscillators.

The loop is opposed by the spread of natural frequencies. Oscillators whose \(|\omega_i|\) exceeds \(Kr\) cannot follow the mean field and keep drifting. The balance sets a threshold coupling \(K_c\), derived in Critical Coupling.






Exercise



Suppose the \(N\) phases are independent and uniform on \([0, 2\pi)\). Show that \(\mathbb{E}[r^2] = 1/N\). What does this imply for the value of \(r\) you measure in an incoherent simulation?








Solution





\[
r^2 = \left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_j e^{i\theta_j}\right|^2 = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{j,k} e^{i(\theta_j - \theta_k)}.
\]
The \(N\) terms with \(j = k\) equal \(1\). For \(j \ne k\) the phases are independent, so \(\mathbb{E}[e^{i(\theta_j-\theta_k)}] = \mathbb{E}[e^{i\theta_j}]\,\mathbb{E}[e^{-i\theta_k}] = 0\). Hence \(\mathbb{E}[r^2] = N/N^2 = 1/N\). An incoherent population with \(N = 100\) shows \(r\) of order \(0.1\), not \(0\). You will see this floor in Finite-Size Effects.









Exercise



Compute \(r\) for three oscillators at phases \(0\), \(2\pi/3\) and \(4\pi/3\), and for three oscillators at \(0\), \(0\) and \(\pi\).








Solution





The first three points are the cube roots of unity, which sum to zero, so \(r = 0\). For the second set, \(e^{0} + e^{0} + e^{i\pi} = 1\), so \(r = 1/3\) and \(\psi = 0\).

Tip: blitting requires you to return artists If you set blit=True, your update function must return an iterable of the artists that changed, as shown above. If you forget to return them, the animation will run but the plot will not update (it will look frozen).
Move the function update_animation inside run_simulation so it can access the state variables with nonlocal.






Hint





Use the tail trick. Store the last TAIL_LEN positions:

shift the tensor with np.roll(...),
write the newest positions into the last slice.

This avoids creating new arrays each frame.









Solution





def update_animation(frame: int):
    nonlocal \
        xy, \
        xy_tail, \
        theta, \
        noise_eta, \
        v0, \
        radius_interaction, \
        box_size
    xy, theta = vicsek_equations(
        xy,
        theta,
        v0=v0,
        dt=dt,
        radius_interaction=radius_interaction,
        box_size=box_size,
        noise=noise_eta,
    )

    # Update tails
    xy_tail = np.roll(xy_tail, shift=-1, axis=2)
    xy_tail[:, :, -1] = xy
    plt_particles.set_data(xy_tail[0].flatten(), xy_tail[1].flatten())
    plt_current.set_data(xy[0], xy[1])

    return (plt_particles, plt_current)

text:
Create the Animation Object
Matplotlib uses FuncAnimation. Inside run_simulation, after defining update_animation, create the animation object:
ani = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update_animation, interval=0, blit=True)

interval=0 makes it as fast as your computer can handle.
You can set a larger interval (e.g. 20 ms) to reduce CPU usage.

Full Script
At this point you have built every piece.






Exercise



Assemble run_simulation(): parameters, initial state, figure, particle artists, the update function and the animation object. Run the script and check that the particles move and align.








Solution





This version has no order plot, noise plot or sliders yet. It focuses on the particle animation.
def run_simulation(dt: float = 1.0) -> None:
    # Parameters
    num_boids = 100
    noise_eta = 0.5
    box_size = 10.0
    radius_interaction = 1.0
    v0 = 0.03

    # Initialize state
    xy, theta = initialize_particles(num_boids, box_size)

    # Order parameter history and noise diagnostic
    # will be initialized here

    # Create figure and axes
    fig, ax_plane = make_figure()

    # Initialize plots
    xy_tail, plt_particles, plt_current = init_particles_plot(ax_plane, xy, box_size, tail_len=20)
    # The order plot and noise plot will go here

    # Sliders will be added here

    # Define the animation update function
    def update_animation(frame: int):
        nonlocal xy, xy_tail, theta
        xy, theta = vicsek_equations(
            xy,
            theta,
            v0=v0,
            dt=dt,
            radius_interaction=radius_interaction,
            box_size=box_size,
            noise=noise_eta,
        )
        xy_tail = np.roll(xy_tail, shift=-1, axis=2)
        xy_tail[:, :, -1] = xy
        plt_particles.set_data(xy_tail[0].flatten(), xy_tail[1].flatten())
        plt_current.set_data(xy[0], xy[1])
        return (plt_particles, plt_current)

    # Create the animation object
    ani = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update_animation, interval=0, blit=True)

    # The slider callbacks will come here

    plt.show()

title: Relaxation Oscillations
text: A relaxation oscillation alternates slow build-up with fast release. Van der Pol introduced the term for self-oscillating electrical circuits (vanderpol1926relaxation?). The standard example is his oscillator with strong nonlinearity (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.5).

title: Relaxation Oscillations
section: The Van der Pol oscillator for large \(\mu\)
text:
The Van der Pol oscillator for large \(\mu\)
The equation \(\ddot x + \mu(x^2 - 1)\dot x + x = 0\) has negative damping for \(|x| < 1\) and positive damping for \(|x| > 1\). With \(F(x) = x^3/3 - x\) and \(y = \dot x/\mu + F(x)\) it becomes
\[
\dot x = \mu\bigl(y - F(x)\bigr), \qquad \dot y = -\frac{x}{\mu},
\tag{1}\]
which is the form in amlab/odes_2d/van_der_pol.py (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.5).
For \(\mu \gg 1\), \(\dot x\) is of order \(\mu\) and \(\dot y\) of order \(1/\mu\). Away from the cubic nullcline \(y = F(x)\) the trajectory jumps almost horizontally, in a time of order \(1/\mu\). On the outer branches of the cubic it creeps slowly, in a time of order \(\mu\). When it reaches a knee of the cubic (\(x = \pm 1\)) it jumps to the other branch.

title: Relaxation Oscillations
text:
The period
Strogatz computes the period from the time spent on the slow branches. On a slow branch \(y \approx F(x)\), so \(\dot y = F'(x)\dot x = (x^2 - 1)\dot x = -x/\mu\). Integrating from \(x = 2\) to \(x = 1\) and doubling for the two branches gives
\[
T \approx 2\mu \int_1^2 \frac{x^2 - 1}{x}\,dx = (3 - 2\ln 2)\,\mu \approx 1.61\,\mu,
\tag{2}\]
with corrections that vanish relative to \(\mu\) as \(\mu \to \infty\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.5).








Figure 1: Van der Pol oscillator for mu = 10. Left: limit cycle and cubic nullcline in the Lienard plane. Right: x(t), with slow drifts and fast jumps.

title: Relaxation Oscillations
text:
Numerical check
Measure the period from upward zero crossings of \(x(t)\) and compare with Equation 2.

for mu in [5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0]:
    t_end = 12 * mu
    s = solve_ivp(van_der_pol, (0, t_end), [2.0, 0.0], args=(mu,), method="LSODA",
                  t_eval=np.linspace(0, t_end, 40000), rtol=1e-8)
    x = s.y[0]
    up = s.t[1:][(x[:-1] < 0) & (x[1:] >= 0)]
    period = np.mean(np.diff(up[1:]))
    print(f"mu = {mu:4.0f}: T = {period:6.2f}, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu = {(3 - 2 * np.log(2)) * mu:6.2f}")

mu =    5: T =  11.61, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu =   8.07
mu =   10: T =  19.08, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu =  16.14
mu =   20: T =  34.68, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu =  32.27
mu =   40: T =  66.50, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu =  64.55


The relative error falls as \(\mu\) grows, as expected for an asymptotic formula.

title: Relaxation Oscillations
text:
Where you meet it again
The FitzHugh-Nagumo model has the same geometry: a fast variable with a cubic nullcline and a slow recovery variable (FitzHugh-Nagumo Model). When its fixed point sits on the middle branch, the system produces relaxation oscillations; when it sits on an outer branch, the system is excitable.






Exercise



Evaluate the integral in Equation 2.








Solution





\(\int_1^2 (x - 1/x)\,dx = [x^2/2 - \ln x]_1^2 = (2 - \ln 2) - 1/2 = 3/2 - \ln 2\). Multiplying by \(2\mu\) gives \((3 - 2\ln 2)\mu\).

title: CDIMA: Phase Plane
text:
Reading




Course material: Hopf Bifurcation and The Phase Plane; Strogatz (2024), Section 8.3.
The CDIMA model (chlorine dioxide-iodine-malonic acid reaction) is a two-variable chemical oscillator (lengyel1991modeling?; Strogatz 2024, sec. 8.3):
\[\begin{aligned}
\dot x &= a - x - \frac{4xy}{1+x^2} \\
\dot y &= bx \left( 1 - \frac{y}{1+x^2} \right)
\end{aligned} \tag{1}\]
where \(x\) and \(y\) are the dimensionless concentrations of I\(^-\) and ClO\(_2^-\). The parameters \(a, b > 0\) depend on the empirical rate constants and on the concentrations assumed for the slow reactants (Strogatz 2024, sec. 8.3).

title: CDIMA: Phase Plane
text:
Prediction






Exercise



From Hopf Bifurcation: for \(a = 10\) the Hopf point is \(b_c = 3.5\). With \(b = 4\), do you expect trajectories to converge to the fixed point \((2, 5)\) or to a limit cycle?








Solution





The fixed point is stable for \(b > b_c = 3a/5 - 25/a = 3.5\). With \(b = 4\) you are on the stable side, so trajectories should spiral into \((2, 5)\). The validation at the end of this page confirms it.

title: CDIMA: Phase Plane
text:
Implementation
To understand the dynamics, we can analyze the phase plane. A phase plane is a 2D plot whose axes are the state variables (here, \(x\) and \(y\)). Each point \((x,y)\) represents the system’s state at a given time, and the differential equations define a vector field on this plane that indicates how the state evolves. Trajectories (solution curves) show how \((x(t),y(t))\) moves through the plane, revealing features such as equilibrium points, nullclines, limit cycles, and their stability.








Figure 1: Phase plane of the CDIMA system with a = 10, b = 4. Trajectories are shown for different initial conditions (IC as x-y, marked black). Generated with scipy.integrate.solve_ivp() and matplotlib.





Generating this phase plane in Python is simple. We will follow the same approach as in 1D: define the right-hand side as a function, choose a time span and evaluation grid, and integrate with scipy.integrate.solve_ivp(). Follow the steps below.

Define the ODE Function






Exercise



Define the cdima() function for Equation 1. Remember that any ODE (in any dimension) can be written as:
def ode(t, state, *params):
    # state represents the current values of the variables (e.g., x, y)

    # params are any additional parameters needed to compute the derivatives
    # each of them is separated by commas

    return dstate_dt  # this should be a sequence of the same length as `state`
Write the cdima() function in this format.








Hint





def cdima(t: float, state: tuple[float, float], a: int, b: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Remember the docstring and type hints!"""
    x, y = state  # unpack the state variables
    dxdt =  # compute dx/dt
    dydt = # compute dy/dt
    return (dxdt, dydt)  # return the derivatives as a list









Solution





def cdima(t, state, a, b):
    """CDIMA (Lengyel-Epstein) model, Strogatz Section 8.3."""
    x, y = state
    dxdt = a - x - 4 * x * y / (1 + x**2)
    dydt = b * x * (1 - y / (1 + x**2))
    return (dxdt, dydt)
The reference version is cdima in amlab/odes_2d/cdima.py.





Solve the Initial Value Problem
Next, we need to solve the initial value problem (IVP) for a given initial condition and parameters. The workflow is similar to 1D, but now we have a vector of state variables instead of a single variable. The solve_ivp() function will return the trajectories for both \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\), which we can then plot in the phase plane.






Exercise



Use scipy.integrate.solve_ivp() and your cdima() function to solve the IVP for \(a=10\), \(b=4\) and \((x_0,y_0) = (0,3)\). The output should be the trajectories of \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\), two arrays of the same length. You can see this trajectory in Figure 1. What is the state of the system at \(t=5\)?








Hint





from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
import numpy as np

# Define parameters
a, b = 10, 4
# Define initial condition
x0, y0 = 0, 3 
# Define time span and evaluation points
t_span = (0, 20) # Start at t=0 and end at t=20
t_eval = np.linspace(t_span[0], t_span[1], 2000)  # Return 2000 points between t=0 and t=20
# Solve the IVP
sol = solve_ivp(cdima, t_span, [x0, y0], args=(a, b), t_eval=t_eval)
# sol.y[0] will give you x(t) and sol.y[1] will give you y(t)









Solution





Integrate up to \(t = 5\) and read the last column of sol.y.

from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
import numpy as np

from amlab.odes_2d.cdima import cdima

a, b = 10, 4
x0, y0 = 0, 3

t_span = (0, 5)
t_eval = np.linspace(t_span[0], t_span[1], 500)
sol = solve_ivp(cdima, t_span, [x0, y0], args=(a, b), t_eval=t_eval)
final_state = sol.y[:, -1]  # Get the last column of sol.y, which corresponds to the state at t=5
print(f"State at t=5: x={final_state[0]:.2f}, y={final_state[1]:.2f}")

State at t=5: x=2.08, y=4.13







Plotting the Phase Plane
Finally, you plot the trajectories in the phase plane using matplotlib.pyplot.






Exercise



Reproduce Figure 1 by plotting \(y(t)\) against \(x(t)\) for the initial conditions \((0, 3)\), \((0, 1.5)\) and \((2, 0)\). Mark the initial conditions to see where the trajectories start.








Solution





import matplotlib.pyplot as plt 

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for x0, y0 in [(0, 3), (0, 1.5), (2, 0)]:
    sol = solve_ivp(cdima, [0, 20], [x0, y0], args=(a, b), t_eval=np.linspace(0, 20, 2000))
    ax.plot(sol.y[0], sol.y[1], label=f"IC: ({x0}, {y0})")  # Plot y vs. x
    ax.plot(x0, y0, 'o', color='black')  # Mark the initial condition
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("y")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

title: CDIMA: Phase Plane
text:
Validation
For \(a = 10\), \(b = 4\) all trajectories in Figure 1 spiral into the same point near \((2, 5)\). This agrees with the prediction: \(b > b_c = 3.5\), so the fixed point \((a/5, 1 + (a/5)^2) = (2, 5)\) is a stable spiral.

title: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
text:
Optional extension



This page is optional. It applies the Session 3 workflow to a second rate law, with saturation instead of bistability.
Michaelis-Menten kinetics is one of the standard examples of a saturating nonlinear rate law (Michaelis and Menten 1913). The classical instantaneous rate is
\[
v(s) = \frac{V_{\max} s}{K_m + s},
\]
where \(V_{\max}\) is the maximum rate and \(K_m\) is the Michaelis constant.
In the reference script used in this course, the same saturating expression is reused as a simple teaching ODE,
\[
\dot s = \frac{V_{\max}s}{K_m + s}
\tag{1}\]
This is not a full enzyme-substrate mass-action model. It is a compact one-dimensional example that lets you study how saturation changes both the rate curve and the time evolution of the state variable.

title: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
text:
Small and Large Concentration Regimes
The rate law has two useful asymptotic regimes:
\[
v(s) \approx \frac{V_{\max}}{K_m} s \quad \text{for } s \ll K_m,
\qquad
v(s) \approx V_{\max} \quad \text{for } s \gg K_m.
\]
So the system is approximately linear at small \(s\) and nearly constant-rate at large \(s\).

title: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
text:
Reference Implementation
See:

amlab/odes_1d/michaelis_menten.py

The helper plot_michaelis_menten(...) produces:

\(s(t)\) over time
\(v(s)\) with guides at \(s=K_m\) and \(v=V_{\max}/2\)

title: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
text:
Render-time Figure








Figure 1: Michaelis-Menten: time series \(s(t)\) and rate curve \(v(s)\).

title: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
text:
Interpret the Parameters

Increasing \(V_{\max}\) raises the saturation plateau.
Increasing \(K_m\) shifts the curve so larger values of \(s\) are needed before the rate is close to saturation.
In the teaching ODE used here, larger \(V_{\max}\) also makes the state variable evolve faster in time.

title: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
text:
Exploration






Exercise



Use plot_michaelis_menten to answer both questions.

Increase \(V_{\max}\) and observe how the rate curve changes.
Increase \(K_m\) (lower affinity). How does the saturation point shift?









Solution





Doubling \(V_{\max}\) doubles \(v(s)\) at every \(s\): the plateau rises and the half-saturation level \(V_{\max}/2\) rises with it, but it is still reached at \(s = K_m\). Increasing \(K_m\) moves the half-saturation point to the right, so you need a larger \(s\) before the rate is close to \(V_{\max}\). The initial slope \(V_{\max}/K_m\) falls.

import numpy as np

from amlab.odes_1d.michaelis_menten import michaelis_menten

s = np.array([0.5, 1.0, 5.0])
for vmax, km in [(1.0, 0.5), (2.0, 0.5), (1.0, 2.0)]:
    print(f"vmax={vmax}, km={km}: v(s) = {np.round(michaelis_menten(0, s, vmax, km), 3)}")

vmax=1.0, km=0.5: v(s) = [0.5   0.667 0.909]
vmax=2.0, km=0.5: v(s) = [1.    1.333 1.818]
vmax=1.0, km=2.0: v(s) = [0.2   0.333 0.714]

text:
Run Locally
python amlab/odes_1d/michaelis_menten.py

title: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
text:
Limitations
In the classical mechanism the substrate is consumed, so \(s\) decreases. The teaching ODE above has a positive rate and makes \(s\) grow without bound. Use it only to study the shape of the saturating law, not as a model of an enzyme reaction.

title: Compartmental Models: SIR and SIS
text:
Reading




Compulsory: (britton2003essential?), chapter on epidemic models.
Recommended: (murray2002mathematical?), chapter on the dynamics of infectious diseases.
Compartmental models divide a population into groups according to infection status and describe the flows between them. The SIR model goes back to Kermack and McKendrick (Kermack and McKendrick 1927); (hethcote2000mathematics?) and Keeling and Rohani (2008) review the family.

title: Compartmental Models: SIR and SIS
text:
The SIR model
Let \(S\), \(I\), \(R\) be the fractions of the population that are susceptible, infectious and removed (recovered and immune, or dead). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot S &= -\beta S I,\\
\dot I &= \beta S I - \gamma I,\\
\dot R &= \gamma I .
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]

\(\beta\) is the transmission rate: a susceptible person meets infectious people at a rate proportional to \(I\), and each contact transmits with a fixed probability.
\(\gamma\) is the recovery rate. The infectious period is exponentially distributed with mean \(1/\gamma\).
\(S + I + R = 1\) is conserved, so only two equations are independent.

The SIR model describes a single outbreak of a disease that gives lasting immunity, such as measles in a population without vaccination (hethcote2000mathematics?).

title: Compartmental Models: SIR and SIS
text:
The SIS model
If recovery gives no immunity, recovered individuals return to \(S\):
\[
\dot S = -\beta S I + \gamma I, \qquad \dot I = \beta S I - \gamma I .
\tag{2}\]
With \(S = 1 - I\) this reduces to one equation, \(\dot I = \beta I (1 - I) - \gamma I\), which is a logistic equation for \(I\). Its long-run state is a disease-free equilibrium or an endemic equilibrium (hethcote2000mathematics?). SIS models are used for some bacterial infections and sexually transmitted diseases that do not confer immunity (Keeling and Rohani 2008).

title: Compartmental Models: SIR and SIS
text:
Assumptions
Each assumption is a simplification you should be able to defend or replace.

Well mixed. Every individual is equally likely to meet every other. Real contacts are structured by households, schools, age and geography.
Constant rates. \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) do not change in time. Seasons, behaviour change and interventions all change \(\beta\).
Closed population. No births, deaths or migration during the outbreak. This is reasonable for a short epidemic, not for an endemic disease over decades.
Exponential infectious period. Recovery happens at a constant rate, so some people recover almost immediately and others stay infectious for a long time.
Deterministic and continuous. Fractions change smoothly. This fails at the start of an outbreak, when there are only a few cases and chance matters.







Exercise



In Equation 1, show that \(S(t)\) is decreasing and \(R(t)\) is increasing for all \(t\). Can \(I(t)\) increase?








Solution





\(\dot S = -\beta S I \le 0\) and \(\dot R = \gamma I \ge 0\) because \(S, I \ge 0\). \(\dot I = I(\beta S - \gamma)\) is positive when \(S > \gamma/\beta\). So \(I\) grows while the susceptible fraction is above \(\gamma/\beta\), then decreases. This threshold is the subject of the next page.

title: Sensitivity and Chaos
text:
The Lorenz attractor is deterministic, but long-term prediction is still limited because nearby trajectories diverge over time (Lorenz 1963; Strogatz 2024). This is sensitivity to initial conditions. On the attractor the separation grows on average like \(e^{\lambda t}\), with a largest Lyapunov exponent \(\lambda \approx 0.9\) for the standard parameters (Strogatz 2024, sec. 9.3).
Figure 1: Two nearby Lorenz trajectories and their separation over time.

title: Sensitivity and Chaos
text:
Compare two nearby initial conditions
To test sensitivity, keep the parameters fixed and change only the initial state by a tiny amount.
initial_state_a = (0.0, 1.0, 1.05)
initial_state_b = (0.0, 1.0, 1.05001)

trajectory_a = simulate_lorenz(initial_state=initial_state_a, dt=0.01, num_steps=3000)
trajectory_b = simulate_lorenz(initial_state=initial_state_b, dt=0.01, num_steps=3000)
At first, the two runs are nearly indistinguishable. Later, they separate enough that their detailed future motion no longer matches.

title: Sensitivity and Chaos
text:
Measure the separation
The most direct diagnostic is the Euclidean distance between the two trajectories at each time step:
\[
d_n = \left\|\mathbf{x}_n^{(1)} - \mathbf{x}_n^{(2)}\right\|.
\]
separation = np.linalg.norm(trajectory_a - trajectory_b, axis=1)
times = 0.01 * np.arange(len(separation))

plt.semilogy(times, separation)
plt.xlabel("Time")
plt.ylabel("Separation")
plt.show()
If the separation grows rapidly from a tiny initial perturbation, then the predictability horizon is short even though the equations themselves are deterministic.

title: Sensitivity and Chaos
text:
What chaos means here
In this context, chaos does not mean that the model is random.

The update rule is fixed.
The same initial condition gives the same trajectory.
Small errors in the initial state can still lead to very different long-run outcomes.

This is why deterministic chaos matters in modeling. Exact equations do not guarantee exact long-term forecasts.

title: Sensitivity and Chaos
text:
Parameter variation
The parameter r strongly influences the geometry of the trajectories. A useful first comparison is to simulate one run with a smaller value such as r=10 and another with the standard value r=28.
trajectory_low_r = simulate_lorenz(dt=0.01, num_steps=3000, r=10)
trajectory_standard = simulate_lorenz(dt=0.01, num_steps=3000, r=28)
That comparison helps separate two ideas:

sensitivity to initial conditions at fixed parameters,
and qualitative changes driven by the parameter regime.

title: The Spruce Budworm Model
text:
Reading




Compulsory: Strogatz (2024), Section 3.7, “Insect outbreak”.
Recommended: (ludwig1978qualitative?).
The spruce budworm is a forest insect whose outbreaks defoliate balsam fir forests. Ludwig, Jones and Holling modelled the budworm and forest system of New Brunswick, Canada, with the budworm as a fast variable and the forest as a slow one (ludwig1978qualitative?). On this page you keep the forest fixed and study the budworm alone, as in Strogatz (2024), Section 3.7.

title: The Spruce Budworm Model
text:
The dimensional model
Let \(N(t)\) be the budworm density. With the forest held fixed,
\[
\frac{dN}{dt} = RN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right) - \frac{BN^2}{A^2 + N^2}.
\tag{1}\]

\(RN(1 - N/K)\) is logistic growth with rate \(R\) and carrying capacity \(K\). The carrying capacity depends on the amount of foliage.
\(p(N) = BN^2/(A^2 + N^2)\) is predation, mainly by birds. It saturates at the maximum rate \(B\) when budworms are abundant. It vanishes like \(N^2\) at low density, because birds switch to other food when budworms are rare. This is a Holling type III functional response (ludwig1978qualitative?).
\(A\) sets the density at which predation starts to saturate: \(p(A) = B/2\).

Ludwig et al. chose these forms because they need few parameters, and they state that the conclusions depend only on the qualitative shape of the terms (ludwig1978qualitative?).








Figure 1: Type III predation term p(N)/B as a function of N/A. It is small at low density and saturates at 1.

title: The Spruce Budworm Model
text:
Removing the units
Equation 1 has four parameters \(R, K, A, B\). Rescale the density by \(A\) and time by \(A/B\):
\[
x = \frac{N}{A}, \qquad \tau = \frac{B}{A}t .
\]
Since \(dN/dt = B\, dx/d\tau\), dividing Equation 1 by \(B\) gives
\[
\frac{dx}{d\tau} = r x\left(1 - \frac{x}{k}\right) - \frac{x^2}{1 + x^2},
\qquad
r = \frac{RA}{B}, \quad k = \frac{K}{A}.
\tag{2}\]
Only two dimensionless groups remain (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.7). Ludwig et al. obtain the same groups under the names \(R\) and \(Q\) (ludwig1978qualitative?, eqn 8).

\(r\) compares the budworm growth rate with the maximum predation rate.
\(k\) is the carrying capacity measured in units of the predation scale \(A\).

The rest of the module uses Equation 2. Parameter values quoted as \(r\) and \(k\) are always the dimensionless ones.






Exercise



Check that \(r\) and \(k\) are dimensionless. Assume \(N\) is measured in larvae per acre and \(t\) in years.








Solution





\(R\) has units 1/year. \(A\) has units larvae/acre. \(B\) is a rate of larvae eaten, so it has units larvae/acre/year. Then \(RA/B\) has units (1/year)(larvae/acre)/(larvae/acre/year), which cancel. \(K/A\) is a ratio of two densities.

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
In the SIS model recovered individuals become susceptible again (hethcote2000mathematics?). With \(S = 1 - I\),
\[
\dot I = \beta I (1 - I) - \gamma I .
\tag{1}\]

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
Prediction
From The Reproduction Number: for \(R_0 = \beta/\gamma > 1\) the solution should approach the endemic level \(I^* = 1 - 1/R_0\); for \(R_0 < 1\) it should decay to 0.






Exercise



Sketch \(\dot I\) against \(I\) for \(R_0 = 2\) and mark the fixed points, as you did for the budworm.








Solution





\(\dot I = I\bigl(\beta(1 - I) - \gamma\bigr)\) is a downward parabola with zeros at \(I = 0\) and \(I^* = 1 - \gamma/\beta = 0.5\). It is positive between them and negative for \(I > 0.5\). So \(I = 0\) is unstable (slope \(\beta - \gamma > 0\)) and \(I^* = 0.5\) is stable (slope \(-(\beta - \gamma) < 0\)).

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
Implementation






Exercise



Write the right-hand side of Equation 1 in the form solve_ivp expects. The state i arrives as an array with one element.
def sis_model(t, i, beta, gamma):
    didt = # TODO: right-hand side of the SIS equation
    return [didt]








Solution





def sis_model(t, i, beta, gamma):
    return [beta * i[0] * (1 - i[0]) - gamma * i[0]]
The reference version is amlab.epidemics.sis_rhs.

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
Validation

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

from amlab.epidemics import sis_endemic_level, sis_rhs

gamma = 0.1
t = np.linspace(0, 200, 800)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for r0, color in [(0.8, "tab:gray"), (1.5, "tab:blue"), (3.0, "tab:red")]:
    sol = solve_ivp(sis_rhs, (0, 200), [0.01], args=(r0 * gamma, gamma), t_eval=t)
    ax.plot(sol.t, sol.y[0], color=color, label=f"R0 = {r0}")
    ax.axhline(sis_endemic_level(r0), color=color, ls=":")
    print(f"R0 = {r0}: I(200) = {sol.y[0, -1]:.4f}, 1 - 1/R0 = {sis_endemic_level(r0):.4f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (days)")
ax.set_ylabel("I")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

R0 = 0.8: I(200) = 0.0002, 1 - 1/R0 = 0.0000
R0 = 1.5: I(200) = 0.3328, 1 - 1/R0 = 0.3333
R0 = 3.0: I(200) = 0.6664, 1 - 1/R0 = 0.6667








Figure 1: SIS model with gamma = 0.1 and three values of R0. Dotted lines: endemic level 1 - 1/R0.

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
Experiment






Exercise




Start from \(I(0) = 0.9\) with \(R_0 = 1.5\). Does the solution approach the same level from above?
Take \(R_0\) close to 1, for example 1.05. How long does it take to get close to \(I^*\)? Relate the time scale to the linearization \(f'(I^*) = -(\beta - \gamma)\).









Solution





The endemic equilibrium attracts every \(I(0) > 0\), from above or below. Near it, perturbations decay like \(e^{-(\beta - \gamma)t}\). For \(R_0 = 1.05\) and \(\gamma = 0.1\), \(\beta - \gamma = 0.005\) per day, so the relaxation time is about 200 days.

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
Interpretation and limitations
The SIS model has no epidemic peak followed by extinction: the disease settles at a constant endemic level. In a finite population the deterministic endemic state hides random fluctuations, and the infection can go extinct by chance when the number of infected individuals is small (Keeling and Rohani 2008).






Optional extension



The SIS equation is a logistic equation. Solve it analytically and compare the formula with the numerical solution.

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text: An SIR epidemic always ends with some susceptibles left. How many people are infected in total can be computed without solving the ODE in time (Kermack and McKendrick 1927; hethcote2000mathematics?).

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text:
The final size relation
Divide \(\dot S = -\beta S I\) by \(\dot R = \gamma I\):
\[
\frac{dS}{dR} = -R_0 S \quad \Longrightarrow \quad S(t) = S(0)\, e^{-R_0 (R(t) - R(0))} .
\]
As \(t \to \infty\), \(I \to 0\). With \(R(0) = 0\) and \(R(\infty) = 1 - S(\infty)\) you get
\[
\ln\frac{S(0)}{S(\infty)} = R_0 \bigl(1 - S(\infty)\bigr) .
\tag{1}\]
For a small initial seed, \(S(0) \to 1\), and the fraction ever infected, \(z = 1 - S(\infty)\), satisfies
\[
z = 1 - e^{-R_0 z} .
\tag{2}\]
For \(R_0 \le 1\) the only solution in \([0, 1]\) is \(z = 0\). For \(R_0 > 1\) there is a unique positive solution, and it is the final size (hethcote2000mathematics?).

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text:
Solving it numerically
Equation 2 has no closed-form solution in elementary functions, but a root finder solves it instantly.

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq

for r0 in [1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0]:
    z = brentq(lambda z: z - 1 + np.exp(-r0 * z), 1e-9, 1.0)
    print(f"R0 = {r0}: final size z = {z:.3f}, herd immunity threshold = {1 - 1 / r0:.3f}")

R0 = 1.5: final size z = 0.583, herd immunity threshold = 0.333
R0 = 2.0: final size z = 0.797, herd immunity threshold = 0.500
R0 = 3.0: final size z = 0.940, herd immunity threshold = 0.667
R0 = 5.0: final size z = 0.993, herd immunity threshold = 0.800


The final size is larger than the herd immunity threshold \(1 - 1/R_0\). The epidemic overshoots: when \(S\) reaches \(1/R_0\) the number of infectious people is at its maximum, and they still cause many infections on the way down.

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text:
Peak prevalence
The same trick gives the maximum of \(I\). From \(dI/dS = -1 + 1/(R_0 S)\),
\[
I_{\max} = I(0) + S(0) - \frac{1}{R_0} - \frac{1}{R_0}\ln\bigl(R_0 S(0)\bigr),
\]
valid when \(R_0 S(0) > 1\) (hethcote2000mathematics?). amlab.epidemics.peak_prevalence implements this formula.






Exercise



Check the final size relation against a simulation for \(R_0 = 3\) (\(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\)) with \(I(0) = 10^{-4}\).








Solution






from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

from amlab.epidemics import final_size, sir_rhs

sol = solve_ivp(sir_rhs, (0, 400), [1 - 1e-4, 1e-4, 0.0], args=(0.3, 0.1), rtol=1e-9)
print(f"Simulated: {1 - sol.y[0, -1]:.4f}")
print(f"Relation:  {final_size(3.0, s0=1 - 1e-4) + 1e-4:.4f}")

Simulated: 0.9405
Relation:  0.9405


The simulated fraction \(1 - S(\infty)\) matches Equation 1 including the initial seed.

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text:
Extensions
The SIR model is the starting point of a large family. Each extension relaxes one assumption from Compartmental Models.

SEIR: an exposed class \(E\) for people infected but not yet infectious. It changes the timing of the epidemic but, in the simplest case, not \(R_0\) (hethcote2000mathematics?; Keeling and Rohani 2008).
Vital dynamics: births and deaths allow endemic equilibria and recurrent epidemics (hethcote2000mathematics?).
Age structure: contact rates that depend on age (hethcote2000mathematics?; Keeling and Rohani 2008).
Spatial structure and networks: contacts limited to neighbours or to a contact network. Module 5 studies epidemics on networks (Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015).
Stochastic models: needed when the number of cases is small, for example to compute the probability that an outbreak dies out by chance (Keeling and Rohani 2008).

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text:
Next
Session 6 implements these models and fits them to data.

title: The Reproduction Number
text: The basic reproduction number \(R_0\) is the average number of secondary infections caused by one infectious individual in a fully susceptible population (hethcote2000mathematics?; Keeling and Rohani 2008).

title: The Reproduction Number
text:
R0 in the SIR model
In the SIR model of Compartmental Models, one infectious person infects susceptibles at rate \(\beta S \approx \beta\) when \(S \approx 1\), during an infectious period of mean length \(1/\gamma\). Hence
\[
R_0 = \frac{\beta}{\gamma} .
\tag{1}\]

title: The Reproduction Number
text:
The threshold
The infectious equation is \(\dot I = \gamma I (R_0 S - 1)\). At the start of an outbreak \(S(0) \approx 1\), so

\(R_0 > 1\): \(I\) grows at rate \(\gamma(R_0 - 1) = \beta - \gamma\), and an epidemic occurs;
\(R_0 < 1\): \(I\) decays and the infection dies out.

This is the threshold theorem of Kermack and McKendrick (Kermack and McKendrick 1927; hethcote2000mathematics?). During the epidemic, the relevant quantity is the effective reproduction number \(R_{\text{eff}}(t) = R_0 S(t)\). The number of infectious people peaks exactly when \(R_{\text{eff}} = 1\), that is when \(S = 1/R_0\).
The same threshold appears in the SIS model. The endemic equilibrium of \(\dot I = \beta I(1 - I) - \gamma I\) is
\[
I^* = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0},
\]
which exists and is stable only for \(R_0 > 1\) (hethcote2000mathematics?).

title: The Reproduction Number
text:
Herd immunity
Suppose a fraction \(p\) of the population is immune before the outbreak, so \(S(0) = 1 - p\). An outbreak cannot start if \(R_0 (1 - p) < 1\). The critical immunization fraction is
\[
p_c = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0} .
\tag{2}\]
Vaccinating more than \(p_c\) of the population protects the whole population, including those not vaccinated (hethcote2000mathematics?; Keeling and Rohani 2008). The formula assumes random mixing and a vaccine that gives full, lasting immunity.








Figure 1: Critical immunization fraction p_c = 1 - 1/R0.

title: The Reproduction Number
section: What R0 does not tell you
text:
What R0 does not tell you

\(R_0\) depends on the disease and on the population: the same pathogen has different \(R_0\) values in different contact patterns (hethcote2000mathematics?).
In the SIR model, only \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) together determine the shape of the outbreak. Early data, which grow like \(e^{(\beta - \gamma)t}\), determine \(\beta - \gamma\) but not \(R_0\). You will see the consequences in Predicting the Peak.







Exercise



A disease has \(\beta = 0.3\) per day and a mean infectious period of 10 days. Compute \(R_0\), the early growth rate, the doubling time of cases, and the critical vaccination coverage.








Solution





\(\gamma = 0.1\) per day, so \(R_0 = 3\). The early growth rate is \(\beta - \gamma = 0.2\) per day, giving a doubling time \(\ln 2 / 0.2 \approx 3.5\) days. The critical coverage is \(p_c = 1 - 1/3 \approx 0.67\).

title: Budworm: a Streamlit App
text: With the functions from Budworm: the Model in Code and Budworm: Integration and Time Series, you can build an interactive app in which a slider changes a parameter and the plots update immediately. See the Streamlit documentation.

title: Budworm: a Streamlit App
text:
Setup
Streamlit runs on your own machine, not in Google Colab. Follow the instructions in the README of the course repository to set up your environment.
Create a script spruce_budworm_app.py. Either import your functions from a module (for example spruce_budworm_model.py) or paste them into the script. A separate module is better practice. Run the app with
streamlit run spruce_budworm_app.py

title: Budworm: a Streamlit App
Budworm: a Streamlit App
text:
Interactive features

Display the differential equation with the current parameter values.
Show the rate plot from the rate plot section and the time series from the time series section.
Add an “Evolve” button that continues the simulation and updates the plots.
Store the time and population arrays in st.session_state. Streamlit reruns the whole script on every interaction, so anything not stored there is reset.

title: Budworm: a Streamlit App
text:
Layout
import numpy as np
import streamlit as st

from your_module import (
    evolve_spruce_budworm,
    plot_spruce_budworm,
    plot_spruce_budworm_rate,
)

st.title("Spruce Budworm Population Dynamics")

r = st.sidebar.slider("Intrinsic growth rate (r)", 0.0, 1.0, 0.5)
k = st.sidebar.slider("Carrying capacity (k)", 0.1, 10.0, 10.0)
x0 = k / 10

# Initialize session state on the first run
if "sbw_x" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state["sbw_t"] = np.array([0.0])
    st.session_state["sbw_x"] = np.array([x0])

t_eval = st.sidebar.slider("Time", 1, 100, 10)
button = st.sidebar.button("Evolve")

t = st.session_state["sbw_t"]
x = st.session_state["sbw_x"]

if button:
    t, x = evolve_spruce_budworm(t, x, r=r, k=k, t_eval=t_eval)
    st.session_state["sbw_t"] = t
    st.session_state["sbw_x"] = x

fig1, ax1 = plot_spruce_budworm_rate(x[-1], r=r, k=k)
st.pyplot(fig1)

title: Excitability
text:
Reading




Compulsory: Strogatz (2024), Section 7.5 on relaxation oscillators.
Recommended: (ellner2006dynamic?), chapter on neural and excitable dynamics.
A system is excitable if it has a stable rest state, small perturbations decay back to rest, and perturbations above a threshold produce a large excursion before the system returns to rest. Nerve cells behave this way: a small current injection changes the membrane potential slightly, while a larger one triggers an action potential (hodgkin1952quantitative?; Strogatz 2024).

title: Excitability
text:
Background: the Hodgkin-Huxley model
Hodgkin and Huxley described the membrane potential \(V\) of the squid giant axon with four ODEs: one for \(V\) and three for gating variables \(m\), \(h\), \(n\) that control the sodium and potassium conductances (hodgkin1952quantitative?):
\[
C\dot V = I - \bar g_{\text{Na}} m^3 h (V - V_{\text{Na}}) - \bar g_{\text{K}} n^4 (V - V_{\text{K}}) - g_L (V - V_L),
\]
with each gating variable relaxing to a voltage-dependent steady state. The model reproduced the shape and speed of the action potential measured in experiments. Hodgkin and Huxley shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with John Eccles, for discoveries on the ionic mechanisms of excitation and inhibition in nerve cell membranes.
Four variables are hard to analyse geometrically. The two-variable models of this session keep the essential structure and can be studied in the phase plane (FitzHugh 1961; morris1981voltage?).

title: Excitability
text:
The ingredients

A fast variable (membrane potential) with an S-shaped, or cubic, nullcline. The middle branch has positive feedback: a small depolarization opens channels that depolarize further.
A slow recovery variable that eventually pulls the fast variable back.
A separation of time scales: the fast variable changes much faster than the slow one, so trajectories jump quickly between the outer branches of the cubic nullcline and drift slowly along them (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.5).

The threshold is not a sharp number in general. In FitzHugh’s analysis it is a narrow band in the phase plane near the middle branch of the cubic nullcline (“quasi-threshold”) (FitzHugh 1961).








Figure 1: FitzHugh-Nagumo model at rest (I_app = 0, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 0.5, epsilon = 0.01). Initial kicks v(0) of 0.05 and 0.11 decay; kicks of 0.2 and 0.3 produce a full spike before returning to rest.





The response is all or nothing: the spikes started from \(v(0) = 0.2\) and \(0.3\) have almost the same height, far above the size of the kick.






Exercise



In Figure 1 the rest state is \((v, w) = (0, 0)\). Use the Jacobian to show that it is stable.








Solution





With \(f(v) = v(1-v)(v - \alpha)\), \(f'(0) = -\alpha\). The Jacobian at the origin is \(\begin{pmatrix} -\alpha/\epsilon & -1/\epsilon \\ 1 & -\gamma \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -10 & -100 \\ 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}\), with \(\tau = -10.5 < 0\) and \(\Delta = 5 + 100 > 0\). The origin is stable. Excitability is a global property: it cannot be seen in the linearization.

title: Predicting the Peak
text: Given the data up to today, can you predict when the epidemic curve will peak? Castro, Ares, Cuesta and Manrubia argue that during the expansion phase you cannot: the time of the turning point cannot be determined with certainty before it is reached, there is only a short horizon for reliable prediction, and this persists even in error-free synthetic data (castro2020turning?). They reach this conclusion with an SIR model extended by confinement and a Bayesian fit to COVID-19 data from Spain. Here you reproduce the main effect with the plain SIR model.

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Prediction
Before you run the experiment, write down how many days of data you think you need to predict the peak day within \(\pm 3\) days, for an epidemic that peaks around day 55.

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Implementation
For each cut-off day \(T\):

take the first \(T\) days of the data;
fit \(\beta\), \(\gamma\), \(I(0)\) and \(N\) with fit_sir_incidence(..., fit_population=True);
simulate the fitted model forward and record the day of maximum incidence.

To see the spread caused by noise, repeat this for ten synthetic epidemics with the same true parameters and different noise seeds.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from amlab.epidemics import fit_sir_incidence, sir_incidence, synthetic_sir_cases

N = 1e6
horizon = np.arange(1, 301)
true_peak = sir_incidence(horizon, 0.3, 0.1, 1e-5, N).argmax() + 1
cutoffs = [30, 40, 50, 60, 70]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for T in cutoffs:
    peaks = []
    for seed in range(10):
        d, c = synthetic_sir_cases(seed=seed)
        f = fit_sir_incidence(d[:T], c[:T], population=N, fit_population=True)
        peaks.append(sir_incidence(horizon, f["beta"], f["gamma"], f["i0"], f["population"]).argmax() + 1)
    ax.plot([T] * len(peaks), peaks, "o", color="tab:blue", alpha=0.6)
    print(f"T = {T}: predicted peaks from {min(peaks)} to {max(peaks)}")
ax.axhline(true_peak, color="k", ls="--", label=f"true peak (day {true_peak})")
ax.plot(cutoffs, cutoffs, ":", color="gray", label="today")
ax.set_xlabel("Days of data used (T)")
ax.set_ylabel("Predicted peak day")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

T = 30: predicted peaks from 33 to 69
T = 40: predicted peaks from 43 to 74
T = 50: predicted peaks from 51 to 65
T = 60: predicted peaks from 54 to 58
T = 70: predicted peaks from 55 to 57








Figure 1: Predicted peak day against the number of days of data used in the fit, for ten synthetic SIR epidemics (R0 = 3) with different noise. The dashed line is the true peak of the expected incidence.

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Validation
After the peak (\(T = 60\) and \(T = 70\)) the predictions cluster around the true peak. This confirms that the fitting code works when the data contain enough information.

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Interpretation
Before the peak, the predictions spread over several weeks, even though the model is exactly right and only the reporting noise differs. The reason is the identifiability problem from Fitting an Epidemic to Data: the rising part of the curve fixes \(\beta - \gamma\) but not \(R_0\) or \(N\), and the peak time depends on those. Castro et al. show that this sensitivity is a property of exponential growth, and conclude that forecasts should be given as probabilities of different outcomes, not as a single date (castro2020turning?).

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Limitations

The model used for the fit is the model that generated the data. With real data the model is also wrong, which adds uncertainty.
Least squares with ten noise realizations is a rough substitute for a proper uncertainty analysis such as the Bayesian fit of (castro2020turning?).







Optional extension



If you have real incidence data, save them as data/epidemic/cases.csv (schema in data/epidemic/README.md) and repeat the experiment with a moving cut-off. Compare the predicted peaks with the observed one.

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Exit question
Two groups fit an SIR model to the first 30 days of an outbreak. Group A reports “\(R_0 = 2.9\), peak on day 57”. Group B reports “\(R_0\) between 2 and 200, peak between day 40 and day 70”. Which report is more useful, and why?






Answer





Group B’s report is more useful. With only early data, the fit determines the growth rate but not \(R_0\) or the peak time. A single number hides this uncertainty and invites decisions based on false precision. A range, or better a probability distribution, states honestly what the data support (castro2020turning?).
